caseno: Appeal from Original Decree No. 106 of 1987.
lawyer:
MI Farooqui with M Salimullah ----- For the Appellant. 
Kaiseruddin Ahmed, DAG ----- For the Respondents.
parties:
Zaher (Md) ----- Appellant 
Vs. 
Bangladesh & ors ----- Respondents.
full_judgment:
Nurul Haque Bhuiyan J: This appeal at the instance of the plaintiff is directed against the judgment and decree dated 27.6.87 passed by the learned Subordinate Judge, 1st Court, Dhaka in Title Suit No. 66 of 1985 and arises out of a suit for declaration that the suit property is not an abandoned property and in the alternative for recovery of possession of the suit property and for realisation of rent or, in the alternative, for mesne profit.

2. The appellant as plaintiff instituted Title Suit No. 682 of 1982 against the respondents as defendants in the 4th Court of Subordinate Judge, Dhaka and on transfer to the 1st Court of Subordinate Judge, Dhaka the suit was re-numbered as Title Suit No. 66 of 1985. The plaintiffs case, in short, is that the plaintiff is a national of Bangladesh and has been living as such in this country. He took 99 years' lease of the suit land from DIT and on taking loan from the House Building Finance Corporation he constructed two-storied building thereon. While he was in possession of the suit property defendant No. 7 requisitioned the property in Requisition Case No. 2158 on 14.2.72 and took possession thereof on 16.2.72. The plaintiff repeatedly requested the defendants to fix the rent in respect of the suit property and ultimately the defendant No. 6 by memo dated 20.11.76 asked the Estate Officer defendant No. 4 to arrange payment of rent of the suit property and defendant No. 4 by a memo dated 21.1.77 informed the plaintiff that the suit property was being treated as abandoned property. Thereafter the plaintiff sent various representations to the abandoned property authority for realisation of rent and for releasing the suit property from the Abandoned Property authority without success. Hence the suit.

3. The defendant Nos. 1-4 contested the suit by filing a joint written statement contending, inter alia, that the Deputy Commissioner, Dhaka requisitioned the suit property on 14.2.72 and placed the same under the defendant No. 4. Defendant Nos. 1-2 allotted the suit property to the Embassy of Iraq. The whereabouts of the plaintiff having not been known the suit property was treated as abandoned property under the Bangladesh Abandoned Property (Control, Management And Disposal) Order, 1972 (PO No.16/ 72). The plaintiff did not produce any paper in support of his claim before 20.11.76. Brigadier Shamsul Islam has been possessing the suit property as an allottee. The suit should be dismissed as it is not maintainable in law.

4. The learned Subordinate Judge framed the following issues:

1. Is the suit maintainable in the present form?

2. Is the suit property an abandoned property under PO No. 16 of 1972?

3. Is the suit barred under law?

4. Has the plaintiff right, title and interest in the suit property?

5. Is the plaintiff entitled to get the reliefs prayed for?

6. What other reliefs is the plaintiff entitled to in this suit?"

5. The learned Subordinate Judge considered the evidence of DW 1 Azizur Rahman, a Deputy Director of the Directorate of Housing, Ministry of Works and the evidence of DW 2 Fazlul Karim, an Office Assistant of the Requisition Branch of Dhaka Collectorate and Ext. A—the requisition order of the suit property, Ext. B — a letter of plaintiff of the year 1976 relating to rent of the suit property, Ext. C-memo of the Estate Officer dated 21.1.77 informing the plaintiff that the suit property was being treated as abandoned property, Ext. 1— a certificate dated 8.5.78 for retirement of the plaintiff from government service issued by MA Hashem, Section Officer, Cabinet Division, Ext. 2—an affidavit sworn on 21.7.72 by the plaintiff before a First Class Magistrate owing allegiance to Bangladesh, Ext. 3—memo of the Ministry of Home dated 27.2.79 addressed to the plaintiff to the effect that the plaintiff did not en-list his name with the International Red Cross for re-turning to Pakistan, Ext. 3(a)—citizenship certificate from First Class Magistrate dated 2.4.73 to the effect that the plaintiff is a citizen of Bangladesh, Ext.3 (b)—passport issued to the plaintiff on 21.6.76, Ext 4—letter of DIT dated 6.9.60 in respect of suit property addressed to the plaintiff, Ext. 4(a)—lease agreement dated 12.11.63 in favour of the plaintiff in respect of the suit property, Ext. 4(b)—receipt of loan petition dated 12.3.69 from House Building Finance Corporation, Ext. 5—the order of requisition dated 14.2.72, Ext. 6 series—petition sent by the plaintiff to the government from 1972 to 1976 for fixation of the rent of the suit property, Ext. 7—memo from the office of Deputy Commissioner, Dhaka dated 20.11.76, Ext.8—Memo of the Estate officer dated 21.1.77 informing the Deputy Commissioner that the suit property was being treated as abandoned property, Ext.9—letter on behalf of the plaintiff to the Estate Officer dated 20.5.77 to make payment of arrear rent in respect of the suit property, Ext. 10—memo of the Estate Officer dated 2.7.77 asking the plaintiff to contact the Ministry of Works for payment of rent in respect of the suit property, Ext. 11—plaintiffs letter dated 7.8.77 to the Secretary, Ministry of Works for release of the suit property. Ext. 12—Memo of the Section Officer, Ministry of Works dated 9.11.77 requesting the plaintiff to appear before him at 10-AM on 19.11.77 with documents in support of his claim, Ext. 12 (a)—plaintiffs letter dated 19.11.77 addressed to the Secretary, Ministry of Works in respect of the release of the suit property, Ext. 12(b)—memo of the Section Officer, Ministry of Works dated 13.12.77 requesting the plaintiff to appear before him at 10 AM on 28.12.77 with documents, Ext 12(c)—memo of the Section Officer, Ministry of Works dated 15.3.78 re-questing the plaintiff to submit two copies of his re-cent passport size photographs, Ext. 12(d)—notice demanding justice dated 4.8.80, Ext. 13—copy of the Writ Petition No. 648/80, Ext. 14—memo of the Section Officer, Ministry of Works dated 3.9.80 to the plaintiffs Advocate Mr. MI Farooqui, Ext.15—letter of plaintiffs Advocate Mr. MI Farooque, dated 6.6.81, Ext. 16—notice demanding justice dated 19.6.81. Ext. 17—copy of the Writ Petition No.540/81 dated 27.7.81, Ext. 17(a)-certified copy of the order dated 27.7.81 in Writ Petition No. 540/81, Ext. 18—plaintiffs letter to the Secretary, Ministry of. Works dated 5.7.82 in respect of release of the suit property, Ext. 19—Findings of the Sub-Divisional Officer (S). Dhaka dated 27.4.83, Ext. 20—Cash deposit by plaintiff dated 6.7.71 in respect of instalment of House Building Finance Corporation, Ext, 21—cash deposit by the plaintiff dated 13.1.77 in respect of ground rent bill, Ext. 22-plaintiffs ration card. Having regard to the findings of the Sub-Divisional Officer (S) to the effect that the plaintiff is a national of this country and his recommendation dated 27.4.83 that the suit property should be released from the list of abandoned property and having considered the citizenship certificate Ext. 3 (a), plaintiffs affidavit Ext. 2, Memo of the Ministry of Home Affairs dated 27.2.79, Ext. 3, plaintiffs passport, Ext. 3(b) and other papers, the learned Subordinate Judge found that the plaintiff is a citizen of this country and he resides in this country. Having regard to the remark of the Process Server on the reverse page of the requisition order dated 14.2.72 Ext.A that the guard of the house received the notice of the requisition order, the learned Subordinate Judge found that the plaintiff was in possession of the suit property. Having regard to the fact that after the requisition on 14.2.72 it was disclosed for the first time in the memo of the Ministry of Public Works dated 21.1.77 Ext. C that the suit property was being treated as abandoned property, the learned Subordinate Judge found that the suit property was never derequisitioned after its requisition in 1972. The learned Subordinate Judge also found that the plaintiff got no scope to file objection as per provisions of the President's Order No. 16 of 1972 and there arose no cause for objection and therefore the plaintiff was entitled to get relief. The suit property having been included in the list of abandoned buildings taken possession under PO No.16/72 published in the official Gazette namely, the Bangladesh Gazette Extra-Ordinary dated 28.4.86 under PO No. 16/ 72 published under section 5(1) (a) of the Abandoned Buildings (Supplementary Provisions) Ordinance, 1985 (Ordinance No. XIV of 1985) the learned Sub-ordinate Judge held the view that the present suit was not maintainable. Accordingly, the learned Subordinate Judge dismissed the suit by his judgment and decree dated 27.7.87. Against the decision of the learned Subordinate Judge dated 27.7.87 the plaintiff has preferred this appeal in this court.

6. Mr. MI Farooqui, the learned Advocate appearing for the appellant, has submitted that the suit. property having been taken over by the Government as requisitioned property the same cannot be treated as abandoned property because the abandoned property as defined in Article 2(1) (ii) (b) of PO No. 16 of 1972 does not include any property which was in the possession or under the control of the Government under any other law which was in force at the time when the President's Order No. 16 of 1972 came into force.

<u>7. Mr. Kaiseruddin Ahmed, the learned Deputy Attorney-General appearing for Bangladesh, has sub-mitted that the requisition was not complete in the present case and as such there was no bar for treating the suit property subsequently as abandoned property by the Government. The abandoned property is defined in Article 2(1) of PO No. 16 of 1972 as follows:</u>

<u>"2. In this Order, unless there is anything repugnant in the subject or context,—</u>

<u>(1) abandoned property' means any property owned by any person who is not present in Bangladesh or whose whereabouts arc not known or who has ceased to occupy, supervise or manage in person his property, including—</u>

<u>(i) any property owned by any person who is in a State which at any time after the 25th day of March, 1971, was at war with or engaged in military operations against the People's Republic of Bangladesh;</u>

<u>(ii) any property taken over under the Bangladesh (Taking over of Control and Management of Industrial and Commercial Concerns) Order, 1972 (Acting President's Order No. 1 of 1972), but does not include—</u>

<u>(a) any property the owner of which is residing outside Bangladesh for any purpose which, in the opinion of the Government, is not prejudicial to the interest of Bangladesh.</u>

<u>(b) any property which is in the possession or under the control of the Government under any law for the time being in force.</u>

<u>Explanation—"Person who is not present in Bangladesh includes any body of persons or company constituted or incorporated in the territory or under the laws of a State which at any time after the 25th day of March, 1971, was at war with or engaged in military operations against the People's Republic of Bangladesh;"</u>

<u>The section 2(1) (ii) (b) clearly provides that any property which was taken over by the Government under any other law before President's Order No. 16 of 1972 came into force could not be treated as an abandoned property. Admittedly the suit property was requisitioned on 14.2.72 as per the order of requisition Ext. A and was taken possession as such on 16.2.72 by the Govt. before President's Order No. 16 of 1972 came into force. That being the position the suit property could not be treated as abandoned property.</u>

<u>8. The learned Advocate for the appellant has next submitted that section 5 of the Ordinance No. LIV of 1985 applies to the buildings the possession of which was taken over by the Government as abandoned property under PO No.16/72 or building in respect of which notice for surrendering or taking possession as abandoned property under President's Order No. 16 of 1972 was issued but in the instant case the suit building was requisitioned under section 3 of the East Bengal (Emergency) Requisition of Property Act (XIII of 1948) on 14.2.72 before PO No. 16 of 1972 came into force on 10.3.72 and as such section 5 of the Ordinance No. LIV of 1985 has no manner of application in the suit buildings. Section 5 of the Ordinance No. LIV of 1985 which provides for publication of list of abandoned property runs as follows:</u>

<u>"5. Publication of lists of buildings-(1) The Government shall, after the 31st day of March, 1986, and before the 30th day of April, 1986, publish in the official Gazette,-</u>

<u>(a) a list of buildings the possession of which have been taken as abandoned property under the President's Order;</u>

<u>(b) a list of buildings in respect of which notice for surrendering or taking possession as abandoned property under the said Order have been issued:</u>

<u>Provided that no such list shall include any building in respect of which—</u>

<u>(a) any decree or order has been passed, at any time before the publication of the list in the official Gazette, by any court declaring the building not to be an abandoned property or not have vested in the Government under the President's Order or declaring the possession by the Government of the building as an abandoned property under that order to be illegal or invalid or directing the Government or any officer or authority subordinate to it to return, restore or transfer the building to any person, or</u>

<u>(b) a suit, appeal, application or legal proceeding is pending before any court, immediately before the date of publication of the list in Official Gazette, in which the vesting in, or possession of, the Government of the building as abandoned property under the President's Order has been called in question in any manner whatsoever or any prayer has been made for return, restoration or transfer of the building by the Government or by any officer or authority sub-ordinate to it to any person.</u>

<u>(2) The lists published under sub-section (1) shall be conclusive evidence of the fact that the buildings included therein are abandoned property and have vested in the Government as such."</u>

<u>9. From clauses (a) and (b) of sub-section (1) of section 5 as quoted above, it is evident that the list of buildings for publication in the official Gazette refers to buildings the possession of which has been taken over as abandoned property by the Government under President's Order No.16 of 1972 or the building in respect of which notice for surrendering or taking possession as abandoned property under PO No.16 of 1972 has been issued. Admittedly the suit property was requisitioned on 14.2.72 by the Government under section 3 of the East Bengal (Emergency) Requisition of Property Act, 1948 as per order of requisition Ext. A before the promulgation of PO No. 16/72 and this requisition was final and complete, the possession of the suit property was taken over by the Government as requisitioned property on 16.2.72 and the suit property was never taken over by the Government as abandoned property. For the above reasons section 5 of the Ordinance No. LIV of 1985 has no application in the suit building. For the same reasons section 6 of the Ordinance has no application in the suit building. Section 6 of the Ordinance runs as follows:—</u>

<u>"6. No suit to lie in respect of certain buildings —Save as otherwise provided in this Ordinance, no suit or other legal proceedings shall lie before any court for—</u>

<u>(a) specific performance of contract in respect of any building the possession of which has been taken by the Government or a notice for taking such possession has been issued under the President's Order immediately before the date of publication of the list in the official Gazette, or</u>

<u>(b) a declaration that a building is not an abandoned property and has not vested in the Government under the President's Order or the right or interest of any person in any building has not been affected by the provisions of that order, or</u>

<u>(c) a direction to the Government or to any officer or authority subordinate to it to restore, return or transfer any building the possession of which has been taken by the Government as abandoned property under that Order to any person."</u>

10. The Government has not produced any pa-per in support of their claim that the suit property was subsequently being treated as abandoned property or that the suit property was derequisitioned except the memo of the Estate Officer, Ext. C to the effect that the suit property was being treated as abandoned property and this Ext. C alone cannot prove that the suit property was subsequently treated as abandoned property in the face of order of requisition Ext. A and absence of derequisition of the suit property and the findings of the SDO (South) Dhaka as aforesaid.

<u>11. The learned Advocate for the appellant has further submitted that even assuming that section 5 of the Ordinance No. LIV of 1985 applies to the suit building then also the suit building cannot be included in the list of abandoned buildings in view of proviso (b) to clauses (a) and (b) of sub-section (1) of section 5 of the Ordinance No. LIV of 1985 and the suit building having been included in the list of buildings published in the official Gazette in contravention of the said proviso (b) the civil Court had jurisdiction to try the suit on merit. The plaintiff instituted the suit on 9.12.82 for a declaration, inter alia, that the suit property was not an abandoned property and when the list including the suit building was published in the official Gazette on 23.9.86 in supersession of the Gazette notification dated 28.4.86 the present suit, in which vesting in possession of the Government of the suit building as abandoned property was called in question, was pending in the trial Court. Therefore, the suit building was included in the list published in the official Gazette on 23.9.86 in contravention of proviso (b) to clauses (a) and (b) of sub-section (1) of section 5 of the Ordinance No. LIV of 1985 referred to above and as such the civil Court namely, the learned Subordinate Judge, had obviously jurisdiction to try the suit on merit and he clearly fell into error in holding the view that merely because the suit building was included in the official Gazette dated 28.4.86 the suit was not maintainable.</u>

<u>12. In the above circumstances, we hold that the suit property is not an abandoned property and the plaintiff is entitled to get a decree that the suit property is not an abandoned property and a decree for recovery of possession of the suit property and the Government having disclaimed the suit property as requisitioned property and the same having not been found to be an abandoned property as claimed by the Government the Government is liable to restore possession of the suit property to the plaintiff. We further hold that the Government is liable to pay rent/compensation to the plaintiff under the provisions of the East Bengal (Emergency) Requisition of Property Act, 1948 for use and occupation of the suit property for the period from 14.2.72 till restoration of possession of the suit property to the plaintiff by the Government. The learned Advocate for the plaintiff-appellant has forgone the plaintiff's claim for mesne profit in respect of the suit property.</u>

13. It is found that the judgment and decree of the learned Subordinate Judge suffer from error and illegality as noted above and as such the same call for interference.

14. In the result, the appeal is allowed without any order as to costs. The judgment and decree of the learned Subordinate Judge are set aside and the suit is decreed without costs. The plaintiff will be entitled to rent/compensation from the Government under the provisions of East Bengal (Emergency) Requisition of Property Act, 1948 for Government's use and occupation of the suit property for the period from 14.2.72 till restoration of the suit property to the plaintiff by the Government.

End.

lawyer:
Habibul Islam Bhuiyan with MA Wahab Mia & Abul Hashem, Advocates ------- For the Petitioner. 
Fakrul Islam, Assistant Attorney-General and Dr. Delwar Hossain, AAG ------- For the Respondent No. 2.
parties:
Halima Bibi------- Petitioner.
Vs.
The Chairman & another ------- Respondents
full_judgment:
Syed Fazle Ahmed, J.: At the instance of the petitioner Halima Bibi a Rule Nisi under Article 102 of the Constitution of the People's Republic of Bangladesh was issued calling upon the Respondents to show cause why the judgment and order dated 9.5.87 passed by the Court of Settlement as contained in Annexure 'P' should not be declared to have been passed without any lawful authority and is of no legal effect.

2. Pending hearing of the Rule Respondent No. 2 was restrained from selling or transferring the property in question in any manner.

3. Facts giving rise to this rule may briefly be stated thus:

Petitioner is an old lady and a citizen of Bangladesh. Building situated at Municipal holding No. 3, Bhitar Bari Lane, PS Kotwali, Dhaka corresponding to CS Khatian No. 2718, Plot No.134, Ward No. 4, Sheet No. 50 mouza Sahar Dhaka originally belonged to one Dhum Chand Bashak and on his death aforesaid building devolved on his heirs namely Sakuntala Bashak (widow), Shantash Chandra Bashak (son) and Kani Lal Bashak (son). The heirs of Dhum Chand Bhasak sold the aforesaid building to one Hari Ballab Bashak by a registered sale-deed No. 1740 dated 18.4.1945. Original sale deed is annexed and marked as Annexure 'A' to the petition.

4. Hari Ballab having possessed the sale property for more than seven years, transferred the same in favour of one Pire Mohammad by registered deed of perpetual lease No. 10172 dated 21.11.1952 which was again followed by a perpetual lease on 20.1.1960. Photostat copy of the original perpetual lease deed is annexed hereto and marked as Annexure 'B' to the Petition.

5. Thereafter Pire Mohammad transferred the said property having possessed for more than eight years to one Syed Musaheb Ali by registered deed of perpetual lease No. 1930 dated 20.1.1960. Photostat copy of said original deed of perpetual lease is annexed hereto and marked as Annexure 'C' to the petition. After purchase of the same property Syed Mosaheb Ali mutated his name in the Revenue Records of the Govt. and in the Municipal records as owner thereof. He also paid rents and levies. Photostat certified copies of mutated SA Khatian and Municipal Tax-receipt arc annexed hereto and marked as Annexure D1 and E respectively.

6. The family of Syed Musaheb Ali is bilingual and they migrated from Calcutta in 1947 and settled at Patharkhola, Pabna. Later on he came and started living at Dhaka since 1960 and he was all along present in Bangladesh and his whereabouts were not unknown and he did not cease to occupy, supervise and manage the property in person till he sold the same to the petitioner on 12.2.74 and as such the property was never abandoned in any sense of the term as defined in section 21 of PO 16 of 1972. Mosaheb Ali lived and died in this country. During the war of liberation beginning from 25th March up to 16th of December, 1971 he was in possession of the said property as its lawful owner and continued to possess the same after liberation of Bangladesh till be transferred the said property to the petitioner Halima Bibi by registered sale deed No. 5147 dated 12.2.74. Original sale deed is annexed and marked as Annexure F to the petition.

7. Syed Mosaheb Ali owned another property at 13, Bitar Bari Lane and he never abandoned his property situated at holding No. 3 and 13 Bitar Bari Lane and his property were neither declared or taken over as abandoned property by the competent authority. He handed over peaceful and vacant possession to the petitioner on 12.4.74 and since then the petitioner has been possessing the said properties as its lawful owner till before eviction, Petitioner after purchase mutated her name in the revenue record of the Government by initiating mutation proceeding and paid rent to the Govt. and also paid tax to the Municipality. Photostat copy of the mutated SA Khatian, Municipal taxes receipts and rent receipts are annexed and marked as Annexure G, H, I and J respectively to this petition.

8. Petitioner while in lawful and peaceful possession of the said property was suddenly evicted there from on 7.8.75 by Officer of the Respondent No. 2 without any prior notice and without giving her chance to show cause as to why the property should not be treated to be abandoned and to defend and to prove her lawful title in the said property. Against this said illegal and arbitrary act of eviction petitioner made several representations and prayed for release of the property in her favour and the office of the Respondent No. 2 made several correspondence with petitioner asking her to produce original title deeds in respect of the said property and to furnish information as to the place of birth and home address of Syed Musaheb Ali.

9. Petitioner submitted documents and furnished the information sought for but Ministry of Works with a malafide motive kept quiet and passed no order of release of the property in spite of repeated requests. Petitioner's letter dated 19.3.84, Ministry of Works letter dated 16.11.83, 18.4.84, 5.6.84 and 12.1.85 are annexed and marked Annexure K, L, M, N and O respectively to the petition.

10. Meanwhile, Ordinance No. LIV of 1985 came into force which provided for final publication of the list of abandoned property. Accordingly list KA was published mentioning therein the building of the petitioner as abandoned property. The said law also provided for constitution of the Court of settlement of exclusion of the property from the abandoned list or restoration of the building on the ground that the building is not an abandoned property and vested in the Government under PO 16 of 1972. After the constitution of the Court of Settlement, the petitioner filed an application before the same for exclusion of her property from the abandoned list and restoration of the possession thereof on the ground that her building is not abandoned property and the same as neither vested in the Government nor her title being affected by the provision of PO 16 of 1972 stating that her vendor Mosaheb Ali was the Bangladeshi citizen and in peaceful possession of the building in question from his purchaser on 2.1.1960 till he sold the same to the petitioner on 12.2.74 and during the period of war of liberation beginning from 25th March to 16th December, 1971 Syed Mosaheb Ali neither abandoned the said property nor left the country, rather he was in peaceful possession therein. In support of her claim petitioner filed all necessary papers which included Annexure A to O to this petition before the Court of Settlement.

11. Before the Court of Settlement the Respondent No. 2 did not file any written statement in controverting or denying the assertion made by the petitioner. But the Court of Settlement without considering the facts and circumstances of the case and without applying judicial mind passed an order dismissing the application by its judgment and order dated 5.4.87 vide annexure P to the petition. The finding of the Court of Settlement to the effect the perpetual lease created by Hari Ballav  Bashak in favour of Pir Mohammed vide perpetual lease deed dated 20.1.1960 in respect to the property in question is hit by the provision of section 75A of the SAT Act, 1950 is wholly misconceived and contrary to law inasmuch relevant gazette notification under the provision of State Acquisition and Tenancy Act, 1950 was published in the official Gazette on 1st August, 1963. Photostat copy of the same is annexed and marked as Annexure Q to the petition. The photostat copy of the Ministry letter dated 14.6.87 is annexed hereto and marked as Annexure 'R' to the petition. There being no other efficacious remedy provided in law against the impugned judgment and order of the Court of Settlement, petitioner invoked the writ jurisdiction and preferred this application.

12. Respondent No. 2, Secretary, Ministry of Works. Secretariat Building appeared and filed affidavit-in-opposition denying the material allegation set out in the writ petition and stating therein that during war of liberation and after war the whereabouts of Syed Mosaheb Ali were not known and the property vested in the Govt. as abandoned under PO 16 of 1972. The sale deed alleged to have been executed and registered by Syed Mosaheb Ali in respect of the property in question is false, forged, without consideration and sham paper transaction and in the relevant period Syed Mosaheb All was not present in Bangladesh. Syed Mosaheb Ali's another property at 13, Bitarbari Lane was never abandoned and this property neither declared as abandoned property by relevant authorities of the Govt. and that he handed over peaceful possession of the aforesaid property to the petitioner on 12.2.74 and since then the petitioner has been possessing the said property as lawful owner are all denied. The properties of Syed Mosaheb Ali was rightly declared to be abandoned property and Syed Mosaheb Ali never handed over possession of the property to the petitioner on 12.2.74 and the petitioner has never been in possession of the property. So her eviction on 7.8.75 from the said property by officer of the respondent No. 2 is concoction. The petitioner made several representations before the Ministry of Works. The finding of the Court of Settlement to the effect that perpetual lease created by Hari Ballaw Bashak in favour of Pir Mohammad in respect of the property in question is hit by provision of section 75A of State Acquisition and Tenancy Act, 1950, that the statement made in paragraph 15 of the Writ Petition that the respondent No. 2 being emboldened by the aforesaid judgment of the Court of Settlement has decided to sell the property in question and to that effect issued a letter to the tenant and asking them to submit bids is denied. The property in question has been rightly declared as abandoned property. All other allegations set out in the writ petition have been categorically denied in the affidavit-in-opposition.

13. It is urged by the learned Advocate appearing for the petitioner that the property in question does not come within the mischief of definition of abandoned property as mentioned in section 2 of the Abandoned Order, 1972 (PO 16 1972).

A property to be declared as abandoned property must come within the mischief of section 2 of the Order (Control, Management and Disposal Order, 1972) hereinafter to be referred as Order. The definition as mentioned in section 2 of the Order reads thus:

(1) "abandoned property" means any property owned by any person who is not present in Bangladesh or whose whereabouts are not known or who has ceased to occupy, supervise or manage in person his property, including.

(i) 	any property owned by any person who is a citizen of a State which at any time after the 25th day of March, 1971, was at war with or engaged in military operations against the People's Republic of Bangladesh;

(ii) 	any property taken over under the Bangladesh (Taking over Control and Management of Industrial and Commercial Concerns) Order, 1972 (Acting .President's Order No.1 of 1972), but does not include.

(a) 	any property the owner of which is residing outside Bangladesh for any purpose which, in the opinion of the Government, is not prejudicial to the interest of Bangladesh;

(b) 	any property which is in the possession or under the control of the Government under any law for the time being in force.

Explanation: "Person who is not present in Bangladesh" includes anybody of persons or company constituted or incorporated in the territory or under the laws of a State which at any time after the 25th day of March, 1971, was at war with or engaged in military operations against the People's Republic of Bangladesh;

(IA) "authorised officer" means an officer authorised by the Government for the purpose of this Order).

The definition of the abandoned property quoted above shows that the word "abandonment" connotes of that owner vacating the property with the intention of never returning to it. But mere temporary absence or absence in certain circumstances is not sufficient to warrant an inference of abandonment. To establish abandonment some positive act than mere non-residence requires to be proved. The desertion of the property must have coincided with the positive intention to give up right vested in the property. The owner of the property may not always be in possession of it and thus mere absence of physical possession is not sufficient to treat the property as abandoned.

<u>14. According to the definition 'abandoned property' means any property owned by any person who is not present in Bangladesh. It implies that there should be some information to the Govt. that the owner is outside Bangladesh but sub-clause II (a) further conveys the idea mere absence from Bangladesh will not render the property abandoned unless the activity of the owner of the property outside Bangladesh is prejudicial to the interest of the country. In other words the owner in the opinion of the Government by indulging in activity prejudicial to the interest of the State. Sub-clause 11 (a) of clause 1 of Article 2 is to be read with clause 1 of Article 2. In the case of M/s Speed Bird Navigation Vs. Government of Bangladesh reported in 27 DLR 170, their Lordships have expounded this provision of law holding that the clause referred above appears to be that the properties of those absentee owners about whose purpose of staying outside the country the Government has not yet formed any opinion whatsoever cannot be also regarded as abandoned properties, but the properties of those persons about whose purpose of staying abroad the Government has formed an adverse opinion, shall be deemed to be abandoned properties. This decision of the High Court Division was upheld by the Appellate Division which has been reported in 30 DLR (AD) page 101 and in that decision of their Lordships of the Appellate Division confirmed the view taken by their Lordships of the High Court Division and further held that the power regarding the formation of the opinion cannot be delegated to other Government officials. Their Lordships further held that" there cannot be any vesting of absentee owners of properties in the government unless there is Government's opinion expressed to the effect that his absence from the country is detrimental to the interest of the State."This definition clause is to be read as a whole in the light of the title and the preamble and also as an integral part of the Presidential Order.</u>

15. Whenever any question arises as to the property of the absentee owner if it can be taken as abandoned property, it shall have to be seen if there is any necessary opinion as to his purpose of absence. In the absence of such opinion the property of absentee cannot be regarded as abandoned property.

16. Thus from this decision the conclusion that can be arrived at is that the owner must be absentee from the country and second, that the Government has expressed opinion that his absence from the country is due to a purpose prejudicial to the interest of the State. It is not possible to presume that the legislature had intended that any one absent from Bangladesh being not prejudicial to the interest of Bangladesh would be coming within the mischief of PO 16 of 1972 and the property thereof is to be taken as abandoned property.

<u>17. Now it is to be seen if whereabouts of Syed Mosaheb Ali from whom petitioner purchased the property as per sale deed vide Annexure F dated 12.2.74 were not known. The expression where about of the owner not known implies that the properties are not in his possession and under his control and management and he is hiding in the country or has left Bangladesh. It should be mentioned here that many of the owners who collaborated with Pakistani Army left the country or want into hiding abandoning their property without making arrangement for administration of the said property. One living outside of the country will not render the property abandoned unless there is opinion from the Government that the activity of the owner outside the country is prejudicial to the State Syed Mosaheb Ali owned two premises one at 93 Bitar Bari Lane and another at holding No. 3 Bitar Bari Lane and both of his properties were never declared as abandoned or taken over as abandoned property by Government. The holding situated at 13 Bitar Bari Lane was not declared or taken over as abandoned properties though it was owned by Syed Mosaheb Ali. But the holding No. 3 was taken over as abandoned property despite the fact that Syed Mosaheb Ali never left the country and that he died on the soil of Bangladesh. In support of this contention -a death certificate of Syed Mosaheb Ali which is lying with the lower Court record was filed before the Court of Settlement. From the death certificate it appears that death of Syed Mosaheb Ali occurred on 13.3.76 and that place of death occurred at holding No. 3 Bitar Bari Lane. Since the petitioner was evicted from holding No. 3 Bitar Bari Lane on 7.8.75 by officers of Respondent No.2 and death of Syed Mosaheb Ali occurred on 13.3.76 ie after eviction, the learned Court of Settlement observed regarding the authenticity of the death certificate. It has already been referred above that Syed Mosaheb Ali owned two properties which were located side by side at 3 and 13 Bitar Bari Lane. From the death certificate of Syed Mosaheb Ali, it is evident that death of Syed Mosaheb Ali occurred in Bangladesh at holding No. 3. The learned Court of Settlement did not treat it to be the authentic document but no reason has been assigned to cast any aspersion regarding its genuineness. In absence of any attack regarding the authenticity of the death certificate it cannot be said that the entry made in the death certificate was not correct. It appears from the death certificate that death of Mosaheb Ali occurred on the soil of Bangladesh.</u>

18. The registered sale deed vide Annexure 'F' by which Syed Mosaheb Ali transferred this property in favour of petitioner Halima Bibi and from the endorsement appearing in the registered sale deed it appears that it was presented for registration by Syed Mosaheb Ali before the Sub-Registrar concerned and Syed Mosaheb Ali admitted the execution of the sale deed Annexure 'F' and he was identified before the Sup-Registrar by an advocate. Further, it appears that Syed Mosaheb Ali executed an affidavit wherein he asserted himself to be the citizen of Bangladesh and owned allegiance to Bangladesh and further declaration has been made that property in question was not abandoned property.

19. So the fact of presentation of the sale deed Annexure 'F' coupled with admission of its execution and further execution of affidavit asserting himself to be the citizen of Bangladesh owing allegiance to Bangladesh are the facts which appear to have been overlooked by the learned Court of Settlement.

<u>20. The learned Advocate appearing for the 	petitioner has submitted that as per clause 3 of Article 7 of the Order, a person in occupation of abandoned properly if sought to be evicted there from is entitled to show cause notice or period i.e. 7 days within the service of notice and if he failed to do so, the Deputy Commissioner or the Sub-Divisional Officer shall take possession of the property in such manner as may be prescribed.</u>

<u>21. Thus it is evident that as per clause 3 of Article 7 of the Order petitioner before being evicted is entitled 10 show cause notice. But in the instant case no such notice was served. The petitioner was evicted there from though she did have valid title thereto inasmuch as Syed Mosaheb Ali who is the owner of the properly transferred it by executing and registering a sate deed Ext. F on receiving valuable consideration.</u>

22. The regard being had to the definition of abandoned property mentioned in Article 2 of the Order that there should be some information to the Government that owner is outside Bangladesh and that sub-clause 11(2) further conveys the idea that mere absence from Bangladesh will not render the property abandoned unless the activity of the owner of the property outside Bangladesh is prejudicial to the interest of the country.

<u>23. Evidence on record proves affirmatively that petitioner Syed Mosaheb Ali died in Bangladesh and there is no material on record to warrant inference that Syed Mosaheb Ali even if presumed to have left Bangladesh indulged in activity prejudicial to the interest of the State. Therefore, the property in question does not fall within the mischief of definition of abandoned property. This aspect of the matter was not considered by the learned Court of Settlement.</u>

24. In the result, the Rule is made absolute and the judgment and order dated 9.5.87 passed by the Court of Settlement as contained in Annexure 'P' to the petition be declared to have been passed without any lawful authority and is of no legal effect, The property in question stands excluded from the list of abandoned property.

We, however, make no order as to cost.

End.

parties:
Sunil Kumar Ghosh & ors ------ Petitioners.
Vs.
The State & others ------ Opp.–Parties.
full_judgment:
This Rule is at the instance of the plaintiffs. It is directed against a judgment and decree of the learned Additional District Judge, Patuakhali in Title Appeal No. 37 of 1978 reversing those of the learned Subordinate Judge of that place in Tale Suit No. 102 of 1976.

2. The petitioners, as plaintiffs, brought the suit for a declaration that the enemy property proceeding as described in schedule 'Ka' to the plaint were illegal, ultravires and without jurisdiction.

<u>3. The case of the plaintiffs, in short is, that plaintiff Nos. 1 and 2 and their brother Arun Kumar, predecessor of plaintiff No 3 being the sons of one Debendra Nath Ghose inherited 3/5th share of the property left by him. Before his death Debendra Nath purported to make a gift of his entire land in favour of plaintiff Nos 1, 2 and Arun Kumar and put them in possession thereof. Arun Kumar having died his share devolved on his son, No. 3. Their further case is that Debendra Nath Chose put-chased the interest recorded in the name of Paresh Nath Chose, But as a matter of fact, the said property belonged to Paresh Nath's father Janaki Nath Chose who died leaving wife Charu Bala as his only heiress. By a deed dated 20.3 48 she sold all her interest in the property in favour of the said Debendra. Debendra had another co-sharer namely Bibhuti who went to India during the war of liberation leaving the property of his share in possession of the plaintiffs, In this way plaintiffs have been in possession of the holding in their entirety. Bibhuti also executed a power of attorney in favour of the plaintiffs. The property could not be and did not vest as enemy property but the Government started enemy property proceedings mentioned in schedule 'Ka' to the plaint treating the same as enemy property in (1972-73). All the proceedings are illegal, ultra vires and without jurisdiction.</u>

4. The suit was contested by defendant Nos. 1 and 2 by filing a joint written statement denying the claim of the plaintiffs. Their case, inter alia is that out of the recorded tenants Arun Kumar, Santi Ranjan, Jnanendra, Bibhuti and Paresh left for India and they are living there permanently. Their property has therefore been legally vested as enemy property. The plaintiffs admitted the said fact and took lease of the property and as they did not get the lease renewed the same has been leased out to defendant No. 4.

5. Defendant No. 4 filed a separate written statement but did not turn up at the time of trial.

The learned Subordinate Judge, on consideration of the evidence on record, decreed the suit on contest with costs against defendant Nos. 1 and 2 and ex parte against the rest without costs. Stated briefly, his findings are that the suit is maintainable in its present form, that the suit is not barred by limitation and that the property in suit was inherited by the plaintiffs and that even if it be found that some of the heirs of co-shares of the holdings are living in India the property being ejmali could not be leased out to others without any partition and hence the impugned proceedings are illegal.

6. Being aggrieved defendant Nos. 1 and 2 preferred an appeal being Title Appeal No. 37 of 1978 to the learned District Judge, Patuakhali and the appeal was eventually heard by the Additional District Judge of that place. The learned Judge reversed the decision of the trial court dismissing the suit mainly on the ground that the suit was not maintainable without a prayer for declaration of title. One of the considerations that weighted with the learned Judge in arriving at the conclusion that the plaintiffs failed to prove the alleged gift by Debendra in their favour and that the power of attorney which was executed by Bibhuti empowering the plaintiffs to deal with the property in his share being dated 10.1.1976 long after the starting of the enemy property proceedings had nothing to do with those proceedings. The learned judge further found that the plaintiffs had full knowledge of the proceedings since 1972 and since the suit was not brought within one year from the date of knowledge it was barred under Article 14 of the Limitation Act.

7. It is the propriety of this decision which has been called in question in the present Rule.

Mr. P.C. Guha, learned Advocate appearing for the petitioners assailed the decision on various grounds. It is first contended that the learned Additional District Judge has misdirected himself in law in taking the view that Article 14 of the Limitation Act shall apply to the facts and circumstances of the case. According to him, Article 14 has application to a suit for setting aside an order and it has no applicability to a suit for declaration. He has, therefore, submitted that the instant suit being a suit for declaration simpliciter is governed by Article 120 of the Act and consequently the learned Additional District Judge has fallen in to an error of law in holding that the suit was barred by limitation. He has cited the decision in the case of Province of East Pakistan Vs. A.K.M. Rezaul Karim, reported in 21 D.L.R. (Dhaka) 492 in support of his contention. In the face of that decision the learned Deputy Attorney General finds it difficult to support the finding of the learned Additional District Judge on the point of limitation. The contention of the learned Advocate for the petitioners is, therefore, sustained.

<u>8. It is next urged by the learned Advocate for the petitioners that regard being had to the pleadings of the parties and the prayer of the plaintiffs in the suit, the learned Additional District Judge has committed an error of law resulting in an error in the decision occasioning failure of justice in holding that intricate questions of title are involved which cannot be adjudicated in simple suit for declaration. It is borne out from the materials on record that the plaintiffs have sought for a declaration as to the legality of certain enemy property proceedings precisely on the basis that they are co-sharers in exclusive possession of the disputed holdings. According to them one of the co-sharers namely Bibhuti left this country during the war of liberation and so the property could not be declared as enemy or vested property. While laying the foundation of their title to the property, the plaintiffs have specifically pleaded that the plaintiff Nos. 1 and 2 being the sons of Debendra and plaintiff No 3 being the son of Arun Kumar since deceased inherited 315th of the share by Debendra in the disputed property, They have further pleaded that Debendra acquired the interest recorded in the name of Paresh Nath Ghose, by way of purchase from his mother Charu Bala. In this respect the learned Additional District Judge has clearly found that Paresh Nath Ghose predeceased his father Janaki Nath and Debendra Nath Ghose, father of the plaintiffs No. 1 and 2 acquired good title over the property by purchase from Charu Bala as per Ext. 1. There is no dispute as to the quantum of the share held by Debendra in the property nor is the claim of 3/5th share of the plaintiffs by inheritance under challenge. What is challenged in the written statement is that the plaintiffs cannot lay any claim to the 16 annas interest of Debendra's share in the holding. True the plaintiffs asserted that Debendra gifted this entire property in favour of plaintiff Nos. 1 and 2 and Arun Kumar, predecessor of plaintiff No. 3 by an unregistered deed of gift and delivered possession thereof to them, but as the deed of gift is an unregistered one they did not claim any title thereunder. They simply sought to use it for collateral purpose to show their entry into the whole of the disputed property. The learned Additional District Judge rejected this document as being manufactured. Learned Advocate for the petitioners has challenged this finding on the ground that there is no legal basis for the said finding. It is strenuously urged by the learned Advocate for the petitioners that Exts. A to A (3) which are the order sheets of the impugned proceedings clearly show that the said proceedings were started on the basis that Bibhuti Bhusan was a non-resident owner and as such the property of his share became enemy property. The property of Debendra was not the subject matter of those proceedings. So there was no occasion for the plaintiffs to produce only document in support of their title before the vested property authority. The learned Additional District Judge found the deed of gift to be a manufactured one upon an assumption that had the deed been in existence the same would have been produced before the vested property Authority. This assumption of the learned Addl. District Judge is a conjecture in disregard of the positive evidence adduced by the plaintiffs in proof of the document. An assertion was made in the written statement that Arun Kumar is alive but there is not an iota of evidence in this respect. On the other hand, P.W. 1. and P.W. 2 stated in one voice that Arun died and his property devolved on plaintiff No. 3. In view of the above facts and circumstances I am unable to find that there is any intricate question of title involved in the suit which cannot be adjudicated. The learned Additional District la, has, therefore, fallen into an error of law in holding that the suit was not maintainable.</u>

9. The next contention of the learned Advocate for the petitioners is that Bhibuti had left the country for India during the war of liberation and so there being no existence of the state of war at that time his property could not become enemy property within the meaning of the term as defined in the Defence of Pakistan Rules and be vested as such in the Dy. Custodian of Enemy Property inasmuch as there was no order of vesting as required under Rule 182(1)(b) of the said Rules. It is, therefore, submitted that the said property could not and did not vest in the Government of Bangladesh under President's Order No. 29 of 1972 as amended by President's Order No. 134 of 1973 and under Act XLV of 1974.

<u>10. In order to appreciate the point it is necessary to examine the relevant provisions of the law governing enemy properties in their true context. On the outbreak of war between India and Pakistan on the 6th September, 1965 the President of Pakistan proclaimed emergency in the country and on that very day he promulgated the Defence of Pakistan Ordinance (Ordinance No. XXIII of 1965) in exercise of his power under clause (4) of Article 30 read with clause (2) of Artie e 131 of the Constitution. it authorised the Central Government to frame Rules and accordingly, the Defence of Pakistan Rules, 1965 were framed. Rule 161 of the Defence of Pakistan Rules defined an "enemy" to mean a state or Sovereign of a State at War with or engaged in military operations against Pakistan, or any individual resident in enemy territory. Rule 169 (1)(9 defined "Enemy Subject" as any individual who possesses the nationality of a state at war with Pakistan, or having possessed such nationality of a state at war with Pakistan, or having possessed such nationality at any time has lost it without acquiring another nationality. Rule 169 (4) defined "enemy property "to mean "any property for the time being belonging to or held or held or managed on behalf of an "enemy" as defined in Rule 161, "an enemy subject or any enemy firm, but does not include property which is "Evacuee property" under the Pakistan (Administration of Evacuee Property Act, 1957.</u>

<u>Provided that where an individual enemy subject dies in Pakistan, any property which, immediately before his death, belonged to or was held by him or was managed on his behalf, may notwithstanding his death continue to be regarded as enemy property for the purpose of Rule 183."</u>

<u>11. Under Rule 182 (1) the Central Government was authorised to appoint Custodian, Deputy Custodians and Assistant Custodians of Enemy Property and to vest or provide for and regulate the vesting of such enemy property by appropriate order.</u>

<u>The relevant provision of the Rule as it stood after amendment on 2.11.65 reads as under:-</u>

<u>"Rule 182 (1) with a view to preventing the payment of moneys to an enemy firm and to provide for the administration and disposal by way of transfer or otherwise of enemy property or matters concerned therewith or incidental thereto, the Central Government may appoint a Custodian of Enemy Property for Pakistan and one or more Deputy Custodians and Assistant Custodians of such local areas as may be prescribed and may by order-</u>

<u>(a) …………………..</u>

<u>(a) Vest or provide for and regulate the vesting, is the prescribed Custodian, such enemy property as nay be prescribed;"</u>

12. In exercise of this power conferred by sub-rule (I) of Rule 182 an order called the Enemy Property (Custody and Registration.) Order, 1965 was made on the 9th September, 1965 Paragraph 4 of this Order was in the following terms :—

"4(1). Whenever by order (emphasis added) made under sub-rule (1) of Rule 182, the property of an enemy is vested in the custodian, the Custodian may take or authorise the taking of such measures as he considers necessary or expedient for preserving the property, and where the property belongs to an individual enemy subject, may incur such expenditure out of the property as he considers necessary or expedient for the maintenance of that individual or of his family in Pakistan."

It may be noted that both the rule and the paragraph quoted herein above clearly provided that vesting of enemy property in the prescribed custodian could be made by appropriate order of the Government.

13. The Proclamation of Emergency was revoked on the 16th February, 1969 resulting in the repeal of the Defence of Pakistan Ordinance and the Rules framed thereunder but the provisions of the Defence of Pakistan Rules relating to the control of trading with enemy and the control of enemy firm and the administration of property belonging to the enemies were made to continue by the Enemy Property (Continuance of Emergency Provisions) Ordinance, 1969 (Ordinance No. 1 of 1969).

14. It will be noticed that in order that the Authority concerned could exercise its power under the Defence of Pakistan Rules or any order framed thereunder, with regard to the properties which came under the definition of enemy properties within the meaning of said Rules it was necessary that the State of war between Pakistan and India continued as, otherwise, such properties would cease to have the character of enemy properties and the provisions of the said Rules would be inapplicable thereto.

<u>15. The Appellate Division, by its decision in Bangladesh Enemy Property Management Board awl others Vs. Md. Abdul Majid, 27 D.L.R. (4.D.) 52 held that the state of war between India and Pakistan did not come to an end merely on the revocation of the proclamation of emergency. The view of their Lordships in this regard has been expressed in the following words (at page 58 of the report ):-</u>

<u>"It, therefore, appears that the question whether the state of war between India and Pakistan had come to an end on the date of the order of vesting in the instant case depended on the question whether an announcement to that effect had been made by the then Government of Pakistan and since admittedly no such announcement to that effect had been made, no presumption that the state of war had ended can be drawn  from the mere fact that the proclamation of emergency was withdrawn."</u>

<u>16. The Appellate Division, however, appears to have taken a different view on this question in its subsequent decision in the case of M/S. Dulichand Omraolal Vs. Bangladesh, 33 D.L.R. (A D.) 30 to the effect that the state of war between the aforesaid two countries ceased to exist on the revocation of the state of Emergency i.e. with effect from 17.2.69. Their Lordships have expressed this view in the said case in the following manner (at page 34 of the report ) : "The principal ground for promulgation of Emergency was the threat of war to Pakistan and that heat with the revocation of Emergency had ceased to exist on any from 17th February, 1969 and so there cannot be any supposed state of war or military operation which may be said to exist in the eye of law Interpreted in this way, there cannot be any question of supposed continuation of any state of war or military operation after 16th February, 1969."</u>

17. It thus appears according to the later decision of the Appellate Division that the state of war between India and Pakistan reeled on the 16th February, 1969.

There appears to be nothing in Rule 182 to show that property belonging to an Indian owner or resident could, on a mere assumption of enemy character, automatically vest in the concerned authority if as a matter of fact there had been an appropriate order of vetting under Rule 182 (1)(b) of the Defence of Pakistan Rules during tie continuance of the state of war between the two countries. No order of vesting of such property could he made nor could any step be taken to take over such a property after the cessation of the state of war inasmuch as such property had ceased 'to be enemy property on the cessation of the said state of war.

<u>18. It has been suggested that it has been laid down in the aforesaid judgment in the case of M/s Dulichand Omraolal Vs Bangladesh, 33 D.L R. (A.D)30 that a property which became an enemy property at any time within the period of the state of war continued to be so even after the expiry of the said period and could as such be taken over by the Government at any time after the cessation of the state of war notwithstanding the fact that there was no appropriate order of vesting during the continuance of the said state of war. There are no doubt certain expressions in the said judgment from which such a conclusion has been suggested. There is, however, no positive statement of law to the said effect in the said judgment and there appears to have been no occasion also, it may be respectfully stated, to express such a view, as in the aforesaid case there was in fact an order of vesting of the firm of M/S. Dulichand Omraolal in the Additional Custodian of Enemy Property on 6/10/1968 i.e. within the period of the state of war. It appears that the question of the contingency of the absence of a vesting order was not within the consideration of their lordships. With great respect I may say that their Lordships wanted to imply in substance in the said case was that if during the continuance of the state of war there had been an appropriate order of vesting of a property which was an enemy property and actual steps to take over such property had not been taken by the concerned authority at that time, subsequent taking over of such property is permissible.</u>

19. However, the period of time when the owner concerned of the disputed property in the instant case is alleged to have left the country and gone to India, is subsequent to the emergence of the independent Sovereign State of Bangladesh.

After the emergence of Bangladesh only those properties which were vested under Rule 182 (1)(b) of the Defence of Pakistan Rules in the Custodian or Deputy Custodian of Enemy Property have been vested in the Government of Bangladesh under Articles 2 (1) of the President's Order No. 29 of 1972 as amended under President's Order No. 134 of 1972 as  held by the Appellate Division in the above mentioned case of Bangladesh Enemy Property Management Board and others Vs. Md. Abdul Majid, 27 D.L.R. (A.D) 52.

<u>20. Subsequently, another Act called the Enemy Property (Continuance of Emergency Provisions) (Repeal) Act, 1974 (Act XLV of 1974) was promulgated. By this Act the Enemy Property (Continuance of Emergency Provisions) Ordinance, 1969 (Ordinance 1 of 1969) was repealed and under section 3(1)(a) thereof all enemy properties which were vested in the Custodian, Dy. Custodian of Enemy Property appointed under the provisions of the Defence of Pakistan Rules have been vested in the Government. After the vesting of the properties under President's Order No. 29 of 1972 there could not be any fresh vesting of the property in law in the Government of Bangladesh as contemplated in Act XLV of 1974. After such vesting under the said President's Order No 29 of 1972 the purported exercise of the powers by the Deputy Custodian of Enemy Property under ordinance No. 1 of 1969 till its repeal and the purported vesting of the said properties thereafter again in the Government of Bangladesh under Act XLV of 1974 do not seem to be consistent with the correct position of law. In any view of the matter, only those properties which had vested in the Custodian or Deputy Custodian of Enemy Property under Rule 182 (1)(b) of the Defence of Pakistan Rules, 1965 may be deemed to have been vested in the Government of Bangladesh either under President's Order No. 29 of 1972 or under Act XLV of 1974.</u>

21. As a matter of fact, the then Governor of East Pakistan under authority delegated to him by the Central Government issued on 3rd December, 1965 an omnibus notification being No. 1199-Gen. of that date under sub-rule 1(b) of Rule 182 of the Defence of Pakistan Rules. The notification was published in the Dhaka Gazetted Extra-Ordinary on 4.12.65 and it runs thus :-

"Whereas the Central Government have directed the Provincial Government to exercise the powers and duties under Rule 182 of the Defence of Pakistan Rules: Now, therefore in exercise of the power conferred by clause (b) of sub-rut." (1) of Rule 182 of the said Rules, the Government is pleased to order:

(a) that all lands and buildings which are enemy property within the meaning of sub-rule (4) of Rule 169 of the said Rules and which are not connected with enemy firm,' as defined in sub-rule (2) of that Rules, shall vest in the Deputy Custodian of Enemy Property (Land and Buildings) with effect from the date of this order;)

22. By this notification the lands and buildings which became enemy property within the meaning of sub-rule (4) of Rule 169 of the said Rules on that date and which were not connected with ''enemy firm" as defined in sub-rule (2) of that Rule had been vested in the Deputy Custodian of Enemy Property (Lands and Buildings) with effect from that date. As already pointed out that the state of war continued up to the revocation of the state of emergency and it was not inconceivable therefore, that a property could become enemy property within the meaning of sub-rule (4) of Rule 169 of the Defence of Pakistan Rules, 1965 after 3rd December, 1965 but no further order of vesting as required under sub-rule (1)(b) of Rule 182 appears to, have been made with respect to such enemy property not connected with an enemy firm.

2<u>3. The real criterion for determination whether a particular property is a vested property or not, therefore, seems to be whether it was an enemy property within the meaning of the term as defined in Rule 169 (4) of the Defence of Pakistan Rules on 3rd December, 1965 and not on any day subsequent thereto, as it is only those properties which had vested in the Deputy Custodian of Enemy Property by virtue of the notification on 3rd December, 1963 and had subsequently vested in the Government of Bangladesh either under President's Order No. 29 of 1972 as amended under President's Order No. 134 of 1972 or under Act XLV of 1974. There having been no subsequent order of vesting under Rule 182 (1)(b) of the Defence of Pakistan Rules, 1965 with respect to enemy properties which were not connected with any enemy firm, the properties which might have become enemy properties after 3rd December, 1965 did not get any scope for vesting in the Custodian of Enemy Property or any other authority. The said properties have naturally ceased to have the character of enemy properly on the cessation of the state of war between India and Pakistan in respect of the territory now comprised in Bangladesh.</u>

<u>24. In the instant case, admittedly Bibhuti had left the country for India during the war of liberation. In any view, the state of war between India and Pakistan so far as the territory which is now Bangladesh is concerned having ended on the emergence of the sovereign state of Bangladesh thereat on the 26th March, 1971 there was no existence of the state of war as conceived in the Defence of Pakistan Rules, at that time. So there was no scope for vesting of his property in the Deputy Custodian of Enemy Property (Lands and Buildings). It is also nobody's case that Bibhuti was an enemy within the meaning of the term as defined in Rule 161 (a) of the Defence of Pakistan Rules on 3rd December, 1965. Moreover, even if the property is taken to have become an enemy property at that for argument's sake, such enemy property cannot be deemed the have been vested in the Deputy Custodian of Enemy Property (Lands and Buildings) by virtue of Notification No. 1199-Gen. dated 3rd December, 1965 referred to above and consequently vested in the Government either under President's Order No. 29 of 1972 or under Act XLV of 1974. I, therefore, find substance in the submission of the learned Advocate for the petitioners. Lastly, the learned Advocate for the petitioners has contended that even if it be accepted for the sake of argument that someone of the absentee co-sharers of the plaintiff petitioners was an enemy and his property vested in the Government under law, the petitioners being co-sharers in exclusive possession of the disputed property are entitled to retain possession thereof till partition of the share of the absentee owner. There is considerable force in this submission also.</u>

25. For the foregoing reasons I am clearly of the opinion that the learned Additional District Judge has committed errors of Jaw resulting in an error in the decision occasioning failure of justice.

In the result, the Rule is made absolute. The judgment and decree of the leaned Additional District Judge are set aside and those of the learned Subordinate Judge are restored. There shall be no order as to costs.

End.

lawyer:
SS Haider with Sadananda Rana, Advocate  and Chandi Charan Paul, Advocates ------ For the Petitioner. 
M Gholam Rabbani, Advocate ------ For Respondent No.3.
