parties:
Abdul Quddus ------ Petitioner.
Vs. 
Government of Bangladesh ------ Respondents.
full_judgment:
Mainur Reza Chowdhury, J. : This Rule Nisi under Article 102 of the Constitution was issued upon the respondents to show cause why the judgment and order dated 11.7.87 passed by respondent No. 4 the Court of Settlement in Case No. 34/87 (Ka-89,-Block-F, Mohammadpur, Dhaka, Holding No. 11A/8, Block 'F' Mohammadpur, Dhaka) should not be declared to have been passed without any lawful authority and to be of no legal effect and why the respondents should not be directed to cancel, rescind or withdraw the impugned judgment and order.

2. The petitioner Abdul Quddus's case is that the holding No. 11-A/8 of Block 'F remained vacant during the liberation war and after the war also the respondent No. 3 Md. Alauddin, the allottee of the said holding, took shelter in 'Geneva Camp' Mohammadpur. The petitioner after enquiry about position of the holding took permission to occupy the said holding as a member of the Freedom Fighter's family as the elder brother of the petitioner was an Army Havildar and freedom fighter soldier. The petitioner entered into occupation of the said holding on and from 1.1.72. Since he was occupying the said holding the petitioner prayed for settlement of the said holding as the same was declared abandoned property and the office of the Respondent No.1 issued Mice upon the petitioner to deposit rent at the rate of Tk. 100.00 per month from 1.1.75 to 28.2.75—Tk. 3,800.00 within 10.7.73 in the Bangladesh Bank. The petitioner deposited the arrear rent and continued to deposit at the same rate on different dates till 17.4.84. He obtained a certificate of deposit of Tk. 18,512.50 for the period 1.1.72 to 30.4.84.

3. The Respondent No. 2, Senior Section Officer, Section XII, Ministry of Public Works, Government of Bangladesh by a letter dated 12.4.84 offered to sell the said holding to the Petitioner as a legal occupier at a price of Tk. 1,29,654.00. The offer to sell was accepted by the petitioner and an agreement to sell the said holding for Tk. 1,29,654.00 was signed on 19.5.85 and the petitioner paid Tk. 25,930.00 on 7.5.85 as the first instalment of the said agreement of sale. The Respondent No. 3 Md. Alauddin filed Writ Petition No. 169 of 1986 on 14.4.86 challenging the order dated 28.12.85 issued by the Respondent No. 2 that agreement for the sale of the said building had been signed and it was not possible to release the said building to Respondent No. 3. The said Writ Petition and the Rule was discharged for non-prosecution on 18.3.1987.

4. The Respondent No. 3 filed an application under section 7 of Ordinance No. LIV of 1985 before Respondent No. 4 the Court of Settlement being case No. 347 (Ka-89, Block 'F' 8 Mohammadpur, Dhaka, holding No. 11-A/8 Block 'F' Mohammadpur, Dhaka) for releasing his property from the list of abandoned property published in the Gazette Notification dated 23.9.1986 being serial No. 89 of the area Mohammadpur Block 'F' in which the petitioner was made a party but Respondent No. 4 did not allow the petitioner to file the written statement.

5. The case of Respondent No. 3 before the Respondent No. 4 (Court of Settlement ), was that the holding No. 11-A8 of Block 'F' of Mohammadpur Housing Estate was allotted to him by the Government vide Memo No. 1945 AO dated 27.9.62 followed by lease deed bearing No. 5686 dated 29.3.1962. The holding was delivered to him on 4.11.62. He cleared all dues. The miscreants forcibly ousted the respondent in December, 1971 and took possession of the building. The respondent submitted several petitions to various authorities from time to time to get possession of the house but to no effect although the petitions were duly received. On hearing that the holding (house) was being sold the respondent filed an application to the Ministry of Works on 1.12.85. In response he received a reply under Memo No. Sec. XII/F 17/84/335 dated 28.12.85 informing him that the agreement for sale of the house had been executed and, as such, it was not possible to entertain any application for its release. Then he submitted an application to the Joint Secretary on 1.12.85. The Government (Housing Estate) received the remaining dues of the Government in respect of the house from the Respondent and issued clearance certificate on 1.12.85 under Memo No. 1407 AO. He is a Bangladeshi and is permanently and continuously residing in Bangladesh since 1.2.1952 and that he never went outside Dhaka even for a single day. He submitted domicile certificate dated 10.5.1963 issued by the Ministry of Home Affairs and a nationality certificate issued by local Ward Chairman of Dhaka Municipal Corporation. He holds Bangladeshi Passport No. E-137774. He is a cobbler by profession who worked as such in the Army and was discharged in 1955 on account of an accident causing one of his legs to be broken. He is residing at 5/616 Block 'F' Joint Quarters, Mohammadpur, Dhaka, The Respondent No. 3 submitted the following documents:

(1) Domicile Certificate in original.

(2) Allotment letter dated 27.9.62 in original (3) Lease deed in Original dated 29.2.1962.

(4) Possession letter dated 12.6.62 from AO Mohammadpur Housing Estate.

(5) Receipts of Housing and Settlement (AO Housing Estate).

(6) Municipal receipts- 10.

(7) Chairman Certificate of Housing and Settlement.

(8) Letters to the Ministry dated 9.11.75. 15.9.76, 5.12.77, 12.4.78, 24.7.79, 31.8.80, 6.5.82, 18.4.83, 1.12.85 and 30.12.85.

(9) Memo No. 1047 dated 1.12.85 received by AO Mohammadpur Estate showing clearance of all Government dues.

6.	 Respondent No.1 as the respondent in the case before the Court of Settlement contested the application of Respondent No.3 stating that the Respondent No. 3 was not a voter, he opted for Pakistan. He did not submit any representation during the period from 1972-1975 that a certificate of clearance of the Govt. was obtained after illegally paying the same and the Writ Petition filed by him was dismissed on 18.3.1987 for non-prosecution.

7. The respondent No. 4, the Court of Settlement after considering the facts and circumstances of the case held that the building had been illegally included in the list of the buildings prepared under President's Order No. 16 of 1972 read with the provisions of Ordinance LIV of 1985, and ordered that the building be excluded from 'Ka' list of the abandoned buildings prepared under PO 16 of 1972 read with the provision of Ordinance LIV of 1985 and ordered the building be restored to the Respondent No.3 by ousting the petitioner there from forthwith.

8. Being aggrieved by the said judgment and order of the Respondent No. 4 the petitioner has filed this petition challenging the legality of the said order mainly on the following grounds.

9. The Court of Settlement committed an error in law in releasing the property from the list of abandoned buildings on the ground that the Respondent No. 3 is a citizen of Bangladesh on the basis of certificate issued by a Ward Chairman of Municipal Corporation without considering that he had no authority to issue said certificate.

10. The certificate of domicile cannot be treated as a certificate of citizenship of Bangladesh as the respondent No. 3 was against the independence of Bangladesh and he opted for Pakistan and he was given shelter for 17 years till today by International Authority and as such he cannot be treated as a citizen of Bangladesh.

11. Respondent No. 3 was ousted from his possession in December, 1971 and since then till " 10.4.74 no application and or approach was made to any authority to release the property.

12. The Court of Settlement cannot declare the property as abandoned property and therefore the decision is illegal and without jurisdiction.

13. The Respondent No. 1 has filed an affidavit-in-opposition stating, inter-alia, that the property is an abandoned property within the meaning of PO No. 16 of 1972. During Liberation movement and afterwards the whereabouts of the owner were not known and the owner ceased to control, supervise and manage the property. Hence the property vested in the government as abandoned property. The property has been under the control and management of the respondent through its allottee the petitioner. The respondent has entered into an agreement to sell the property to the petitioner for Tk. 1,29,654.00 and the petitioner has already paid Tk. 25,930.50 as down payment. The Respondent No. 3 never appeared or applied to this respondent for the release of the house prior to 1985. The Respondent No. 3 has opted for Pakistan and has been residing at Geneva Camp and he is not a citizen of Bangladesh.

14. The Respondent No. 3 has filed affidavit-in-opposition stating inter alia, that he does not reside and never resided at the 'Geneva Camp'. Since December 1971 he is residing at 5/16, Joint Quarter Block 'F' Mohammadpur. He owns and possessed the house and had to leave the said house in December, 1971 and take shelter in the aforesaid house at 5/16 Joint Quarter Block 'F Mohammadpur. He denied that he opted for Pakistan or that since December, 1971 he was given shelter in 'Geneva Camp' Mohammadpur or that he was not a national of Bangladesh or that he sent all his family member to Pakistan or that they are residing in Pakistan. He also submitted that the petitioner had no locus standi to be a party in the Court of Settlement or to contest the same.

15. The question before us is whether or not the property in question is an abandoned property under President's Order No. 16 of 1972.

16. Mr. SS Halder, the learned Advocate appearing for the petitioner, has submitted that the property is an abandoned house under President's Order No. 16 of 1972 in that the Respondent No. 3 admittedly left the house vacant in December, 1971 and the petitioner having occupied the said house on and from 1.1.72 the Respondent No. 3 ceased to occupy, supervise or manage the property in person. He further submitted that the Respondent No. 3 after leaving the said house has been living in Geneva Camp at Mohammadpur and has opted for Pakistan waiting to be repatriated to that country by the International Committee of Red Cross, and thereby deceased to be a citizen of Bangladesh. He also submitted that the whereabouts of the Respondent No. 3 was not known to the Government (Respondent No. 1) until 1985 and therefore the property vested in the Government under President's Order No. 16 of 1972.

17. Let us now see what is an abandoned property under the President's Order No. 16 of 1972. Article 2 of the Order has defined abandoned property as follows:

"(1)"Abandoned property" means any property owned by any person who is not present in Bangladesh or whose whereabouts are not known or who has ceased to occupy, supervise or manage in person his property, including.

(i) any property owned by any person who is a citizen of a state which at any time after the 25th day of March, 1971, was at war with or engaged in military operations against the People's Republic of Bangladesh,

(ii) any property taken over under the Bangladesh (Taking Over of Control and Management of Industrial and Commercial Concern) Order, 1972 (Acting President's Order No. 1 of 1972) but does not include.

(a) any property the owner of which is residing outside Bangladesh for any purpose which, in the opinion of the Government, is not prejudicial to the interest of Bangladesh

(b) any property which is in the possession of or under the control of the Government under any law for the time being in force.

18. The Respondent No.3, who is the owner of the property, has stated in his affidavit-in-opposition that he owned and possessed the house "but due to known circumstances" he had to leave the said house in December, 1971 and to take shelter in the house at 5/16 Block 'F' Mohammadpur and has been living there since then. Admittedly he never left Bangladesh although the petitioner has alleged that the Respondent No. 3 has been living in the "Geneva Camp" at Mohammadpur. Now the question is whether by leaving his house in December, 1971 the Respondent No. 3 "ceased to occupy, supervise or manage in person his property" The Respondent No. 3, who is an immigrant from the province of Bihar in India, was afraid and in apprehension about his security at the time immediately following liberation which he has referred to as 'known circumstances.' We believe that it was not unnatural for him to feel insecure and therefore he left the house for security. Leaving the house in such mental state does not mean that he gave up his right to the property with the intention of not returning to it. Therefore, it cannot be said that he ceased to occupy, supervise or manage in person so as to render the property abandoned simply on the ground that he left the house. Further, the petitioner has stated that he entered the house on 1.1.72 i.e. before the promulgation of President's Order No.16 of 1972 on 26.2.1972 and only 15 days after liberation and has been occupying the same since then, and that being the position, the Respondent No. 3 could not occupy, supervise or manage in person the property with the petitioner in the house.

<u>19. It has been stated by the petitioner and Respondent No. 1 that the Respondent No. 3 did not approach or appeal for the release of the property until 1985, but it appears from the judgment of the Court of Settlement that the Respondent No. 3 did write several letters for the release of his house between 1975 and 1985. Mr. Gholam Rabbani, the learned Advocate appearing for Respondent No. 3, submitted that the property had not been treated as abandoned property until 1975, and the Respondent No.3 came to know about it only when the Government for the first time issued the letter on 15.3.75 (Annexure 'A' to the petition) to the petitioner for payment of rent of the property as an abandoned property from 1.1.1972 to 28.2.1975. It was then that the Respondent No. 3 applied to the government for the release of his property. The petitioner has not annexed any paper or document dated earlier than 15.3.75 to show that the property was being treated as an abandoned property or that he was permitted to occupy the property from 1.1.72. We are, therefore, of the opinion that Respondent No. 3 cannot be said to have ceased to occupy, supervise or manage in person his property on the ground that he made no representation for its release.</u>

<u>20. It has not been denied that the Respondent No. 3 was in Bangladesh during the liberation war in 1971 and continued to be in the country after liberation till date. In such circumstances can it be said that the whereabouts of the Respondent No. 3 were not known and therefore his property was abandoned within the meaning of President's Order No. 16 of 1972. Whereabouts of the owner not known would, in our opinion, mean a person whose property is not in his possession for his control and management and he may be hiding in the country or has left Bangladesh or who cannot be traced. In Government of Bangladesh Vs. M/s. Ispahani as reported in 40 DLR (AD) 116 the Appellate Division of the Supreme Court of Bangladesh observed PO No. 16 was promulgated on 28.2.72 immediately after emergence of Bangladesh as an independent nation. Hundreds of West Pakistani industrial/business entrepreneurs had left the Country. Mills, factories, establishments; etc. had been abandoned for which specific law was promulgated. Such absentee owners had left their assets, properties e.g. house buildings, etc. Such property was the subject matter of PO 16 and the definition has been given in the PO itself. "</u>

<u>This observation by the Appellate Division clearly and correctly indicates the intention of the legislators was not to include properties of persons who were in Bangladesh and who may have left their property out of fear to stay in some other place in Bangladesh for shelter. Such temporary absence from their property cannot mean that their whereabouts were not known. We are, therefore, of the opinion that the absence of Respondent No.3 from his house did not amount to his whereabouts being unknown to the Government so as to make his house an abandoned property under PO No. 16 of 1972.</u>

21. The property does not come within the clause (1) of Article 2 because Respondent No. 3 does not come within the expression "person who is not present in Bangladesh" nor it is the case that his whereabouts are not known, nor can it be said that he ceased to occupy, supervise, or manage in person his property because the petitioner himself took over the possession of the house from 1.1.72.

22. The next question is whether he will come within the clause (i)" any property owned by any person who is a citizen of a State which at any time after the 25th day of March, 1971 was at war with or engaged in military operations against the People's Republic of Bangladesh."

23. Mr. SS Halder, Advocate for the petitioner, had submitted that the Respondent No.3 had opted for Pakistan and has been living in the 'Geneva Camp (which has been denied by the respondent) and therefore he ceased to be a Bangladeshi citizen as from December, 1971. He has annexed three certificates Annexure P2, P3 and P4 in support. Annexure P2 is a copy of certificate dated 20.11.89 from Sub-Inspector Mohamrnadpur Police Station and P3 is a certificate dated 8.12.89 from the local Relief Committee. Both these certificates state that the Respondent No. 3 has been living in the Geneva Camp and he is waiting to be repatriated to Pakistan. The documents being dated the year 1989 they were not submitted before the Court of Settlement and so the fact stated therein was not proved or determined by that court after examination. Annexure P3 is a photocopy of certificate dated 11.2.86 from the Government of Bangladesh purported to have been signed by one Md. Shahjahan Sr. Scale Section Officer of the Ministry of Home Affairs, Immigration Section V, stating that Respondent N0. 3 opted for repatriation to Pakistan.

24. President's Order No. 149 of 1972 provides for citizenship of Bangladesh. Article 2 thereof provides that any person shall be deemed to be a citizen of Bangladesh:

(i) who or whose father or grandfather was born in the territories now comprised in Bangladesh and who was permanent resident of such territories on the 25th day of March, 1971 and continues to be so resident, or (ii) who was a permanent resident of the territories now comprised in Bangladesh on the 25th day of March, 1971 and continues to be so resident and is not otherwise disqualified for becoming a citizen by or under any law for the time being in force."

25. Respondent No. 3 does not come under clause (i) of Article 2 but he comes under clause (ii) in view of the fact that he was a permanent resident" of the territories comprising Bangladesh on 25th March, 1971 and continued to be so. "Now does he lose his citizenship by opting for Pakistan and living in the Geneva Camp (fact which he denies). In Mukhtar Ahmed Vs. Government of Bangladesh as reported in 34 DLR 29 this Court has held" the mere fact that he filed an application for going over to Pakistan cannot take away his citizenship. The Bangladesh Citizenship Order, PO No. 149 of 72 has enumerated different situations in which a person shall be denied to be a citizen of Bangladesh, but it has not discriminated among its citizens no matter in which they may have become citizens of this country. So the petitioner is on the same footing as any other citizen. His citizenship therefore clings to him. He could voluntarily renounce it or he could be deprived of it if he had incurred any disqualification"

We agree with the view taken by this Court. The Respondent No. 3 has not renounced his citizenship nor has he incurred any disqualification by alleged option for Pakistan. We find that he had not pursued his alleged application for repatriation to Pakistan. On the contrary he has got a Bangladeshi Passport which is a prima facie evidence of his citizenship of the country. He has not acquired citizenship of any other country, his citizenship of Bangladesh which he acquired long before cannot just disappear or evaporate and he continues to be a citizen of Bangladesh.

<u>26. In the circumstances we hold that Respondent No. 3's property is not an abandoned property because he has neither acquired citizenship of Pakistan nor has ceased to manage his property nor his whereabouts are unknown to the government.</u>

<u>It has been submitted on behalf of the petitioner that Court of Settlement does not have any power to release an abandoned property. The Abandoned Buildings (Supplementary Provisions) Ordinance, 1985 (Ordinance LIV of 1985) provides in section 10(2) that for the purpose of hearing an application a Court of Settlement shall have all the powers of a Civil Court while trying a suit under the Code of Civil Procedure, 1908 (Act V of 1908) in respect of the following matters:</u>

<u>(a) Summoning and enforcing the attendance of any person and examining on oath.</u>

<u>(b) requiring the discovery and production of any document.</u>

<u>(c) requiring evidence on affidavit</u>

<u>(d) requisitioning any public record, or copy thereof from any office; and</u>

<u>(e) issuing commissions for the examination of witnesses and documents.</u>

27. Section 10(3) provides that any proceeding before a Court of Settlement shall be deemed to be a judicial proceeding within the meaning of section 193 of the Penal Code. (Act XLV of 1860). and section 109 (5) provides, "A Court of Settlement shall, after such enquiry as it may deem necessary and after giving reasonable opportunity to the parties concerned of being heard and also adducing evidence, both oral and documentary, if any, make such decision on the prayer of the applicant as it deems fit."

28. The Court of Settlement therefore is competent and within its jurisdiction to allow the prayer of any petitioner to exclude a building from list of the abandoned buildings and order the building to be restored to him.

We do not find the judgment and order dated 11.6.87 passed by Respondent No.4, the Court of Settlement, in case No. 347/89 (Ka-89), Block-F', Mohammadpur, Dhaka. Holding No. 11A/8, Block 'F' Mohammadpur, Dhaka, to have been passed without any lawful authority and to be of no legal effect Therefore, we have no reason to interfere with the judgment and order.

In the result, the Rule is discharged. We make no order as to costs.

End.

case_source: (From the Judgment and Order dated 19.1.1982 Passed by the High Court Division in F.M.A. No.428 of 1981)
full_judgment:
Fazle Munim, C.J.:—This appeal arises from First Miscellaneous Appeal No. 428 of 1981 decided by a Bench of the High Court Division on January 19, 1982.

Respondent No. 1 instituted Partition Suit No. 118 of 1980 in the court of Subordinate Judge, 1st Court, Sadar, Chittagong against the appellants and respondents Nos. 2 to 29 for partition of his share after deducting the area sold by him out of his share to the outsiders, namely, defendants Nos. 4 to 10. In three schedules to the plaint, schedule No.1 comprises 15 gandas, schedule No. 2 comprises ganda and schedule No. 3 comprises 5 gandas of land. Schedules 1 and 2 are tenanted premises and schedule 3 is the homestead. Schedules 1 and 2 properties originally belonged to Habibullah Khan, father of the appellants and respondent Nos. I and 2, Schedule 3 originally belonged to Safiunnessa, their mother. Father died in 1954 and mother died on June 22, 1978 leaving them as heirs to their respective properties. Respondent Nos. 11 to 39 are proforma-defendants being tenants in schedules I and 2 properties.

2. The suit was filed on September 12, 1980. Later, on September 29, 1980 two applications were filed, one under Order 39, rule 1 of the Civil Procedure Code for restraining defendant Nos. 1 to 10 from transferring or changing the nature of the schedule properties and the other was filed under Order 40, rule 1 of the Civil Procedure Code for appointment of receiver.

3. In the application for injunction the trial court passed an order directing the parties to maintain status quo which order was made absolute on December 2, 1980 and in the application for appointment of receiver an order to issue notices was passed.

4. So far as the prayer for appointment of receiver was concerned, respondent No. I expressed grievance that after the death of their father in 1954, appellant No. 1 as male member and also his guardian took charge of schedules 1 and 2 properties, did not pay anything to their mother who died in 1978 and realised rents from proforma-defendant Nos. 11-39. His further allegation was that since for nonpayment of Government dues, four certificate cases had been started, and the need had arisen to prevent the properties from being illegally transferred, there was necessity for appointment of a receiver.

5. Written objections were filed by the appellants controverting the allegations made in the application under Order 39, rule I of the Civil Procedure Code. He stated that the application was malafide and aimed at suppressing the plaintiff's misdeeds, namely, transferring properties of schedule 1 to defendant Nos. 4-10 who are tenants in possession of the premises of schedule 1 and the suit as well as the application were filed by him in collusion with them. Appellant No. 1 maintained the whole family out of the income of the disputed property since 1954, when his father died and plaintiff-respondent No. 1 was married in 1978 by spending Tk. 35,000/- taken on loan. Plaintiff-respondent No. 1 sold almost his entire share from the property of schedule No. 1 to defendant. Nos. 4-10. It is on the refusal of plaintiff-respondent No. 1 to pay the dues of certificate cases to the extent of his share and on his refusal to hand over the rent receipts and the kabalas for schedules 2 and 3 lands, appellant No. 1 paid the entire dues of the certificate cases on December 30, 1980, January 2, 1981 and August 11, 1982 respectively. No certificate case was started with regard to the property of schedule No. 1.  For the protection and improvement of properties, appellant No. 1 mortgaged the properties and due to improvement effected thereto with the help of the loan so raised the rent has been increased enormously. As all the co-sharers, being transferees from respondent Nos. 1 and 2 were not impleaded in the partition suit it was not maintainable and, therefore, the prayer for appointment of receiver was also not maintainable. Further, the order of status quo, having been made absolute on September 29, 1980 the prayer for appointment of receiver was not maintainable. Also, all the properties inherited by the plaintiff and defendant Nos. 1-3 from the parents were not brought into hotchpot which is necessary for the maintenance of a partition suit.

6. On May 25, 1981 the trial court passed an order for appointment of receiver. Against this order, appellants preferred the aforesaid first miscellaneous appeal in the High Court Division. The learned Judges who heard the appeal affirmed the decision of the trial court on the landing that there was mismanagement and there was necessity for appointment of receiver for better management and presentation of the disputed property.

<u>7. Leave to appeal from their judgment was granted by the Court to consider whether there was any scope or necessity for appointment of a receiver when they have already been restrained by an order of temporary injunction from transferring the properties in question or causing any damage thereto and also when there was neither any specific allegation of mismanagement or damage to the property nor any finding of an instance of such management or damage.</u>

8. Mr. Rafique-ul-Huq, Counsel for the appellants, submitted that though the appellant No. 1 objected vehemently to the appointment of receiver and never expressed in favour of such appointment, the learned Judges of the High Court Division wrongly observed that "the appellant No. I was not altogether against the appointment of receiver". The Counsel referred to the relevant paragraphs from the written objection against the prayer for appointment made in the petition under Order 40, rule 1 of the Civil Procedure Code. He further submitted that if any appointment of receiver is made the entire property and income derived therefrom will be eaten up by the receiver. Since, due to the effort of appellant No. 1, the dispute property is earning such income, there cannot be any better instance of good management of the property concerned, As already observed, no specific allegation of mismanagement or damage to the disputed property having been made or established before the Court, there is no case for the appointment of a receiver. Appellant No. 1, being the eldest ion, not only took care of his mother and his brothers and sisters including plaintiff-respondent No. 1 whom he brought up from childhood and spent considerable amount of money over his marriage, but also managed well the property left by his father. Due to his single efforts, great improvements have been effected leading to increase in income, municipal taxes have been paid and all the dues under certificate, cases have also been paid. The learned Counsel submitted that these activities were not instances of negligence, extravagance or any other lapses, so as to justify the appointment of the receiver.

9. As against these claims of appellant No. 1 which, if accepted, would negative the necessity of any receiver, Mr. M.H. Khondker, Counsel for the plaintiff-respondent No. 1, made feeble attempts to justify the order of appointment of receiver, relying solely on the alleged non-payment of municipal taxes and dues in the certificate cases. In face of the assertion of appellant No. 1 regarding full payment of all such taxes and dues payable in respect of the disputed property, plaintiff-respondent No, 1 would seem to have no legs to stand upon. Broad facts remained that it is appellant No. 1 who maintained the entire family since his father's death in 1954 and effected impressive improvements in the property left by his father by taking initiative and lead. Existence of these facts negative the necessity for the appointment of a receiver, Moreover, the conduct of plaintiff-respondent No. 1 in relation to appellant No. 1 as well as his dealings with the disputed property are not at all satisfactory. His preference for strangers only shows his indifference and callous attitude.

Quite a number of cases have been cited by the learned Counsels for and against the appointment of a receiver. I would refer a few amongst them.

<u>10. As a general rule, the appointment of a receiver in a particular suit has not met the approval of the Court. The existence of dispute offers no ground whatsoever for appointing a receiver. In Govind Narain Rao Desai vs. Vallabhrao Narayantao Desai, AIR 1920 Bom. 321, it has been observed that in a partition suit between members of a joint family the Court will not appoint a receiver except by consent, and especially where the family property consists of land. Special circumstances must be proved before the Court will make such appointment. The plaintiff-must satisfy the Court that the property in possession of the defendant is in danger of being wasted,</u>

<u>11. Other legal principles in the matter of appointment of a receiver should also be kept in view. These principles require the exercise of caution about putting a third party as a receiver of properties of a join family which are being possessed and enjoyed by the members of the family. If there is no fear that the property in question is going to be destroyed or dissipated, the Court should be reluctant to extend any relief by appointing a receiver. In support, reference may be made to Chaitanya Naiko vs. Kandhino Naiko, AIR 1965 Ori 217.</u>

<u>12. The reason that a plaintiff has prima facie case does not establish the necessity for appointment of a receiver. Such appointment may be made if it is considered just and convenient. Relief by way of appointment of a receiver is discretionary with the Court. Appointment of a receiver cannot be claimed as a matter of course. Without allegations of wastage or destruction of property, it requires to be proved that not merely the plaintiff's interest but also the interest of all the parties in the suit and the property concerned need be protected. The power to appoint a receiver as conferred by Order 40, rule 1, C.P.C. should, therefore, be sparingly used. These aspects were considered in Sardar Wall Muhammad vs. Sardar Muhammad Iqbal Khan Mokal, PLD 1975 Lah 492.</u>

<u>13. The provisions for the appointment of a receiver is to be considered as one of the harshest remedies for the enforcement of rights to property. It should, therefore, be exercised only in extreme cases. Where there is not merely apprehension of possible danger but the peril or danger to the property in question appears to be great and imminent, such appointment may be made. This finds support in Mst. Ghulam Zainab vs. Mst. Tahira Sultana, PLD 1977 Lah. 830.</u>

<u>14. Mere apprehension that the property in question will be transferred by the defendant offers no justification for appointment of receiver particularly when an undertaking has been given by him that no transfer will be made vide Serajul Won vs. Bimal Chandra Sen, (1982) 34 DLR 297.</u>

15. In an early case the Calcutta High Court while considering the provisions of Order 40, rule 1, C.P.C. observed that though the preservation of properly from waste and alienation must be proved in seeking the exercise of discretion under them, they have substantially provided the scope of the Court's discretion. If, therefore, it is found in a suit of partition of joint family property that the plaintiff has been kept out of possession of his share in the property with the result that all supplies were cut of from him, the case though involves no case of waste, order may be passed for the appointment of the receiver vide, Ramji Ram Vs. Saligram, (1909) 14 CWN 248.

16. Though the case of Kali Kumari Vs. Bachhan Singh (1913) 17 CWN 974 involves the question of appointment of a receiver in respect of the properly of an infant in a suit under the Guardians and Wards Act, 1890 from the members of the family Here, the principle for selection and appointment of particular person as a receiver has clearly been stated. The exercise of discretion being judicial must be exercised according to the circumstances of the case.

17. In Suprasanna Roy Vs. Upendra Narain Roy, (1913) 18 CWN 533, the Calcutta High Court in deciding the legality of an order in a partition suit for the appointment of a receiver considered a few principles relating thereto. According to this decision, the Court will not hesitate to appoint a receiver if it is just and convenient to do so. The necessity for the appointment of receiver is much stronger if a party to the suit is in sole occupation. The Court may, of course, allow the parties in exclusive possession to elect to pay an occupation rent to others. But it may require security from the co-owner in exclusive occupation to account for their share of the rents to the other co-owners. Further, one of the parties to the suit should not ordinarily be appointed a receiver except in very exceptional circumstances.

<u>18. In Basant Ram Vs. Dasondhi Mal, AIR 1929 Lab 497, one of the principles for appointment of receiver has been stated to be the deprivation of other co-sharers from share in the profits arising from the property in question which is in the hands of one co-sharer. Where it is found that the defendant's conduct is not absolutely straight forward and above board thus giving sufficient justification to the plaintiff to urge that he has no more any confidence in his honesty and integrity the defendant was allowed to be a joint receiver of the property in question along with a third person, and they are to remain under the control and direction of the Court.</u>

<u>19. Having regard to the principles enunciated in the decisions cited before us, it appears that there is no reason for appointment of a receiver in the present case, particularly when the courts below did not find any mismanagement or damage to the property in question and there is an order of injunction restraining the transfer of any property in question.</u>

<u>For the reasons stated above the judgment and order of the High Court Division is set aside and the appeal is allowed with costs.</u>

End.

case_source: From the judgment and order dt. June 3, 1980 passed by the High Court Division in Second Appeal No. 1245 of 1962
full_judgment:
Ruhul Islam, J:-This appeal by special leave arises from the judgment and decree of the High Court Division in Second Appeal No. 1245 of 1962 affirming those of the Subordinate Judge, Bogra in Title Appeal No. 73 of 1961 reversing the decision of the Munsif, First Court, Bogra in Title Suit No. 317 of 1959 The question involved in this appeal is whether the defendants held the suit property in occupancy right which is protected or it is an under tenure holding, If it is found that the suit land appertains to an under tenure holding, then the plaintiff must succeed to recover possession by evicting the defendant on the basis of his auction purchase of the touzi in revenue sale, and on annulment of encumbrances, but if it is found that the suit land appertains to an occupancy holding as claimed by the defendants, then the suit must fail, because occupancy holding being a protected interest it could not be annulled at the instance of the auction purchaser of the touzi in revenue sale.

<u>2. The plaintiff brought the suit for declaration of his title to and recovery of khas possession in the suit land by evicting the defendants on the basis of his purchase of Touzi No. 314 in revenue sale, and delivery of possession of the same in 1951 after confirmation of the sale, and annulment of encumbrances in Miscellaneous Case No. 151 of 1951. According to the plaintiff he got khas possession in all the lands of the Touzi excepting 'Kha' schedule land which is in possession of the defendant. Hence the suit. Defendant No. 1 contested the suit contending, inter alia, that the suit land does not constitute an under tenure holding but it is an occupancy holding. He claimed that the plaintiff's father settled the disputed land with the defendant and others by 4 pattas on 3.12.1927 and on the same day they made a waqf of the said property by a registered deed of waqf and the defendant was made the Mutwalti. The defendant claimed to have raiyati mokarari right in the land settled with them by the father of the plaintiff. He claimed that since he has acquired a right of occupancy in the suit land he is not liable to be ejected.</u>

3. The learned Munsif on consideration of the pattas and other documents produced by the party and subsequent user of the land by the tenants dismissed the suit on the finding that the defendant is an occupancy raiyat. On appeal the Subordinate Judge interpreted the pattas as creating tenure holding in favour of the defendant and decreed the suit. This decision was affirmed by the learned Single Judge of the High Court Division.

The relevant portion of the patta which is identical in all the 4 pattas marked Exhibit-D series runs in the following terms:

“লিখিতং শ্রীকেরা মতুল্লা মন্ডল,….চিরস্থায়ী স্থির জমার মোকররী জোতের পট্যকপন্ন নিলাম খরিদসূত্রে পন্ডনী তালুক স্বত্বে স্বত্ববান ও দখলকার আছি।তনদুর্গত নিন্ম তপশীল চৌহাদ্দির বর্ণিত মত্তাজী ৭০ শতাংশ জমির কাত শালীয়ানা ১ টাকা ছয় আনা জমা ধার্য্যে তোমরা চিরস্থায়ী স্থির জমার বন্দোবস্ত করিয়া লওয়ার প্রার্থনা করায়…. স্বীকার ও অংগীকার করিতেছি যে নিম্নলিখিত কিস্তিবন্দি মোতারেক সন সন কিস্ত কিস্ত খাজনা কায্যকারককে দিয়া সেরেস্তায় প্রচালিত্যাচেক দাখিলা রীতিমত হাসিল করিতে থাকিবা…তোমরা অদ্য হইতে চিরস্থায়ী স্থির জমার মোকররী স্বত্বে স্বত্ববান ও দখলকার হইয়া দান বিক্রয় আদি সর্ব প্রকার হস্তান্তর ও অবস্তান্তর করনের ও অধীন প্রজা বিলি পস্করিনী খনন ও ভরন উষ্টক নির্মিত পোওশ দালান কি মসজিদ আদি কি রক্ষাদি রোপন ও ছেদন করনের ক্ষমতা যুক্তে পরম সুখে পত্র পৌত্রাদি ওয়ারীশানগণ ক্রমে চিরকাল ভোগ দখল ও তছরুপ করিতে থাকহ।…তাং ৩-১২-২৭”

4. It appears that land measuring 1.90 acres recorded in C.S. Khatian No. 528 appertaining to Touzi No. 314 is the subject matter of the suit for khas possession. Plaintiff claimed it on the basis of his auction purchase of the Touzi in revenue sale held on 27-9-50 which was confirmed on 27.11.50 and delivery of possession given on 7.4.51. Thereafter all the under tenures appertaining to the said Touzi were annulled in a regular proceeding; and the plaintiff got possession of all lands excepting the suit land. According to the plaintiff he has already possession of .43 acres of land of the said khatian which has been described in schedule "Ka". The suit land has been described in schedule "Kha", to the plaint. C. S. Khatian No. 528 is directly under C.S. KhatianNo. 527 which records the tenure right of the predecessor of the plaintiff. Keramaullah Talukder, father of the plaintiff settled the disputed land with (1) Rabiullah and Yeadullah, (2) Keramatullah, (3) Banari Bibi, and (4) Sonaullah by 4 pattas dated 3.12.27. According to the defendant the pattas created a mokararijote right but according to the Plaintiff it created an under tenure holding.

5. Decision of the case depends on interpretation of terms of the pattas. The defendant in support of his case referred to a registered waqfnama dated 3.12.27 by which waqf was created in respect of the land settled by the plaintiff's father Keramatullah Talukder. Sonaullah Talukder was appointed as the Mutwalli. Defendant further showed that the plaintiff's father and after him the plaintiff all along treated the land as mokararijote right and realized rent from the settlement holder. In this connection defendant also referred to a decree in Title Suit No. 171 of 1947 obtained by the plaintiff's father in respect of .43 acres of land purchased by him in a rent sale, and suit was filled for declaration of his title and partition of the same. Plaintiff's father got a decree in that suit. The trial Court in consideration of the evidence led by the parties and referring to the recitals in the pattas arrived at the finding that the defendant was a cultivating raiyatin actual possession of the suit land and so the trial Court held that the defendant acquired occupancy right which was a protected interest. On appeal by the plaintiff the learned Subordinate Judge, however, arrived at a different finding with regard to the nature and character of the interest created by the pattas. Relying on the provisions in the pattas authorizing the settlement holder to engage tenants, and settlement of mokari right at fixed rate, was of the view that the incidents of the settlement indicate beyond any shadow or doubt that it was a tenure and not an occupancy right granted to the defendant by the pattas. According to him the original purpose being use of land by engaging tenants, tenant's mere user of the same as a cultivating raiyat, cannot change the nature and character of the holding, the learned Subordinate Judge arrived at the finding that inception of the tenancies shows in clear terms that the defendant took settlement of the tenure and not of raiyati right, and as such be cannot acquire occupancy right in the tenure by cultivating the land for a long time nor he can acquire any occupancy right by virtue of his being a settled raiyat in that village. The learned Subordinate Judge concluded with the finding that the defendant is not an occupancy raiyat but a tenure holder, so his interest is not protected under section 37 of the Revenue Sale Law. This decision was affirmed by the learned Single Judge of the High Court Division in second appeal.

6. Mr. B. B. Roy Chowdhury, the learned Advocate, appearing for the appellant submitted that the learned Subordinate Judge as well as the learned Single Judge of the High Court Division failed to properly appreciate section 5 of the Bengal Tenancy Act, which has defined "tenure holder" and consequently failed to appreciate the pattas Exhibit D series in the light of the said definition, and this led to an erroneous, decision that the pattas created a tenure holding and not a raiyati holding Mr. Roy Chowdhury further submitted that the dakhilas Exhibit A series, the decree passed in Title Suit No. 171 of 1947, Exhibit E series clearly show that the landlord treated the right of the defendant in the disputed property as a raiyati tenancy.

<u>7. The tenure-holder as defined in section S of the Bengal Tenancy Act means primarily a person who has acquired from a proprietor or from another tenure-holder a right to hold land for the purpose of collecting rents or for bringing it under cultivation by establishing tenants on it, and includes also the successors-in-interest of persons who have acquired such a right. The definition of raiyat as it was before the amendment of 1928 was that-means primarily a person who has acquired a right to hold land for the purpose of cultivating it by himself or by members of his family or by hired servants or with the aid of partners and includes also the successor in interest of persons who had acquired such a right. The definition was slightly modified by the amendment of 1928. After amendment "Raiyat" means primarily a person who acquired a right to hold land for the purpose of cultivating it by himself or by members of his family or by servants or labourers or with the aid of partners and also includes successors in interest of persons who have acquired such a right. Sub-section (1) of section 5 deanes "Tenure holder". A tenure-holder means primarily a person who has acquired from a proprietor or from another tenure holder a right to hold land for the purpose of collecting rents or bringing it under cultivation by establishing tenants on it and includes also the successors in interest of persons who have acquired such a right. The pattas in question being prior to the amendment of the Bengal Tenancy Act by Act IV of 1928, the old sub-section (2) of section 5 should be referred to for the definition, "Raiyat" means primarily a person who has acquired a right to hold land for the purpose of cultivating it by himself or by members of his family or by hired servants, or with the aid of partners, and includes also the successors in interest of persons who have acquired such a right Sub, section (4) of section 5 provide the guidance to find out whether a tenant is a tenure-bolder or a raiyat. It provides that the Court shall have regard to-</u>

<u>(a) local custom; and</u>

<u>(b) the purpose for which the right of tenancy was originally acquired, Sub-section (5) provides that when the land held by a tenant exceeds 100 standard bighas, the tenant shall be presumed to be a tenure- holder until the contrary is shown.</u>

<u>8. The definition of tenure-holder is not exhaustive. Similarly the definition of raiyat is also not exhaustive. Whether a person' is a tenure-holder or a raiyat depends on questions of fact and one must look to the attendant circumstances to judge the purpose of the lease. Normally the original purpose determines the nature of tenancy. If the original purpose is not known, subsequent conduct of the parties may be looked at in order to determine the nature of tenancy the mode of user of the land may give a valuable clue to the original purpose for which the tenancy was created.</u>

9. In the instant case the trial Court dismissed the suit on the finding that the defendant was a cultivating raiyat in actual possession of the disputed land and as such he acquired right of occupancy which is "a protected interest, and the plaintiff isnot entitled to recover possession by evicting the defendants. On appeal by the plaintiff e learned Subordinate Judge reversed the decision on the view that the original purpose of creation of a tenancy will be the guiding factor to determine whether the tenant as an occupancy raiyat is a tenure-holder. He found that inception of the tenancy shows in clear terms that the defendant took settlement of the tenure and not of raiyati right. So the defendant could not acquire occupancy right in the tenure by cultivating the, land for a long time nor can he acquire any occupancy right by virtue of his being a settled raiyat in that village. The learned Subordinate Judge found that since the defendant is atenure-holder his interest is not protected under section 37 of the Revenue Sale Law.

10. In second-appeal the learned Single judge of the High Court Division took the view that mere cultivation of the land by the tenant himself does not change the nature of the tenancy if the original purpose was to create tenure or an under tenure.

The patta dated 3.12.17 clearly recites that-

তোমার অদ্য হইতে চিরস্থায়ী স্থির জমার মোকররী স্বত্বে স্বত্ববান ও দখলকার হইয়া দান বিক্রয় আদি সর্ব প্রকার হস্তান্তর ও অবস্থান্তর করনের ও অধীন প্রজা বিলি পুঙ্করিনী খনন ও ভরস হষ্টক নির্মিত পোন্ডশ দালান কি মসজিন আদি কি রক্ষাদি রোপন ও ছেদন করনের ক্ষমতা যক্তে পরম সুখে পত্র পৌত্রাদি ওয়ারিশানগম ক্রমে চিরকাল ভাগ দখল ও তচরুপ করিতে থাকহ।

<u>11. The above noted recitals show that the lessee was allowed to hold the land at fixed rate of rent; and it authorized the lessee to collect rent by setting up tenants on the land. The pattas land was recorded in C S. Khatian No. 528 as “মধ্যস্বত্ব চিরস্থায়ী স্বত্বের”…… With reference to the terms in the pattas the lower Appellate Court held that defendant is a tenure bolder. According to him, since the inception of the tenancy shows in clear terms that the defendant took settlement of the land with the right of a tenure-holder and not with a raiyati right. Thus it appears that the learned Subordinate Judge confined his consideration on the question of nature of the tenancy merely with reference to recitals of the patta but without any consideration as to the nature of use of the land by the lessee since its inception. The plaintiff in this suit prayed for khas possession of 1 90 acres of land recorded in C.S. Khatian No. 528 on the basic of his auction purchase in revenue sale of Touzi No. 314 of Bogra Collectorate. According to the plaintiff’s case, he has already got possession of.43 acres or land of the same khatian, but due to obstruction he did not succeed in taking possession of 1.90 acres of land of the said khatian. Defendant No.1 gave a total denial about the annulment of the encumbrance and their knowledge about the said proceeding with regard to .43 acres in the possession of the plaintiff. His case is that the plaintiff's father Keramatullah Talukder took khas possession of it as putnidar in Title Suit No. 171 of 1947 of the Munsif, First Court, Bogra. According to the defendant, plaintiff never took possession of it. The defendant's further case is that plaintiff's father settled the disputed land with (1) Rabiullah and Yadullah; (2) Karamatullah Talukder, (3) Banari Bibi, and (4) Sonaullah by 4 pattas dated 3-12-1927 in makarrarijote right, and on the same day they made a wakf by a registered deed of wakf and the defendant became the mutwalli. The mere fact that a person has acquired from a proprietor or from another tenure-holder a right to hold land for the purpose of collecting rent is not sufficient to prove that he is a tenure-holder. It must be proved on evidence that since the inception of the tenancy land was let out for agricultural or horticultural purpose. This principle, as it appears from the judgment of the lower Appellate Court and that of the High Court Division, was not followed in determining the controversy between the parties on the question of nature of the tenancy created by the pattas Exhibit D series dated 3.12.1927.</u>

<u>12. The defendant's specific case is that by the patta a raiyati with occupancy right was created and not a tenure as claimed by the plaintiff, and this gets support from the use of the land by the defendant from the very inception of the tenancy. The defendant led the evidence to prove that the land has been under direct cultivation of the defendant. Defendant filed certain dakhilas Exhibit. A to A(5) of which Exhibit A is in the hand-writing of the plaintiff and Exhibits A to A( 5) are in the hand writing of Keramatullah Mondal, plaintiff's father. C.S. Khatian No. 528 is included in all these dakhilas except A(2) and A(3). With reference to these dakhilas the learned Munsif rightly observed that it no longer lies in the mouth of the plaintiff to say that defendants are "Niskar tenure-holder as recorded in khatian and not raiyati." The defendant also filed a decree made in Title Suit No. 171 of 1947 (Exhibit E) which shows that the suit was brought by Keramatullah Mondal on the basis or auction purchase of schedule "Ka" land in rent sale. The decree also belies the statement of the plaintiff that he got possession of schedule 'Ka' land on the basis of revenue sale and got possession through the Collectorate. With reference to the above mentioned materials the learned Munsif correctly arrived at the finding that by the pattas raiyati with occupancy right was created, and the suit land does not appertain to an under-tenure holding as claimed by the plaintiff. By the pattas dated 3-12-1927 a tenancy in the nature of makarrari jote right was created and the interest thus acquired by the defendant is protected from annulment under section 37 of the Revenue sale law. In this context it may be mentioned that the recitals in the pattas lend considerable support to the defendant's case that “স্বাধীন প্রজালিলি” was not the dominant purpose of creation of the tenancy by the pattas Exhibit D series. It mentions that the pattas created an occupancy raiyati interest with fixed jama. It recites, inter alia-</u>

<u>“চিরস্থায়ী স্থির জমার মোকররী স্বত্বে স্বত্ববান ও দখলকার হইয়া…”</u>

<u>The pattas also authorize the tenant to enjoy the tenancy with the rights amongst others- “পঙ্করিনী খনন ও ভরন ইষ্টক রিম্মিত পোন্ডশ দালান কি মসজিদ আদি কি বক্ষাদি রোপন ও ছেদন করনের ক্ষমতাযক্তে পরম সাথে পত্র পৌত্রাদি ওয়ারীশানগণ ক্রমে চিরকাল ভোগ দখল ও তছরুপ করিতে থাকহঃ”</u>

<u>The tenancy was created in 1927 and the suit was filed in 1959,"and during this long period of 32 years the Ian has although been used by the tenant for cultivation by himself and for other purposes In view of the rights conferred upon the tenant by the pattas and the admitted fact that the defendant never set up any tenant on the land and he used the land for himself by cultivation and for other purposes. I am of the opinion that by the pattas Exhibit D series mokarrari jote with fixed rent with occupancy right was created in favour of the patta holders, including the defendant; and such tenancy is protected from annulment. The learned Subordinate Judge on misconception of law and facts erroneously reversed the judgment of the trial Court and learned Judge of the High Court Division affirmed the same.</u>

<u>In that view of the matter the appeal is allowed with costs. Judgment and decree of the High Court Division and those of the lower Appellate Court are set aside and those of the trial Court restored.</u>

End.

full_judgment:
This Rule, issued at the instance of the plaintiffs, calls in question the order No. 14 dated 21.11.85 passed by the Munsif, Sadar, Sylhet, in Title Suit No. 196 of 1985 allowing the application of the opposite party Nos. 5-7 to implead them as defendants in the suit in accordance with Order 1, rule 10 of the Code of Civil Procedure.

2. There is a petition for amendment of the revisional application, supported by an affidavit, filed today in the Court in respect of the present pendency of the suit concerned in the First Court of Subordinate Judge, Sylhet, bearing No. 297 of 1986. This petition be treated as allowed.

3. Factual matrix of the present matter appears to be a competition in benevolence. The petitioners and the opposite party Nos. 5-7 are rival donors of properties for housing the Alankari Post Office under Biswanath Upazila. The petitioners as plaintiffs filed Title Suit No. 196 of 1985 in the First Court of Munsif, Sadar Sylhet, against the defendant opposite party Nos. 1-4, the concerned government officers, for declaration that the order of shifting of the Alankari Post Office from the present building donated by the petitioners to some other site is void and without jurisdiction as it would be in violation of the agreement entered into between the plaintiff petitioners and defendant Nos. 1-4, in pursuance of which the plaintiffs petitioners donated .05 decimals of land by a document registered on 20.3.84 and constructed the present building thereon according to the specifications given by the defendant opposite party Nos. 1-4. It was alleged in the plaint and it is also not disputed that in pursuance of an order made by the defendant opposite party No.3, the Deputy Post Master General, and communicated under his Memo. No. H-1-4/81-82 dated 9-2-85, the Post Office, which was formerly in the outer house of one Rashid Ali, had been actually shifted to the building provided by the plaintiffs petitioners. It is grievanced in the plaint that some people of the locality has secured an order from the Minister of the concerned Ministry for shifting of the said Post Office from the present building to some other place and the Ministry communicated the order to the defendant opposite party No. 1, Upazila Nirbahi Officer, who, in his turn, under his Memo No. 846 dated 20.8.85, asked the defendant opposite party No. 2, the Assistant Commissioner, to shift the Post Office. It is further alleged that neither the plaintiffs petitioners nor defendant opposite party No. 3, the Deputy Post Master General, had been consulted in the matter of shifting of the Post Office.

4. In pursuance of this suit the plaintiffs petitioners obtained an order of temporary injunction under Order 39, rule 1 of the Code of Civil Procedure from the learned Munsif on 16.9.85 restraining the opposite party Nos. 1 and 2 from shifting the said Post Office from its present site to any other place. On 5.11.85 the defendant opposite party Nos. 5-7 filed an application before the learned Munsif under Order 1, rule 10 of the Civil Procedure Code to implead them as defendants in the suit alleging that they got the Post Office provisionally established at the outer house of one Rashid Ali and subsequently they donated a piece of land by a deed dated 8.5.84 and created a permanent building thereon according to the desire of the authorities, but the petitioners collusively managed to get the Post Office shifted to its present site. They further stated that the defendant opposite party Nos.1-4 had decided to shift the Post Office to the donated property of the defendant opposite party Nos. 5-7 to which the plaintiffs petitioners could have no objection.

5. The learned Munsif impleaded the opposite party Nos. 5-7 as defendants by his order as follows:

"The petition under Order 1, rule 10 Civil Procedure Code by one Abdul Wahid and 2 others for impleading them as defendants is put up today. Prayer is allowed. Amend the plaint and the G.R. accordingly. To 18.12.85 for W/s."

6. Being aggrieved by the aforesaid order of the learned Munsif the plaintiff petitioners have obtained this Rule.

7. Mr. Dewan A.M.S. Zaman, the learned Advocate for the petitioners, has submitted that the impugned order of the learned Munsif suffers from illegality occasioning a failure of justice as the order is against the patent provision of law and the decisions of the superior courts.

8. Mr. S.H. Md. Nurul Huda Jaigirdar, the learned advocate for opposite party Nos. 1 5,6 and 7, on the other hand, supported the order of the learned Munsif and submitted that the order passed by the learned Munsif under Order 1, rule 10 of the Code of Civil Procedure was passed in discretion of the court for proper adjudication of the case; and that defendant opposite parties 5-7 were proper parties, if not necessary parties. He submitted that this court will not interfere in its revisional jurisdiction with an order passed in his discretion by the learned Munsif when it has not occasioned any failure of justice. In sup-port of their respective contentions the learned Advocates for both sides cited decisions. Before glancing at them it will be profitable to examine the relevant rules in respect of impleading defendant in a suit.

9. To begin with, I may quote Order 1, rules 9 and 10(2) of the Code of Civil Procedure for easy reference. Order 1, rule 9 is as follows:-

"No suit shall be defeated by reason of the misjoinder or non joinder of parties, and the court may in every suit deal with the matter in controversy so far as regards the rights and interests of the parties actually before it."

Order 1, rule 10, sub-rule (2), is as follows:-

"The court may at any stage of the proceedings, either upon or without the application of either party and on such terms as may appear to the court to be just, order that the name of any party improperly joined, whether as plaintiff or defendant, be struck out, and that the name of any person who ought to have been joined, whether as plaintiff or defendant, or whose presence before the court may be necessary in order to enable the Court effectually and completely to adjudicate upon and settle all the questions involved in the suit, be added".

10. The plain construction of the provisions of Order 1, rule 9 and Order 1, rule 10 sub-rule (2) make it clear that the Court is required to deal with the matter in controversy so far as regards the rights and interests of the parties are actually before it and the name of any person whose presence before the court may be necessary in order to enable the Court to effectually and completely adjudicate upon and settle all the questions involved in the suit may be added either as plaintiffs or as defendants.

11. Therefore, it comes up for consideration whether the controversy regarding rights and interests of the plaintiffs petitioners and defendant opposite party Nos. 1-4 may be effectually and completely adjudicated upon and souled without impleading the defendant opposite party Nos. 5-7 in the suit. If such adjudication is possible without the defendant opposite party Nos. 5-7 they are not only not necessary parties but also not proper parties. The plaintiff petitioners have sought to enforce their right to retain the Post Office in the present premises on the basis of an agreement made between the plaintiff- petitioners and the defendant opposite party Nos. 1-4 in pursuance of which the plaintiff petitioners gifted on 20.3.84 the present premises for the Post Office. So far as the agreement between the defendant opposite party Nos. 5-7 and defendant opposite party Nos. 1-4 is concerned, it is distinct and separate, being of a subsequent date. So the rights, liabilities and obligations as between the plaintiff petitioners and the defendant opposite party Nos. 1-4 can be adequately and completely adjudicated upon in the absence of the defendant opposite party Nos. 5-7. As such adjudication is possible without impleading the defendants opposite party Nos. 5-7 as defendants in the instant suit, the impugned order is beyond the ambit of Order 1, rule 10 sub-rule (2) of the Code of Civil Procedure.

12. Mr. Dewan A.M.S. Zaman, the learned Advocate for the petitioners, cited before me as many as 6 decisions upon this aspect of the case. The first citation is 27 D.L.R. (AD) 129: Mst. Jahanara Begum versus A.L. Md. Shamsul Huq. In this decision a test has been laid down for finding whether or not certain parties are necessary or proper parties for adjudication of the case. Their Lordships have spelt out that one test which has been recognised as of great importance is that if in the absence of a party the court cannot give an effective remedy that party is a necessary party. Besides, in order that a party may be considered a necessary party two conditions must be satisfied, first, that there must be a right or some relief against him in respect of the matter involved in the suit and, secondly, that his presence should be necessary in order to enable the court effectively and completely to adjudicate upon and settle the question involved in the suit.

13. The next decision is in 31 D.L.R. page In this decision in the case of Safiuddin Ahmed Siddiqui Versus The Deputy Custodian, Enemy Property Management Board, it was held by learned brother Mr. Abdur Rahman Chowdhury, J. (as he then was) that a lessee holding his lease under E.P. (Lands and Buildings) Administration and Disposal Order, 1966, is not a necessary party in a suit for establishment of title between parties claiming title adversely to each other, because presence of lessees is not in any way necessary in order to effectively adjudicate upon and settle the question involved in the suit, particularly when the lessor, the Enemy Property Authority has been contesting the suit.

14. The third decision cited is 39 DLR (Appellate Division) 111, Md. Ayub versus Bangladesh represented by the Secretary, Ministry of Works and others. In this case the High Court Division impleaded two persons as respondent Nos. 6 and 7 in a Writ Petition on consideration that they were in possession of the property when the Writ petition was brought by the appellant challenging the validity of Government order declaring the disputed property as abandoned property and himself claiming it as the owner thereof. Their Lordships of the Appellate Division found that Rules 7 and 9 of the High Court Rules, which are akin to Order 1, rules 9 and 10 of the Code of Civil Procedure, conceived that only persons whose presence would be necessary for proper adjudication of a case should be impleaded as parties and none else. Their Lordships accordingly allowed respondent No. 6 to remain impleaded as respondent on the ground that according to the Writ Petition itself he was a tenant under the petitioner from before taking over of the property by the Government as abandoned. Their Lordships excluded the opposite party No.7 on the ground that he was inducted after taking over of the property by the respondent as Abandoned Property and his presence was not necessary or proper for adjudication of the case.

15. Besides these decisions of our Courts, the learned Advocate for petitioners has also cited the decision in A.I.R. 1960 (J & K) 67. In this decision in the case of Mst. Bindru versus Sadda Ram and others, it has been stated that a party cannot be added under Order 1, rule 10 of the Code in order to enable him to import an altogether new cause of action into the pending litigation. The addition of the new party must be consistent with the scope and the setting of the pending litigation. It has been further observed in this decision that it will be proper exercise of discretion to add a party if his presence is absolutely necessary to further the cause set up by a party to the pending suit. When dispute arises out of one contract or one transaction or one subject matter it will be proper to implead all the persons who are parties to the concerned contract or transaction.

<u>16. In the instant case we find that the defendant opposite party Nos. 5-7 were not a party to the contract between the plaintiff petitioners and the defendant opposite party Nos. 1-4 nor any such contract or rights of the opposite party Nos. 5-7 had been in-fringed upon. The contract between the plaintiff petitioners and the defendant opposite party Nos. 1-4 was admittedly of earlier date. So we find that the ratio decidendi of decisions in all the aforesaid cases is very definite and it only supports the view that the opposite party Nos. 5-7 do not deserve to be impleaded as defendants in the instant case.</u>

17. The learned Munsif has passed the order in a non-speaking manner. He did not at all state why or how the presence of the opposite party Nos. 5-7 was necessary for proper adjudication of the dispute between the plaintiff petitioners and the defendant opposite party Nos. 1-4. This is also a reason why the impugned order cannot stand.

<u>18. The next question that arises is whether this illegality has occasioned a failure of justice. This may be considered in the light of the decision reported in A.I.R. 1969 (Punjab) 57: Banarash Das Durga Prashad versus Panna Lal Ram Richpal Oswal and others, cited by the learned Advocate for the petitioners. In this decision it has been stated that a person may not be added as defendant merely because he would be incidentally affected by the judgment, for his case is not covered by the provision of Order 1, rule 10 sub-rule (2) of the Civil Procedure Code. There is no justification to add a party merely because that would save a third person from the expenses and botheration of a separate suit for adjudication of a collateral matter, which was not directly and substantively in issue in the suit in which he seeks intrusion. Furthermore, as a rule, the court should not add a person as a defendant in a suit when the plaintiff is opposed to such addition. The reason is that the plaintiff is the dominus litis. He is the master of his suit and he cannot be compelled to fight against a person against whom he does not wish to fight and against whom he does not claim any relief.</u>

<u>19. I am in respectful agreement with the above views expressed in the Banarash Durga Prashad Das case (Supra). I am of the view that unnecessary stress would be laid upon the plaintiff petitioners if their suit be allowed to be encumbered by addition of parties whose presence is not really necessary or proper for adjudication of the dispute between them and the opposite party Nos. 1-4. I find that the impugned order of the learned Munsif has occasioned a failure of justice and calls for interference.</u>

20. Mr. S.H. Md. Nurul Huda Jaigirdar, the learned Advocate for the opposite party Nos. 5, 6 and 7, has cited the decision in 36 DLR(HC) page 303: Abdul Hashem versus. Saleh Ahmed. In that case the petitioner was allowed to be added as defendant as proper party in a suit for Specific Performance of Contract as he was a subsequent purchaser of the suit property and he claimed to have purchased the land for value without notice of the contract sought to be enforced. The Court found that in view of section 27(b) of the Specific Relief Act, he had an interest to protect in the litigation, although he was not a party to the contract sought to be enforced. In other words, he had a vested right in the suit property subject to the agreement sought to be enforced. The decision, therefore, has no application to the facts and circumstances of the present case. The other decision placed before me by the learned Advocate for opposite party Nos. 5-7 is 30 DLR(SC) 244: Amal Kumar Maitra versus Md. Mashiur Rahman. Their Lordships of the Supreme Court have stated in that case that the revisional jurisdiction under section 115 of the Code of Civil Procedure is meant primarily for correcting errors made by the Subordinate Courts in the exercise of their jurisdiction and not those which are made in their discretion, unless the discretion is exercised fancifully or arbitrarily. Order 1, rule 10(2) of the Code of Civil Procedure empowers the court to add parties at any stage of the proceeding either upon or without application, who ought to have been joined whether as plaintiff or as defendant or whose presence before the court maybe necessary in order to enable the court effectually and completely to adjudicate upon and settle the questions involved in the suit. This power is discretionary and unless this power is exercised arbitrarily or fancifully it cannot be interfered with under section 115 of the Code of Civil Procedure. Even an improper or wrong exercise of discretion is not open to revision unless the order is contrary to legal principles governing the exercise of such discretion or the court has acted perversely.

21. It has been urged by the learned Advocate for opposite party Nos. 5-7 "that once the learned Munsif has decided to exercise his discretion to implead the opposite party Nos. 5-7 as defendants, even if the impugned order is not proper, interference with such order by this court in its revisional jurisdiction is not called for. But one may notice that in the cited decision itself it has been stated that the discretionary power exercised must not be contrary to legal principles governing the exercises of such discretion. The impugned order of the learned Munsif has been passed in clear violation of the principles emanating from the provisions of Order 1, rule 9 and rule 10(2) Id of the Code.

22. The learned Munsif has passed the impugned order arbitrarily and fancifully and not in accordance with the legal principles governing the exercise of his discretion in respect of addition of parties and as such it calls for interference. The impugned order be set aside and the Rule be made absolute without any order as to costs.

End.

caseno: Appeal from Original Order No. 227 of 1987
lawyer:
Appeal dismissed. Fazlul Karim, Advocate, with A.K.M. Nurunnabi Khan, Advocate. ----- For the Appellant. 
A.T.M. Monwaruddin, Advocate, with Shirin Nahar, Advocate. ------ For the Respondent No.1 
B. Hossain, Advocate. ------ For the Respondent No.2
parties:
Harun-or-Rashid Talukder ------ Appellant 
Vs. 
District Manager, Pubali Bank, Jamalpur ------ Respondent
full_judgment:
Mustafa Kamal, J:-This First Miscellaneous Appeal has been preferred under Article 36(1) of the Bangladesh Legal Practitioners and Bar Council Order, 1972 (P.O. No. 46 of 1972) against the judgment and order dated 5.7.87 passed by Tribunal No. II of the Bangladesh Bar Council in Tribunal Case No. 4 of 1983, finding the appellant guilty of gross professional misconduct under Clause (1) of Article 32 of P.O. No.46 of 1972 and suspending him for a period of 8 years and debarring him from practicing in any Court or authority in Bangladesh during the period of suspension with immediate effect. 

2. The proceeding before the Tribunal was initiated by P.W. 1 Md. Liakat Ali Khan, District Manager, Pubali Bank, Jamalpur Branch by addressing a letter of complaint on 6.6.83 to the President Bangladesh Bar Council, invoking legal action against the appellant on the facts stated therein. The appellant replied to the allegations by his letter dated 25.8.83 to the President, Bangladesh Bar Council. Thereafter the Bangladesh Bar Council proceeded against the appellant by instituting Case No.4 of 1983 before the Tribunal No. II. Issues were framed on 11.2.84. The appellant was also permitted to amend certain portions of his reply dated 25.8.83. 

3. In the inquiry before the said Tribunal, the complainant examined himself as P.W. 1 He also examined Mr. Sk. Nowsher Ali his immediate predecessor District Manager of Pubali Bank, Main Branch, Jamalpur as P.W. 2. The appellant examined himself as D.W. 1 and he also adduced 2 other witnesses D.Ws. 2 and 3. All the witnesses were crossexamined by the other side. Several documents were exhibited by both parties. 

4. The said Tribunal discussing the entire case and evidence on record by its judgment and order under appeal found the appellant guilty of gross professional misconduct and sentenced him as aforesaid. 

5.Thereafter the appellant has preferred the present appeal. 

6. A large part of the facts involved in this appeal is mutually admitted by the parties. Admittedly, the appellant Harun-or-Rashid, an Advocate of erstwhile Mymensingh bar and later of Jamalpur bar was the legal advisor of Pubali Bank and he used to file and conduct all suits of Jamalpur area in the Courts of Subordinate Judges at Mymensingh on behalf of the said bank. In 1979 upon the instruction of P.W. 2 Sk. Nowsher Ali who was the Manager of Pubali Bank, Main Branch, Jamalpur, the appellant filed in the 4th Court of Subordinate Judge, Mymensingh, Money Suit No. 3A/79 against one Kafiluddin Islami for recovery of a loan of Tk. 50,000/- which was obtained by Kafiluddin in 1975. The appellant obtained on 22.6.79 an ex parte order of attachment before judgment of the property mortgaged in the suit. Such properties were mentioned in the schedule to the application for attachment before judgment and the appellant knew the schedule very well, being the conducting lawyer of the bank. 

7. It is further admitted by both the parties that the said Money Suit No. 3A/79 was decreed exparte in favour of the Pubali Bank. Upon the instruction of the bank the appellant filed Money Execution Case No.2 of 1980 of the 4th Court of Subordinate Judge, Mymensingh. Jamalpur was made a district and in December, 1980 the District judge's Court at Jamalpur started functioning. The appellant shifted his place of practice from Mymensingh to Jamalpur shortly thereafter. The records of the said execution case were sent to Jamalpur and the Money Execution Case was re-numbered as Money Execution Case No. 4 of the Court of Subordinate Judge, Jamalpur. 

8. Thereafter the story of the complainant and the appellant differs. The complainant contends that during the pendency of Money Execution Case No.4 of 1982 in which the petitioner bank prayed for realisation of the decrial amount by sale of the attached property, namely, plot No. 1489 of mouza Chandra comprising an area of 1.04 acre and plot No. 1082 of mouza Shinghajani measuring 10 acre, the appellant being the engaged lawyer of the bank and knowing full well that the above-mentioned properly was the subject matter of the aforesaid execution case, purchased the said land in his own name and in the name of his wife and children and also in the benami of his cousin D.W. 2 Md. Mahfuzul Hoq Talukdcr by 4 registered kabalas dated 25.8.81, Ext.3, 3(1), 3(2) and 3(3). When the bank came to know of this transaction the complainant P.W. 1 requested the appellant to return the brief. He returned the case file P.W. 1 also requested the appellant to pay up the bank's dues assuring that in such an event the bank will not take any legal action against the appellant. But the appellant did not comply with that request. Thereafter a legal notice was served on the appellant demanding the bank's money within a certain period failing which the matter would be referred to the Bar Council [or professional misconduct. The appellant received the notice, but did not reply. The bank has been affected by the purchase in question. The complainant prayed that suitable action be taken against the appellant for gross professional misconduct. It was further stated by the complainant in his evidence that the schedule-property of the execution case is under the occupation of the appellant. He has started construction thereon and has since started his professional activities therefrom by opening his chamber thereon. He is also residing there with his family. 

9. It is admitted by the appellant that by 5 different registered deeds dated 25.8.81 the appellant has purchased part of the suit property under attachment in his name and in the names of his wife and children. D.W.2 Md. Mahfuzul Hoq Talukder, his cousin, is the co-purchaser of the-remaining part of the suit property.
