Since purchase he and D.W. 2 have possessed the suit property under attachment. 7 1/ 2 acres of land covered by the said sale deeds are situated at Jamalpur town and the appellant has himself stated that he has already constructed puce buildings thereon. His explanation is that P.W. 2 Sk. Nowsher Ali who was manager of Pubali Bank, Main Branch, Jamalpur from 30.12.74 to 13.8.81 made an unauthorised advance of Tk. 50,000/- to the defendant Kafiluddin Islami in 1975. He obtained an equitable mortgage of the suit property under attachment from Kafiluddin Islami, as security for the loan, but there was no registration of the mortgage. When Jamalpur was made a separate district and the District Judge's Court started functioning at Jamalpur, the appellant shifted his practice from Mymensingh to Jamalpur. P.W.2 Sk. Nowsher Ali gave out in June 1981 that he was going to be transferred from Jamalpur. P.W. 2 pressed the appellant hard for an early disposal of the aforesaid money execution case. At about this time defendant Kafiluddin was also trying to sell out the suit property under attachment to third parties. Successive signboards affixed upon the suit property stating that the same was under attachment were mysteriously disappearing for which P.W.2 sought police help. P.W.2 came to an understanding with defendant Kafiluddin that the suit properly would be sold for realisation of bank's dues. P.W.2 requested the appellant to purchase the suit property, but he declined stating that a lawyer was under a legal disability to purchase the same. Besides, the appellant had no fund to buy the property. The appellant was given the proposal that he was required to pay Tk. 75,000/-, the bank's dues, to the bank by installment. He needed to pay defendant Kafiluddin the balance of the consideration money. At this stage the appellant agreed to purchase the suit property for Tk. 10,05,00/- out of which the bank's claim was Tk.80,000/- only and the appellant actually paid Tk. 30,000/- only to defendant Kafiluddin. The appellant did not pay any money to the bank at the time of purchase. Uptil now he has not paid even a single penny to the bank. It is also the case of the appellant that on the basis of mutual agreement between the parties. Tk. 5000/- was remitted by the bank in favour of defendant Kafiluddin at the instance of P.W. 2 Nowsher Ali. As the appellant had no sufficient funds to buy the suit property, he requested his cousin D.W. 2 Mahfuzul Hoq Talukder to join him to purchasing the suit property. P.W. 2 Nowsher Ali came to the chamber of the appellant many times in connection with the above claim of the bank. Mr. Nowsher Ali was transferred and he made over charge to his successor P.W. 1 Liakat Ali on 13.8.81. The new manager was also in the know of the matter. The appellant was informed by a letter dated 18.9.81 that he was no longer the legal advisor of the bank and that Mr. Amjad Hossain, another Advocate, replaced him. After making representations to the Managing Director of the bank and having received no reply thereto the appellant made over charge to the said Mr. Amjad Hossain. The appellant came to know of the demand of the bank by legal notice dated 2.11.82. According to the appellant himself he has filed as many as 3 applications under Order 21 Rule 58 C.P.C. for being added as a party to the aforesaid execution case, 2 which were rejected and the last one of which is still pending. He has also stated in his reply to the allegations of the complainant that he filed O.C. Suit No. 71/83 on 26.6.83 in the Court of Subordinate Judge, Jamalpur, for a declaration that the Pubali Bank had no claim on him with respect to the land of the aforesaid money execution case. 

10. Mr. Fazlul Karim, learned Advocate for the appellant has based his submissions solely and completely on the aforesaid story of the appellant and has soulful argue, in the first place, that the appellant having not acquired "an interest" adverse to the bank in the property involved in the execution case, is not guilty of professional misconduct. He has argued secondly that it is under circumstances of a peculiar nature that the appellant had merely exercised an ill judgment. He became the victim of an inducement and was merely used as a pawn by the outgoing manager P.W. 2 SK. Nowsher Ali. The Tribunal did not notice the effect of the inducement made by P.W. 2 Nowsher Ali. Lastly, Mr. Fazlul Karim submits, the facts and circumstances of the case do not warrant imposition of a harsh sentence of suspension from practice for 8 years. At best, the appellant can be reprimanded. 

11. To appreciate the first point made by Mr. Fazlul Karim it is necessary to set down Clause (I) of Chapter II entitled "Conduct with regard to clients" occurring in the "Canons of professional Conduct and Etiquette" prepared by the Bangladesh Bar Council:- 

"(I) An Advocate shall not acquire an interest adverse to a client in the property or interest involved in the case." 

12. Mr. Fazlul Karim submits that an Advocate cannot acquire an interest adverse to his client in the property until and unless by the transaction in question he acquires a title to the property. Both Section 64 and Order 21 Rule 64 C.P.C. make It quite clear that if a person purchases a property under attachment without permission from the Court then the whole transaction is void. The attached properly is liable to sale notwithstanding the unauthorised purchase. Therefore, the bank has sustained no loss and has incurred no disability at all by the appellant's purchase of the suit property. It's remedy of sale of the suit property under attachment IS still available, notwithstanding the appellant's purchase. Mr. Fazlul Karim argues that when the appellant has thus acquired no title to the suit property under attachment by viture of Section 64 c.P.c. then it cannot be said that he has acquired any interest adverse to the bank in the property. He is, therefore, not guilty of any professional misconduct. Specially Clause (I) of Chapter II is inapplicable to him. 

13. It is difficult to uphold the aforesaid contention of Mr. Fazlul Karim. A client does not always have a proprietary interest in the suit property. He may have a possessory interest, a contingent interest and even a trespasser's interest in the suit property. It is enough to attract the mischief of Clause(l) of Chapter II if the Advocate engaged by the client transgresses upon any such interest held by the client. In the present case the bank's interest in the suit property under attachment is total. It has an interest in the right, title and possession of the suit property. Upon his own admission the appellant sought to create a title in him by purchasing the suit property admittedly under attachment at a time when he was the engaged Advocate of the bank to conduct the execution case. He admits that he has not only taken possession of the suit property under attachment but has also constructed a building thereon. To acquire an interest adverse to the bank in the instant case it is not necessary that the appellant should acquire a valid title to the suit property. It is enough that he has created several documents of title in his favour and has entered into possession of the suit property. He has thereby prejudiced the interest of the bank in the suit property. On his own admission he has filed as many as 3 applications, one of which is pending, for being added as a third party to the execution case. He has thus sought to place himself in the shoes of defendant Kafiluddin. The bank is thus obliged to prosecute the execution case not only against defendant Kafiluddin but also against the bank's own lawyer, the appellant, who is claiming an interest in the suit property, valid or otherwise. It is because of the appellant's repeated efforts to get himself added as a third party in the execution proceedings that the execution proceedings have been delayed. The appellant has thus compromised his position as a conducting lawyer of the case. Not only that, he has himself stated in his reply to the complainant's allegation (at page 42 of the paper book) that on 26.6.83 he has filed O.C. Suit No. 71/83 in the Court of Subordinate Judge, Jamalpur, praying that the bank has no claim upon him with respect to the land of Money Execution Case No. 4/82 pending in that Court. Apart from proceeding against defendant Kafiluddin the bank is now saddled with the additional burden of facing and meeting the appellant's pleas and submissions. It is absolutely immaterial whether by virtue of Ext. 3 series the appellant has acquired a valid title to the suit property under attachment or not. This issue will be decided in an appropriate forum by the concerned parties. For the purpose of disposing of this professional misconduct case the Tribunal will only see the various kinds of interest that a client has over the property or interest involved in the case and as to whether the Advocate concerned has acquired any of the interests adverse to the client. The facts arc palpably clear and we have no manner of doubt that the Tribunal has come to the correct conclusion that the appellant in purchasing the suit property under attachment and in taking possession thereof and constructing a building thereon has definitely acquired an interest adverse to the bank in the suit property. 

14. Of course Mr. Fazlul Karim next submits that if the appellant has been able to show that everything was done in the interest of the bank as part of a package with the knowledge and with the blessing of the local manager, then his action may be branded as reprehensible, but he cannot be saddled with the delinquency of professional misconduct. He further submits that the appellant has exercised a mere ill judgment and that the circumstances were such that he was induced to exercise such an ill judgment without realising the consequence thereof. 

15. The appellant contends that the loan given to defendant Kafiluddin was an unauthorised advance. There was no registered deed of mortgage of the suit property. P.W. 2 Sk. Nowsher Ali was nervous about this particular case because the advance money would be realised from him when he would leave the station if it still remained unpaid. So he was in a hurry to realise the loan and it was on his initiative that a tripartite agreement was made between him, the appellant and defendant Kafiluddin providing that the property would be purchased by the appellant for only Tk. 1,05,000/- out of which defendant Kafiluddin would be paid only Tk. 30,000/-. The appellant would pay to the bank Tk. 80,000/- by installments. 

16. Of course the appellant as D.W. I has-asserted those facts in his evidence. P.W. 1 and P.W. 2 were given the suggestion in their cross-examination that the advances made to defendant Kafiluddin were unauthorized and that the appellant purchased the suit property by way of an arrangement. They denied the same. P.W. 2 Nowsher Ali on the contrary has deposed that he was given two promotions after his transfer from Jamalpur. There is absolutely no written agreement between the appellant, P.W. 2 Sk. Nowsher Ali and defendant Kaflluddin. There is not a single witness other than D.W. 1 who has deposed a word about the talk that the appellant allegedly had with P.W. 2 Sk. Now sheer All and defendant Kafiluddin. There is no corroborative evidence regarding the exact terms of the so-called tripartite agreement. D.W. 2 Mahfuzul Hoq Talukder, admittedly a cousin of the appellant and admittedly a co-purchaser of the suit property under attachment, has of course wanted to say that in August, 1981 he was taken to the house of the appellant by defendant Kafiluddin and there he found bank manager P.W. 2 Sk, Nowsher Ali. There D.W. 2 learnt that the land of Kafiluddin was mortgaged with the bank and that Kafiluddin wanted to sell the same. D.W. 2 further stated that manager P.W. 2 Sk. Nowsher Ali then proposed to the appellant and D.W. 2 that they may purchase the property in question under attachment and for that they were not required to pay the bank at that time. They could pay the bank later on by installments. Consequently they purchased the suit property. D.W. 2 purchased 50% of the agricultural land while the rest of the property was purchased by the appellant. 

17. It is in the evidence of the appellant deposing as D.W. 1 that the proposal to purchase the suit property was made to the appellant alone, but the appellant declined on the ground that as a lawyer he was under a legal disability to purchase the same. D.W. 1 has further stated that he agreed to purchase the suit property while it was suggested to him that he need not pay the bank's money all at a time. He could, pay by installments. He further said he had no sufficient fund. So he requested his cousin D.W. 2 to join them in purchasing the suit property. D.W. 1 nowhere makes out a case that in August, 1981 D.W. 2 was taken to the house of the appellant by defendant Kafiluddin and P.W. 2 Sk. Nowsher Ali was present there. D.W. 1 nowhere stated that on that occasion D.W. 2 came to know about the mortgaged property. It is nowhere in his evidence that P.W. 2 Sk. Nowsher Ali proposed to D.W. 1 and D.W. 2 jointly that they should purchase the property under attachment. D.W. 1 obviously was telling one story and D.W. 2 another. No one corroborates the other. Each one is telling a different story.

18. The appellant has finally introduced D.W. 3 A.T.M. Nurul Hossain who was a retired railway guard, then a teacher in a High School. He wanted to say that he found P.W. 2 Sk. Nowsher Ali in the chamber of the appellant in July 1981 when the manager requested the appellant to purchase a bank property, but the appellant refused. 

19. This witness is a purely chance witness. D.W. 1 nowhere says that D.W. 3 was present when P.W. 2 made him the offer. He cannot be accepted as a corroborating witness. Besides, he had no account in the Pubali Bank and therefore it is highly unlikely that he even knew the manager of the bank. It was suggested to him that he was deposing falsely at the instance of the appellant, which he denied, but from the nature of his deposition we have no doubt in our mind that he was brought in as an obliging witness for the appellant. 

20. Besides, it is in the evidence of P.W. 2 Sk. Nowsher Ali that he was the Manager of Pubali Bank, Main Branch, Jamalpur from 30.12.74 to 13.8.81 P.W. 1 also says in his evidence that he joined Jamalpur Branch on 6.8.81 and took over charge of the branch on 13.8.81. The registered sale deeds of the suit property are dated 25.8.81, i.e. after P.W. 2 handed over charge to P.W. 1. D.W. 2 says in cross-examination that 10/12 days after the silting in the house of the appellant the sale deeds were registered. This means that P.W. 2 finalized the arrangement with the appellant when he was no longer the manager and had already handed over charge to P.W. 2. It is very hard to believe such a story. 

21. We find no material whatsoever that the advance made to defendant Kafiluddin was an unauthorised advance. We find no reason why P.W. 2 Sk. Nowsher Ali should be nervous about the advance before his departure from Jamalpur. He had made an advance to Kafiluddin in 1975. Kafiluddin failed to repay the loan. He instituted the money suit in 1979. He obtained ancabaret decree therein. The suit property was already under attachment before judgment. He has instituted a money execution case. When he left Jamalpur the position was that the suit property could be sold in the execution case at any time on the prayer of the bank. P.W. 2 Sk. Nowsher Ali had a perfect explanation both in respect of the loan and in respect of the steps he had taken for realising the loan. He had no compulsion to enter into a dubious verbal arrangement with the appellant for sale of the suit property. When he was enjoying the protection of a full-proof money execution case in his favour, he will be a fool indeed to enter into a verbal arrangement with the appellant and leave Jamalpur with not a single penny as actual recovery from that questionable transaction. Besides, he left no documents for his successor to follow up. We find that this is a completely cock and bull story invented by the appellant to save his skin. There were absolutely no compelling circumstances whatsoever necessitating the transfer of the suit property in favour of the appellant and his family members. We are quite clear in our mind from the evidence on record that the appellant wanted to strike a bargain in his favour by presenting the bank with a fait accompli. As soon as P.W.2Ieft Jamalpur he purchased the suit property by registered deeds, thinking that the incoming manager P.W.l will not know much about the matter. 

22. His next defence is that the incoming manager P.W. 1 Liakat Ali in his bid to induct his distant relation Mr. Amjad Hossain Advocate as the legal adviser of Pubali Bank concocted a false story against the appellant and ultimately Mr. Amjad Hossain succeeded the appellant as the legal advisor of Pubali Bank, Jamalpur Branch. This is an another flight of imagination on the part of the appellant. Pubali Bank, Jamalpur Branch, had only the present execution case on its file. Mr. Amjad Hossain was asked to conduct only this case in place of the appellant after the questionable transaction came to the knowledge of the bank. Mr. Amjad Hossain was not a: recipient of a huge favour from the bank. The sale deeds in question were executed and registered 15 days after P.W. 2 Sk. Nowshaer Ali handed over charge. There is absolutely no evidence that his successor P.W. 1 Liakat Ali was also in the know of this alleged arrangement and in any case there is absolutely no evidence that P.W. 1 was in any way connected with the execution and registration of the sale deeds Ext. 3 series. There is also no evidence that Kafiluddin was allowed a remission of interest to the extent of Tk. 5,000/- because of the so-called arrangement. The evidence is that he was offered the remission provided he paid the bank's dues all at a time. He did not pay. 

23. The main planks of the appellant's various defense’s have thus fallen through like a house of cards. 

24. Finally, it has been submitted by Mr. Fazlul Karim that the Tribunal ought not have inflicted a severe punishment by way of suspending the appellant from practicing for 8 years because, in his submission, the appellant's guilt, if any, was merely one of wrongful exercise of discretion which could have been appropriately corrected by a reprimand. 

25. We have in details set out the facts, circumstances and evidence recorded in the case. We have no manner of hesitation in concurring with the Tribunal that "the purchase of the property in question by the opposite party (appellant) in his own name and in the names of his wife, children and cousin against the interest of the bank, whose cause he was representing, possession of the property in question by the opposite party (appellant), construction of building in a portion of the suit property, repeated attempts by him to block the progress of the money execution case in question are the clearest manifestations of the unholy desire of the opposite party (appellant) to acquire the attached property in question by any means, fair or foul, and in doing so he has clearly acted against the interest of his client, acting against his professional pledge and responsibility. Such course of action, indeed, deserves highest condemnation and calls for deterrent punishment". 

26. Article 32(1) of P.O. No. 46 of 1972 provides as follows: - 

"(1) An Advocate on the roll may, in the manner hereinafter provided be reprimanded, suspended or removed from practice if he is found guilty of professional or other misconduct." 

27. Hence reprimand is the mildest punishment that can be meted out to an Advocate found guilty of professional or other misconduct. Suspension from practice is a sentence of a higher degree but it really belongs to the intermediate class of punishment. Removal from practice is the ultimate punishment that can be meted out to a delinquent Advocate. Considering that the appellant was of fairly advanced age and was in bruised health the Tribunal decided to award him the intermediate punishment of suspension from practice for 8 years. In the facts and circumstances of the case we do not think that the Tribunal misjudged the punishment that is appropriate in the case. The Tribunal acted completely within its discretion in not awarding the severest sentence in view of some extenuating circumstances. We do not find any reason why the intermediate punishment should now be relegated to the softest one. All the defense’s of the appellant have been proved to be completely cooked up. From the moment he received the legal notice from the bank up to the present moment his attitude is one of defiance, contest and challenge. He has no regrets, no remorse, no repentance either. He has chalked out a path of destructive self-justification. He must pay for his defiance. We find no extenuating circumstances whatsoever to reduce the sentence. 

28. In the result the appeal is dismissed but without any order as to costs. 

Md. Mozammel Hoque, J. I agree.

End.

caseno:
Civil Revision No. 3375 of 1991 (Dhaka)
Civil Revision No. 114 of 1986 (Barisal)
lawyer:
Abdul Quayum with AKM Zahirul Huq, Advocates ----- For the Petitioner
Shahidul Alam Chowdhury, Advocate ----- For the Opposite Parties.
parties:
Laxmi Kama Roy ----- Petitioner
Vs.
Upazila Nirbahi Officer and another ----- Opposite Parties
full_judgment:
This Rule was issued directing the opposite parties to show cause as to why the Judgment and Decree passed by the learned District Judge, Bansal, in Title Appeal No. 112 of 1985 reversing the Judgement and Decree passed by the learned Upazila Munsif, Agailjhara, in Title Suit No. 4 of 1984 (Previously TS No. 60 of 1981) should not be set aside.

2. Plaintiff is the petitioner before this Court It was his short case that the suit land was leased out to the plaintiff and one Azahar Bahadur by the owners of the property in 1351 BS on receiving salami and also at a rental of Taka 2.25 by issuing Amaldari and Dakhilas and delivered possession to the plaintiff and others. Since 1351 BS the plaintiff was in peaceful possession of Ka schedule land by residing in the homestead portion, planting trees in the garden portion and cultivating the same land of the schedule on paying rent to the landlord continuously and without any interruption from any quarter. Though the plaintiff took settlement of the suit land in the year 1351 BS in the SA record his name was not recorded and for correction of record of right the plaintiff filed Title Suit No. 258 of 1976 in the Court of Munsif, Barisal and obtained a compromise decree on 14.5.76. Thereafter the plaintiff filed an application under section 54 of the State Acquisition and Tenancy Act which was registered as Mutation Case No. 193G/75-76 in the Office of the Circle Officer (Rev) Gournadi and accordingly, a separate khatian was opened with regard to Ka schedule land. Since then he has been paying rent to the Government. The land is not enlisted as Vested and Non-resident property. It is alleged that on the basis of a false report from the Tahsildar, the Sub-Divisional Officer, Sadar, (North) Barisal started the impugned VP Case No. 142 of 1980 and was also threatening to lease out the suit property to others by dispossessing the plaintiff from there. The plaintiff had no knowledge about the aforesaid VP Case and he came to learn it on 21.1.81 and that is why the plaintiff instituted the suit for declaration that the VP Case No. 142 of 1980 is illegal, collusive, fraudulent and without jurisdiction and also for permanent injunction restraining the defendants from leasing out the suit property to anybody else.

3. The defendant No. 1, Sub-Divisional Officer (Sadar) North, Barisal, filed written statement denying the allegations made in the plaint. It is further stated in the written statement that the suit was not maintainable in the present form and manner. The story of lease in 1351 BS is false and the plaintiff never took lease of the land from the recorded tenant and possessed Ka schedule land. Specific defence of the defendants is that the original recorded owner of the suit property left the country before 1965 and as such the property vested in the Government as Enemy Property, now vested property, and the Assistant Custodian leased out the same to one Bhuban Chandra Roy in lease Case No. 142 of 1980 who had been possessing the same. The suit was originally filed in the 2nd Court of Munsif, Barisal Sadar and numbered as Title Suit No. 60 of 1981. Thereafter it was transferred to the court of the learned Assistant Judge, Agailjhara Upazila, and renumbered as Title Suit No.4 of 1984 the Upazila Nirbahi Officer Agailjhara was substituted as defendant No. 1 who contested the suit upon the written statement filed by previous defendant No.1, the Sub-Divisional Officer.

4. In this case both the parties adduced evidence both oral and documentary. After hearing the parties and perusing materials on record the trial Court decreed the suit in favour of the plaintiff by his Judgment dated 9.7.85. Against the aforesaid Judgment and Decree the defendant No. 1 preferred appeal before the learned District Judge, Bakerganj, in Ti tie Appeal No. 112 of 1985. The learned District Judge, Bakerganj, by his judgment and decree dated 31.5.86, allowed the appeal reversing the Judgment and Decree of the trial Court and dismissing the suit. Being aggrieved by the aforesaid Judgment and Decree of the learned District Judge, Bakerganj the plaintiff-petitioner preferred this revisional application and obtained the present Rule.

<u>5. At the very outset it has drawn my attention in this case as to whether the institution of the VP Case No. 142 of 1980 was maintainable in the eye of law. The Defence of Pakistan Ordinance and Rules came in the year 1965. The Defence of Pakistan Ordinance and Rules were repealed in the year 1969, but by Ordinance No. 1 of 1969 promulgated by the then Central Government of Pakistan, some of the provisions of the Defence of Pakistan Rules were kept alive and continued. Thereafter by Act No XLV of 1974, the Ordinance No. 1 of 1969 was repealed on 23.3.74. After the repeal of Ordnance No. 1 of 1969 in 1974 whether any proceeding under the said Ordinance and Rules could be started. Admittedly, the present Vested Property case was started in the year 1980. Unfortunately, this point was neither raised by the learned Advocate for the plaintiff, nor the learned Judges had taken notice of the law which was repealed in the year 1974. This point was not specifically agitated and no issue was framed on it. Mr. Abdul Quayum, the learned Advocate appearing for the petitioner, submits that since it is a question of law it can be agitated in this Court at this revisional stage. In this case Mr. Quayum has referred to the case of Nittya Gopal Roy Barman Vs Pran Gopal Nandi and others, 32 DLR 11. In the aforesaid Judgment it is categorically held by his Lordship that after repeal of the Ordinance No. 1 of 1969 by Act No. XLV of 1974 on 23.3.74 the authority was not competent to start such vested property proceeding in the eye of law. In the aforesaid Judgment his Lordship held as follows:</u>

<u>"Mere claim of the Assistant Custodian that the property of the deceased testator is an enemy property in respect of which an enemy property 'case was started in 1978 is not sufficient for coming to a conclusion that the property is an enemy property".</u>

<u>I fully agree with the view of his Lordship expressed in the aforesaid decision. Since the law on Enemy Property itself died with the repeal of Ordinance 1 of 1969 on 23.3.74 by Act XLV of 1974, no further vested property case can be started thereafter on the basis of the law which is already dead. So I find that the starting of the vested property case No. 142 of 1980 in the year 1980 is absolutely without jurisdiction and has no legal basis at all.</u>

6. Learned Advocate appearing for the opposite parties submits that the present case comes within the saving clause as provided in section 3 of Act XL V of 1974. but in support of such contention the learned Advocate failed to produce any papers whatsoever in order to show that such a property assumed the character of Enemy Property or any proceeding was started in respect of this property under the vested properties Law before repeal of Ordinance No. 1 of 1969. I have perused the papers and documents filed in this case and I am of the view that the instant case does not come within the saving clause of section 3 of Act XLV of 1974. So, the contention of the learned Advocate does not find any merit in the case.

7. Let me consider the suit on merit. The lower Appellate Court found that the plaintiff failed to produce any document to show that whether the plaintiff took lease of it in the year 1351 BS. Mr. Quayum submits that Ext. 3 and Ext. 4 solen am a were filed in Title Suit No. 256 of 1976. He submits that for some reason the plaintiff could not produce lease document and dakhilas of the year 1351 BS but the fact remains that since his name was not recorded in the SA record he filed the suit for correction vide Title Suit No. 258 of 1976 which was decreed on compromise on 14.5.76. Thereafter he started a Mutation Case under section 54 of the SAT Act and separate khatian was opened in his name in respect of Ka schedule land. Since then he has been paying rent to the Government. Mr. Quayum submits that had the suit property been, enlisted as enemy property, his name would not have been recorded in the SA record of right in the aforesaid Mutation Case and his rents could not be accepted by the Government. Mr. Quayum submits that in the year 1976 the aforesaid Title Suit was instituted but the suit property was enlisted as enemy property in 1980. I find substance in the contention of Mr. Quayum. Mr. Quayum submits that on 14.5.76 compromise decree was passed in Title Suit No. 258 of 1976 and in pursuance of the aforesaid decree plaintiff mutated his name in the SA record of right and had been paying rent to the Government regularly. Rightly or wrongly a decree was passed in the year 1976 when the property was not shown listed as enemy property. The aforesaid compromise decree still stands valid. Unless and until a decree of a court is set aside by a competent court it will remain as a valid decree.

8. Mr. Quayum further submits that once the Government allowed the plaintiff to record his name in the SA record of right and started taking regular rent from the plaintiff, the Government is estopped from declaring the suit property as enemy property. I find substance in the above contention of Mr. Quayum. In this view of the matter I find that since a decree is passed in Title Suit, No. 258 of 1976 which still stands good and lias not yet been set aside by any competent court the plaintiff is entitled to get benefit of the aforesaid decree.

9. The lower Appellate Court found fault with the plaintiff as in the present suit the plaintiff did not implead the Government as a party. The lower Appellate Court found that the Government was a necessary party under President's Order 142 of 1972 under Article 6 clause A and since mandatory provision of aforesaid President's Order was not complied with the present suit was not maintainable. In this respect Mr. Quayum has referred to President's Order 142 of 1972 and along with it he has referred to the case of Fakir Chand Mia being dead his heirs and legal representatives Asadunnessa and others Vs. Quamaruzzaman and others, 26 DLR 233. In the aforesaid decision a Division Bench of this Court held as follows:

"20. The preamble of President's Order No142 of 1972 which has been called the Bangladesh Transfer of Immovable Property (Temporary Provisions) Order, 1972 runs as follows:

"Whereas it is expedient to make provisions for restricting the transfer of immovable property in Bangladesh in public interest. "The Article 6 of the said Order is to the following effect:

"No person shall without joining the Government which shall be a necessary party, file or proceed with any suit-.

(a) for the specific performance of any contract relating to the transfer of any immovable property or for declaration of title to or assertion of ownership of any such property.

(b) for enforcement of mortgage securing in relation to any immovable property except where the mortgagee is the Government or a local authority or a schedule bank or a statutory Corporation or a Co-operative Society or (c) for partition of immovable property where total area of the property involved exceeds one hundred standard "big has."

Now, the question is whether suit for declaration of title or assertion of ownership as is contemplated in clause (a) of the said Article is the kind of suit out of which the present appeal arises. The obvious object of the legislation as found in the preamble of the Order and also in its substantive provisions appears to be the prevention of certain transfers of immoveable property in derogation of some legislative enactments. If we keep this dominant purpose of the enactment in view, it will be clear that the words "any such property" as used in clause (a) of the Article will not be referable to any immovable property, but to any immovable property which was the subject matter of a contract relating to transfer. To interpret this provision in any other way so as to make it applicable to any suit for declaration of title to or assertion of ownership of any immovable property does not appear to be reasonable at all because that will make this provision absolutely pointless and needlessly harassing. We are, therefore, of the opinion that the provision of Article 6 of the President's Order No. 142 of 1972 has no application to the present case and so the Government of Bangladesh is not a necessary party in this case."

<u>10. In the aforesaid decision the self-same question arose as to whether in a suit for declaration of title Government is a necessary party under President's Order 142 of 1972. From the aforesaid decision it appears that their Lordships are of the view that provision of Article 6 of President's Order 142 of 1972 has no application to the case of any suit for declaration of title. The aforesaid provision was only applicable in a suit for specific performance of contract relating to transfer of any immovable property or for declaration of title or assertion of ownership of any such property regarding such transfer. Their Lordships are of the view that when the title in respect of some property in a suit for specific performance of contract is to be determined, the government is a necessary party. I am of the view that plaintiff prayed in the present suit for a declaration that the VP Case No. 142 of 1980 was illegal and inoperative and without jurisdiction and for permanent injunction restraining the defendants from leasing out the suit property to any person. So, the lower Appellate Court committed an error of law in holding that the present suit is not maintainable inasmuch as the government was not impleaded as a party as per provision of President's Order 142 of 1972. I hold that in the present suit Govt. is not a necessary party, as it does not involve any question of title relating to a suit for specific performance of contract.</u>

11. Mr. Quayum further submits that no papers or documents whatsoever as regards declaration and/or treating the suit property as enemy property were produced before Court at any stage of the proceeding. He submits that no papers whatsoever were produced by the defendant before Court showing that the suit property was ever treated as enemy property or a notice was issued and investigation was started to ascertain as to whether the present property can be treated as enemy property. Only in the year 1980 they started the aforesaid VP Case No. 142 of 1980. I have gone through the records of the case to see as to how, when and why this property was treated as enemy property. Since no papers or documents as regards alleged proceeding were produced before Court, I am of the view that in fact there is no proceeding in respect of the suit property till the time when the vested law was repealed in 1974. For the first time in 1980 the defendants started vested property case without any basis or material whatsoever. The lower Appellate Court has considered oral evidence of PW s and DWs. After considering the evidence of DWs, the lower Appellate Court solely relied upon some interested witnesses and came to a finding that the property is vested property. Such finding cannot be accepted in law without record of VP Case. Just on the basis of some oral evidence of some interested persons this property cannot be treated as enemy property after 1974 when the law itself ceased to exist. It is their case that before 1965 the owner of the suit land left this country for India and as such after 1965 the property stood vested in the Assistant Custodian as enemy property. This omnibus stand of the defendants without any materials and papers cannot be accepted.

12. Mr. Shahidul Islam Chowdhury, the learned Advocate appearing for the opposite parties, submits that the property in question vested in the Assistant Custodian in the year 1965. Some properties were detected and some were not. Since this property was not detected as vested property before 1980, Government started VP Case in 1980 as soon as it was detected. Before 1965 the owner of the suit land left for India and by operation of law in December, 1965 all such properties stood vested in the Assistant Custodian. Such argument of Mr. Shahidul Islam Chowdhury cannot be accepted. He failed to produce any papers as regards character of this property before or after 1965. Since the Vested Property law was repealed in 1974, such an argument is absolutely an absurd one for a case which was started in the year 1980. Without materials or basis whatsoever such a finding of the lower Appellate Court arrived at on the depositions of DWs cannot be entertained at all inasmuch as after 1974 a property can be treated as vested property only if it comes within the purview of saving section 3 of Act XLV of 1974 and in no other case.

13. Considering the facts and circumstances of the case and my discussions above, I hold that the lower Appellate Court committed an error of law in its decision resulting in an error occasioning failure of justice in setting aside the judgment and decree of the trial Court and as such the judgment and decree of the Lower Appellate Court cannot be sustained in law.

14. In the result, this Rule is made absolute without any order as to cost and the Judgment and Decree passed by the learned District Judge, Bakerganj in Title Appeal No. 112 of 1985 are hereby set aside and those of the trial Court are hereby affirmed.

Send down the lower courts record immediately.

End.

caseno: Appeal from Appellate Decree No. 588 of 1966.
lawyer:
B.N. Chowdhury -------- For the Appellant.
B.B. Roy Chowdhury -------- For the Respondent.
parties:
Shefalika Debi -------- Appellant   
VS
Belarani Debi and ors -------- Respondents.
full_judgment:
This Second Appeal has been preferred by the plaintiff against a judgment of reversal. Plaintiff is the wife of one Narendra. Defendant No. 1 who contested the suit is the widow of Jitendra, a younger brother of Narendre. The suit was one for declaration of title and recovery of possession of the suit land measuring 3.79 acres of C.S. Khatian No. 315 of Moues Jibanpur. According to the plaintiff, an area of land measuring 6.63 acres appertaining to that Khatian was held in joie right by Haridas Biswas under the landlord Harendra Kishore Roy Chowdhury. Haridas died leaving 5 sons, Nareudra, Upendra Jitendra, Suradas and Jatindra. Some persons purchased some land out of tins khatian. For arrears of rent the entire khatiaa comprising of 6.63 acres of land was auction-sold. All the 5 brothers and the part-purchasers were judgment-debtors. The plaintiff auction-chased the entire khatian of 0.03 acres of land with her money on 2.10.00 and took delivery of possession through Court on 30.11.50. Out of that auction-purchased land of 6.63 acres, 3.79 acres is the suit land. Plaintiff possessed the suit land and cultivated it sometimes by hired labourers and sometimes through bargadars. Plaintiff settled in korfa right 21½ decimals of her auction-purchased land to one Mohanta Majhi. In Baisakh, 1368 B.S. the defendants without any right, title, interest or previous possession dispossessed this plaintiff from the suit land.

2. Defendant No. 1 contesting the suit contended that the plaintiff never auction purchased the suit land nor took delivery of possession. She had no capacity to purchase the property. She is only a benamdar of her husband Narendra. Narendra was a cripple from birth. He was deprived from his father's property according to Hindu Law and he lived separately in mess and property from the very beginning. With an eye to grabbing paternal property Narendra has caused the auction-sale in conspiracy with others. Except the husband of the plaintiff the 4 sons of Haridas were in ejmali possession of the suit land after the death of Haridas. Suradas died leaving son Nihar. Jatindra moves from place to place and is callous to worldly affairs. Upendra used to look after thelamily properties. The husband of defendnt No. 1 was also not experienced in worldly affairs. As a result of partition Upendra moved to West Bengal entrusting Narendra with the management of family properties. Upendra died in West Bengal. Taking advantage of Upendra's absence Narendra caused the auction-sale in the benami of his wife for illegal gain of paternal property from which he was deprived. The brothers of Narendra on learning about the deceitful auction-purchase put pressure on him and Narendra offered to register their 4/5th share of the suit land by kabala at his own cost which he never did. The husband of the defendant No. 1 died, Jatindra was a vagabond, Upendra and Mier, son of Soradas, also moved out of the country. Taking advantage of the helpless position of the defendant No. 1 Narendra with a view to driving her out from her homestead has instituted this and other false litigations. The defendant No. 1 has been possessing the suit land through abraders since the last 16/17 years. The plaintiff has no right, title and interest in the suit land.

3. The trial Court disbelieved the defendant's case that Narendra was a cripple from birth. The fact of Narendra living in separate mess and property also could not be proved, Ext. 5 series shows Kabuliyats in favour of all the 5 sons of Haridas. So the trial Court held that it is baseless to allege that Narendra did not inherit anything from his father. Ext. 6 series the kabales show that Shefalika the plaintiff, purchased and transferred properties from much before and so the trial Court held that the plaintiff auction-purchased the suit land wills her own money. The trial Court referred to Ext. A, a letter written by Narendra to Upedra in West Bengal immediately after the auction-purchase which was admitted into evidence on admission. Narendra slated therein that he purchased the suit land "in the name" of his wife. The trial Court held that since the word benami has not been used in the letter it has not been proved that the plaintiff's husband purchased the property in the benami of the plaintiff. The defendant No. 1 also failed to establish any fraud in the auction-sale. Her story of title is a sort of adverse possession which could not be substantiated. She cannot name the bargadars of her husband, nor can she give the exact area under her own cultivation through her own bargadars, not can she give the exact area of the suit land. The defendant's witnesses do not speak of her title and possession, except Dews 2. & 8 whose statements as alleged bargadars are not free from doubt. The plaintiff's witnesses and documents on the whole substantiate the case of the plaintiff. The trial Court, therefore, decreed the suit in favour of the plaintiff.

4. The appellate Court below comes to the finding that the properties left by Haridas were not partitioned and that in the auction-sale, which was at first denied but later on admitted by the defendant, Narendra as well as the 4 other sons of Haridas were parties. Narendra was therefore a judgment-debtor and if he had purchased the suit-land in the benami of his wife he was evidently barred to do so under section 173(1) of the Bengal Tenancy Act. Referring to Ext. A, the appellate Court below finds that the trial Court was wrong in holding that Narendra did not auction-purchase the suit land in the benami of his wife simply because the word "benami" was not there in the letter. It held that the letter was a sufficient indication that Narendra auction-purchased the suit land in the benami of his wife. He has done so in contravention of the provisions of section 173 (1) of the Bengal Tenancy Act. The position of law according to the appellate Court below, is that if a judgment-debtor auction-purchases the suit holding in contravention of section 173(1) of the Bengal Tenancy Act, his purchase will ensure to the benefit of his other co-sharers, if any, or in other words, the position of a judgment-debtor auction-purchaser is like that of a trustee. So Narendra is debarred from excepting defendant No. 1 as one of his co-sharers and his auction-purchase of the suit land in the benami of his wife enured to tire benefit of his co-sharers. There is no case of any ouster. The plaintiff cannot get the relief prayed for bemuse she was simply a benamdar of her husband. The appellate Court below allowed the defendant's appeal and dismissed the plaintiff's suit.

5. Mr. B.N. Chowdhury, learned Advocate for the appellant, submitted that the judgment of the appellate Court below is not a proper judgment of reversal inasmuch as there is no reversal of the trial Courts' finding that the plaintiff auction-purchased the suit holding from her own money. This part of the learned Advocate's submission appears to be factually correct, but it is equally correct, as contended by Mr. B. B. Roy Chowdhury, learned Advocate for the respondent, that the appellate Court below on a reading of Ext. A has given a clear finding that Narendra auction-purchased the suit holding in the benami of his wife. Ext. A is expressly admitted to have been written by Narendra himself both in his examination-in-chief and in his cross-examination as PW 2. It leaves no manner of doubt whatsoever that he admits therein that it is he who auction-purchased the suit holding in the benamy of his wife. There' s no evidence on record that the plaintiff had independent sources of income. Ext. 5 series which are some kabalas show that some lands were purchased by the plaintiff before the auction-sale. They do not show that the plaintiff had independent source of income. In the face of the clear admission of Narendra P.W. 2 I am of the opinion that the substance of the trial court's finding in respect of the banami or benami purchase of the suit khatian stands sufficiently reversed by the appellate Court below.

6. Mr. B. N. Chowdhury submitted next that the appellate Court below has fallen in an error of law in holding that if a Judgment-debtor auction purchases the suit holding in contravention of section 173(1) of the Bengal Tenancy Act, his purchase will enure to the benefit of his other co-sharers and that his position will be that of a trustee. Mr. Chowdhury submitted that an advantage gained by a qualified owner is governed by section 90 of the Trusts Act, which is as follows:-

"Where a tenant for life, co-owner, mortgagee or other qualified owner of any property, by availing himself of his position as such, gains an advantage in derogation of the right of the other persons interested in the property or where any such owner, as representing all persons in such property, gains any advantage, he most hold, for the benefit of all persons so interested, the advantage so gained, but subject to repayment by such persons of their due share of the expenses properly incurred, and to an indemnity by the same persons against liabilities properly contracted, in gaining such advantage."

7. Mr. Chowdhury then refers to the case of Balgbhadra Vs. Nirmala Surulari Debi (AIR 1954 Orison 33) where the applicability of section 90 of the Trusts Act in situations similar to the present cases has been stated to he as follows:-

"For granting equitable relief a co-sharer who subsequently purchased the property in the revenue sale must be guilty of some kind of sharp practice which would be inconsistent with any relation of mutual confidence between co-sharers. Where there can be no question of one co-sharer being misled by the other and the latter is not guilty of any sharp practice the equitable principles of s. 90 cannot be invoked" (PP. 28-29)

8. Mr. Chowdhury refers next to the case of Mohammad Khan Vs. Kedarmal (AIR 1943 Nagpur 302), wherein it was held as follows :

"There is ordinarily no fiduciary relation between tenants in common so as to impose an obligation on one co-owner to protect the interest of other co-owners. Section 90 does not apply unless one co-owner is placed in such relation to another by the act or consent of another, that he becomes interested for him and with him in any subject or property or business and being in that position he, acting for himself or as representing another, gains an advantage in derogation of another's rights. Where a co-owner, who has purchased the property at an auction sale in default of the payment of land revenue is not bound to pay the land revenue and does not represent the interests of his co-owners, s. 90 has no application in the absence of suggesting that the default was due to the machinations on the part of the purchaser."

9. To the some effect is the third case cited by Mr. Chowdhury, namely, the case of Amish Nath vs. Dwarka Nath (AIR 1939 PC 66). The Privy Council held therein that as fraud or bad faith towards co-sharers had not been proved the other co-sharers could not claim to recover their former interest in a zamindari estate by paying proportionate portion of the purchase price.

10. Mr. Chowdhury submitted that in the absence of any evidence and finding that Narendra was entrusted with the management of the cumuli property or that he was guilty of some sharp practice, his purchase cannot be said to have endured to the benefit of his co-sharer. He is entitled under the law to hold it for himself.

11. Mr. B. B. Roy Chowdhury, on the other hand, referred to illustration (b) of section 90 which is as follows:-

"(b). A village belongs to a Hindu family. A, one of its members, pays nazrana to Government and thereby procures his name to be entered as invader of the village. A holds tire village for the benefit of himself and the other members."

He argued that section 90 of the Trusts Act itself and the illustration (b) thereof amply make it clear that if a co-owner gains an advantage by availing of his position as such, the mischief of section 90 is attracted. The co-owner need not be in a fiduciary relationship with the other co-owners nor need he be guilty of any sharp practice. Mr. Roy Chowdhury relies upon the following observations of the Privy Council in the case of Deo Nandan Prasad V. Jakhi Singh and others (AIR 1916 PC 227):-

"The relative of co-owners, one towards the other, demands from each co-owner such measure of candid dealing and good faith as would ensure that co-sharer would not be tempted to make a deliberate default with a view to ousting his co-sharers and appropriating to himself their common property. A co-owner or an usufructuary mortgagee of a co-owner's share, has a duty to perform which is inconsistent with his becoming a purchaser of the property and consequently his title by purchase of the property in a sale for arrears of venue on account of the co-owners default cannot operate to the exclusion of the other co-owners. The sale may stand good but the property purchased must be held for the benefit of all the co-sharers according to their several interest."

12. In the aforesaid case the co-sharer mortgagee had a previous agreement with his other co-sharers that he would pay his quota of the Government revenue. He himself was the defaulter in payment of his quota to the Government and he purchased the estate in a revenue sale. The default was brought about deliberately without the knowledge of the other co-sharers. The Privy Council observed the above view in the aforesaid circumstances, after disagreeing with the view expressed in Doorga Singh V Shree Porshad Singh, reported in ILR 16 Cal 194. The Calcutta High Court, explaining Doorga Singh's case in a later case, namely, Kurshed Ali V. Dinanath Surma (AIR 1919 Cal 431) ob-serves that the mere fact that the purchaser of an estate in a revenue sale was one of the co-sharers was not sufficient to attract the equitable principles of section 90 of the Trusts Act. There must be something unfair, something amounting at least to sharp practice, in the conduct of the purchaser. The Orissa, case AIR 1954 0 23), earlier referred to, deals with this aspect of the matter thoroughly and notes approvingly of a subsequent decision of the Calcutta High Court, namely, the case of Akshay Kumar P. Ahmed Ali (AIR 1931 Cal 434) wherein the principles enunciated in the Privy Council (AIR 1916 PC 277) were applied in the case of a deliberate and intentional default in the payment of land revenue.

<u>13. I, therefore, hold that in order that section 90 of the Trusts Act is attracted the co-sharer auction-purchaser must not only be co-sharer, but must also be guilty of some kind of sharp practice in the transaction m question.</u>

14. Mr. Roy Chowdhury, however, points out that notwithstanding the main defence of the defendant that Narendra was separate in mess and property from the very beginning there is evidence that he was managing the ancestral property after Upendra’s departure to West Bengal. He refers to Narendra's statement in cross-exmination, "I myself was a debtor for rent I could not pay off the dues of all which shows that he was responsible for paying of the dues of all. Again in the letter Ext. A he states that he has collected khajana to the extent of Rs. 150/175 which also shows that he was managing the ejmali properties.

15. It appears, however, that the state of evidence in this respect is not at all favorable to the defendant. Defendant's case in the written statement is that Upendra, on leaving for West Bengal, entrusted Narendra with the management of ejmali properties. Narendra PW.1 has repeatedly denied this. In her evidence as DW. 1, the defendant No. 1 nowhere states that Narendra was in-charge of the management of the ejmali property. She merely says, "Narendra used to look after my property." Both the Courts below  have found that the suit land was anomaly property and therefore by "my property" the defendant No. 1 surely could not have meant the suit land. Mr. Roy Chowdhury relies upon Ext. A and submits that the very offer of Marinara to recovery 4/5th share of the suit land to his other co-sharers at his own cost even after auction-purchase with his own money shows that Narendra was conscious that he perpetrated a fraud upon his co-sharers and that he realized he was holding the suit land for the benefit of himself and his co-owners. Mr. B.N. Chowdhury, on the other hand, contends that Ex. A is a clear proof that Narendra had no malafide in auction-purchasing the suit land. He offered to recovery the suit land within 30 days of the sale, before the sale was confirmed, as a noble gesture, but none of the co-sharers responded. The husband of the defendant No. 1, Jitendra was alive at the time, which is in evidence, and he did not come forward to accept Narendra's offer to set aside the sale. I am of the opinion that the evidence on record nowhere shows that Narendra was entrusted with the management of ejmali properties or that he was guilty of any sharp practice. As such, the finding of the appellate court below that Narendra holds the snit land for the benefit of himself and his other co-sharers cannot be sustained. Narendra holds the suit land for his own benefit to the exclusion of hit co-sharers.

16. Mr. B. N. Chowdhury submitted next that the appellate Court below erred in law in holding that the plaintiff cannot get the relief prayed for because she was simply, a benamdar of her husband. Mr. Chowdhury submitted that a' benamdar has a right to bring a suit claiming title and for possession except against the real or beneficial owner. He has cited the case of Damodar Mondal Vs. Karamai Ali (Khan), reported in AIR 1913 Cal. 536, in support of the proposition. That was a case where the suit was dismissed on the ground that a benamdar has no right to bring a suit claiming title and for possession where he is suing in effect the beneficial owner. This case supports Mr. Chowdhury's contention negatively. Mr. Chowdhury, however, refers to a Privy Council decision, namely, the case of Gar Narayan and others Vs. Sheo Lal Singh & others (2) wherein the Privy Council observes as follows:-

"On the question whether a person who has no beneficial interest in the property which stands in his name, or is acquired in his name, can maintain as action in respect thereof, there seems to be considerable diversity of judicial opinion in India. The system of acquiring and holding property and even of carrying on business in names other than those of real owners, usually called the benami system, is and has been a common practice in the country. There is nothing inherently wrong in it, and it accords within its legitimate scope, with the ideals and habits of the people.

<u>17. So long, therefore, as a benami transaction does not contravene the provisions of the law the courts are bound to give it effect. As already observed, the benamdar has no beneficial interest in the property or business that stands in his name ; he represents, in fact, the real owner, and so far as their relative legal position is concerned he is a mere trustee for him. Their Lordships find it difficult to understand why, in such circumstances, an action cannot be maintained in the name of the benamdar in respect of the property although the beneficial owner is no party to it....</u>

<u>Mr. Chowdhury has also cited the case of Mst. Amanat V. Mahboob Hussain, reported in PLD 1959 Kar 362 wherein the above decision of the Privy Council has been followed.</u>

<u>18. Mr. Roy Chowdhury did not dispute the above contention of Mr. Chowdhury. His contention is that the plaintiff did not sue as a benamdar. She sued as the real owner. It is the court which finds her to be a benamder. Her case of independent title having been disbelieved, she cannot maintain the present action. I am of the opinion that it matters not whether the plaintiff sued as a real owner or as a benamdar. If she is found to be a benamder by the Court, her capacity or legal ability to proceed with the suit is not affected thereby, because a benamdar can maintain an action except against the real and beneficial owner. That being the position I am of the opinion that the plaintiff is entitled to a decree in the suit. The appellate court below, I find, has not reversed the trial Court's finding that the defendant had no title and possession of suit land and that the plaintiff possessed it after the auction-purchase till her dispossession.</u>

19. In the result, the appeal is allowed without any order as to costs. The judgment and decree of the appellate court below are set aside and those of the trial mourn are restored herewith.

20. Mr. B.B. Roy Chowdhury, the learned Advocate for the respondent prays for leave under clause 15 of the Letters Patent. In view of section 3 of the Law Reforms Ordinance, 1978, no such prayer is necessary.

The leave prayed for is refused.

End.

full_judgment:
In this Rule the petitioner has challenged a decision of the lover appellate court reversing a decision of the trial court in pre-emption case under section 96 of the State Acquisition and Tenancy Act, Initially the pre-emption case was instituted at the instance of a contiguous owner. Upon service of notice to all the co-sharers, a co-sharer by inheritance was also made a co-applicant in the pre-emption case. Thus, both a contiguous owner and a co-sharer were claiming pre-emption of the self same land. The trial court allowed the pre-emption claimed by the contiguous owner and disallowed the claim of the co-sharer on the ground that it was time barred. The lower appellate court did just the opposite by allowing the pre-emption in favour of the co-sharer and disallowing it against the contiguous owner. While doing so, the lower appellate court came to a finding of fact on consideration of the evidence on record and in the facts and circumstances of the case that the claim of the co-sharer for pre-emption was made within the statutory period of 4 months from the date of the personal knowledge of the co-sharer about the impugned transfer and such finding of fact made by the lower appellate court in the absence of any apparent error of law on the face of the record is otherwise conclusive. In this connection it may be mentioned that the lower appellate court did not reverse the finding of the trial court about the filing of the pre-emption case by a contiguous owner within the statutory period of limitation of 4 months from the date of the knowledge of the impugned transfer.

<u>2. The only question for determination in this Rule is thus as to who will have priority in claiming pre-emption in between a co-sharer and a contiguous owner. Sub-section (1) of section 96 of the State Acquisition and Tenancy Act providing for a right of pre-emption has mentioned a co-sharer in the first instance and subsequently a contiguous owner has been added. From the reading of section 96 (1) of the State Acquisition and Tenancy Act it would clearly appear that the co-sharer comes first in priority over a contiguous owner. Further, a co-sharer can always be divided into co-sharer by inheritance and co-sharer by purchase. Even if it is assumed that a co-sharer by inheritance or purchase and a contiguous owner are put on the same footing for the purpose of enabling any of them to claim pre-emption under section 96 of the State Acquisition and Tenancy Act, upon a clear equitable principle a co-sharer by inheritance shall have the highest priority followed by a co-sharer by purchase and thereafter a contiguous owner. The very purpose of granting pre-emption to avoid any stranger in any joint holding or neighbourhood would be frustrated if such priority as held herein before is not maintained for ends of justice.</u>

3. In view of the above observations the impugned judgment of the lower appellate court allowing pre-emption in favour of a co-sharer by inheritance as against a contiguous owner does not suffer from any error of law to warrant any interference by this court exercising its discretionary revisional jurisdiction. This Rule is accordingly discharged without any order as to costs.

End.

case_source:
(From the Judgment and decree dated 3.5.1984 passed by the 
High Court Division, Sylhet Bench, Sylhet in Second Appeal No. 1509 of 1968).
full_judgment:
M. H. Rahman, J.: This appeal, at the instance of the heirs of defendant No.1, is directed against the judgment of the High Court Division, Sylhet Bench passed in Second Appeal No. 1509 of 1968.

2. The plaintiff-respondents instituted Title suit No. 22 of 1962 in the Court of Munsif, First Court, Sadar, Sylhet for partition of the undivided family homestead in the suit and also prayed for purchasing the share of defendant No. 1, a stranger-purchaser of a portion of the suit homestead from some co-sharers of the plaintiffs. Their case, in brief, is that the two brothers Hadu Shah and Nadu Shah took lease of southern half of the disputed homestead from the landlords. Subsequently Nadu Shah alone took lease of the northern half. Hadu Shah got 1/4th and Nadu Shah got 1/4th share of the homestead. Hadu Shah died leaving two daughters Feroja and Hafiza and brother Nadu Shah. The plaintiffs, being the heirs of Nadu Shah, claimed 5/6th share of the suit property. There was no previous partition. As the plaintiffs demand for an amicable partition was not conceded they filed the present suit for partition. Further case of the plaintiffs is that they were entitled to purchase the share of defendant No. 1, a stranger purchaser, under section 4 of the Partition Act and read with section 44 of the Transfer of Property Act.

3. Defendant No. 1, alone contested the suit, His case was that Bedu Shah was the original owner of the suit land. He died leaving two sons, Hadu and Nadu, and a daughter, Modina. Hadu Shah died leaving one son, Sadu Shah, two daughters Firoza and Hafiza, and a widow, Kutibibi. Kuti Bibi died leaving Firoza and Hafiza who sold their interest to Ambor and others. Modina died leaving one son Amjad, who leaving two sons Ambor and Amfor.  Amfor and minor children of Ambor sold half of the home stead to defendant No. 1 by a kabala dated 15.2.87 and since then he was in continuous possession in the specific portion of the land he purchased. It was further contended that the plaintiffs claim was excessive and section 4 of the Partition Act was not applicable in this case.

4. The suit was once decreed on contest but on appeal the matter was remanded to the trial Court. Thereafter the suit was again decreed by the trial Court. The trial Court found that defendant No. 1 was a stranger and he only acquired 4/5 share by his purchase. The plaintiffs were given 7/15th share of the suit homestead on partition and were allowed to purchase Defendant No. 1's share.

5. On appeal the learned Subordinate Judge affirmed the decree of the trial Court as to defendant No. 1's share. He observed: "The present suit land is no doubt homestead land but is not a dwelling house of an undivided family". He allowed the appeal in part by holding that defendant No. 1 was not a stranger and he was already in possession of a specific portion of the homestead and therefore he should also get a separate saham.

6. In second appeal the High Court Division restored the decree of the trial Court after affirming the finding of the trial Court that the plaintiffs and the co-sharers-defendants had their dwelling house in their suit property and they were entitled to purchase 4/15th share of defendant No. 1 by purchase from the co-sharer-defendants of the plaintiffs.

7. On behalf of appellants it contended that the High Court Division erred in law in not considering that the vendors of defendant No. 1 had been in possession of a specific portion of the homestead and that defendant No. 1 had also been residing there for a long time since his purchase on 15.2.1957 and that he was no longer a stranger in the suit property. It is also urged that the plaintiffs can easily get a separate saham for their 7/15th share in the homestead land by maintaining the existing possession of co-sharers as far as possible causing least disturbance to other co-sharers in possession.

8. On the other hand, the respondents submit that the lower appellate Court's finding that defendant No. 1 was no longer a stranger is based on a misconception of both fact and law because the suit property was never previously partitioned by metes and bounds.

9. The High Court Division upheld the plaintiffs contention and restored the decree of the trial Court after considering Md. Tazammul Hossain Vs. Purni Agarwalini 10 DLR 318 and Md. Magdu Bhuiya Vs. Jabban Huq 11 DLR 355 and Md. Habibullah Patwari Vs. Pran Ballav Bhakta & others 9 DLR 119 and some cases of Indian jurisdiction. In this case we need not reconsider those decisions.

<u>10. After considering the mores of our people, the co-sharers attachment to their ancestral house and their anxiety to preserve the purdah and privacy a of the members and inmates of the undivided dwelling house, the legislators made the provisions of section 4 of the Partition Act. The expression a dwelling house belonging to an undivided family is to be liberally construed. We have done so in Sree Jugal Kishori Sarker Vs. Azizur Rahman & ors 40 DLR (AD) 150. A co-sharer's prayer to buy up a stranger-purchaser may not be refused on a technical ground.</u>

<u>11. The appellate Court's finding that "the suit land is no doubt a homestead, but is not a dwelling house of an undivided family" is utterly misconceived. In the suit land an undivided dwelling house is situated. The defendant himself claimed to be residing in a portion there. The suit property never lost its character of an undivided homestead because there had admittedly been no partition by metes and bounds by any previous arrangement. The impartible character of the suit property remained undisturbed when the suit was filed in 1962. There is no time limit for filing an application under section 4 of the Partition Act. In the instant case the plaintiffs' claim d cannot be called stale. The defendant's claim of continuous possession since purchase would be of no consequence. The claims of the patties in a case are to be determined with reference to their respective positions existing at the time of the filing of the e suit. Hence we do not find any substance in the appellant's second contention that the plaintiffs could get a separate saham by maintaining the existing possession of the co-sharers. If an application under section 4 of the Partition Act is filed to buy-out a stranger-purchaser after an inordinate delay from the date of the purchase then the applicant himself may suffer. When an applicant's prayer is allowed under section 4 of the Partition Act it involves a kind of forced sale for the stranger-purchaser. And hence the Court would in equity determine the valuation of the transferred share on the date of the filing of the application for permission to purchase the share of the stranger-purchaser.</u>

12. In view of the above, the appeal is dismissed. No costs in this appeal.

End.
