case_source: From the Judgment and Decree dated 1st June, 1979 passed by the High Court Division in S. A. No. 486 of 1964.
full_judgment:
Ruhul Islam, J:—This appeal by special leave arises from the judgment and decree dated June 1, 1976 of the High Court Division in Second Appeal No. 486 of 1964 reversing the concurrent finding of the Courts below and decreeing the suit in favour of the heirs of deceased plaintiff Abdul Latif Bhuiyan who instituted the suit for pre-emption under the Mohammedan Law.

2. Facts in short necessary for disposal of the appeal may be stated thus : On September 28, 1962 the plaintiff instituted Title Suit No. 124 of 1962 in the second court of Munsif at Brahmanbaria for pre-emption under the Mohammedan Law against the appellants stating, inter alia, that one Jonah Ali Daroga owner for the suit plots in tenure right sold half of the property to the respondent and other half to Nishikanto Chowdhury who sold the same to Zahurul Huq and Anwarul Huq who sold the same to the appellant by a registered kabala dated October 12, 1957. On October 13, 1957 the plaintiff came to learn about the sale and he immediately made Talab-i-mowasibat in presence of some persons and he duly performed Talab-i-issad. Thereafter without taking steps for institution of a suit for pre-emption, filed an application under section 26F of the Bengal Tenancy Act for pre-emption of the suit land and lost it upto the Appellate Court on July 19, 1962. Thereafter the suit was filed on September 28, 1962 against the appellants for a decree of pre-emption under the Mohammedan Law. The suit was contested mainly on the grounds of limitation and non-performance of the formalities as required under the Mohammedan Law, because, according to the plaintiff's own showing the formalities performed by him were premature as the formalities were completed before registration of the kabala.

The learned Munsif dismissed the suit on the finding that the formalities observed by the plaintiff were premature as they were before the registration of the sale deed. This judgment was affirmed in appeal. In second appeal by the plaintiff the learned Single Judge of the High Court Division decreed the suit on the finding that-the suit was not barred by limitation under article 10 of the Imitation Act, because, the plaintiff-respondent having been dispossessed from the suit plot in 1962, the period of one year provided for institution of a suit for pre-emption is to be counted from the date of dispossession in 1962, and the suit was filed well within time.

<u>3. Leave was granted to examine the following questions raised by the appellants viz:—</u>

<u>i) Whether the learned Judge was justified in disturbing the concurrent findings of the Courts below on the question of performance of formalities required under the Mohammedan Law as well as on the question of plaintiff-respondent's possession of the transferred land.;</u>

<u>2) whether the learned Judge has correctly applied Article 10 of the Limitation Act in the facts of the instant case and holding that the suit is not barred by limitation.</u>

<u>Right of 'shufa' or pre-emption under the Mohammedan Law is a right which enables the owner of an immovable property to acquire by purchase an immovable property which has been sold to another person.</u>

4. The right of pre-emption or `shufa' means a right to be substituted in place of the transferee of some immovable property by the exercise of such right, that is, a right to acquire by compulsory purchase some immovable property in preference to all other persons by means of pre-emption. The law of `shufa.' has been developed out of some 'hadises' (tradition) of the Prophet of Islam. Its foundation seems to be based on the principle, that all members of the society should attempt to preserve joint nature of their ancestral property. It may appear to be contrary to the modern idea of freedom of alienation of property, and so it is considered as a restriction on the right of ownership. But this law; in some form or other has been prevalent almost in every part of the world since the ancient time, but it is difficult to trace its origin. In all those countries the Law of pre-emption was not developed as a scientific exposition of substantive law, but the Mohammedan Law of pre-emption is highly developed and a scientific exposition of a very difficult branch of law. The Mohammedan Law of pre-emption contains well defined principles restricting the individual rights of property and yet is in complete harmony with principles of equity, justice and good conscience. In this field of law Imam Abu Hanifa and his disciples have left a unique and distinct mark on the theory of jurisprudence.

<u>5. The right of pre-emption arises only out of a valid, complete and bonafide sale. It does not arise out of gift (hiba), sadaqat, wakf, inheritance, bequest or a lease even though in perpetuity. The right does not arise also out of a mortgage even though it may be by way of conditional sale. Under the Mohammedan Law a sale is an exchange of property for property, the exchange consisting in payment of price by the purchaser to the vendor and delivery of possession by the vendor to the purchaser. Under the Mohammedan Law execution of instrument of sale is not necessary to complete the sale; the sale is complete with the passing of consideration and delivery of possession.</u>

<u>6. There is some controversy on the question, whether a sale though not complete as contemplated under section 54 of the Transfer of Property Act, but is otherwise. complete under the Mohammedan Law, gives rise to the right or pre-emption. The main factor is that the sale must be a complete sale. Under the Mohammedan Law the sale is complete with the payment of price and delivery of possession. Under the Transfer of Property Act, of course, completion of sale is dependent on the execution of the instrument of sale, and if value of the property is Tk. 100/-or upwards, on its registration. Delivery of possession is not so vital as in the case of sale under the Mohammedan Law. There are a number of decision of different superior Courts supporting the view that the personal law regarding transfer of property cannot override the statutory law, that is the Transfer of Property Act, where it applies. According to this view, the territories where the Transfer of Property Act is applicable, unless the sale is complete as provided under section 54, that is, by registration of the instrument of sale, the right of pre-emption does not arise.</u>

7. Essential part for a valid claim for pre-emption is "demands" ; and the demands are to be made as provided under the Mohammedan Law. No person is entitled to purchase by pre-emption unless—

(1) he has declared his intention to assert the right immediately on receiving information of the sale. This formality is called talab-i-mowasibat—literal meaning demand of jumping ; and unless,

(2) he has with the least practicable delay affirmed the intention, referring expressly to fact that the talab-i-mowasibat had already made, and has made a formal demand—

(a) either in the presence of the buyer, or the seller, or on the premises which are the subject of sale, and

(b) in the presence of at least two witnesses. This formality is called talab-i-ishhad--demand with invocation of witnesses.

8. In the instant case, according to the plaint case, the disputed sale was completed by registration of the kabala Exhibit B on 12-10-57 corresponding to 25th Aswin, 1364 B.S. The plaintiff Made demands on the following day, that is, on 13-10-57. In fact the kabala was presented for registration on 12-10-57 and the vendors admitted execution on the same day, but registration with the necessary entries as provided' under sections 60 and 61 of the Registration Act was completed on 24-10-57 and as per section 54 of the Transfer of Property Act the sale was complete on 24-10-57. The learned Munsif dismissed the suit on the finding that neither party's case being that possession of the property was delivered on the date of sale, that is, on 12-10-57, the alleged demands for pre-emption were premature. According to the learned Munsif, the right of pre-emption arose only when the transfer of the property became operative under section 54 of the Transfer of Property Act. The suit was also dismissed on the ground of limitation as the suit was filed on 28-9-62 which was long after the period of limitation of one year as provided under Article 10 of the Limitation Act. The learned Munsif also noticed that the plaintiff after making the alleged demands for pre-emption, instead of filing the suit within one year from the sale, filed a pre-emption case with a prayer for recovery of khas possession. Plaintiff's case that he was all along in possession of the land till middle of 1962 when he was dispossessed, and then he instituted the suit within one year from the said dispossession, was not accepted by the lower Appellate Court, because, the plaintiff's possession could, not be proved by his witnesses. The lower Appellate Court accepted the evidence of the witnesses of the defendants who proved that defendants are in actual possession of the disputed land according to their share since later part of Kartick, 1364 B.S. The Appellate Court concurred with the finding of the trial Court that the suit was barred by limitation.

9. In second appeal the learned Single Judge set aside the judgments of the courts below on taking the view that .the demands were not premature. According to the learned Judge demand of pre-emption under Muslim Law at this stage is not premature since the sale is to be completed under the Muslim Law and the person claiming the right of pre-emption cannot wait till registration thereof. In taking this view the learned Judge accepted the plaintiff's case that he was in possession of the suit land and continued to remain in possession as such till 1962 when he was dispossessed. The learned Judge observed that the question of delivery of possession by the vendor to the vendee under the kabala executed on 12th October, 1957 did not arise, because, the plaintiff claiming to be in possession of the land in question demanded pre-emption under Mohammedan Law by way of talab-i-mowasibat on October 13, 1957 when evidently the kabala had already been executed and the price thereof paid.

10. The learned Counsel appearing for the appellants contended that the learned Judge was not correct in taking the above view, inasmuch, as, delivery of possession being one of the main factors of a sale under Mohammedan Law, mere execution of the kabala and passing of the consideration would not be sufficient to complete the sale under the Mohammedan Law. In this cow text the learned Counsel submitted that the provision of sale as provided under the Mohammedan Law having been superseded by the statutory provision of the Transfer of Property Act, the sale until completed on compliance of the requirements of sections 60 and 61 of the Registration Act, the right of pre-emption did not arise and the question of making demands also did not arise. In support of this contention the learned Counsel referred to a number of decisions of different superior Courts of the subcontinent wherein view has been taken that the law relating to sale under the Mohammedan Law has been superseded by the statutory provision as contained in section 54 of the Transfer of Property Act, and the right of pre-emption does not arise until the sale is completed on completion of registration of the deed of sale; and registration is not completed until compliance of the requirements, of section 61 of the Registration Act.

11. It has already been mentioned above that the plaintiff's suit for pre-emption was dismissed by the Courts below on the concurrent finding that it is neither party's case that the defendants were put into possession on the date of execution of the deed of sale, that is, on 12-10-57. The learned Single Judge set aside the judgments without adverting to these concurrent findings of the Courts below and without taking into consideration the effect of absence of delivery of possession of the land in suit to the vendee. According to him the sate concluded on the execution of the deed of sale. From this he assumed that the sale as contemplated under the Mohammedan Law was complete, and hence the demand made on 13-10-57 for pre-emption was not premature but a valid demand. In this context it would be relevant to mention that while considering the question as to whether the suit was barred by limitation under Article 10 of the Limitation Act, the learned. Judge accepted the case of the plaintiff' that the property sold on 12-10-57 continued, to remain in possession of the plaintiff, and he was dispossessed only in 1962, and the suit having been filed on September 28, 1962 being well within one year from the date when the defendant took physical possession of the property sold; the suit was not barred by limitation. The learned Judge completely overlooked the implication of the factum of possession of the property on the right of pre-emption.

12. Under the Mohammedan Law the sale becomes complete only on payment of price by the vendee to the vendor and delivery of possession by the vendor to the vendee. Therefore, even if we do not accept the arguments advanced by Mr. Pal that the right of pre-emption under the Mohammedan Law does not arise until the instrument of sale is registered and necessary steps as required under sections 60 and 61 of the Registration Act are completed, the judgment under appeal cannot be sustained.

13. Let me first examine whether section 54 of the Transfer of Property Act, 1882 supersedes the Mohammedan. Law relating to pre-emption under section 54 a sale of immovable property of the value of Tk. 100/- and upwards is not complete unless made by a registered instrument. This provision has been construed by some of the superior Courts of the subcontinent to mean that right of pre-emption does not arise until the sale is completed on completion of registration of the instrument of sale, and registration is completed only on compliance of requirements of sections 60 and 61 of the Registration Act.

14. The other view, which has been supported in a number of decisions, is that the Transfer of Property Act, 1882 did not alter the law of pre-emption under the Mohammedan Law. It has been forcefully canvassed therein that it was not the intention of the Legislature, in passing the Transfer of Property Act, 1882, to alter directly or indirectly the Mohammedan Law of pre-emption as it existed and was understood for centuries prior to the passing of the Act. According to this view when the vendor and the vendee intended the transaction of sale to be completed and consideration passed, and the vendee was put into possession, but the parties, omitted to observe the necessary legal formality of having a registered instrument, the transaction gave rise to the right of pre-emption.

15. At the outset it may be mentioned that Patna and Calcutta High Courts are on the opinion that section 54 of the Transfer of Property Act abrogated Mohammedan Law of sale giving rise of pre-emption; and no right of pre-emption arises until the sale has been completed by registration of the transferred as provided under the Registration Act, 1908. The Supreme Court of India has approved this view which will be discussed later. In Budhar Sardar Vs. Sonaullah Mridha, 18 CWN 890 a Division of the Calcutta High Court expressed the opinion that the statutory law has superseded the personal law, that is, Mohammedan Law of transfer of immovable property. The reason given is that as under the Mohammedan Law the right of pre-emption does not arise until after the cessation of two vendor's title, the point of time at which the right is to be taken to arise at the present day should be determined by the statutory law of sale which has superseded the Mohammedan Law. Kheyali Prosad Vs. Mullick Nazrul Islam, 20 CWN 1048 a Division Bench of the Patna High Court expressed similar opinion. As a sale is not complete till legal ownership passes, no matter whether there has been payment and delivery of possession, the pre-emption's right in the case of a property valued Rs. 100/- and upwards does not accrue till after registration. The learned Judges observed. "It would be against equity, justice and good conscience to apply in such a case the Mohammedan Law of sale which is no longer in force and to attach to a mere contract for sale an incident which Mohammedan lawyers intended to attach only to an actual sale."

16. The Supreme. Court of India expressed the opinion in the same line as noted above. In Radhakisan Luxminarayan Toshniwal Vs. Shridhar Ramchandra Alshi, AIR 1960 SC 1368=(1961) 1 SCR, it has been held that the transfer of property, where the Transfer of Property Act applied, Mohammedan Law or any other personal law is inapplicable to transfer and no title passes except in accordance with that Act, and the Mohammedan Law of transfer of property cannot override the statute law.

17. In the case of Ram Saran Lal Vs. Domini Kuer, AIR 1961 SC 1747, by majority judgment it has been held that the demand for pre-emption must be made after completion of the sale as contemplated under section. 54 of the Transfer of Property Act read with sections 60 and 61 of the Registration Act. The judgment does not show any indication of taking into consideration the intention of the parties as to when the sale was to be treated as complete, which turns upon the intention of the parties, as it has been held consistently in a number of decisions of the different superior Courts of the subcontinent. Even in the above mentioned case two of the learned Judges, in their dissenting judgment put much stress upon the intention of the parties, if it is expressed, to determine as to when the sale to take effect.

18. In this case the question for consideration was whether the talab-i-mowasibat which was required to be made after completion of the sale, was made before or after such completion of the sale. The making of the demand was not in dispute, but the dispute was as to when the sale was completed. The facts which gave rise to the question may in short be stated thus: On January 31st, 1946, the Pandey's executed a deed of sale in favour of the respondent-purchaser in respect of their house. The appellants having their residential house contiguous to the said house claimed right of pre-emption on this sale. Consideration was Rs. 2,000/-, and on account of a subsisting mortgage a sum of Tk. 200/- was to be left with the purchaser for satisfying the mortgage debt. The deed also recited that the Pandey's received Rs. 400/- and the remaining Rs. 1400/- in cash at the time of exchange of equivalents, that is, at the time of handing over of the receipt on registration of the deed. The sale deed further recited "on receipt of the whole and entire amount of consideration money we have put the said claimed into possession and occupation of this vended property as absolute owner in place of us, the executants and our heirs and representative". The deed further stated, "the sale deed becomes operative from the date when we the executants affixed our signature thereon. Whatever title we the executants and our heirs had …with respect to this vended .property has become extinct, inoperative and null and void and the same has now been transferred to and acquired by the claimant." Obviously by the word "claimant", the respondent purchaser was referred to. The deed was presented at the registration office for registration by the Pandeys on the day it was executed and it was left with the Registrar in the Registration Office for necessary entries and copies and receipt being given to the Pandeys. On February 2, 1946, the appellants on coming to hear of the sale made the talab-i-mowasibat. On February 7, 1946 the receipt was made over by them to the respondent purchaser who thereupon paid the balance of the price as stipulated in the deed. On February 9, 1946, the documents were copied in the Registrar's book and thereupon the registration became complete as provided in section 61 of the Registration Act. The respondent purchaser thereafter received the deed of sale on February 13, 1946. The appellants filed their suit for pre-emption on September 9, 1946. The suit was decreed by the trial Court and this decision was maintained by the Appellate Court. The High Court in second appeal set aside judgment of the Courts below and dismissed the suit. Against this judgment the pre-emptor took the matter to the Supreme Court in further appeal.

19. It was contended on behalf of the appellants relying upon section 47 of the Registration Act that since the sale is to be deemed to have been completed on the day the sale deed was executed, the talabs which were performed on February 2, 1946 were performed by the appellants after the right of pre-emption accrued and it was valid talab-i-mowasibab. The contention was not accepted by the majority of the learned Judges. The learned Judge took the view that a sale is not complete until the registration of the sale is complete, and the registration is not completed until section 61 of the Registration Act is complied with, and until the registration is completed the sale does not give rise to any right of pre-emption. According to the learned Judges since admittedly the talab-i-mowasibat was made before registration of the instrument of sale was completed, the talab could not be said to have been validly made. On this view, by the majority judgment the appeal was dis-missed. The learned Judges, however, did not consider it necessary to examine the recitals of the instrument of sale to find out the intention of the parties when the sale was intended to be effective.

20. The minority view is based on consideration of intention of parties gathered from construction of the recitals of the document. According to this view, since the recitals in the document clearly showed the intention of the parties that the sale was to become effective on January 31, 1946, that is, the date when the deed was executed by the vendors, on receiving the entire consideration money and possession delivered to the vendee, the performance of the two talabs by the appellant on February 2, 1946, would be in time, legal, proper and effective to cloth the pre-emptor with a right to demand conveyance in her favour, In taking this view the learned Judges referred to the recitals in the sale deed which contain inter alia:-

"On receipt of the whole and entire amount of consideration money we have put the said claimant, into possession and occupation of this vended property as absolute owner in place of us the executants and our heirs and representatives."

As if to reinforce their statement relating to intention the deed goes on to state after the words of conveyance "I have executed the deed of absolute sale and jointly received Rs. 2,000/- as per recitals in the body."

The recitals also showed that the passing of title the vendee was not to be postponed to any date beyond the date of execution of the document. Intention of the vendor was made further clear by the statement.

"It is desired that the said claimant should enter into and remain in possession and occupation of the vended property as an absolute owner"—

Which was to be from and after the date of the execution of the deed.

21. Another paragraph contains an express stipulation as regards when the transfer should be deemed effective. It says: "This sale deed becomes operative from the date when we the executants affixed signatures thereon. This recital was repeated and reinforced by the following paragraph, wherein dealing with the title of the vendors it is stated that the said title with respect to the vended property has become extinct inoperative and null and void and the same has now been transferred to and acquired by the claimant."

22. Keeping in view the recitals of the sale deed and requirement of section 61 of the Registration Act the learned Judges observed as follows:

"In the face of these recitals, covenants and stipulations which clearly express the intention of the parties that the deed should have effect from the date of its execution it seems to us that the argument that it could be postponed to a later date—either the date when the-registration was complete under the terms of Section 61 of the Indian Registration Act or to February 7, 1947; When on the registration receipts having been handed over to the vendee, 'the vendor received the balance of Rs. 1,400/- is hardly tenable."

According to the learned Judges, as per stipulation in the deed of sale became complete "immediately on the execution of the document on January 31, 1946, the performance of the two talabs by the appellants on February, 5, 1946 would be in time, legal, proper and effective to cloth her with a right to demand a conveyance in her favour." The learned Judges, therefore, allowed the appeal and set aside the judgment of the High Court.

23. In the controversy on the question as to whether it is the principle of the Mohammedan Law would determine the point of time when the sale is taken to be complete or whether in view of enactment of the Transfer of Property Act, it is the statute the former view found favour with the majority of the learned Judges of the Full Bench, of the Allahabad High Court in Begum vs. Mohammad Yakub, ILR 16 All. 344; and this view was approved by the Privy Council in a later case. Of course the Supreme Court of India in Radha Kishan vs. Sreedhar Ramchandra, AIR 1960 SC 1368 ; and Ram Saran Lal vs. Domini Kuer, AIR 1961 SC 1747 hold that the provisions of the Transfer of Property Act superseded the principles of the Mohammedan Law, that is to say, one should look to the statute to find when a sale is complete in order to give rise to the right of pre-emption and not the sale deed. This view has been followed in a number of other cases by different High Courts. With due respect, I find it difficult to agree with the above view. In my opinion the right of pre-emption is not dependent on the completion of sale by registration of the instrument of sale, and the pre-emptor's claim should be determined on the basis of the intention of the parties to complete the sale. In the absence of any express words in the statute, if the right of pre-emption is made dependent on registration of the instrument of sale, the right can be very conveniently defeated by a device adopted by the parties. Once the owner of the immovable property agrees to sale his property and the terms are settled between the vendor and the vendee and consideration money is paid, partly or fully and possession is delivered on the vendee, the vendor ceases to have any right in the property. The owner de facto ceases to have any title to the property, for all practical purpose, after he excites the instrument of sale on accepting the consideration money; and he is only required to complete the formalities of transfer as per requirement of the statute. Once the instrument is executed by the vendor, in the matter of registration of the document the vendor has nothing to do excepting admitting the execution before the registration officer, after the document is presented for registration. Thereafter the rest is to be completed by the Registration Officer as a matter of course. The above proposition gets support from the decision of the Privy Council in Situram Bhaurao Doshmukh vs. Jiaul Hasan Khan, AIR 1923 P.C. 41=48 IA 475. It does not appear from above mentioned decisions that this Privy Council case was at all cited in any of those cases. In this case one of the co-sharers in the property sold to the appellants (Hindus) a part of his undivided share on October 14, 1908 for a consideration of Rs. 29,999/-, Rs. 1,000 was paid on the completion of the negotiation and the remainder was payable in two installments. There was to be a deed of sale, obviously it would be registered. The vendor being a nephew of the plaintiff wrote him a letter on October, 14, 1908 in these terms:

"My dear uncle, I beg to intimate that I have this day sold my one-quarter share in the villages of Waha and Patadhi, for a sum of Rs. 29,999- to,"---the first Appellant and his brothers." As you are in Inamdar of the three-fourths share in the said villages 3, give you this notice that if you are desirous of purchasing the said villages for the sum aforesaid you will be good enough to send me a cheque for the amount, viz Rs. 29,999/-, by return" of post and in the event of your not replying to this or paying the money within two days after receipt hereof, I shall, without any further intimation to you, close the bargain and obtain the sale proceeds."

<u>23. The letter dated October 14, 1908 was not received until the afternoon of 15th, and two days from the date of receipt thereof, which was expressly used in the letter, would not be until the 17th. The uncle replied by a letter dated 17th October. In the letter he claimed his right of pre-emption and thereby performing the ceremonies. The uncle died, and ultimately an Administrator was appointed. The nephew treating the demand for pre-emption as invalid being out of time completed the sale by executing the instrument of sale. Ultimately a suit, for pre-emption was instituted  by the Administrator of the uncle. The main question for fore adjudication at the trial was as to whether the suit for pre-emption was maintainable on the basis of the demands made by the pre-emptor before completion of the sale by registration of the document. The plaintiff succeeded in the trial Court and the decision was affirmed by the High Court. On the question when the sale took place, which was material, inasmuch as; it was with regard to that date that the question whether the requisite religious and other formalities had been performed at the proper time, the learned Judges of the Bombay High Court took the view that for determining the question they thought they ought to look to what the parties represented to each other; and in this respect they followed a decision of the Calcutta High Court in Jadu Lal Sahu vs. Janki Koer (1900) 35 Cal. 575. In that case the question was as to whether there had been a sale for the purpose of determining the application by applying the principle of Mohammedan Law of pre-emption. It was held that the real solution was to be found by determining in each case what was the intention of the parties. On the evidence led by the parties it was held that there was no doubt that the vendor and vendee did not regard the sale complete until the price had been paid and the deed registered. The Hindu purchaser ultimately brought the matter to the Privy Council by special leave. With reference to the recitals of the letter dated October 14, 1908 from the nephew to the uncle informing him his intention to sell the property provided the latter was prepared to purchase the same for the sum of Rs. 29,999/- as agreed by the vendee, within the time fixed therein, their Lordships observed that the effect of the document was an admission that there was a law of pre-emption which was doubtless, from the way in which it was referred to, was a general law. Their Lordships held that it was the general law to which reference should be made to see what these rights were. Their Lordships agreed with the learned Judges of the Bombay High Court in taking the view that the parties represented a full sale as having taken place on October 14, 1908, sufficient to justify the uncle in proceeding at once to perform the ceremonies, treating that the date of execution of sale deed as the crucial time. In this connection their Lordships approved the view taken by Sir John Edge, C.J. of the Allahabad High Court in Begum vs. Mohammad Yakub (1894) 16 All. 344 (F.13.), referred to above. On the question whether the Transfer of Property Act which requires registration to complete a sale of immovable property altered the principle of the Mohammedan Law of pre-emption in respect of performance of the ceremonies claiming pre-emption, the learned Chief Justice observed:</u>

<u>"I cannot think that it was the intention of the Legislature, in passing Act No. IV of 1882" (the Transfer of Property Act), "to alter directly or indirectly the Mohammedan Law of pre-emption as it existed and was understood for centuries prior to the passing of Act No. IV of 1882."</u>

24. Their Lordships of the Privy Council -finding that correct principle had been followed by the High Court, dismissed the appeal, and concluded with the following observation:

"The conclusion is, that, you are to look at the intention of the parties in determining what system of law was, to be taken as applied and what was to be taken to be the date of the sale with reference to which the ceremonies were performed."

Three clear views emerge from the decisions of different superior Courts of the sub-content—

(i)	the right of pre-emption under the Mohammedan Law accrues the moment sale is complete under the Mohammedan Law; and

(ii)	the right of pre-emption under the Mohammedan Law does not accrue until sale is completed by the execution and registration of a deed of transfer ; and registration is not completed until sections 60 and 61 of the Registration Act are complied.

(iii)	For the purpose of making demands one should look at the intention of the parties as to whether sale is governed by the Mohammedan Law, that is, personal law or the general law that is Transfer of Property Act and the Registration Act.

<u>25. The controversy has arisen on the question of determining the point of time when demands for pre-emption are to be made. Valid demand is a pre-requisite for claiming pre-emption under Mohammedan Law. Legal demands are to be made immediately on getting the information about sale of the immovable property. Under the Mohammedan Law, for a valid sale execution of an instrument of transfer is not necessary. For a valid sale requirements are—offer by the vendor, acceptance by the vendee passing of the consideration money, as settled in the contract ; and delivery of possession. After negotiation is complete, the moment the vendor accepts the consideration money and puts the vendee into possession, sale is complete, and it give rises to the right of pre-emption. According to this view, if a pre-emptor claiming his right under the Mohammedan Law is required to wait till the deed of transfer is registered in accordance with sections 60 and 61 of the Registration Act, his right may be defeated by various devices. Reasons for the other view are that section 54 of the Transfer of Property Act supersedes the law of pre-emption as provided under the Mohammedan Law to the extent that the right of pre-emption does not arise until registration of the deed of sale is completed in accordance with the law. These are two extreme views taken by different superior Courts of the sub-continent on the question when the pre-emptor is to make demands in exercising his right. The third view, so to say is a compromise between the first two views. According to this view the intention of the parties ascertainable from the terms of the contract indicating whether sale is governed by the Mohammedan Law or the general law, will determine the time when formal demands are to be made. If the intention of the parties is clear from the terms of the contract for sale, the pre-emptor is not be required to wait till the, deed of transfer is registered. To me third view appears to be fallacious, because, it is not based on sound reasons. It is not difficult to conceive a case when vendor desiring to exclude his co-sharer or contiguous neighbor from exercising his right of pre-emption by adopting a device in agreement with the vendee can postpone registration of the deed of transfer, and thereby defeating the pre-emptor's right.</u>

26. The third view gets support from some of the observations of the Privy Council in A.I.R. 1923 P.C. 41. Relevant portion of the judgment has, been quoted above, that it is within the competence of the parties to state in the contract by agreement as to what system of law would be taken as applied and what would be taken to be the date of the sale. This decision clearly shows that the second view was not approved. Their Lord-ships of the Privy Council approved the view taken by the Allahabad High Court that it was not the intention of the Legislature to alter directly and indirectly the Mohammedan Law of pre-emption. In view of this decision it is no longer a valid proposition that Transfer of Property Act, 1882 superseded the Mohammedan Law of pre-emption. Therefore, observations to the effect that "it would be, against equity, justice and good conscience to apply the Mohammedan Law of sale which is no longer in force" do not provide sound guidance in resolving the controversy.

27. On the question when sale is effected, reference may be made to the decision of the Calcutta High Court in the case of Naresh Chandra Dutta Vs. Girish Chandra Das, LL.R. 62 Calcutta 972. The learned Judges while considering the question when "sale takes place" observed as follows:

"...there may be three points of time at one or other of which the sale can possibly be taken to have been effected, the first is the point of time at which a part of the consideration money having been paid the vendor put the vendee in possession; the second, when the transfer became operative under section 54 of the Transfer of Property Act; and the third, any other point of time at which the parties may have intended the sale to be effective."

<u>28. According to the above mentioned Calcutta decision when the vendor on receiving the consideration money put the vendee into possession of the property transferred, sale has been effected. Thus the sale as contemplated under the Mohammedan Law has been recognized.</u>

<u>The Rules, of Mohammedan Law provide that the formalities are to be strictly performed by the pre-emptor. Delay in observing formalities is fatal to the claim of pre-emption. If the pre-emptor is required to wait until registration is completed observance of the requisite formalities as provided under the Rules of the Mohammedan Law practically loses all significance. Registration of a document is not complete on the day it is presented, that is, endorsements made by the Registering Officer under sections 59 and 60 of the Registration Act. Section 61 of the Registration Act provides that endorsements and certificate referred to and mentioned in sections 59 and 60 shall thereupon be copied into the margin a the Register book and the copy of the map or plan (if any mentioned in section 61 shall be filed in Book No. 1 Registration of the document shall thereupon be deemed complete, and the document shall then be returned to the person who presented the same for registration, or to such other person (if any) as he has. nominated in writing in that behalf on the receipt mentioned in section 52. It is now a matter of common experience that it takes quite a long and indefinite time for complying with the requirements of section 61. If the right of pre-emption is made dependent on completion of registration of the deed of transfer, the pre-emptor would be placed in the most unobvious position, because he will be required to keep a constant watch over the progress of the work in be Registration office; and if he succeeds in getting the information when registration is completed in accordance with section 61 of the Registration Act, then he will exercise his right by observing the formalities. Such observance of the formalities on the completion of registration of the document cannot be said to be in accordance with the Rules of Mohammedan Law.</u>

29. The Mohammedan Law of pre-emption does not provide a right of re-purchase from seller or buyer but it provides right of substitution, entitling pre-emptor to stand in the shoes of the buyer. When the law does not provide for re-purchase, completion of transfer as contemplated under section 54 of the Transfer of Property Act does not appear to be relevant. The law enables the pre-emptor to be accepted as the vendee. Even when the deed of transfer is executed and registered, and thereby transfer is complete and the vendor is divested of his title in the property, on allowing pre-emption it is the vendor who is required to execute the necessary document, in favour of the pre-emptor and not the vendee.

<u>30. In my, opinion pre-emption case relating to immovable property of the value of Tk. 100/- and upwards under the Mohammedan Law, appears to have been unnecessarily fettered by referring to section 54 of the Transfer of Property Act. The transfer in favour of the pre-emptor claiming under the Mohammedan Law, is not in any manner in contravention of section 54 of the Transfer of Property Act. Even under the Transfer of Property Act sale without a registered document is permissible if the tangible immovable property is worth less than Tk. 100/-. In such a case sale as contemplated under the Mohammedan Law has been recognized. It is only in the case of tangible immovable property worth. Tk. 100/- and upwards the requirement of law is that such transfer can be made only by a registered instrument. Section 54 merely provides that transfer of tangible immovable property of the value of Tk. 100/- and upwards can be made only by a registered, instrument, but it does not say as to when sale is effected; which is an essential ingredient in the case of pre-emption. In the Transfer of Property Act there is nothing in section 54 that the property passes as soon as the instrument is registered, because, it is dependent on the intention of the party. Sale as contemplated under the Mohammedan Law provides a sure test of divesting vendor's title in the immovable property sold. I am of the view that the intention of the legislature in passing Transfer of Property Act (Act IV of 1882) was not to alter directly or indirectly the Mohammed Law of pre-emption and as such the law of pre-emption as provided under the Mohammedan Law has not been superseded; and the decisions following contrary view cannot be approved.</u>

<u>31. Even in the case of sale of property worth More than Tk. 100/- by an unregistered deed status of the vendee has been changed by incorporation of section 53-A of the Trans of Property Act. Section 53-A creates rights which were not in existence before the enactment was passed in 1929. This section imports in modified form the equity of part performance as developed in England. By virtue of this section although the' transfer 'has not been completed in the manner prescribed thereof by the law, the transferee's right to possess and enjoy the property is now protected. The transferor or any person claiming under him shall be de-barred from enforcing against the transferee and persons claiming under him any right in respect of the property of which the transferee has taken possessions By the corresponding amendment of section 49 of the Registration Act by inserting a proviso there to, the sale deed though not registered is admissible as evidence of the contract of sale. In view of the above noted provisions, that is, section 53-A of the Transfer of Property Act and amendment, of section 49 of the Registration Act, the status or right of a purchaser of immovable property under an unregistered deed of sale or even under a written contract of sale, is not protected. Keeping in view the provisions of law discussed above I have least hesitation to hold that right of pre-emption under the Mohammedan Law is not dependent on registration of the deed of sale; and therefore, one claiming pre-emption under the Mohammedan Law must make necessary demands on the completion of sale of the property as contemplated under the Mohammedan Law. The moment consideration is paid and possession of the property is given to the vendee the right of pre-emption accrues; and the pre-emption is required to promptly make the necessary demands in accordance with the Rules of Mohammedan Law. The Transfer of Property Act, of course, will apply to effect transfer of title between the parties of property worth Tk. 100/- and above; and both the laws operating in its own field.</u>

<u>32. In the present case the ceremonies were admittedly performed after execution of the sale deed but before its registration. The sale in question could not be treated as complete even under the Mohammedan Law because admittedly possession was not delivered to the purchaser. In the absence of any evidence showing that sale according to the Mohammedan Law was completed, the ceremonies performed by the plaintiff cannot be said to have been performed in accordance with law. Therefore, in the absence of the ceremonies validly, performed, the plaintiff cannot succeed in the suit for pre-emption.</u>

<u>33. On the question of limitation the learned Single Judge of the High Court Division has taken the view that, since the plaintiff was dispossessed from the suit properties only in, 1962 and the suit having been filed on September 28, 1962, the suit was not barred by limitation. The view taken by the learned Judge is not consistent with the view taken on the first question, namely, as to performance of the ceremonies demanding pre-emption. Once the ceremonies are complete in accordance with Mohammedan Law, treating the sale complete, the question of limitation running from the date of dispossession of the plaintiff did not arise of the plaintiff was in possession of the property sold on the date of sale, then filing of the suit could not be deferred beyond one year, from the date of registration. However, in view of the decision on the first question, consideration of the second question has become mere academic and I do not propose to express any opinion on this question in the facts of this case.</u>

<u>In the result, the appeal is allowed with costs. The judgment of the High Court Division is set aside and those of the Courts below are restored.</u>

End.

full_judgment:
Kemaluddin Hossain, C. J:- This appeal arises out of a writ petition wherein the appellants attempted to get an order of the Enemy Property authority declared as without lawful authority but had not succeeded.

2. Facts are that the properties in appeal had been declared as enemy property by the Assistant Custodian of the Enemy Property by his orders dated 29-12-69 and 14-9-70 in E.P. Cases No. 228/70-71, 229/70-71 and 230/70-71. The properties were owned and possessed by (1) Hari Bandhu Nath, son of late Kamini Kumar Nath (2) Promoda Sundari Devi, wife of late Kamini Kumer Nath and (3) Sabitri Prova Devi, wife of late Krishna Bandhu Nath (son of late Kamini Krishna Nath). "The property comprised in E.P. Case No. 22R/70-71 originally belonged to Gour Chandra Karmakar and others and then it was transferred to Krishna Sundar Majumder, who in turn, sold the same to Kamini Kumar Nath by a registered Kabala dated 27-10-43. Kamini Kumar Nath was in possession of the property since his purchase. Kamini Kumar mortgaged the property to Nath Bank (Pakistan) Ltd. by a registered deed of mortgage dated 28-12-44. The Bank filed Mortgage Suit No. 84 of 1954 in the Court of Subordinate Judge, Noakhali against the mortgage on the death of Kamini Kumar, Promoda Sundari Devi and Sabitri Devi were substituted in his place. The suit was disposed of on compromise on 22-9-75. It was claimed that Had Bandhu Nath, Promoda Sundari Devi and Sabitri Devi were nationals of Bangladesh by birth and were permanent residents of Noakhali District and they never migrated to India either after partition or during the Indo-Pakistan War, 1965 nor during the liberation war of 1971. Hari Bandhu Nath, Promoda Sundari and Sahitri Devi sold these properties to the deceased appellant and his son and brother and others by registered kabalas dated 19-8-75 (registered on 20-8-75) It was alleged that respondent Md. Golam Mostafa, a neighbor was trying to grab the property. He moved the authority to treat the said property as abandoned property but when he failed in his attempt, he got the property declared as enemy property by unfair means. An enquiry was made into the matter to ascertain whether the property was an enemy property by Mr. SUM Zahirul Islam, Magistrate, 1st Class, Sadar, and Noakhali. The Magistrate submitted his enquiry report on 3-3-76, on examination of witnesses and held that appellant's vendors never migrated to India either in 1947 or in 1965 or in the year 1971. The enquiry report was not accepted by the Joint Secretary, Land Administration & Land Reforms, Administration Division and he held that the property vested as Non-Resident-Property (Administration Cell), and that the property was rightly declared as Enemy Property by the Assistant Custodian. This order was passed on 5-10-76. The appellant being aggrieved by the aforesaid order of the Joint Secretary moved the High Court Division under Article 102 of the Constitution.

3. The dispute centered round the question whether the vendors of the deceased appellant migrated from the then East Pakistan some time before the war of Indo-Pakistan in 1965. The High Court Division held that it was a disputed question of fact and so it could not be decided in the writ jurisdiction, and the learned Judges were of the view that the order passed by the Enemy Property authority declaring the property as enemy would stand and that is under challenge.

4. Leave was granted to consider whether the High Court Division has rightly allocated the onus on the appellant about the migration of his vendors and whether the property could be declared as enemy property in 1975 and whether the High Court Division was correct in holding that the question of migration being a disputed fact the order of the Enemy Property authority would stand.

<u>5. On hearing Mr. M.H. Khondoker, learned Counsel for the appellant and Mr. Anwarul Huq Chowdhury, Deputy Attorney-General who appeared on 26-11- 79 for Respondents 1 and 2, it appears that a question of law was raised in the writ petition which the learned Judges of the High Court Division have not considered but Which has a bearing on the merit of writ petition in that the property in question was mortgaged to Nath Bank by the predecessor of the vendors of the appellant and the mortgage suit was compromised and the property released in favors of the vendors of the appellant who got the property by a Kabala and also got possession. If the property was declared an enemy property, it is not explained how the mortgage suit could proceed till 1975 long after coming into operation of the enemy property laws without the said, authority being impleaded. Apart from this, the appellant has asserted his possession in the property and the Government in their affidavit-in-opposition though has challenged the validity of the sale deeds yet have admitted that the appellant was in possession after his purchase on 20-8-75. On these unchallenged facts, we come to the first question to see whether the High Court Division has allocated the onus on the parties on right principle. The other grounds of the leave order are defendant on the first facts. The High Court Division has proceeded on the basis that the appellant has not been able to establish that the predecessors of the vendors of the appellant or they never migrated to India, a fact which has been characterized as a disputed one on which the High Court Division has refrained from deciding. It is an admitted case of both parties that the predecessors of the appellant were Pakistani nationals and the appellant on purchase of the properly from his vendors is in possession of the property and it requires to be explained by the Enemy Property authority or the Government, which has not been attempted at all. How the property could be treated as enemy property. It was for the Enemy Property authority, in the premises of the facts to establish that the predecessor of the vendors of the appellant or they, in fact, migrated to India earlier to the Enemy Property law came into operation in 1965, so that the property left by them came within the mischief of enemy property law but the High Court Division has erroneously assumed as a fact which the Enemy Property authority was to prove. The onus was misplaced on the appellant. This finding which is based on wrong allocation of onus cannot be sustained. It has been stated earlier that the appellant's possession of the property, the pendency of the mortgage suit from 1954 to 1975 and the total lack of any evidence from the side of Enemy Property authority that the vendors of the appellants ever migrated to India make it manifest that, the challenged order declaring the property in question as enemy property was without jurisdiction. The decision on the first ground covers the third ground of leave order and the appeal succeeds on these two grounds, and so the second need not be discussed in this appeal. In that view of the matter, the order of the High Court Division cannot stand.</u>

<u>In the result, this appeal is allowed without any order as to cost. The order of the High Court Division is set aside and the impugned order of the Enemy Property authority is declared to be illegal and without any lawful authority.</u>

End.

lawyer:
M. Golam Rabbani, Ranesh Chandra Moitra ------ For the Petitioner. 
M. M. Haque ------ For the Respondents.
parties:
Hiralal Agarwala ------ Petitioner.
Vs.
Deputy Commr. Bogra & ors ------ Respondents.
full_judgment:
Shahabuddin Ahmed, J.-These 2 Rules under Article 102 of the Constitution have been heard together and are going to be disposed of by this judgment as common question of law and facts are involved in them. This relates to certain Order of the Additional Deputy Commissioner (Revenue), Bogra treating certain property as enemy and vested property and also certain action in taking over possession of the property.

2. In writ Petition No. 609 of 1977, the petitioner Hiralal Agarwala claims that a piece of land measuring 5.31 acres within Kahaloo police station, as described in the petition belonged to him to his late paternal uncle Prahallad Agarwala and one Hiralal Agarwala. Hiralal Agarwala got 8 annas share whereas the remaining 8 annas share belonged to him (petitioner) and his uncle Pahallad Agarwala. His uncle was childless all his life, and, as such, had entrusted to him the duty to look after all his properties. The petitioner entered into a partnership business under a registered partnership deed dated 30.12.58. with Hariram Agarwala for carrying on business under the style and name Sree Balajee Rice Mills, on a part of their land. Petitioner's share in the business is 8 annas and since the establishment of this Rice Mill, the petitioner and his partner Hariram Agarwala have been carrying on the business till 5.2.75 when Hariram Agarwala transferred his 8 annas share in the business as well as in the land to one Mukabbar Hossain Talukder, respondent No. 5. The petitioner then entered into another partnership business under registered-partnership deed dated 5.2.75 with Mukabbar Hossain Talukder and has been carrying on business with Mukabbar Hossain since then. But on some false representation the Revenue Deputy Collector, Bogra, respondent No. 5, went to the premises of the Rice Mill on 3.9.76 and stated that the Mill was an Enemy Property and as such it would be leased out. The petitioner, apprehending immediate danger of dispossession filed a suit-O.C. Suit No. 232 of 1976 in the Court of Subordinate Judge, Bogra but the Additional Deputy Commissioner by his Order dated 28.8.76 declared the entire property including the land and the Rice Mill as Enemy Property which vested in the Government and proceeded to lease it out; on the order of the Deputy Commissioner the Revenue Deputy Collector took possession of the 8 annas share in the property on 2.9.76 and after 5 days leased it out to respondent No. 5. In view of this dispossession the petitioner failed to obtain an order of temporary injunction in his suit which was then withdrawn and this Court was moved under Article 102 of the Constitution.

3. The case of the petitioner is that he has got both right and title as well as possession in the 8 annas share of the entire property including land and business and this share was never an enemy property to vest in the Government. The impugned order and action of the Government, as stated above, are without lawful authority and malafide.

4. The respondent, Government of Bangladesh, contested the Rule by filing affidavit in opposition denying altogether the petitioner's claim of ownership and title in the 8 annex of the property including the Rice Mill. Their contention is that Parallax Agarwala who had 8 annals share in the property was a lift long bachelor and he went to India before 1965 whereupon his 8 annas share in the property automatically became an enemy property which ultimately vested in the Government; the petitioners got no right, title at all in this 8 annas share of Prahallad Agarwala. As to the business under the name and style Sree Balajee Rice Mill, the contention of respondents is that the Rice Mill also belonged to Prahallad Agarwala in which the petitioner did not contribute anything but he was simply a partner in the business with Prallad's co-sharer Hariram Agarwala. Both the Rice Mill and Land in respect of 8 annas share having become enemy property ultimately vesting in the Government the impugned order of the respondent Government is perfectly wrongful and there is malafide in it. Further contention of the respondent is that the petitioner took resort to falsehood by setting up one Laxmi Devi respondent No. 4 widow of Prahallad Agarwala whereas Prahallad Agarwala died bachelor ; in the said O.C. Suit No. 232 of 1977 which was filed by the petitioner along with the said Laxmi Devi praying for declaration of their title to the 8 annas share of property it was withdrawn by them when a written statement was filed by the respondents disclosing the real facts and when the Civil Suit for title was withdrawn, the petitioner is not entitled to the remedy under writ jurisdiction as an order under Article 102 of the Constitution in this case would amount to declaration of the petitioner title which had failed to be proved in the Civil Court.

5. In Writ petition No. 610 of 1977 the same petitioner Hiralal Agarwala has challenged certain action of the same Additional Deputy Commissioner, Borga in treating another property consisting of Rice, Oil and Flour Mills at Talura as an Enemy Property allegedly having belonged to same Prahallad Agarwala who went to India before 1965. In this case, the petitioner's claim is that he had purchased by 2 registered kabalas in the year 1963 and 1965 the entire land at Talura as described in the petition by valuable consideration and that he, with his own money, established Flour, Rice and Oil Mills and it was never an enemy property. The Rule was contested by the respondents, the Government of Bangladesh and others taking the contention that the said property was purchased by Prahallad Agarwala the benami of his nephew, the petitioner Hiralal Agarwala and as such when it became an enemy property and vested ultimately in the Government, the respondents were justified in treating the property as an enemy property. The petitioner in this case also was dispossessed by the respondents who already leased out the land as an Enemy (vested) Property.

<u>6. We shall take up the Writ Petition No. 610 of 1977 first as the facts are rather very simple. The petitioner has produced 2 registered sale-deeds showing that he had purchased the land in question. As against these registered instruments respondents failed to prove and produce anything to show that the land was purchased by Prahallad Agarwala. The only basis of their claim is that Prahallad had purchased it in the benami of his new phew, the petitioner. But in absence of any evidence we failed to understand how the Additional Deputy Commissioner could treat it, the land, having been purchased by Prahallad Agarwala in the benami of his nephew unless it has been declared in a competent Court that the transaction was benami and that the real purchaser was Prahallad Agarwala who went over to India and became an alien enemy, the Additional Deputy Commissioner or for that purpose the Custodian of Enemy Property have no authority to treat as an enemy property. Onus of proof that it is a benami transaction lies heavily upon the person who raised this question. The impugned action of the respondent in treating the property i.e. the Rice, Oil and Flour Mills at Talura as an Enemy and Vested Property is illegal and without any lawful authority and as such this action not only declaring the property as vested but also taking possession thereof must be interfered with.</u>

7. Now coming to the other petition, petition No. 609 of 1977 we have heard Mr. M, Golam Rabbani, the learned Advocate for the petitioner and Mr. M. M. Huq, the learned Assistant Attorney General appearing for the respondent Government. The facts which are not disputed in this case are that Prahallad Agarwala and Hariram Agarwala were the recorded owners of the land measuring 5.31 acre in equal shares. Petitioner's claim that he got some share in the 8 annas share of his uncle Prahallad Agarwala has no basis or any evidence except his oral claim. As such this claim cannot be accepted and it is, therefore, found that Prahallad Agarwala was the owner of the 8 annas share of this land. As to Prahallad Agarwala there is also no basis of the petitioner's claim that Prahallad Agarwala remained in India and thereafter in Bangladesh till 1971. On the other hand, the contention of the respondent is that Prahallad Agarwala went over to India before 1965 where he died appears to be borne out by facts as such he was an enemy alien and in his absence his share of the property became an enemy property under the Defence of Pakistan Rules and thereafter it vested in the Government. The petitioner along with one Laxmi Devi filed a Title Suit No. 232 of 1977 for declaration of their title to 8 annas share of the property left by Prahallad Agarwala but the suit was ultimately withdrawn. We need, not discuss whether Prahallad Aagrwala had left any widow or he died a bachelor put since Laxmi Devi respondent No. 4 is not coming before us claiming to be an heir of Prahallad Agarwala the petitioner's claim is to be rejected outright. But the case of the petitioner is that even if he got no right, title in the 8 annas share of Prahallad Agarwala he got right, title as well as possession in the 8 annas share of the business under name and style Sree Balajee Rice Mill which was set up under registered partnership deed dated 31.12.58 and as such this 11 annas share in the business Which never belonged to Prahallad Agarwala is not an Enemy Property and never vested in the Government. Mr M. M. Huq does not dispute the partnership deed, Annexure A dated 30.12.58 does not challenge this partnership deed which is a registered one. But his contention is that this relates to a partnership in the businesses between the petitioner and Hariram Agarwala but the petitioner did not contribute any capital and since the Rice Mill was set up in the land which belonged to Prahallad Agarwala and his co-sharer Hariram Agarwala it is presumed that the Mill belonged to these 2 co-sharers. But recital in the partnership deed does not support Mr. Huq since there is nothing mentioned in it as to what would be the relation between the petitioner Hiralal Agarwala and his uncle Prahallad Agarwala in respect of the Rice Mill. It is true that the land on which the Rice Mill was set up did not belong to the petitioner. But his partnership deed also does not say anything whether the petitioner, one of the 2 partners in the business, would be treated as a licensee or lessee in respect of the portion of the land covered by Rice Mill. The partnership deed simply shows that the 2 partners, Hiralal Agarwala and Hariram Agarwala, would have equal share in the business profits. Mr. Huq contends that at least this recital shows that the petitioner did not contribute any-thing to the capital of the business. Similarly it does not also show that Prahallad contributed anything by way of capital either. That Prahallad Agarwala was 8 annas owner in respect of the land does not necessarily show that he had contributed the 50% of the Rice Mill and started business. Unless it is shown that 8 annas share in the business and the Rice Mill belonged to Prahallad Agarwala this 8 annas share could not have been treated as Enemy Property. Admittedly, the petitioner has been in joint possession and control as well as management of this business since 1958 along with his partner Hariram Agarwala and if the land did not belong to him he could not be treated as trespasser either, for when he entered into the land for the purpose of business he was certainly authorised by the other owner, namely, Prahallad. That without approval he could not have become a partner in the business in that land. Mr Huq has stressed that there is no evidence to show that the petitioner got any share in the capital. The petitioner may not have any share in the capital but he has certainly got 8 annas share in the business property and this interest in the business cannot be affected by the declaration of the property i.e. the land is vested property. Mr. Rabbani has submitted that there is no disturbance at all so Iong the petitioners original business partner Hariram Agarwala is there. But disturbance started when respondent No. 5 Mokabbar purchased the 8 annas share of Hariram Agarwala. It further appears that respondent No. 5 also entered into a partnership under registered partnership deed dated 5.2.75 with the petitioner. That had 8 annas share in possession of the  petitioner been an Enemy Properly and subsequently vested then respondent No. 5 would not have entered such partnership business. From this fact it is clear that it is respondent No. 5 Mokabbar Hossain who manipulated everything in the matter so as to oust the petitioner from his share in the business. The impugned order dated 28.8.76 so far as it affected the petitioner's right in the Rice Mill and business is found to be without any lawful authority no matter the petitioner got no right, title in the land which originally belonged to Prahallad Agarwala and now vested in the Government.

<u>8. In the result, the Rule in Writ Petition No. 610 of 1977 is made absolute and the impugned action treating it as a vested property and leaving it out to some other person is declared to have been without lawful authority and of no legal effect. The Rule in Writ Petition No. 609 of 1977 is made absolute to the extent that the order of the Additional Deputy Commissioner treating the Rice Mill and business as the vested property and leasing cut of the property is declared to have been made without any lawful authority and of no legal effect. The respondents are directed to pay costs in Writ Petition No. 610 of 1977 which we assessed at Taka 2000,00 and there is no cost in Writ Petition No. 609 of 1977.</u>

Rafiqur Rahman J.—I agree.

End.

parties:
Salimuddin Munshi and another ----- Petitioners
Vs.
Abdur Rashid Mridha and another ----- opposite Parties
full_judgment:
This Rule was issued at the instance of the petitioners directing the opposite party No. 1 to show cause as to why the judgment and decree dated 29.9.1993 and 7.10.1993 respectively passed by the learned Additional Assistant Judge, Gazipur Sadar, Gazipur in Title Suit No. 100 of 1992 should not be set aside.

2. The facts of the case are, that the opposite-party No. 1 as plaintiff filed Title Suit No. 44 of 1991 against the present petitioners and opposite party No. 2 under section 9 of the Specific Relief Act for recovery of Khas possession of the suit land described in the plaint stating, inter alia, that he purchased the suit land from the real owner by two registered sale deeds dated 25-7-1984 and 28-10-1981 respectively, and since purchase he has been possessing the same on payment of rent. Thereafter defendant Nos. 1 and 2 tried to dispossess him from the land and the plaintiff filed a Title Suit being No. 81 of 1990 praying for permanent injunction and got a decree against him. Subsequently while the plaintiff opposite-party was in possession of the land the defendant petitioners dispossessed him from the suit land on 4-12-1991 and then the plaintiff opposite party filed a suit being No. 100 of 1992 under section 9 of the Specific Relief Act for recovery of khas possession of the suit land. The present petitioners contested the suit by filing a written statement stating, inter alia, that the plaintiffs are not the real owner of the suit land and that they never possessed the suit land. The learned Assistant Judge after hearing both the parties decreed the suit against the petitioners. Being aggrieved at this judgment and decree the petitioners preferred this petition under section 115 (1) of the Code of Civil Procedure and obtained the present Rule.

3. The learned Advocate for the petitioner submits that the defendant petitioners have no interest in the suit land and they have dispossessed the plaintiff opposite party on 4.12.1991 and that in the deposition PWs 2 and 3 stated that one Mr. Shamsul Huq constructed a tin-shed but on the suit land and has been possessing the same since 1991 and that the said Shamsul Huq is not made party in the suit. He further submits that since the petitioners have no interest in the suit land, the plaintiff-opposite party has filed this suit against wrong persons and, as such, the judgment and decree passed by the court below is not binding upon the petitioners. It appears from the lower court records that the opposite party No. 1 filed a suit for permanent injunction being Title Suit No. 81 of 1990 in the Court of the learned Senior Assistant Judge, Gazipur against the present petitioners and in that suit the petitioners contested and opposite party No. 1 got a decree on 8-5-1991. It shows that the opposite party No. 1 had possessed the suit land having prima facie good title. It is alleged that the petitioners dispossessed the opposite party No. 1 on 4.12.1991. The court below after discussing the evidence disbelieved the petitioners previous possession in the suit land and believed that the petitioners dispossessed the opposite party No. 1 who is the plaintiff of the suit, on 4.12.1991. PWs 2 and 3 admitted that one Shamsul Huq constructed tin shed but on the suit land about two years back. These two PWs. deposed before the court in the month of August, 1993. Accordingly, Shamsul Huq's possession in the suit land was from August, 1991, that is, after filing the suit before the Court by the opposite party No. 1 against the petitioners under section 9 of the Specific Relief Act. So Shamsul Huq was not in possession in the suit land when the suit was filed and, as such, question of adding him as party did not at all arise. There is nothing in the evidence on record that the petitioners had no possession in the suit land before 4.12.91. I find no error in the findings of the lower court. Accordingly, I find no substance in the submission of the learned Advocate for the petitioners.

4. Mvi. Md. Wahidullah, the learned Advocate for the opposite party, submitted that in the present application the court cannot go into the title matter of the suit and that the only question before this court is to see whether the court below did irregularity or illegality or any error with resulting failure of justice. He draws our attention to section 9 of the Specific Relief Act which reads as follows:

"If any person is dispossessed without his consent of immovable property otherwise than in due course of law, he or any person claiming through him may, by suit 8....... recover possession thereof notwithstanding any other title that may be set up in such suit.

Nothing in this section shall bar any person from suing to establish his title to such property and to recover possession thereof.

No suit under this section shall be brought against 9 (the 10 Government.)

No appeal shall lie from any order or decree passed in any suit instituted under this section, nor shall any review of any such order or decree be allowed".

<u>5. He referred to a decision reported in 39 DLR 8 (Bisheswar Dutta vs. Sree Copal Chandra Dey and others). In that case his Lordship held that, "The above provision clearly lays down that if a person who has, without his consent, been dispossessed of immovable property otherwise than in due course of law, he is entitled to recover possession thereof by filing a suit. A plea of title is no defence in the suit and any decision that may be made in the suit will be subject to a title suit which may be eventually filed and the person who has title or even a better right shall be competent to ask for recovery of the property on establishment of such right. As the question of title of the respective parties is kept beyond the purview of such a suit the real intendment behind this provision seems to be to provide a quick remedy by way of restitution of possession only. Under section 9 of the Specific Relief Act, the court has therefore, no power to pass a decree for removal or demolition of structures." It appears that the learned Assistant Judge has considered the evidence on record and come to a clear finding that the plaintiff was in possession of the suit land and the present petitioner dispossessed him on 4.12.1991 and the plaintiff filed the suit within time. Accordingly, I do not find that the learned Assistant Judge has committed any error of law or of procedure in arriving at the said finding. So I find substance in the submission made by the learned Advocate for the opposite party No. 1.</u>

6. It is not out of place to mention that the opposite party No. 2 is the Government who is a proforma defendant No. 3 of the suit. Though section 9 of the Specific Relief Act debarred any person to bring any suit against the Government, opposite party No. 1 made Government as party without claiming any relief against her. So, Government is neither a necessary party nor a proper party in the suit and, as such, the suit is not affected by making the Government as proforma defendant in the suit.

<u>7. For the reasons stated above I maintained the impugned judgment and decree of the learned Assistant Judge for recovery of Khas possession of the land in suit.</u>

<u>8. In the result, the Rule is accordingly discharged without any order as to costs. Send down the lower court records at once.</u>

End.

lawyer:
MA Wahab Miah, Advocate, instructed by Md. Aftab Hossain, Advocate-on-Record — For the Appellant. 
Sirajuddin Ahmed Advocate-on-Record (absent) — For Respondent Nos. 1-2.
