full_judgment:
D. C. Bhattacharya, J.—This appeal by special leave is against an order of a Division Bench of the Dacca High Court refusing to exercise its revisional jurisdiction to interfere with an order of appointment of a receiver under Order 40 rule 1 of the Code of Civil Procedure in a suit for partition in which appellants are Defendants No 6 and 7.

2. Respondents No. 1 to 8 instituted Partition Suit No. 90 of 1965 in the Court of Sub-ordinate Judge, Dinajpur on 13.8.65 for partition of the properties described in the schedule to the plaint. It has been alleged in the plaint that the disputed properties originally belonged to one Kasturi Chand Bermecha, the predecessor of the plaintiffs, who belonged to the Mitaksara School of Hindu Law, that defendants No. 1 to 5 are co-parceners of the plaintiffs, that different co-sharers have made over possession of some of the joint properties to defendant Nos. 6 and 7 with a view to transfer the said properties; that defendants. No. 9-27 and 34 are Bharatia tenants, that Defendant No. 28, the Deputy Commissioner, Dinajpur is also a Bharatia tenant in respect of a godown under requisition and that other defendants have been impleaded as they claim some interest in the disputed properties.

After the institution of the suit, hostilities between India and Pakistan broke out on the 6th September, 1965 and the Emergency Laws came into force.

3. On 12.6.67 an application was filed on behalf of defendant No. 28, the Deputy Commissioner of Dinajpur, for transposing the said defendant No. 28 to the category of the plaintiff and permitting him to prosecute the suit on behalf of the plaintiffs. It was stated in the application that the plaintiffs and the principal defendants being Indian Nationals and having resided in India the disputed properties had vested in the applicant defendant under the emergency laws in force, that in the absence of the Indian nationals several interested parties who were proforma defendants in the said suit had been causing damages to the properties and had been attempting to misappropriate the said properties on the plea of false and fraudulent kabalas or exchange deeds and that the applicant defendant being Assistant Custodian of Enemy Property was entitled to prosecute the said suit. The said application was allowed on the 28.6.67 and Defendant No. 28 was transposed to the category of the plaintiff as plaintiff No. 9.

4. Thereafter an application was filed on that date for appointment of a receiver of the disputed properties whereupon the learned Subordinate Judge by another order on the same date appointed Mr. Abdur Rahman, Advocate as receiver of the properties in suit.

5. An affidavit appears to have been filed on the same date on behalf of the original plaintiffs and defendant Nos. 1 to 4 in which it was stated that item Nos. 1-15 and 18 of schedule 'kha' were homestead and shop preimses and the properties described in item Nos. 16 and 17 were agricultural land measuring 14-8 acres, that defendant Nos. 6 and 7 were claiming interest in the disputed properties on the basis of a deed of exchange purported to have been executed by defendant Nos. 2 and 5, that the said two defendants were wrongfully realising rent from the tenants and that they were trying to take other properties in suit in their possession and to withdraw the deposited arrear rent, that plaintiff Nos. 1 to 8 and defendant Nos. 1-5 and defendant Nos. 29-33 were residing in India, that due to the state of emergency in both the countries the said plaintiffs and defendants were not looking after their properties, that in the circumstances defendants No. 6 and 7 were using the properties according to their will, availing themselves of the absence of the aforesaid plaintiffs and defendants, and that they were trying to dispose of the disputed properties mentioned as item Nos. 16 and 17 and cause various kinds of harm to the other properties.

6. Defendant Nos. 6 and 7 appeared in the suit for the first time on 3.7.67 on which date they filed an application praying for vacating the order dated 28.6.67 appointing the receiver, stating, inter alia, that no notice of the suit or of appointment of the receiver was served upon them, that they were in possession of the disputed properties on the basis of various deeds of exchange and that they did carry on jute business on some parts of the disputed properties.

7. The learned Subordinate Judge appears to have taken the view that the said application was not bonafide inasmuch as Defendant Nos. 6 and 7 did not put in any appearance and have not filed any written statement in the suit as yet and observed that defendants 6 and 7 might file written statement, if any, by 29.7.67 and directed to keep their application in abeyance till the said date.

8. Defendants No. 6 and 7 without filing any written statement as directed moved the High Court at Dacca with an application under section 115 of the Code of Civil Procedure, on which a Rule was issued and the said Rule was discharged by a Bench of the said High Court on 28.7.71. Although it has been pointed out in the judgment of the High Court that the impugned order was appealable and that its such the revisional application was not maintainable, the learned Judges, considered the said application on merits and found that there was no substance in the said application.

9. Special leave to appeal has been granted by this Court to the appellants to consider 3 points namely (i) whether further proceeding in the suit was barred under section 83(2) of the Code of Civil Procedure without permission of the Central Government (ii) whether the Deputy Commissioner had any legal authority to join himself in the suit as plaintiff, as the Deputy Commissioner was not an Asstt. Custodian of Enemy Property for lands and buildings and (iii) whether the trial Court was competent to effect dispossession of Defendants 6 and 7, who were in physical possession, by appointment of a receiver, in view of sub-rule (2) of Rule of Order 40 of the Code.

<u>10. It should be pointed out that none of these grounds were pressed either in the Trial Court or before the High Court and ordinarily a party is not allowed to raise such questions for the first time in the highest tribunal as certain questions of fact naturally arise in connection with such grounds. However, as the questions are of general public importance, leave was granted to consider these questions.</u>

11. Mr. Khondker Mahbubuddin Ahmed, the learned Counsel on behalf of the appellants, has submitted at the outset that he would not press the ground No. 2 as he has come to learn that the Deputy Commissioner, Dinajpur became an Assistant Custodian of Enemy Property by virtue of Govt. Notification by which all Deputy Commissioners of the districts were appointed Assistant Custodian of Enemy Property for lands and buildings lying within the area of the respective districts. He has, however, pressed the other two grounds before this Court. But, in our opinion, none of these grounds has any force.

12. Under section 83(2) of the Code of Civil Procedure no alien enemy residing in Pakistan without permission of the Central Govt. or residing, in a foreign country could sue in a Court in Pakistan. In the present case it was not an enemy alien who was seeking to prosecute the suit but it was the Deputy Commissioner, Dinajpur who sought to prosecute the suit as a plaintiff and prayed for appointment of a receiver for the said object. The learned Counsel for the appellants has, however, contended that the Deputy Commissioner being none other than the representative of an enemy alien, the disability which had been created under section 83 of the Code would automatically attach to him. We have failed to appreciate this argument of the learned Counsel. The disability or the incompetence as has been enjoined under the statute is for the purpose of preventing an enemy alien from reaping any benefit out of a legal proceeding during the continuance of a state of war. Moreover, since during such a state of war, it is not generally possible for enemy aliens to act or move for the purpose of their normal avocations of life, provisions were made in the Emergency Laws such as Defence of Pakistan Ordinance and the Rules framed thereunder, for taking custody of the properties of enemy aliens and for management and protection of the said properties during this period of the abnormal conditions. As regards the lands and buildings, which the disputed properties are, provisions were made in rule 182 of Defence of Pakistan Rules for the vesting of the said properties in the Custodian, Addl. Custodian, Dy. Custodian and Assistant Custodian of Enemy Property and for conferring and imposing on the said Custodian, Addl. Custodian, Dy. Custodian, Assistant Custodian such rights duties and responsibilities, as might be prescribed, in respect of the property vested in them. In exercise of the powers under rule 182(1)(b) of Defence of Pakistan Rules was the Government concerned issued a notification dated 3.12.65 where-under all enemy properties not connected with an enemy firm were purported to have been vested in Deputy Custodian of Enemy Property (Lands and Buildings) with effect from the said date. Under a subsequent notification all Deputy Commissioners were made Assistant Custodians of Enemy Properties (Land and Buildings) and were invested with all the powers of Deputy Custodian in respect of the said properties.

<u>13. The properties in suit which belonged to Indian nationals became enemy properties after the promulgation of Defence of Pakistan Ordinance and the Rules framed thereunder on the out-break of war between Pakistan and India in September, 1965 and the said properties vested in the Assistant Custodian of Enemy Properties (Land and Buildings) Dinajpur who happened to be the Deputy Commissioner of the district by virtue of the Notification dated 3.12.65. The rights and duties with which the Assistant Custodian of Enemy Property were invested for the purpose of preservation and Management of the properties of alien enemies had statutory foundation and are legal personality of such an Assistant Custodian of Enemy Property was entirely distinct and different from that of an enemy alien whose properties had vested in the said Assistant Custodian of Enemy Property. The whole object of the legislation dealing with the properties of enemy aliens was to see that the enemy alien did not derive any benefit from the said properties and also to set up a machinery for preservation, management and disposal of the said properties which the owners of the said properties were incapable of doing during the period of the state of belligerency. The provision of Section 83 of the Code of Civil Procedure does not apply to a Custodian, Deputy Custodian, or an Assistant Custodian of Enemy Property in terms nor does the principle underlying the said provision made any of them amenable to the disabilities of the said provision.</u>

14. The Enemy Property (Custody and Registration) Order, 1965 was promulgated under sub-rule (1) of the rule 182 of the Defence of Pakistan Rules conferring specific powers upon the Custodian of Enemy Property including an Assistant Custodian of Enemy Property for management and preservation of enemy properties. Under paragraph 4(1) of the said Order, the Custodian including an Assistant Custodian might take such measure as he considered necessary or expedient for preserving the property of the enemy, and under sub-paragraph (2)(iv) of paragraph 4, the Custodian, including an Assistant Custodian was entitled to institute, defend or continue any suit or other legal proceedings, refer any dispute to arbitration and compromise any debts claims or liabilities. This provision clearly authorised Deputy Commissioner, Dinajpur acting as the Assistant Custodian of Enemy Property to take appropriate steps in the partition suit in question for the preservation of the properties involved, most of which appear to have been enemy properties within the meaning of the Defence of Pakistan Rules.

<u>15. We have already pointed out that section 83 of the Code of Civil Procedure did not in terms apply to the Assistant Custodian of Enemy Property in whom the disputed properties of the enemy aliens had vested. Even if it is imagined as has been suggested in course of the argument on behalf  of the appellants, that the principle of section 83 of the Code of Civil Procedure would be applicable to the case of an Assistant Custodian of Enemy Property as he was managing the properties on behalf of the enemy aliens there would be, in such a ease, it conflict between the provision of Section 83 of the Civil Procedure Code and the Emergency Legislations embodying Enemy Property (Custody and Registration) Order, 1965. It may be pointed out that the Emergency Legislation, which was a special legislation subsequently made, must be deemed to have superseded the general provision of Section 83 C.P. Code which was previously made. The position was also made explicitly clear by section 4 of the Defence of Pakistan Ordinance which provided that any rule made under the Ordinance and any order made under any such rule should have effect notwithstanding its inconsistency with any other enactment.</u>

16. In support of the contention that section 83 of the Code of Civil Procedure has no application to the present case, the learned Counsel for the respondent relied upon a decision of the Dacca High Court in the case Hajee Nurul Islam Chowdhury and others. Vs. The Patya Tea Company Limited (1968) 20 DLR (Dac.) 54 in PLD 1969 Dacca 946 in which it has been held on the basis of the aforesaid provision of section 4 of the Defence of Pakistan Ordinance that in case of conflict, the provision of Enemy Property (Custody and Registration) Order, 1965 will prevail over the provision of Civil Procedure Code and the Custodian does not require special permission from the Central Government for prosecuting a legal proceeding. We approve of this decision which in our opinion has correctly applied the law.

We therefore, hold that there is no substance in the contention of the learned Counsel on this point.

17. The other ground urged by the learned Counsel for the appellants is that there cannot be any appointment of a receiver in respect of the properties in possession of defendants Nos. 6 and 7, as none of the parties to the suit have present right to remove them from the possession of the said properties, as contemplated in sub-rule (2) of Order 40, rule 1 of the Code. The appellants are parties to the suit as defendant Nos. 6 and 7 and they claim right, title and interest in the disputed properties on the basis of some deeds of exchange alleged to have been executed by some of the admitted co-sharers and, therefore, it is submitted, they are not liable to be removed from the possession of the properties in which they are in rightful possession.

<u>18. Sub-rule (2) which purports to exclude the operation of the provision as to the Court's power of removal of any person from possession of a property by appointing a receiver in the case of the "person whom any party to the suit has not a present right so to remove" is a kind of limitation on the Court's power as embodied in clause (b) of sub-rules (1). This sub-rule gave rise, in the past, to a judicial controversy, as to its true meaning and scope. The majority of the High Courts in the Indian sub-continent have taken the view that the words 'any person' in sub-rule (2) should be understood in a restricted sense and the said sub-rule has no application to a person who is a party to the suit. That is to say, the restriction or limitation in the Court's power of removal, as contemplated in the said sub-rule is not attracted in a case where the person who is to be removed from possession by appointment of receiver is a party to the suit.</u>

<u>19. The Allahabad High Court has, on the other 'hand, took a contrary view in the Full Bench case of Anadilal and others Vs. Ram Sarup and others, A.I.R. 1936 All. 495 in holding that the words any person in sub-rule (2) were wide and comprehensive enough to include both persons who were parties and persons who were non-parties. Sulaiman, C. J. as he then was, in delivering the leading judgment of the Bench stressed upon the plain and general language used in sub-rule (2), which, according to him, should be understood in their proper and ordinary meaning and also observed that to interpret the said words in a different way would have the effect of interpolating in the said provision, after the words, 'any person certain new words which were not there, viz. 'other than the parties to the suit'.</u>

<u>The said Allahabad case arose out of a suit for sale on a simple mortgage, and in dismissing an application for appointment of a receiver in such a suit it was held by the Full Bench that as none of the parties to the suit had any present right to remove the mortgagor from possession of the mortgaged property inasmuch as the said mortgagor had the right to remain in possession of the said property till it was sold in pursuance of a decree for sale which might be passed in the said suit, no receiver could be appointed by removing such a person from possession.</u>

20. The Allahabad High Court applied the literal rule of interpretation of statutes in construing the sub-rule without noticing it may be respectfully pointed out the ineffectiveness of the entire provision relating to appointment of receiver, which might result from adoption of the said interpretation.

<u>21. According to section 94(d) of the Code, the Court may, if it is so prescribed, appoint a receiver of any property in order to prevent the ends of justice from being defeated, and Order 40 rule 1(1) of the Code has prescribed that whenever it appears to the Court to be just and convenient the Court may appoint a receiver of any property, whether before or after the decree, remove any person from the possession or custody of the property and commit the same to the possession, custody or management of the receiver. It has been made clear in the said provision that the power to appoint a receiver may be exercised in a suit before the passing of the decree as well as after the passing of the decree. Appointment of a receiver is a kind of interim measure, very often taken recourse to in a suit by way of an interlocutory proceeding, for keeping certain property in the possession of the Court, pending the final adjudication of a certain dispute in the suit, so that the benefit accruing from the said adjudication in favour of any party to the suit, may not .be destroyed or impaired. The powers which can be conferred upon a receiver under sub-rule (1) of Order 40, rule 1 are inter alia, for the realisation, management, protection, preservation and improvement of the said property during the pendency of a certain litigation If the Court is to be satisfied under sub-rule (2) before appointing a receiver as to the present right of a party to the suit to remove another party from the possession of the property in question, there can hardly be found a suit where a receiver can be appointed before the passing of the decree, as the present right to remove a party from the possession of the property can be determined only by the decree in the suit, if such a right is in issue in the said suit. In other classes of suits where such a right is not in issue, the question of appointment of a receiver may not, in all probability, arise at all. In the case of a suit for partition with which we are concerned in the instant case, the present right of a co-sharer to remove another co-sharer from the possession of a particular joint property cannot accrue until the final decree has been passed allotting the said property to a co-sharer other than the possessing one. That is to say, there cannot be any question of appointment of a receiver in a partition suit, till the passing of the final decree. We shall have to be, therefore, extremely cautious in accepting the interpretation suggested by the aforesaid Full Bench decision of the Allahabad High Court, which reduces the provision relating to appointment of receiver to an almost nugatory one.</u>

<u>22. If we keep the object of the provisions of Order 40, as, expressed in section 94, clause (d) of the Code and read the provision of rule 1 of Order 40 as a whole, it becomes clear that the words 'any person', which have been used in sub Rule (2) of the said rule in juxtaposition to the words 'any party to the suit' refer to a person other than a party to the suit. We are, therefore, of the opinion that the said sub-rule has no application to the case of a person who is a party to the suit in which the order of appointment of a receiver is to be made.</u>

<u>23. The consensus of the judicial opinion in the sub-continent except the opinion of the Allahabad High Court, as expressed in the Full Bench case referred to above, has favoured this interpretation of the words 'any person' as used in sub-rule (2) of Order 40, rule 1 As regards the Allahabad High Court, there had been a subsequent reference to another Full Bench for a fresh consideration of the question as to the true import of sub-rule (2), but the Full Bench in the said case, viz. Mt. Tulsha Devi Vs. Shah Chironjeelal and others 1943 All, 1 without going into the said question, recommended that the rule should be amended to leave no doubt as to the true interpretation of the sub-rule. Pursuant to the said recommended the sub-rule has been amended by the Allahabad High Court by adding the words, not being a party to the suit after the words 'any person' in the said sub-rule, with the result that the law as to appointment of receiver in respect of that High Court as well has been brought in conformity to the rest of the sub-continent.</u>

24. Defendants. No. 6 and 7 being parties to the suit are not therefore entitled to plead absence of the present right to remove them from their possession of the properties in suit, in opposing the application for the appointment of a receiver of the properties in suit.

<u>25. There is no doubt that the Court had power to appoint a receiver in respect of the properties which are in the possession of the said defendants. The extent to which the receiver may be authorised to, or may exercise the power to, takeover physical possession of the properties by removing the persons in actual possession thereof will depend upon the facts and circumstances in each case. The Court shall have to decide the said question on the basis of what is just and convenient in each case.</u>

<u>The result therefore is that this appeal fails and is dismissed with costs.</u>

End.

lawyer:
AW Bhuiyan, Additional Attorney-General, instructed by Shamsul Haque Siddique, Advocate-on-Record—For the Appellant
 MI Faruqui, Advocate (M. Salimullah, Advocate with him), instructed by MG Bhuiyan, Advocate-on-Record—For the Respondent No. 1 Not represented—Respondent Nos. 2-6
parties:
Bangladesh, represented by the Secretary, Ministry of Works ----- Appellant
vs
Feroz Ahmed and others  ----- Respondents.
case_source: (From the Judgment and Order dated 10-1-93 passed by the High Court Division in Writ Petition No. 1543 of 1989).
full_judgment:
Mustafa Kamal J : This appeal by leave by the Government-appellant is from the judgment and order dated 10-1-93 passed in Writ Petition No. 1543 of 1989 making the Rule absolute. It raises some questions which strike at the root of the writ petition, namely, whether it was maintainable at all, whether a tentative order passed by prescribed authority under Article 15 of President's Order No. 16 of 1972 can at all be a final order and as to whether a decision of the High Court Division in an earlier writ petition on the same matter has become final after withdrawal of the petition for leave to appeal by Writ petitioner-respondent No 1.

2. Writ petitioner-respondent No. 1 Feroz Ahmed filed the aforesaid Writ Petition for a declaration that the enlistment of holding Nos. 12 and 13, Bara Katra, PS Lalbagh, Dhaka in the 'Ka' list of abandoned properties published on September 23, 1986 in Bangladesh Gazette, Extraordinary should be declared to have been made without lawful authority and of no legal effect and also the orders dated 29-10-88 and 29-1-89 passed by the Court of Settlement (respondent No. 6) in case No. 683 of 1988 should be declared to have been passed without lawful authority and of no legal effect and also for a direction to hand over the physical vacant possession of the holding in question to writ petitioner-respondent No. 1.

3. It was the writ petitioner-respondent's case in the writ petition that he and his parents migrated from Calcutta and came to Dhaka on 1-12-49 for permanent settlement. His parents got themselves domiciled at Dhaka along with their children and had been living in the then East Pakistan as a permanent resident. The writ petitioner became a citizen of Bangladesh by operation of law after the liberation of Bangladesh. On 10-8-73 he had sworn an affidavit before a Magistrate, 1st Class, Dhaka owing allegiance to Bangladesh. An international passport was issued to him by the Ministry of Home Affairs on 20-6-73, after the expiry of the period of which a new passport was issued to him on 11-12-83. The writ petitioner is the absolute and sixteen annas owner of Municipal holding Nos. 12 and 13, Bara Katra, PS Lalbagh, Dhaka which the writ petitioner purchased in 1964 from one Ismail Ahmed Dada Bhai under a registered deed of sale. The writ petitioner leased out the said property on monthly rent to M/s. Waqar & Sons which accommodated its office therein. The said firm M/s. Waqar & Sons was taken over by a Notification dated 13-1-72 by the Ministry of Industries and Natural Resources read with a modified Notification dated 24-1-72 with all properties and assets belonging to the said firm. One Nezamuddin was appointed Administrator of the said firm on 24-1-72 and he arbitrarily stopped payment of rents to the writ petitioner and unauthorisedly let out a portion of the said property and started his own business therein. M/s. Waqar & Sons virtually ceased to function. Subsequently Nezamuddin was suspended and removed by the Government. The writ petitioner made representation to the prescribed authority, the Sub-Divisional Officer, Sadar, South, Dhaka on 28-4-72 stating inter alia that the property in question did not belong to M/s Waqar & Sons, that the said firm was a tenant under him, that the said property was not an abandoned property and that he was a national of Bangladesh. The writ petitioner's application was received by the prescribed authority under receipt No. 1895. The writ petitioner made various representations to the prescribed authority and the Ministry of Works for release and restoration of the said property but to no effect. During the pendency of the writ petitioner's various representations, the Additional Deputy Commissioner (City), Dhaka invited tenders to dispose of the said property and the goodwill of the said firm Waqar & Sons through an advertisement in newspapers. On the writ petitioner's representation the Ministry of Works restrained the said official from putting the said property on auction till the writ petitioner's claim was disposed of. Subsequently on 12-7-82 the writ petitioner filed an application by way of reminder to the prescribed authority to dispose of his claim under Article 15 of President's Order No. 16 of 1972. The prescribed authority kept the matter pending but upon receipt of a Memo. from the Ministry of Works dated 10-11-83 directing finalization of all claims by 31-12-83, the prescribed authority took up the writ petitioner's application for consideration. After hearing the writ petitioner and on perusal of relevant documents and papers the prescribed authority by an order dated 4-2-84 came to the finding that the said property did not belong to M/s. Waqar & Sons and the same may be released and restored to the writ petitioner who is a national of Bangladesh and is the owner of the holding in question. The prescribed authority sent his said findings to the Government which neither preferred any appeal nor revised the findings under Article 16 of President's Order No. 16 of 1972. The writ petitioner made several representations to the Government for release and restoration of the said property after the prescribed authority passed the aforesaid order but upon the failure of the Government to do so the writ petitioner after sending a notice of demand of justice filed writ petition No. 113 of 1986 challenging the action of the Government in keeping and retaining the said property without lawful authority. A Division Bench of the High Court Division rejected the Writ Petition summarily on 10-3-86 holding that the Court had no power to issue the writ as prayed for in view of the provisions of Clause 5(e) of Chief Martial Law Administrator's Order No. 1 of 1985. The writ petitioner preferred CP No. 148 of 1986 to the Appellate Division against the said judgment and order of the High Court Division but subsequently the Appellate Division permitted the writ petitioner on 31-1-89 to withdraw the leave petition allowing the writ petitioner to proceed in the matter in an appropriate forum if he is so advised. During the pendency of the matter in the Appellate Division, the Abandoned Buildings (Supplementary Provisions) Ordinance, 1985 (Ordinance No. 54 of 1985) came into force and the writ petitioner's aforesaid property was included in the 'ka' list of abandoned properties published on September 23, 1986 in Bangladesh Gazette, Extraordinary. To inform the Court of Settlement that the matter is sub judice before the Appellate Division the writ petitioner filed Case No. 683 of 1988 on 10-8-86 before the Court of Settlement. The said case was fixed for hearing on 29-10-88 and on that date it was pointed out that all relevant documents and papers were lying with the learned Advocate of the writ petitioner in connection with CP No. 148 of 1986 then pending in the Appellate Division. The Court of Settlement directed the writ petitioner to file the documents by 29-1-89 with a default order. On 29-1-89 the Court of Settlement in the absence of the writ petitioner passed an ex parte order to the effect that the case stood dismissed. The writ petitioner thereafter filed the instant writ petition in November, 1989.

4. On behalf of the Government-appellant an affidavit-in-opposition was filed and it was stated that the writ petitioner was not a national or citizen of Bangladesh and he has never been living in Bangladesh as a permanent resident. He did not become a citizen of Bangladesh by operation of law. He did not swear any affidavit before any Magistrate owing allegiance to Bangladesh and the alleged affidavit is an ante-dated document and that an international passport can be obtained by anybody within 24 hours without any enquiry. It was specifically asserted that during the liberation movement and afterwards, the whereabouts of the writ petitioner were not known, that he ceased to occupy, supervise or manage the case property and so the case property absolutely vested in the Government as abandoned property legally and lawfully. In respect of the writ petitioner's application dated 28-4-72 and various representations in Annexure-D series the Government appellant stated that those were afterthoughts created for the purpose of the writ petition. In respect of the writ petitioner's application under Article 15 of President's Order No. 16 1972 dated 12-7-82 and the order of the prescribed authority dated 4-2-84 it was stated in the affidavit- n-opposition that the writ petitioner created those papers collusively only to file the writ petition. It was stated that when the case property was included in the Gazette Notification in the 'ka' list on September 23, 1986 the pendency of the writ petitioner's CP No. 148 of 1986 was not known to the respondents. It was again stated the writ petitioner claimed the case property by purchase as an immigrant but during the liberation movement he left Bangladesh for Pakistan with the members of his family, and after liberation he never came back to Bangladesh and his whereabouts were not known and he failed to manage, supervise and control the case property in person and hence the case property absolutely vested in the Government as an abandoned property under President's Order No. 16 of 1972. The Government controlled and managed the case property as abandoned property through Amjad Hossain, Abdul Mutaleb, Md. Shahabuddin, Abdul Jabbar, their allottees, who were given offer of sale of the case property on 11-7-85 fixing the value of the same at Taka 15, 32, 149.00 and the allottees paid 20% down payment to the Government and have also entered into an agreement on 10-10-85 with the Government for the transfer of the case property to them. The writ petitioner never appeared in person before any authority until now but some interested persons are pulling strings from behind with an ulterior motive only to grab the abandoned property after creating some collusive papers and documents.

5. The writ petitioner filed an affidavit-in-reply thereto substantially reiterating the statements made in the writ petition. The High Court Division made the Rule absolute on the ground that by an order dated 4-2-84 the Additional Deputy Commissioner (City), Dhaka, the prescribed authority, passed an order holding that the case property is not an abandoned property and the same may be released and restored to him. By terming the said order as collusive without giving any basis the Government-appellant did not serve the interest of justice and fair play. The High Court Division then relied upon the case of Rana Awan vs. Bangladesh, 43 DLR 139 and two unreported (but not cited) decisions of the High Court Division and came to the conclusion that the prescribed authority under Article 15 of President's Order No. 16 of 1972 is required either to accept or reject the claim of the claimant and not to seek instruction or opinion from anyone or to send the records to any other authority for passing the final order of release. The Additional Deputy Commissioner (City), Dhaka without passing final order sought the opinion of the Government pleader although he was satisfied that the property in question was not an abandoned property and it must be released in favour of the writ petitioner. Nevertheless the said order dated 4-2-84 must be treated as a final order. The High Court Division held that the writ petitioner is a national of Bangladesh and his property in question cannot be treated as an abandoned property. The inclusion of the case property within 'ka' list of abandoned properties was also without jurisdiction, as the writ petitioner's CP No. 148 of 1986 was pending in the Appellate Division till 31-1-89.

6. Mr. Abdul Wadud Bhuiyan, learned Additional Attorney-General appearing for the Government-appellant, submits, first, that the writ petition itself was not maintainable and in spite of a specific point being taken in the Government-appellant's affidavit-in-opposition to that effect, the High Court Division failed to consider the preliminary point of maintainability. He submits that the only authority under Ordinance No. 54 of 1985 to decide the question as to whether a listed property is an abandoned property or not is the Court of Settlement. The writ petitioner filed a settlement case therein. The case was dismissed for default without giving a finding that the Court of Settlement had no jurisdiction in the matter or that the dismissal of the writ petitioner's case for default was of no legal consequence, the High Court Division illegally assumed the jurisdiction to decide as a Court of first instance as to whether the case property is an abandoned property or not. The judgment of the High Court Division has produced an incongruous result in that according to the High Court Division the case property is not an abandoned property but according to the Court of Settlement the case property is an abandoned property.

7. Mr. MI. Faruqui, learned Advocate for writ petitioner respondent No. 1, sought to justify the judgment of the High Court Division on the ground that the prescribed authority having already determined the character of the suit property by its order dated 4-2-84, the subsequent inclusion of the case property in the 'ka' list of abandoned properties by a Gazette Notification dated September 23, 1986 is of no consequence and therefore the Court of Settlement had no further jurisdiction in the matter.

<u>8. It is difficult to uphold the contention of Mr. MI Faruqui. The writ petitioner obtained a Rule Nisi to show cause inter alia why the orders dated 29-10-88 and 29-1-89 passed by the Court of Settlement in Case No. 683 of 1988 should not be declared to have been passed without lawful authority and to be of no legal effect. The High Court Division could not have assumed jurisdiction over the self-same matter without at first purging the Court of Settlement of jurisdiction in the matter and without declaring its orders dated 29-10-88 and 29-1-89 to have been passed without jurisdiction. The High Court Division has made no deliberation on this aspect of the Rule Nisi issued by it. While making the Rule absolute the High Court Division expressly declared that the inclusion of the case property in the 'ka' list has been made without lawful authority and is of no legal effect and directed the respondents to deliver vacant possession of the case property to the writ petitioner, but it has made no declaration in respect of the two impugned orders of the Court of Settlement.</u>

<u>9. Having thus left the question of jurisdiction of the Court of Settlement in the matter absolutely open and inconclusive the High Court Division erroneously assumed jurisdiction in the matter and, as such, we have no difficulty in holding that the entire exercise of the High Court Division in the matter was an exercise in nullity. The writ petition was not maintainable at all.</u>

10. The learned Additional Attorney-General submits next that the writ petitioner's application under Article 15 of  D-20 President's Order No. 16 of 1972 is said to have been filed on 28-4-72 for the first time and the writ petitioner also claims to have filed several representations thereafter, Respondent No. 1 has filed an additional paper book in this Court but even in his paper book containing Government orders in respect of the case property since 1972, there is no reference to his alleged application under Article 15 dated 28-4-72 and the alleged representations thereafter. It is found from the said additional paper book and from Annexure-G to the writ petition that he filed an application under Article 15 of President's Order No. 16 of 1972 for the first time on 12-7-82 i.e. long after three months of the date of commencement of President's Order No. 16 of 1972. It is found from the order of the prescribed authority dated 4-2-84 that he examined the title deed of the writ petitioner and found that the property belonged not to M/s Waqar & Sons but to the writ petitioner. It was never an issue before the prescribed authority as to whether the writ petitioner ceased to occupy, supervise or manage in person his property in question. The prescribed authority referred the matter for legal opinion to the Government pleader only on the issue involved before him, namely, whether the case property belonged to the writ petitioner or to M/s Waqar & Sons. The Government pleader on perusal of the documents opined that the case property belonged to the writ petitioner. Thereafter, the prescribed authority by a letter dated 13-5-84 forwarded the application of the writ petitioner along with the report of his office and the opinion of the Government pleader, Dhaka to the Ministry of Works for taking necessary action. A copy of this letter dated 13-5-84 has been annexed in an additional paper book filed by the Government-appellant. The learned Additional Attorney-General submits that before taking a final decision, in terms of Article 15, rejecting or allowing the application of an applicant wholly or in part, the prescribed authority is fully competent to obtain legal opinion and departmental information from the relevant Ministries and therefore neither his order dated 4-8-84 nor his subsequent letter to the Ministry of Works dated 13-5-84 can be termed as "final order" as erroneously held by the High Court Division. He submits that the prescribed authority was still in seisin of the matter when he wrote to the Ministry of Works on 13-5-84 and the question of the Government preferring an appeal or revising the decision of the prescribed authority under Article 16 of President's Order No. 16 of 1972 does not arise.

11. Mr. MI Faruqui on the other hand submits that after hearing the writ petitioner and obtaining the opinion of the Government pleader the prescribed authority in no uncertain terms held that the property is not an abandoned property and that it should be released in favour of the writ petitioner and the prescribed authority's Memo dated 13-5-84 is nothing but an intimation to the Ministry of Works of the prescribed authority's final decision for the purpose of implementation by the Ministry of Works. He submits that the High Court Division correctly termed the prescribed authority's order 4-2-84 as a "final order".

<u>12. It is true that under Article 15(3) of President's Order No. 16 of 1972 the prescribed authority, on receiving an application from an applicant, "shall hold a summary inquiry in the prescribed manner and, after taking such evidence as may be produced, shall pass an order, stating the reasons thereof, for rejecting the application or allowing it, wholly or in part, on such terms and conditions as it thinks fit to impose". We have perused the order dated 4-2-84 posed by the prescribed authority as at Annexure-G to the writ petition as also in the additional paper book filed by respondent No. 1. We find that the prescribed authority on perusal of the documents furnished by the writ petitioner and upon hearing him found that the property in question did not answer the definition of abandoned property as given in President's Order No. 16 of 1972 and that the same may be released and restored to the writ petitioner. So saying the prescribed authority could have stopped and it would have been a final order for all purposes, but then he sent the case records to the Government pleader for his opinion after obtaining which, he stated, "we may send our findings for taking necessary action to the Ministry of Industries and Commerce (Commerce Division) with a copy to the Ministry of Works". The Government Pleader, we find, on perusal of the documents opined that if the authorities so desire the case property may be released from the list of abandoned property and possession may be restored to the writ petitioner. By an order dated 14-3-84 the prescribed authority, after receiving the report of the Government pleader, noted as follows:</u>

<u>"Let me examine the case for further necessary action".</u>

<u>Thereafter the prescribed authority sent the Memo. dated 13-5-84 to the Ministry of Works, containing no final finding that the case property is not an abandoned property and that the property should be released to the writ petitioner, but merely forwarding i copy of the writ petitioner's application along with the report of his office and the opinion of the Government Pleader to the Ministry of Works "for taking necessary action". In such circumstances it is difficult to hold that the prescribed authority had passed a final order and that the Ministry of Works was only required to implement any final decision taken by the prescribed authority. We have to differ with the High Court Division as to the nature of the order passed by the prescribed authority. We hold that this was not a final order as contemplated under Article 15 of President's Order No. 16 of 1972.</u>

13. The learned Additional Attorney-General next submits that the case of the Government-appellant that the writ petitioner left Bangladesh during liberation movement with the members of his family for Pakistan and that after liberation he never came back to Bangladesh and his whereabouts were not known and that he failed to manage, supervise and control the case property was neither considered by the prescribed authority nor by the High Court Division and therefore the Government-appellant's case has gone by default. As the Court of Settlement dismissed the writ petitioner's case for default, the Government- appellant had no opportunity to place its own case before any forum. He submits that the writ petitioner may have a valid registered deed of sale in his favour but an abandoned property must necessarily have an owner and the moot question in this case is not the ownership of the property in question by the writ petitioner but the fact of the writ petitioner's presence in Bangladesh at the material time, the question of knowledge of the Government of his whereabouts and the fact of the writ petitioner's occupation, supervision or management in person of the case property. That question having not been noticed at all by the High Court Division it is fit and proper in the interest of justice that this core question should be investigated and decided by a competent forum.

14. Again Mr. MI Faruqui in his reply falls back to the order dated 4-8-84 passed by the prescribed authority and submits that the status of the property has already been determined by the prescribed authority and there remains nothing for any other forum to determine the character of the property in question all over again.

15. We find considerable merit in the submission of the learned Additional Attorney-General. The basic issue raised by the Government-appellant in its affidavit-in-opposition has not been touched upon by the High Court Division at all and without adverting to those basic issues the High Court Division could not have pronounced upon the character of the case property. The core issue remains undecided so far and in the interest of justice it must be decided in a competent forum.

<u>16. Finally, the learned Additional Attorney-General submits that when the case property was included in the 'ka' list the writ petitioner's CP No. 148 of 1986 was no doubt pending in the Appellate Division but that petition for leave to appeal was with regard to the maintainability of Writ Petition No. 113 of 1986 which was not concerned with the abandoned character of the case property at all but with the question of release and restoration of the case property to the writ petitioner on the assumption that it was not an abandoned property. As such, its inclusion in the 'ka' list during pendency of CP No. 148 of 1986 was not at all without jurisdiction, as the High Court Division held.</u>

<u>17. Mr. MI Faruqui, on the other hand, submits that although CP No. 148 of 1986 was concerned with the maintainability of Writ Petition No. 113 of 1986, yet the question involved in the writ petition was the character of the case property itself and therefore the High Court Division was correct in its decision that the inclusion of the case property in the 'ka' list during the pendency of CP No. 148 of 1986 in the Appellate Division was without jurisdiction.</u>

<u>18. We have perused the judgment of the High Court Division in Writ Petition No. 113 of 1986. The writ petition was in respect of the alleged failure of the Government to omit to do which it was required by law to do, namely, to release the case property and deliver its vacant possession to the writ petitioner. The basic underlying assumption behind the said writ petition was that it was not an abandoned property and the question was already a settled one. It was then merely a question of release and restoration. Under such circumstances the embargo under section 5 of Ordinance No. 54 of 1985 has no application and the High Court Division was wrong in its finding that the inclusion of the case property in the 'ka' list during the pendency of CP No. 148 of 1986 was without jurisdiction. By the same token we do not accept the submission of the learned Additional Attorney-General that upon the withdrawal of the writ petitioner's leave petition, namely, CP No. 148 of 1986, the High Court Division's order dismissing Writ Petition No. 113 of 1986 became final. Yes, it was final, but only with regard to the maintainability of the said writ petition, not with regard to the abandoned character of the case property which was not the subject matter of the writ petition at all.</u>

In the premises aforesaid the appeal is allowed and remanded to the Court of Settlement for hearing of the case in accordance with law. We set aside the orders dated 29-10-88 and 29-1-89 passed by respondent No. 6 in Case No. 683 of 1988. There will be no order as to costs.

End.

with

lawyer:
Mahmudul Islam with Probir Neogi, Advocates - For the Petitioners (In both the Writ Petitions)
