Thus the Judges of that time, rose to the occasion and checked the exercise of arbitrary powers and saved the nation from the absolute, authoritarian arbitrary rule of a Monarch with absolute power as it was prevalent at that time all over the globe. This bold declaration ushered a glorious beginning of the supremacy of law, enacted by the Parliament and Parliament alone, representing the Commons, the Lords and the King which is still true today.

27. In this era, the ideas of Hobbs (1651) inspired the independent-minded English people to shake off the absolute rule of the Monarch on the basis of their divine right. After a prolonged constitutional struggle, the Bill of Rights was enacted in 1689. It emphatically declared the supremacy of Parliament in enacting any law and transformed gradually the absolute divine right Monarchy into constitutional Monarchy. It was a joint achievement of both Whig and Tory parties.

28. It can be noted in this respect that the Magna Carta (1215), the Petition of Right (1628) and the Bill of Rights (1689), together constitute the Bible of the English Constitution (Lord Chatham), upholding the rights and liberties of the English people.

29. As a matter of fact, from the early eighteenth century, the modern political system in England was beginning to take shape. The Cabinet and the Premiership:

30. From the days of the early Kings, all matters of State were being debated and resolved before the King with his Privy Council. But it was found to be not convenient always because of the usual long debates before its large number of members, specially when the matter was secret and urgent. As such, Charles II preferred to consult a small body of trusted councilors known as cabal or cabinet council. As a matter of fact, earlier even James I had also such secret councilors. During the reign of Charles II, a small group of his confidential advisers used to meet confidentially in a small secret room in the palace. The King in his discretion, consulted such of his advisers in the cabinet or individual ministers. After the decision, it was brought before the Privy Council for its confirmation.

31. It is fascinating to reflect how the cabinet system slowly started to take roots in the English constitutional scheme.

32. After the death of Queen Ann, the first of the Hanoverians, George I (1714-27), the great-grandson of James I and Elector of Hanover, succeeded to the English throne, and welcomed by the Whigs. The King began his reign by appointing a cabinet of fifteen members but although he could speak German and Latin but could hardly understand the English language. Naturally, he found the deliberations in the cabinet very boring and thereafter, rarely attended the cabinet meetings. Robert Walpole, the First Lord of the Treasury, could converse in fluent Latin with the King. As such, the King used to send for Walpole and give instructions to the Cabinet through him. He also, of necessity, worked as a spokesman for the Cabinet. In this manner, although he could neither appoint nor dismiss any of those ministers and was never a prime minister but the people, rather derisively or jokingly, used to call him the 'Prime Minister' of the King. As a matter of fact, when Walpole resigned in 1742, one of the charges against him was that he was the sole prime minister which was denied by him. On his resignation, the King asked William Pulteney, the principal opposition leader, to form an administration. This time Pulteney selected his colleagues, one of the attributes of a prime minister but he himself refrained from taking any office. Even in 1782, when Lord North, the Chancellor of the Exchequer and the First Lord of the Treasury, resigned, he also denied that he had been a Prime Minister but maintained that there should be one man or a cabinet to govern the whole. In 1782, the Civil Establishment Act was passed. It immensely changed the relation between the executive and the legislature. It effectively though gradually ceased the control of the Crown on the executive, rather, by and by, very slowly it went under the control of the Parliament. By the time of William Pitt, the Younger (1783-1804), the concept of Premiership had also been changed. He felt the practical necessity of a Prime Minister who should be the real minister possessing the chief weight in the council and also confidence of the King.

33. So far the cabinet system is concerned its growth was owed and possible because of the indifference of George I and George II to the Kingship of Great Britain. They preferred it to be left in the hands of the offices of the State as far as possible. Since the King was not present in the Cabinet, with the passage of time, the principal ministers and the secretaries of the State, took the opportunity to discuss their mutual problems in respect of their own minis-tries, with one another, apart from their prime duty owed to the King. They also communicated the results of their deliberations through their spokesman, generally the First Lord of the Treasury, sometimes through others and, of necessity, generally in one voice, free from any personal influence of the King. Since it was their own resolution which they wanted to carry, they also, by and by started to become collectively responsible to the House of Commons and no longer to the King. Thus, the Cabinet started as the institution of the Crown, for affording advice to him by the concerned ministers and by the eighteenth century, it was developed as a conference of the senior ministers but still without any Prime Minister as such. The lapse on the part of the Kings to the affairs of the State, allowed the English Constitution to develop by the time of George III in 1760, the system of ministerial government with collective responsibility to the House of Commons. Although the ministers had legal existence but the Cabinet, as such, had none but grew up out of necessity of the State based on practice which in time became a constitutional convention.

34. Under the Reform Act, 1832, the personal influence of the Crown also steadily declined and by the time of William IV in 1834, it was apparent that the King cannot dismiss an administration or a ministry but may choose one or the other.

35. Queen Victoria (1819-1901) during her long reign had immense influence on the affairs of her Kingdom but it never exceeded the constitutional decorum and the personal power of the Sovereign as distinguished from her Regal power was always maintained within constitutional limits.

36. The relationship of the Cabinet with the Crown is aptly explained by William Wart Gladstone thus:

"The association of the ministers with the parliament, and through the House of Commons with the people, is the counter-part of their association as ministers with the Crown and the prerogative ----- what in all circumstances they must bear while they remain ministers, the undivided responsibility of all that is done in the Crown's name.

Of the members of the Cabinet, he said

"Every one of them acts in no less than three capacities: as administrator of a department of state; as member of a legislative member; and as a confidential adviser of the Crown."

37. About his own position, he said:

"The head of the British Government is not a grand vizier. He has no powers, properly so called, over his colleagues: on the rare occasions when a cabinet determines its course by the votes of its members, his vote counts only as one of theirs. But they are appointed and dismissed by the sovereign on his advice."

38. As regards the relationship of the Prime Minister to the Crown and the Cabinet he said:

"As the cabinet stands between the sovereign and the parliament, and is bound to be loyal to both, so he stands between his colleagues and the sovereign, and is bound to be loyal to both.

39. Thereafter, he adds:

"As a rule, the resignation of the first minister, as if removing the bond of cohesion in the cabinet, has the effect of dissolving it The prime minister has no title to override any one of his colleagues in any one of the departments. So far as he governs them, unless it is done by trick, which is not to be supposed, he governs them by influence only. But upon the whole, nowhere in the wide world does so great a substance cast so small a  shadow nowhere is there a man who has  so much power with so little to show for it in the way of formal title or prerogative".

Quoted from Thomas Pitt Taswwell-Langmead on English Constitutional History, 10th Edition, pages-725-727).

40. This is the classic exposition as to how Gladstone saw the office of the Prime Minister and the Cabinet, the head of the administration of the British Empire, in the late 19th century.

41. Thus the Cabinet started as an institution of the Crown although without any legal basis, for the necessary advice for the Crown by the concerned minister and by the end of the 18th century, it was developed as a conference of senior ministers but, even then, without any Prime Minister as such.

42. The office of the Prime Minister was first mentioned in the Treaty of Berlin in 1878 and a royal warrant of 1905. The Ministers of the Crown Act, 1937, first provided for a salary to be paid to the person who is Prime Minister and First Lord of the Treasury, with pensions to the former holder of the office.

43. The present modern Cabinets in the United Kingdom also function, strictly speaking, without any legal basis but on long years of practice bloomed into a constitutional convention.

44. We have narrated the earlier history leading to the establishment of the office of the Prime Minister and the Cabinet in the United Kingdom in some details but not without a purpose, because it is always true that 'a page of history is worth a volume of logic' (Justice Holmes). The creation of modern Governments in many a country around the world is the result of the long and arduous constitutional struggle of the people of the United Kingdom and its leaders. Although we reap the benefit of their labours in a few sentences contained in Articles 55 and 56 of our Constitution which is the fruits of struggle of nearly one thousand years of the people of England and unless we know the history and context, we shall not be able to understand and appreciate the import of the above provisions in its proper perspective. That is why Shahabuddin Ahmed, CJ in his celebrated judgment in the case of Kudrat-e-Elahi Panir vs Bangladesh 44 DLR (AD) 319, traced the history of the local government bodies in this country in deciding the real issue on it.

Three Branches of the Republic-Parliament :

45. Among the three branches of the Republic, the President is the head of the State, the Prime Minister is the head of the Executive Government but all executive actions of the Government are expressed in the name of the President.

46. The Speaker presides over the House of the Nation, the Legislative Branch of the Republic. He represents the House. With him resides the dignity of the House and through him that of the Nation. As such, once elected in the House as the Speaker, he does not owe any loyalty to any particular political party but to the House as a whole and to the House alone. The classic example of singular boldness witnessed nearly four hundred years ago in 1642 when Charles I, on entering the Commons, asked Speaker Lenthall to point out the five members he sought to arrest. The Speaker obligingly, knelt down before his Sovereign and replied:

"May it please your Majesty, I have neither eyes to see nor tongue to speak in this place, but as the House is pleased to direct me, whose servant I am here" (quoted from Encyclopedia Britannica, Vol 17, page - 378,1973).

47. Speaker Lenthall risked his neck but did not give away the identity of the members, sought to be arrested. The present day Speakers can at least risk their wooden chair, if necessary, in order to uphold the dignity of their office by being completely impartial and remain independent and aloof of brow beating of their party bosses in conducting the proceedings of the House.

48. The Chief Justice of Bangladesh is head of the third Branch of the Republic, the Judiciary.

49. We have already noticed by now that in contradistinction to the unwritten Constitution of the United Kingdom, we have a written Constitution based predominantly on the model of Westminster type democracy. According to Thomas Paine, the purpose of the Constitution is:

"A Constitution is not the act of a Government, but of a people constituting a government and a government without a Constitution is power without right   A Constitution is a thing antecedent to a government, and a government is only the creature of a Constitution.  (1792) (Quoted from Hilaire Barnett on Constitutional And Administrative Law, Fourth Edition, 2002, page-7).

50. In this connection, we must acknowledge and appreciate that in the United Kingdom, the Crown is still sovereign under the law and all persons in the Realm without any exception, are his subjects. But Bangladesh is a Republic. Here the people are the sovereign and all functionaries of the State, without any exception, are their servants. So also, the persons in the Service of the Republic. This is the constitutional and political position of all functionaries and the persons in the services of the Republic. This legal position without any ambiguity is enshrined in Article 7 thus:

"7. (1) All powers in the Republic belong to the people, and their exercise on behalf of the people shall be effected only under, and by the authority of, this Constitution.

(2) This Constitution is, as the solemn expression of the will of the people, the supreme law of the Republic and if any other law is inconsistent with this Constitution that other law shall, to the extent of the inconsistency, be void.

51. In explaining this touchstone of the Constitution, BH Chowdhury (as his Lordship then was) at Para 149 of his judgment in the case of Anwar Hossain Chowdhury vs Bangladesh 1989 BLD (Spl) 1 = 41 DLR (AD) 165 held :

"149. Our Article 7 has reflected the wisdom of the past and the learning of the history. Therefore, it has said categorically:

(1) All power in the Republic belongs 'to the people-this is a concept of sovereignty of the people. Sovereignty lies with the people not with executive, legislature or judiciary all these three are creations of the Constitution itself.

52. In the case of Rai Sahib Ram Jawaya vs The State of Punjab AIR 1955 SC 549, on the nature of the Constitutional position of India, BK Mukherjea CJ held at page 556:

"13...... Our Constitution, though federal in its structure, is modeled on the British Parliamentary system where the executive is deemed to have the primary responsibility for the formulation of governmental policy and its transmission into law, though the condition precedent to the exercise of this responsibility is its retaining the confidence of the legislative branch of the State.

14. In India, as in England, the executive has to act subject to the control of the legislature; but in what way is this control exercised by the legislature? Under Article 53(1) of our Constitution, the executive power of the Union is vested in the President but under Article 75 there is to be a  Council of Ministers with the Prime  Minister at the head to aid and advise the President in the exercise of his functions.  The President has thus been made a formal or constitutional head of the executive and the real executive powers are vested in the Ministers or the Cabinet.

..... In the Indian Constitution, therefore, we have the same system of parliamentary executive as in England and the Council of Ministers consisting, as it  does of the members of the legislature is.  like the British Cabinet. "a hyphen which  joins a buckle which fastens the legislative  part of the State to the executive part".

The Cabinet enjoying, as it does, a majority in the legislature concentrates in itself the virtual control of both legislative and executive functions; and as the Ministers constituting the Cabinet are presumably agreed on fundamentals and act on  the principle of collective responsibility, the most important questions of policy are all formulated by them.

53. The people of Bangladesh exercises their sovereignty through their representatives, elected under Article 66, Article 119 and Article 124 of the Constitution, in the House of the Nation. Those representatives of the people are known as the Members of Parliament. The Parliament consists of three hundred directly elected members and forty-five women members.

54. This Parliament although sovereign but is not omnipotent like that of the British Parliament. The powers and functions of the Parliament is subject to the provisions of the Constitution. It cannot override the provisions of the Constitution since it is the embodiment of the will of the people of Bangladesh. As such, it must act within the spirit and form of the Constitution. It cannot enact any law which is ultra virus to the Constitution or violates the fundamental rights of the people as proclaimed in Part III of the Constitution. It has even a limited amending power of the Constitution. The Parliament although supreme and sovereign but it cannot abrogate the Constitution or change its foundation or basic character or feature. The Parliament cannot even enlarge its such limited power of amendment to an absolute power and any amendment is always subject to scrutiny by the Supreme Court, if it is brought to its attention.

55. Subject to the above qualification, the legislative powers of the Republic is vested with the Parliament and under chapter II of Part V of the Constitution it can enact any law save and except in respect of those subjects of which such power had already been vested in some other functionary under the Constitution.

56. Financial control is another important function of the Parliament. It dates back to Magna Carta (1215). Although it was not an Act of Parliament but since the execution of the said Charter, no Monarch could impose any tax or levy any fee in any form on his subjects. The source of discontent between the Stuart Kings and the English Parliament was mainly due to their inability to impose tax without the approval of the Parliament. Even Oliver Cromwell could not maintain his army because of lack of funds in the absence of the Parliament. After all, 'who holds the purse, holds the power' (Madison in the 'Federalist'). This was true then, it is true now. It is through the control of the nation's purse, the Parliament exercises its real authority over the executive.

57. In Bangladesh, there were so very many supra-constitutional situations that this control of the House of the Nation was tampered with freely by the autocrat rulers, although, under the law, no money can be withdrawn from the consolidated fund without an Appropriation Act.

58. But, 'What is the House of Commons for?' Harold J Laski, raised this question in 1938, in his celebrated work, 'Parliamentary Government in England' (Eighth Edition, 1968).

He said:

"The business of making a Government' and providing it, or refusing to provide it, with the formal authority for carrying on the public business is the pivotal function of the House of Commons upon which all other functions turn." (page-142).

He then adds:

If we assume that a Government is in being, what are the functions the House must perform? There is the ventilation of grievance. There is the extraction of information. There is the business of debate, with the attempt, through debate, to sustain public interest, and to educate it, in the significance of what is being done." (page-144).

59. The most important function of the Parliament is the debate and discussions. By these exercises, the House can control the executive. Because, the Constitution makes the Cabinet collectively responsible to the House [Article 55 (3)]. If the policy of the Government is found to be unacceptable to the House, either it has to amend it or has to go for a dissolution. The members, be of Treasury or of opposition, are not only entitled but duty bound as members, to demand information about the various actions and steps of the Government.

60. In an ideal democratic country, the members must remember that although on being selected by their respective parties, they contest the election but once they are elected, they represent all shades of people in their constituency in the House of the Nation and if they fail to perform their functions as such elected members, they will be failing in their duty as such representatives of the people in the House. If they fail to raise their voice, they will be failing the entire nation, frustrating the very concept of a representative Government in a democracy.

61. The members are also entitled to question the individual Ministers in accordance with the Rules on the performance of their departments and the concerned Minister is also obliged to answer any such query. The concerned Minister cannot avoid answering any such question, put to him even by the junior-most member in the House because this is the mechanism by which the executive is made answerable for their actions to the Nation.

62. Laski viewed this function thus at pages 151-154:

"The process of questioning has important results. It brings the work of the Departments of State into the public view. It makes them realize that they are functioning under a close public scrutiny which will continuously test their efficiency and honesty. It mitigates, even if it cannot wholly prevent, the danger that bureaucratic habits will develop in the civil service; men who have to answer day by day for their decisions will tend so to act that they can give a good account of themselves. The minister is made aware that his answers have proved unsatisfactory. He feels that he must go further than the answer his department is able to render. He is anxious to placate a special or general public opinion which continues to insist that more should be known. There is no Fascist country in the world today which makes available to its public opinion truthful statistics about wages and prices, the number of unemployed and their treatment the operation of the judicial system.  There is none, either, that permits discussion even of the results of the half-truths it makes available. To make the facts known, and to work out principles of politics which display the meaning of those facts, is an achievement it would not be easy to over-estimate."

63. Besides questioning, the members, specifically the members of the Opposition, following the procedure, are entitled to criticize any policy or measure of the Government. The concerned Minister or any spokes-man of the Government must explain the interest and purport of the policy or measure to the House and through the House to the entire nation. It is the readiness to be accountable that makes a Government a good Government as Napoleon said that any fool can govern in a state of siege. A Government must prove itself as the representative of the governed in the face of the volley of criticism.

64. Another method of controlling the executive is the debate in the House. A debate initiated on the President's address, on the performance of the Government or an issue raised on the floor gives the members an opportunity to criticize the government policy. Laski addressed the point in his book thus at pages 154-6:

"The House of Commons is, also, a debating assembly A society that is able to discuss does not need to fight; and the greater the capacity to maintain interest in discussion, the less danger there is of an inability to effect the compromises that maintain social peace." Because, he said "A democracy lives by the spoken word, and what is said in print about that spoken word."

65. Besides these methods, the power of the members to ventilate a grievance is one of the oldest means to keep the executive on their toes. The barons, knights and burgesses forced King John to execute the Great Charter in 1215. It was the result of vindication of their grievances. From the earliest time, the local people of the country or borough in England used to approach their knight or other representatives for redress of their collective or individual grievances before the Commons. This practice continues even today. Even in this 21st century, an individual in the United Kingdom freely writes to his Member of Parliament for raising his grievance before the House of Commons for his redress. This is an important right of a citizen in that country and a member of Parliament tries his best to find the expected remedy in vindication of his such right and so also the House itself. This is how an ordinary citizen is given to understand that the House belongs to him, it is his own institution. This is how democratic polity flourishes in that great country.

66. Laski portrayed this power in this manner at page 147:

"After forming a Government, the most essential function of the House of Commons in our system is the ventilation of grievance. No Government can satisfy everybody; and some Governments fail to satisfy some interests, important or unimportant, very badly indeed. It is inherent in the nature of a democratic system that any man, or group of men, who can persuade a member of the House to raise his grievance, should have the opportunity of getting it discussed. It may be Mr. O'Brien, who is arrested without due process of law at the instance of the Home Secretary. It may be Miss Savidge who is severely questioned by the police after being acquitted in a Court of law for the offence charged against her by the police. The Co-operative Movement may feel strongly about the taxation of their profits by a Chancellor of the Exchequer who, as an eminent advocate, had advised them that, as they do not make profits, they cannot be liable for taxation. It may be Mr. Plimsoll heroically struggling against the Government's refusal to impose adequate human standards upon the owners of merchant ships. It may be the official Opposition, either moving a general vote of censure upon the Government, or claiming a day to insist upon what it believes to be some obvious inadequacy in the conduct of foreign affairs. The subject is unimportant. The method may be as humble as a simple question to ministers, or as dramatic as a motion to adjourn the House on a question of urgency. The essential point is that the grievance real or unreal may be ventilated and that the Government as best it can must seek to produce a satisfactory answer to the claim of grievance.

Of the value of this right, no one who has watched it in operation can have any doubt at all. No better method has ever been devised for keeping administration  up to the mark. It assures that what a Government does will, overwhelmingly, have to be done in the light of day and answered for in the light of day also. I do not say that it gives an assurance that justice will be done; it does give an assurance that there will be a careful examination into the accusation of injustice. The minister against whose department the accusation is made knows that he is on trial. He is eager, if he possibly can, to convince the House; he is even anxious, if he can, to persuade his critics to accept his explanation. There are many cases in which the private member, with a serious grievance to pro-test, has been able to secure a prompt movement to redress. In the Savidge case, for example, the whole House, indifferently to party composition, was on the side of the member who moved the adjournment of the House; and the temper of the assembly was such that the Home Secretary had to concede to the setting up of a Royal Commission on Police Powers and Procedure which led to a significant revision of the powers assumed by police authorities."

67. This power of ventilation of grievance, in an ideal democratic State, compels the Government to give its attention to the source of such grievance. Besides, the press in a free society is expected to highlight the grievance in bringing it to the attention of the Nation. In such a situation a responsible Government would do its best to address the grievance promptly in order to avoid, if not for anything else, the adverse publicity. As such, where this power is not encouraged, the scope of tyranny and oppression gets upper hand to the ultimate discredit of the Government unless, of course, it is an autocratic country and the people are too, moderate to raise their eye-brows to the excesses of the Government.

68. The above mentioned various powers are constantly used by the Members of Parliament in the United Kingdom and also in India in exercise of their rights as such members of the House. The members in Bangladesh are also clothed with such powers, functions and obligations. On a plain reading of the Constitution it appears that the members of Parliament in Bangladesh, be a member of the Treasury or of Opposition, following the procedure can criticize the Government for its actions or inactions, ask for any information regarding any step or measure of the Government or raise any grievance before the House. They are not only entitled but it is imperative on their part, as the representative of the people to do so, if the situation so demands.

69. These are the reasons, among others, why Parliament is so very important to the life of any nation. The Parliament is the barometer of civilization of any country.

70. Sir Ivory Jennings in his celebrated work. 'Cabinet Government' Third Edition, 1969, observed cynically, in this respect at page 510 thus:

"Government can be carried on quite successfully without a Parliament. It is indeed, a dilatory and inefficient talking' machine. Yet speed and efficiency are not the only requirements of the government. Justice is the supreme political virtue. Nor is ability to act first and think afterwards, if at all, a quality which commends itself. The British governmental machine is in spite of its many defects one of the most efficient, if not the most efficient constitutional structures of the world. It is reasonably efficient because it can be criticized. It is reasonable just because its actions are proclaimed to the people by those who have no cause to praise it.  It is, in short, a good system because it rests upon Parliament and, through Parliament, upon the willing consent of those who are governed."

71. Referring to what Cromwell said that 'not a dog barked', when he forcibly dissolved the Long Parliament, Sir Ivor retorted, 'The dogs bark in Parliament, if there were no Parliament, they might bite."

Article 70 of the Constitution:

72. The only impediment pointed out by the learned Advocate for the petitioner, is Article 70 of the Constitution. It is very true that this provision imposes certain limitations on the independent workings of a Member of Parliament.

73. This provision has an unhappy history. The framers of the Constitutions are aware about the unfortunate saga of floor crossings of the members in the Provincial Assembly in mid 1950s, bringing down the successive Governments one after the other. This sad experience must have loomed large in the minds of the framers of the Constitution. Dr Kamal Hossain admitted it. Obviously, in order to avoid the horse trading on the members of the House, they, in their apprehension and wisdom, thought it necessary to put an impediment on such free-lance floor crossings in the House when they enacted Article 70 in 1972 thus :

"70. A person elected as a Member of Parliament at an election at which he was nominated as a candidate by a political party shall vacate his seat if he

(a) resigns from that party; or

(b) votes in Parliament against that party;

but shall not thereby be disqualified for subsequent election as a Member of Parliament."

74. This original Article 70 appears to impose reasonable restrictions on a member who wants to resign from the party on whose nomination he was elected. He also vacates his seat if he votes against his party. This provision does not debar a member of the ruling party from criticising any policy or measure of the Government or asking for any information however embarrassing it may appear to the Government. This provision also does not debar him from raising any grievance or participate in any debate. If he does not agree with the views of his party, he may abstain from voting or may even remain absent from any sitting of Parliament. In this manner, even without voting against his party, he may show his own resentment to the decision of his party in Parliament, in exercise of his function as a representative of the people of his constituency with whom his prime and foremost loyalty resides. As such, the original Article 70 although imposed certain restrictions on the independence of an individual member which is neither present in Westminster nor in Lok Sabha but was grudgingly accepted possibly as a necessary evil in order to avoid the earlier instances of free-for-all floor crossings in the House.

75. But section 5 of the Constitution (Twelfth Amendment) Act, 1991 (Act XXVIII of 1991) made an overwhelming change. The amended Article 70 reads as follows:

"70. (1) A person elected as a member of Parliament at an election at which he was nominated as a candidate by a political party shall vacate his seat if he resigns from that party or votes in Parliament against that party.

Explanation.-If a member of Parliament-

(a) being present in Parliament abstains from voting, or

(b) absents himself from any sitting of Parliament ignoring the direction of the party which nominated him at the election as a candidate not to do so, he shall be deemed to have voted against that party.

(2) If, at any time, any question as to the leadership of the Parliament party of a political party arises, the Speaker shall, within seven days of being informed of it in writing by a person claiming the leadership of the majority of the members of that party in Parliament, convene a meeting of all members of Parliament of that party in accordance with the rules of procedure of Parliament and determine its Parliamentary leadership by the votes of the majority through division and if, in the matter of voting in Parliament, any member does not comply with the direction of the leadership so determined, he shall be deemed to have voted against that party under clause (1) and shall vacate his seat in the Parliament.

(3) If a person, after being elected a member of Parliament as an independent candidate, joins any political party, he shall, for the purpose of this article, be deemed to have been elected as a nominee of that party"

76. Under this amended provision, a Member of Parliament is debarred not only from voting against his party but cannot even indirectly oppose any policy or measure by being absent from voting, violating the direction of the party which nominated him at the election.

77. This amended provision, no doubt, greatly impaired the independence of a member of Parliament. He shall have to toe the party line. In effect, he becomes a representative of his party in Parliament but not the representative of the people of all shades in his constituency. Consequently, the expected universality of representation of people in the House is lost.

78. In effect, the supremacy of Parliament in England vis-a-vis the independence of its members, which was the result of relentless struggle of the people there has gone amiss in Bangladesh. The concept of sovereignty of the people of Bangladesh has been severely impaired. By restricting the voice of the representatives of the people, in the House of the Nation, in totes manner, the voice of the people of Bangladesh has been muffled, if not choked, altogether.

79. Let alone the theory, the naked reality is that the political party who gets majority seats in the House, tends to govern but not to serve the Nation. The opposition, members may clamour but would hardly bring any fruitful result when the members of the ruling party themselves are tamed under the whip of Article 70, as amended. This provision makes the member a prisoner of the party he belongs to.

80. This is what we see as the negation of democracy and the lack of consensus of the people in running their country. The people of England after a prolonged and tedious struggle established a Government on the consensus of the people from where the people of Bangladesh carried forward its such torch of democracy based on the concept of a representative Government on the sacrifice of three million martyrs. But the whole effort has now become meaningless without the independent voice of the members of the House of the Nation whether of the Ruling Party or of the Opposition.

81. It may be noted here that the Ruling party, however, in vindication of the democratic spirit in the Constitution, may voluntarily allow its members, at least to speak freely in the House and conduct their other functions without any impediment. Such freedom from the Whips may diminish the disgraceful effect of Article 70 (as amended) on the members, at least to some extent. In the House of Commons, such freedom was allowed on many an occasion.

82. Be that as it may, this is the legal position. Whether the amendment of Article 70 is within the ambit and purport of Article 142 is an altogether different issue and beyond the scope of the present Rule, as such, we contain ourselves in considering Article 70 as it is presented before us.

83. This is the legal position and functions of an elected Member of Parliament.

Executive Branch of Government:

84. Now let us look at the Executive Branch of the Government.

85. We have already considered, to some extent, the growth of the Office of the Prime Minister and the Cabinet system in the United Kingdom.

86. Let us now concentrate on the source of grievance of the petitioner, a member of Parliament. But before considering the question as to whether a Minister of the Government can be appointed in charge of a particular district, let us first examine his position as a Minister under the Constitution.

87. It may be reiterated that we have borrowed the concept of Cabinet and offices of Prime Minister and other Ministers from the English experience as it reached its nadir of development in the 20th century. The result of the long and tedious struggle of the people of England for the last more than one thousand years has been summarized in few sentences in Articles 55 and 56 of our Constitution.

88. Article 55 of the Constitution provides for a Cabinet for Bangladesh while Article 56 provides for appointment of the Prime Minister and other Ministers. Article 55 and Article 56 read as follows:

"55. (1) There shall be a Cabinet for Bangladesh having the Prime Minister at its head and comprising also such other Ministers as the Prime Minister may from time to time designate.

(2) The executive power of the Republic shall, in accordance with this Constitution, be exercised by or on the authority of the Prime Minister.

56.(1) There shall be a Prime Minister, and such other Ministers of State Deputy Ministers as may be determined by the Prime Minister.

(2) The appointments of the Prime Minister and other Ministers and of the Ministers of State and Deputy Ministers, shall be made by the President:

Provided that not less than nine-tenths of their number shall be appointed from among members of Parliament and not more than one-tenth of their number may be chosen from among persons qualified for election as members of Parliament.

(3) The President shall appoint as Prime Minister the member of Parliament who appears to him to command the support of the majority of the members of Parliament.

(4) If occasion arises for making any appointment under clause (2) or clause (3) between a dissolution of Parliament and the next following general election of members of Parliament, the persons who were such members immediately before the dissolution shall be regarded for the purpose of this clause as continuing to be such members."

89. Generally, on the results of a general election, by convention, as in England, the President respecting the mandate of the people calls upon the leader of the party which commands majority in the House to form an administration in the country which is known as a Ministry. As such, of necessity, such leaders in a democratic country must be properly elected, reflecting the support of the majority members of the concerned party. Thus, the practice of democracy in the political party itself is the sine qua non for democracy in any country.

90. The theory is that the electorates, up and down the country, elect their representatives in the House of the Nation and their leader as the leader of the majority, should form the administration, reflecting again, the choice of the people. This is the ideal situation as in the United Kingdom since the 18th century.

91. In this country, the groundwork was laid down in the Government of India Act, 1935. Under the said enactment, elections were held since 1937 in the provinces which although lacked the concept of universal suffrage and even a semblance of popular Government but the people of this sub-continent got its first taste of representative Government although in somewhat restricted manner. But even by that form of election, the Muslims in Bengal in 1946, voted Pakistan into existence. By the Independence of India Act, 1947, the Dominions of India and Pakistan came into existence. Within two years, India got its Constitution and became a Republic, while Pakistan lapsed into a medieval theocratic and police State from which Bangladesh got its liberation in 1971 at a cost of three million martyrs and framed its Constitution within less than one year based on Westminster type democracy but subject to its written Constitution.

92. In our Constitution, the Prime Minister is the apparent chief executive of the country. He is also the leader of the House of the Nation, as such, he with his Cabinet, acts as the bridge between the Executive and the Legislative Branch of the Government.

93. As we have discussed above, earlier in the United Kingdom although the Prime Minister is the first among the equals, primus inter pares, but in the 20th century, according to Jennings, 'He is rather a sun around which planets revolve'. No doubt, the Prime Minister is the king-pin in the Cabinet system of Government. Because it is he who designates other Ministers in the Cabinet and the Council of Ministers. A Prime Minister commands loyalty from his party and he can throw out any Minister from his Council as the head of the Government and also the head of the party. Mackintosh pictures the form of Government as a cone with the Prime Minister at the apex Beneath him is a widening series of rings of senior Ministers, the Cabinet, its committees, non-cabinet Ministers and departments (Quoted from 0. Hood Phillips: Constitutional and Administrative Law, Seventh Edition, page 324).

94. Explaining the position of the Prime Minister, Lord Morley stated thus in 1889:

"...........the Prime Minister is the keystone of the Cabinet arch. Although in the Cabinet all its members stand on an equal footing, speak with an equal voice, and, on the rare occasions when a division is taken, are counted on the fraternal principle of one man, one vote, yet the head of the Cabinet is primus inter pares, and occupies a position which, so long as it lasts, is one of exceptional and peculiar authority." (Quoted from Hilaire Barnett: Constitutional and Administrative Law, Fourth Edition, page-314).

95. Half a century later, Prime Minister Sir Anthony Eden viewed the Office thus:

"A Prime Minister is still nominally primus inter pares, but, in fact, his authority is stronger than that. The right to choose his colleagues, to ask for a dissolution of Parliament and, if he is a Conservative, to appoint the Chairman of the party organization, add up to a formidable total of power."

(Quoted from Hilaire Barnett: Constitutional and Administrative Law, Fourth Edition, page 314).

96. In an ideal situation, even in modern times, the influence and the consequential power of the Prime Minister depends on the support of the Cabinet, Council of Ministers, members in the House and also the party and through them the will of the people who watches the performance of their representatives all the time.

97. Even in England, during the 2nd World War, they had almost a Prime Ministerial Government. However, it also depends on the personality of the concerned Prime Minister. He cannot always ride roughshod over his colleagues. Even with his towering personality Sir Winston Churchill sometimes gave way to the views of his colleagues. In 1940, the people of Great Britain saw their saviour in him but even after the great victory, in the great war, on the question of his policies, he had to bow out before his people in 1945. This is how the supremacy of the will of the people was in actual play. Even Mrs Margaret Thatcher, the invincible Prime Minister who came out successfully in three consecutive general elections, had to step down in 1990 when she lost the confidence of the Cabinet and the party.

98. There we see how the towering personalities with all their might bow down gracefully and submit to the will of the people. There lies the political maturity of the people of the United Kingdom and their leaders. But in most of the Third World countries, the leaders become synonymous with the office they hold, ensuring a hero worship where the democracy takes a back seat and the old feudalistic approach to their political lives takes precedence.

99. Harold Wilson saw in the context of the United Kingdom, the role of the Prime Minister as 'if not that of a managing director, as that of an Executive Chairman (0 Hood Philips) but in many third world countries, the role of the Prime Minister is gradually becoming as that of a managing director of a private limited company, and that is even apparently without any accountability to anyone. Thus, the autocracy seeps through the system and the rot starts. The elected Prime Minister starts to behave like a 16th century hereditary absolute Monarch with the supposed divine right to Rule with all sycophants around him, consequently despotism follows and the people helplessly watch that all their struggles go down the drain. That is why Johm Stuart Mill (1808-1873) warned the people so long ago against allowing uncontrolled power even to a great man which may enable him to thwart the democratic institutions of the Sate. That is why eternal vigilance by the people is so much necessary to safeguard their rights, even if those are written in their Constitution.

100. In our country, under Article 55(3), the Cabinet, not the Prime Minister, is responsible to the Parliament. It is true that under sub-Article 4, all executive actions of the Government are expressed to be taken in the name of the President and the executive powers of the Republic are to be exercised by or on the authority of the Prime Minister, in accordance with the provisions of the Constitution, but neither the President nor the Prime Minister, in his individual capacity is responsible to the Parliament. It is the Cabinet, which includes the Prime Minister and other Senior Ministers of the Government, as a whole, that is collectively responsible to the House of the Nation and through the House to the people of Bangladesh. This responsibility to the House, vis-a-vis the people, as specifically spelt out in sub-Article 3 of Article 55, empowers the Cabinet with the executive authority of the State.

101. Although the executive powers of the Government are expressed to be taken in the name of the President and apparently exercised by the Prime Minister or under his authority but under the scheme of our Constitution, all executive powers actually reside with the Cabinet and not with the Prime Minister. A Prime Minister in Bangladesh, under the mandates of the Constitution, can advise termination of any of his Ministers or may even advise the President to dissolve Parliament but cannot carry out any policy of his Government without the concurrence of the Cabinet. As such, there is no Prime Ministerial Government in Bangladesh, at least in theory. The misuse of power and despotism, if any, is not due to any shortcoming or draw-back in the Constitution but due to lapse and obliging conduct on the part of the members of the Cabinet in derogation to their solemn constitutional obligation to the Parliament.

102. Besides, the standing committees of Parliament, appointed under Article 76, may investigate or inquire into the activities or administration of any Ministry and may require it to furnish relevant information’s and to answer questions. The Committee can ask any Minister to appear before it and reply to the queries. The standing committee after making such inquiries would report back to the Parliament. In this manner, the standing committees play a very import role in keeping the functions of the Executive Branch of the Government open to criticism and also accountable before the House and through it to the people who are the ultimate masters.

103. The faulty party system without democratic practice and the ever apathetic and obliging Election Commission of Bangladesh are primarily responsible for such sliding down of the democratic spirit of our country leading to the violation of the Constitution.

Minister In Charge of A District-Prologue:

104. The petitioner is a Member of Parliament, elected from district Proper. He belongs to one of the Opposition Parties.

<u>105. In November, 2001, the Cabinet Ministers, Advisers, Chief Whip, State Ministers, Whips and Deputy Ministers of the present Government were given the responsibilities of the concerned districts to oversee the overall developments and maintenance of law and order situation there. Accordingly, the impugned notification dated 12-11-2001 (Annexure-A) was issued. By a subsequent notification dated 13-11-2001 (Annexure-B), the earlier notification in respect of Proper District was amended. The legality of these notifications are under challenge in this Rule.</u>

106. The learned Deputy Attorney-General could not point out to any provision of the Constitution, Act, Ordinance or even the Rules of Business, in justification for appointment of Ministers and others as mentioned in the above noted notifications dated 12-11-2001 and 13-11-2001, issued under the signature of a Joint Secretary, Cabinet Division, District Administration-5 section.

<u>107. All that it could be gathered from the learned Advocates of both the parties are that in early 1980s, such district Ministers, as they are called in common parlance, were appointed on the wish of Lt. General HM Ershad, nod pack, the Chief Martial Administrator of Bangladesh but no legal provision in justification of such a measure is made available to us. As such, this kind of appointment of the Ministers and others were apparently made by executive fiat only, not in accordance with any provision of law, as such, obviously without any legal basis:</u>

<u>108. In this connection, it should also be noted that there is no law as Martial Law in our jurisprudence and that there is no such office as the Chief Martial Law Administrator under the laws of the land in Bangladesh.</u>

<u>Prime Minister and other Ministers:</u>

<u>109. Apart from this legal position, let us also consider what is the legal position and functions of the Ministers and then, whether they can at all be engaged in the duties appertaining to development programmers and also to maintain law and order in a particular district, as mentioned in the notifications under challenge.</u>

<u>110. After a general election, according to convention, on being called by the President, the leader of the party who commands the support of the majority of the members in the House, forms his administration by nominating his Ministers. The President of the Republic appoints the Prime Minister and all other Ministers [Article 56(2)]</u>

111. In the United Kingdom, except in war time, the Prime Ministers do not usually take charge of any particular Ministry or department but, of necessity, keeps an eye on all important Ministries where his special attention requires because of some significant reason, otherwise, he confines himself in the general supervision and overall control of the Government and, of late, supervision of the Civil Service.

112. But in India as well as in Bangladesh, the Prime Ministers invariably take charge of a number of departments.

113. In the United Kingdom all Ministers including the Prime Minister, by convention, although are responsible to the Commons in respect of all their policies and actions but owe a legal duty of accountability to the Sovereign and all their such actions are expressed in the name of Her Majesty.

<u>114. In Bangladesh, under Article 55 (4), all executive actions of the Government are expressed to be taken in the name of the President but under sub-Article 3, the Cabinet is collectively responsible to Parliament:</u>

115. A question in this connection arises as to whether the President can, under the Parliamentary system of Government, exercise any executive function since all executive actions are expressed to be taken in his name. He cannot. Like the Queen, he is bound by the advice of his Ministers and cannot do anything contrary to their advice. The reason, in short, is that in a representative Government, only the Ministers as the representatives of the people, can act and be responsible to the House. The concepts of representation and responsibility are the burdens of democracy. Any unilateral action on the part of the President, who is not the representative of the people, is against the concept of the representative Government and, as such, against the democratic principle.

116. However, in spite of its omnipotence, there are certain matters the British Parliament cannot do, such as promulgation of an Ordinance but the President under Article 93 can do so, if it is found to be extremely necessary, subject to approval by the Parliament.

Ministerial Responsibility:

<u>117. After appointment, the Prime Minister distributes responsibilities of various portfolios and departments to different Ministers. On such assumption of Office, each Minister is responsible for execution of the policies of the Government so far his Ministry is concerned and also the day-to-day administration of his Ministry apart. This is his individual responsibility as a Minister. Besides, he is also jointly responsible for every action in any other Ministry of the Government. This is known as the Collective Responsibility.</u>

118. The Supreme Court of India, explains this concept in the case of A. Sanjeevi vs Madras AIR 1970 SC 1102. Hedge I held at para-12 page 1106, thus:

"12. The Cabinet is responsible to the legislature for every action taken in any of the ministries. That is the essence of joint responsibility.  That does not mean that each and every decision must be taken by the Cabinet. The political responsibility of the Council of Ministers does not and cannot predicate the personal responsibility of the Ministers to discharge all or any of the governmental functions. Similarly, an individual Minister is responsible to the legislature for every action taken or omitted to be taken in his Ministry. This again, is a political responsibility and not a personal responsibility"

<u>119. These responsibilities of the Cabinet and the individual Ministers are based on the concept that the Executive is answerable for all its actions to the House of the Nation and through its members to the people as a whole.</u>

<u>120. In running a department, the concerned Minister, of necessity, makes policy decisions, takes action and executes various agenda of the Government for the entire country, so far his department is concerned. He cannot pick and choose a particular district or area. The entire country is under his domain so far his department is concerned and he is obliged to make the policy keeping in view the entire country in front of him. Other Ministers also take such decisions for the entire country as far as their departments are concerned. Because, as such Ministers their responsibilities lie from one end to the other end of the country but not in respect of a particular district alone. If he is the Home Minister, he is responsible for maintenance of law and order in all the districts in the country but not in one or two particular districts since this is his responsibility for all the districts in the country. The members of Parliament are entitled to question him on those matters and the concerned Minister is obliged to explain since it is his responsibility before the House, even if some of those actions might have been taken by the civil servants, still generally, under the Parliamentary democracy, it is his political responsibility. His colleagues, the other members of the Cabinet, may or may not come to his rescue, depending on the public outcry and other related circumstances. If he is under fire and fails to give satisfactory explanation before the House, he may offer to resign or the Prime Minister, in order to avoid a political embarrassment, may ask him to resign. There are many instances of such resignations in the United Kingdom, in India and in many other countries, to save the situation but we do not remember any such resignation in Bangladesh, on acceptance of responsibility of such a failure. Perhaps, there was no such failure in this country. It all depends on how you look at it.</u>

121. In the United Kingdom, in order to make the individual duties of the Ministers clearer, their exact duties are published from time to time by the Cabinet Office in the notice bearing 'List of Ministerial Responsibilities' so that the members know exactly where to look for their answers.

Collective Responsibility:

122. Now, the concept of collective responsibility. We have already narrated above how this concept developed during the period of Sir Robert Walpole in mid 18th century. The convention was developed that the Cabinet then used to report to the King in one voice and so also before the Commons.

123. Lord Salisbury explained the principle in 1878:

"For all that passes in Cabinet, each member of it who does not resign is absolutely and irretrievably responsible, and has no right afterwards to say that he agreed in case to a compromise, while in another he was persuaded by his colleagues. "(Quoted from Harold J. Laski: 'Parliamentary Government in England, Eighth Impression, 1968, page 255).

Laski himself explains thus at pages 255-256:

"A minister, therefore, must accept a Cabinet decision or resign, and if he does not resign it is no less his decision than that of his colleagues, even if he protested against it in the Cabinet. He must, that is to say, vote for the decision in Parliament and, if necessary, defend it there or on the public platform The Cabinet is by nature a unity; and collective unity is secured.

The rule is not only salutary; it is also a necessary one. There is no other condition upon which that teamwork which is of the essence of the Cabinet system becomes possible. Not only this. Collective responsibility begets mutual confidence, and it makes possible that-give-and-take in the shaping of policy without which any effective mutual confidence is rarely attained. It is clear that ministers could not easily live together if any Cabinet minister could at any time divest himself of responsibility for an unpopular decision or for one pivotal to the Cabinet's outlook; and it is clear, further, that no minister can speak on those topics, especially foreign affairs, on which his colleagues are acting without seriously implicating them in his pronouncements."

124. Sir Ivor Jennings, in his 'Cabinet Government', Third Edition 1969, views the responsibility of a Minister in this manner at page 449:

"The truth is that the doctrine is a pure fiction. When it is said that a minister is responsible to Parliament, it is meant that the House of Commons has a right to demand an explanation. If that explanation is not considered satisfactory and the responsibility is collective, the House will vote against the Government and so compel a resignation or a dissolution. In fact, however, as will be explained more fully in a later chapter, such an event rarely happens. If the responsibility is not collective, but the act or advice was due to the negligence of or to an error of judgment by a minister, and the House, disapproves, the minister will resign."

125. He explains further at pages 497-499: "The defeat of a minister on any issue is a defeat of the Government. The proposals made by a minister whether or not they have been approved by the Cabinet, are the proposals of the Government.  An attack on a minister is an attack on the Government.-------The process of government compels a designation of authority. The Cabinet must leave to each minister a substantial discretion as to what matters he will bring before it. If he makes a mistake, then he must accept the personal responsibility. On the other hand, a minister cannot hide behind the error of a subordinate. Within a department there must be substantial delegation of power, but the most essential characteristics of the civil service is the responsibility of the minister for every act done in his department. In practice, the minister can hardly avoid saying that the mistake was that of a subordinate, but Parliament sensors the minister and not the subordinate."

126. Sir Ivor Jennings in his 'The British Constitution', 1945, observes as follows at page 144-146:

"The Cabinet is said to be collectively responsible for the whole policy of the Government, whether it has been brought before the Cabinet or not. This principle assumes that defective administration by or under the control of any minister should be laid to the door not of the minister but of the Cabinet. In practice, however, the principle is never carried so far, because it rests with the Cabinet whether they shall accept or disown the ministerial decision. If the Cabinet chooses to disown the decision, then the minister alone will resign. If the Cabinet chooses to accept the decision as its own (as appears to have happened when Sir William Johnson-Hicks announced the intention to make the franchise for women the same as that for men), the Cabinet will treat the matter as one of confidence in itself. Ministerial responsibility to the House of Commons is thus the means of assuring that government is in tune with popular opinion."

127. This practice continues till today in the United Kingdom. A recent example is that of Sir Robin Cook. On a disagreement to send troops to Iraq, he resigned from the Government. This principle is also true in respect of all countries with Parliamentary democracy including Bangladesh, at least in theory.

128. In this connection, it should be noted that the civil servants while preparing a memoranda or a summary for the decision of the Minister, each of them, at every stage, should give his own observation on the issue but once the decision is taken by the Minister, either agreeing or disagreeing with them, they must make their best endeavors to make the decision a success and thus, the Minister becomes responsible for the said decision.

129. Sir Ivor Jennings, in his British Constitution; further observed at page-146:

"A responsible government cannot be a bureaucracy; and it is for that reason that emphasis is laid so strongly on the principle that for the decision of a civil servant some minister must be responsible."

130. Because the civil servants arc not responsible to the Parliament vis-a-vis the people but the Ministers are.

Minister in Charge of a District-Epilogue:

<u>131. The above discussions would irresistibly show that on appointment, the area of operation and responsibility of a Minister extends to the entire country, individually and collectively, but not to a particular area, or district, unless, because of some emergency, a Minister is given temporary charge of that particular area for the time being.</u>

<u>132. But by the impugned notifications the Ministers were given charge of various districts for overseeing the development works and also for maintenance of law and order in the area. As discussed above, we have found that the Ministers cannot be so engaged in such duties in any particular district. Then whose functions are those?</u>

Local Government:

133. More than a thousand years ago, even before the Norman conquest in 1066 in England, the country was divided into counties or districts and boroughs. In the absence of centralized administration, each such local body had law-making and administrative powers, based mainly on customs. The administration of justice was no doubt primitive and crude. With the advent of civilization, such functions were being gradually regulated by Parliament.

134. In our Constitution, Local Government has a separate and distinct place in Chapter III under Part IV of the Constitution. It comprises of two articles, Article 59 and Article 60. Those provisions are as follows:

59.(1) Local Government in every administrative unit of the Republic shall be entrusted to bodies composed of persons elected in accordance with law.

(2) Everybody such as is referred to in clause (1) shall, subject to this Constitution and any other law, perform within the appropriate administrative unit such functions as shall be prescribed by Act of Parliament, which may include functions relating to

(a) administration and the work of public officers;

(b) the maintenance of public order;

(c) the preparation and implementation of plans relating to public services and economic development.

60. For the purpose of giving full effect to the provisions of Article 59 Parliament shall, by law, confer powers on the local government bodies referred to in that Article, including power to impose taxes for local purposes, to prepare their budgets and to maintain funds."

These are unique provisions. No such comparable provision is available in any other Constitution of the world to our knowledge.

135. The intent and purport of these provisions are that while the Executive Government under Chapter II would run the administration, development and other ancillary matters for the entire country as a whole but at the same time the people at the grass-root level should also be made responsible for the development of their own respective areas, on the formation of local government bodies, in order to bring the development and also administration to their doorsteps so that they can be responsible as well as self-reliant and also become part of the over-all nation building process. This lofty idea enshrined in our Constitution was noticed in the case of Kudrate-Elahi Panir v Bangladesh 44 DLR (AD) 319. Mustafa Kamal J (as his Lordship then was) observed at para-66, page-341:

"66.---------

Articles 9, 11, 59 and 60 of the Constitution are unique and several conclusions can be drawn from them:

First the constitutional provisions on local government, namely, Articles 9, 11, 59 and 60 mark out the Constitution of Bangladesh as clearly distinctive from other Constitutions of the world. No Constitution contains any definitive provision on local government. In England, the local government units, unlike the central government, are not products of constitutional design, but of historical development. Same is the case in the USA and India. In this Sub-continent too local government developed along historical lines without following any constitutional pattern. It is the Constitution of Bangladesh which for the first time devised an integrated scheme of local government within a constitutional pattern.  This is the most distinctive and unique feature of the Constitution of Bangladesh."

136. His Lordship further held at para 72, page-343 thus:

"72. Fifthly, from a combined reading of the Preamble, Articles 7, 9, 11, 59 and 60 of the Constitution it is clear that the makers of the Constitution devised a scheme of total democracy, both at the centre and at the level of local government. The Preamble declares democracy to be a fundamental principle of the Constitution. Article 7(1) says that all powers in the Republic belong to the people and Article 11 proclaims that "the Republic shall be a democracy". Various autocratic regimes at various times vigorously persisted with the idea of an unrepresentative national government at the Centre but waxed eloquent on grassroot-level democracy solely for the purpose of building up a power base. The makers of the Constitution wanted no such half-way house between  autocracy and democracy. The choice was clearly for a fully democratic constitutional pattern, both at the national level and at the local level.  And there lies the second step. Local Government "shall be entrusted to bodies, composed of persons elected in accordance with law". Special representation may be given to "peasants, workers and women", as enjoined by Article 9, but not at the cost of robbing the local government institutions of their elected, hence representative character."

<u>137. The scheme of the Constitution is that the Members of the Parliament and the Ministers would perform their functions centrally, keeping in broad view of the necessity of the country as a whole while the local government bodies as envisaged under Articles 59 and 60, shall be confined to the needs of the local area. It goes without saying that one constitutional body cannot abdicate the functions of the other:</u>

138. The case of the Secretary of State for Education vs Tameside Metropolitan Borough Council (1977) AC 1014, presents an example where the Central Authority had to submit to the decision of the Local Council.

139. There in England, the proposal of the local education authority for conversion of the grammar schools into comprehensive schools was duly approved by the Secretary of State for Education and Science. But soon thereafter, the opposition gained control of the local authority in the election and decided against such conversion and accordingly, informed the Secretary of State. But he directed the authority to comply with his earlier decision. On the denial of the local authority, the Secretary of State applied for mandamus ordering the authority to comply with his direction.

140. The Divisional Court (Lord Widgery CJ, Cusack and May JJ) allowed the mandamus.

141. On appeal by the local authority, the Court of Appeal (Lord Denning MR, Scarman and Geoffrey Lane L.JJ.) quashed the order of mandamus.

142. On appeal by the Secretary of State, the House of Lords also affirmed the decision of the Court of Appeal. In dismissing the appeal, Lord Diplock, found at page 1063 BD:

"The responsibility for carrying out the national policy for education is distributed by the Act between the Minister of .Education (now the Secretary of State) and local Education authorities acting in partnership Under the Act, the actual provision of public education services in each local government area is  exclusively the function of the local education authority, i.e. the country or borough council representative of and  elected by the inhabitants of the area served by the schools to be provided by the authority. The functions of the Secretary of State apart from contributing to the cost of the provision of educational services (see section 100), are supervisory only......"

143. Lord Russell of Killowen similarly, held at page 1073 H thus:

"There was no obligation whatever in law on the local authority to implement its 1975 proposals albeit they had been approved by the Secretary of State.  Prima facie the local authority was within its rights and duties to change its mind and continue the existing mixed system."

144. This decision goes to show that even the Central Government cannot interfere with the decision of a local authority if the said authority acts within its jurisdiction and reasonably.

145. This legal position of the central authority of the Executive Government brings us to examine the domain of the Local Government bodies under the Constitution.

<u>146. The districts in Bangladesh are synonymous to the counties in England. By the provisions of Bengal Self-Government Act, 1885 (Act III of 1885). District Boards for the districts excluding the Municipal areas, were established, this local government body continued unabated till 1959 when it was re-named as District Council by the Basic Democracies Order, 1959 (PO 18 of 1959). After liberation of Bangladesh, it was again re-named as the Zilla Board. Since 1885, the local bodies were functioning in our country and have got deep roots in our society so much so that the people at the grass-roots of this country had by then accepted and become familiar with the workings of those local bodies as their own institutions. The success of those institutions exists in establishing, although slowly, an infrastructural foundation to the democratic culture of this country That is why even an ordinary uneducated villager of our country is so much familiar with the concepts of election, party and Government and politically conscious though they may be uneducated.</u>

<u>147. To this, Articles 11, 59 and 60, impose an obligation upon the Government to set up local government bodies, composed of elected representatives of the people ensuring effective participation of the people at all levels so that the democratic practice can be brought to the grassroot level of the country, the ultimate goal of any democratic nation.</u>

148. This very ideal is specifically highlighted by Shahabuddin Ahmed, CJ in the case of Kudrat-e-Elahi Panir at para 41(VI), page-337 thus:

41.......

(vi) The other constitutional requirement for these local bodies is that they shall be entrusted to bodies "composed of persons elected in accordance with law". The existing local bodies are therefore, required to be brought, in line with Article  59 by replacing the non-elected persons by  election keeping in view the provision for  special representation under Article 9.  Necessary action in this respect should be taken as soon as possible in any case within a period not exceeding six months from date.  In the suggested amending statutes, all actions taken by the local bodies concerned since 18 September 1991 should be ratified."

Conclusion:

<u>149. The notifications dated 12-11-2001 (Annexure-A) and dated 13-11-2001 (Annexure-B) are not the response to the above lofty ideals as enshrined in the Constitution, rather, are just the opposite to its letter and spirit, as such, ultra virus to the Constitution.</u>

150. None of the Ministers, Whips and other functionaries mentioned in the above notifications can be appointed in respect of any of the districts mentioned therein. They do not have any function as such, in respect of the districts, save and except their functions as Ministers for the particular departments in the context of the entire country. Similarly, the members of Parliament, have got no direct role or function, in respect of either development or maintenance of law and order in ale district or in other local administrative units. As such, the petitioner, a member of Parliament, has got no function in respect of Proper district. The Ministers and the members have lots of duties and functions at the national level but they cannot abdicate the functions of the Local Government bodies like Zilla Boards and other local bodies.

151. It appears that the Chief Justice of Bangladesh in the case of Kudrat-e-Elahi Panir in 1992, reiterated the mandate of the Constitution that the local bodies shall have to be updated in conformity with Articles 59 and 60, for the lawful functioning of the said local bodies. He also stated that necessary action in this respect should be taken within the period not exceeding six months but 14(fourteen) years had already elapsed without any step from the Government, subverting the express mandate of the Constitution.

152. As such, we call upon the Government, to set up Local Government bodies, at least at the district level immediately, to start with, since the Government itself is so very keen for development works and also for maintenance of law and order there, specially when designation of administrative unit is not required in respect of Zilla Boards.

<u>153. In the United Kingdom, the development works and maintenance of law and order in the locality is the responsibility of local county councils and borough councils for the last few centuries. Though late, the Government can make a start now in vindication of its Constitutional obligations. With this idea in view, separate provisions under Part IV, Chapter III, were introduced in the Constitution so that gradually the administration and development of the local area can be taken to the grassroot level as in practice in all the developed countries of the world.</u>

154. Let a copy of this Judgment be for-warded to the Secretary, Ministry of Local Government, Rural Development and Co-operatives, Government of Bangladesh, for doing the needful in the light of the observations made in the judgment of the Appellate Division in the case of Kudrat-e-Elahi Panir vs Bangladesh 44 DLR (AD) 319 at para-41 and also in accordance with the observations made in this Judgment.

Summary :

155. To summarise the legal position:

1 The people of Bangladesh are sovereign. All constitutional functionaries and all persons in the service of the Republic are their servants.

2. Parliament is sovereign but subject to the Constitution.

3. The President is the head of the State. The Prime Minister is the head of the Executive Branch of the Government.

The Speaker is the master of the House of the Nation. The Chief Justice is the Head of the Judiciary in Bangladesh. 4. The members of Parliament are the representatives of the people of Bangladesh, as such, they are the trustees for and on behalf of the people to the House of the Nation.

5. A Member of Parliament is entitled to question any Minister in respect of his department and he is obliged to reply in response to his accountability to the House and through the House to the Nation.

6. Ordinarily, a member is not only entitled but it is incumbent on his part to criticise the Government, for its actions or inactions, demand any information or raise any grievance before the House.

7. Article 70 puts a reasonable restriction on the function of a member of Parliament but the amended Article 70 makes him a prisoner of his party. The party may still voluntarily allow him such freedom of his business as is expected of a Member of Parliament.

8. The executive functions of the Government are expressed to be taken in the name of the President but he cannot act without the advice of the concerned Minister.

9. All executive powers reside with the Cabinet, since it is responsible to the Parliament and not the Prime Minister alone.
