10. The Ministers are individually responsible in respect of their own departments and also collectively responsible for the Government, to the Parliament. They have no powers and functions in respect of any particular district, although, they may have supervisory functions, relating to his own department.

11. The members are entitled to ask for any information and raise the grievance of any of their electorates before the House but cannot interfere with the local administration.

12. The Local Government Bodies in every administrative unit of the Republic are charged with the functions relating to administration and the work of public officers in the local area, the maintenance of public order and other nation-building development activities there.

13. Neither the Ministers nor the Members of Parliament can abdicate the functions of the elected members of the Local Government Bodies in respect of their functions in the concerned administrative units.

14. The representative character of the Government and its accountability to the people are the burdens of democracy. If these are not present, the republican character of the nation would be lost.

Order:

156. Under the circumstances, the Notification No. মপবি/জেপ্রঃ-৫/২(৪)৯২/অংশ-১)/১৭২ তারিখ ২৮ কার্তিক ১৪০৮/১২ নভেম্বর, ২০০১ dated 12-11-2001 (Annexure-A) and the notification No. মপবি/জেপ্রঃ-৫/২(৪)৯২/অংশ-১)/১৭৩ তারিখ ২৯ কার্তিক ১৪০৮/১৩ নভেম্বর, ২০০১ dated 13-11-2001 (Annexure-B), both issued under the signature of the Joint Secretary, Cabinet Division, Government of Bangladesh, are declared illegal and without lawful authority.

In the result, the Rule is made absolute but without any order as to cost.

End.

full_judgment:
AK Badrul Huq J: Pre-emptee Md Mofizul Islam Sarkar seeks review of the Judgment dated January 13, 2002 recorded by this Court in Civil Revision No. 3535 of 1999 springing out of a Pre-emption proceeding under section 96 of The State Acquisition and Tenancy Act (for short The Act) on presentation of Review Petition whereupon Rule was issued calling upon Pre-emptor-opposite party Subitri Sundari Mali to show cause as to why Judgment dated 13-1-2002 passed by Division Bench in Civil Revision No. 3535 of 1999 should not be reviewed or such other order or further order or orders be not passed which this Court might deem fit and proper.

2. Portrayal of essential facts forming background of this Review Petition may succinctly be voiced which are:

A. Subitri Sundari Mali in capacity of a co-sharer of Pre-emption proceeding land exercised right of pre-emption in respect of 0.37½(thirty-seven and half) acres of property from plot No. 335 covered in the deed of conveyance dated 18-12-1993 in favour of Pre-emptee-petitioner and one Md Nazrul Islam Sarkar, Pre-emptee-Second-Opposite-Party depicting them as strangers to Pre-emption proceeding land before learned Subordinate Judge (now Joint District Judge), Munshiganj on presentation of a petition under section 96 of The Act. The petition had been numbered as Pre-emption Miscellaneous Case No. 18 of 1994.

B. Pre-emptee-petitioner put up resistance against Pre-emption Miscellaneous case on laying a written objection taking stand that Pre-emptor was not a co-sharer in case holding and, also, that the deed of conveyance was not an out and out sale and it was accompanied by an agreement of reconveyance.

C. Learned trial Judge dismissed Pre-emption Miscellaneous case.

D. Pre-emptor took an appeal before the learned District Judge, Munshiganj. In the appeal Pre-emptor laid a petition for amendment of the petition for pre-emption and restructured his status as contiguous land holder of the land transferred instead of co-sharer of the case holding. Appellate Judge allowed the amendment and sent the case back on remand to Trial Judge.

E. Pre-emption Miscellaneous Case this time, also, was not visited with a favourable verdict.

F. Learned Trial Judge once again dismissed the Pre-emption Miscellaneous Case canvassing ground that the deed of sale was accompanied with an agreement for reconveyance and it was an usufructuary mortgage and the case was not maintainable.

G. Pre-emptor again approached before appellate Judge in an appeal. The appeal met with success. Appeal was allowed and Pre-emption Miscellaneous Case was allowed on reversing the decision of Trial Judge. Appellate Judge could not accept the agreement for reconveyance as genuine.

H. Pre-emptee, thereafter, invoked this Court in Civil Revisional Jurisdiction on presentation of a Revision Petition under section 115 of The Code of Civil Procedure (hereinafter referred to as The Code). Grounds canvassed before High Court Division were:

i. The Court of appeal erred in law in reversing the finding of trial Court that the transaction was an out and out sale without considering oral and documentary evidence led by parties.

ii. The claim of the Pre-emptor to pre-empt the Pre-emption proceeding land in the capacity of a contiguous holder of the land to be transferred on the strength of a petition dated 14-11-1996 stood barred by law and the appellate Court fell into a serious error in allowing Pre-emption case.

iii. Pre-emptor filed Pre-emption case claiming herself to be co-sharer in the case holding and, as such, she did not implead owners of contiguous land holders of the land under Pre-emption proceeding but learned District Judge allowed pre-emption in making out a Third case that the Pre-emptor-opposite party was owner of contiguous land to the land transferred without considering that the contiguous land owners were not impleaded as parties and the court of appeal committed an error resulting in an error in the decision occasioning a failure of justice.

3. This Court did not feel impressed by ground Nos. 1 and 2 and ground Nos. 1 and 2 stood turned down. This Court came in agreement with the decisions recorded by Court of appeal. This Court did not meet third ground which was impleading of owners of contiguous land holders of the land sold.

4. Pre-emptee-petitioner now seeks review of the decisions rendered by this Court on filing this Review Petition contending, inter alia, that after discharging the Rule Sree Sunil Biswas, son of pre-emptor Subitri Sundari Mali gave out in the locality that the Pre-emptee lost his case before Hon'ble High Court Division and he disclosed that during pendency of Civil Revision petition, Pre-emptor transferred the case land to him and he would dispossess petitioner from case land very soon. Thereafter, on searching relevant registry petitioner on 17-1-2001 obtained certified copy of registered Gift Deed No. 2704 dated 27-10-1999 and became specifically aware that during pendency of Civil Revision petition pre-emptor transferred the entire land acquired by her and pre-emptor, thus, lost her right of pre-emption. The certified copy of the Deed of Gift dated 27-10-1999 executed and registered by Pre-emptor Subitri Sundari Mali in favour of Sree Sunil Chandra Biswas has been annexed in Review Petition.

5. Basic grounds pressed into service and contentions advanced are as follows:

I. In order to establish a claim for pre-emption the Pre-emptor must have subsisting interest on the contiguous land throughout the whole proceeding and in the case Pre-emptor transferred the contiguous land by way of gift which was the foundation stone to pre-empt the land under Pre-emption proceeding during pendency of Civil Revision case before High Court Division and, as such, the Pre-emptor lost her right of pre-emption on the case land.

II. The fact that Pre-emptor transferred the contiguous land, that is plot No. 334, during pendency of Civil Revision was not within the knowledge of Pre-emptee-Petitioner and, as such, Pre-emptee-Petitioner could not bring to notice of this Court at the time of hearing of Revision Petition and the execution and registration of the deed of gift matter, if it could be brought before this Court, the fate of Civil Revision case would have been different.

6. Support for the contentions has been sought from Mamijannessa vs Tazaruddin and another, 14 DLR 572, Lakhi Kanta Patibar vs Sunil Kumar Patibar and others, 17 DLR 327 and Chandra Kumar Maladas vs Abdul Motaleb and others, 19 DLR (SC) 36.

7. Pre-emptor Subitri Sundari Mali having been dead her heirs Sunil Chandra Biswas, Parimal Chandra Biswas who are sons and Noni Gopal Biswas who is grandson had been substituted in her place as opposite party Nos. 1(a) to 1(c) respectively in Civil Rule.

8. Substituted opposite party Nos. 1(a) to 1(c) entered appearance in Civil Rule and filed an Affidavit-in-opposition. In the Affidavit-in-opposition statements made are:

(a) Subitri Sundari Mali being an old lady after getting the order of pre-emption from appellate Court wished to make amicable partition of her whole property between two sons and one grandson through pre-deceased son the opposite party Nos. 1(a) to 1(c).

(b) In the deed of gift dated 27-10-1999 Subitri Sundari Mali gifted .72 acres out of .74 acres in contiguous plot No. 334. Subitri Sundari Mali died on 7-1-2001 before final order passed in Civil Revision case and, thus, it could not be said that Pre-emptor lost right of pre-emption in the case. In the Affidavit-in-opposition death certificate of Subitri Sundari Mali evidencing that she died on 7-1-2001 had been annexed as Annexure X.

9. Contentions brought home from the side of substituted opposite parties are as follows:

i. Proceeding during pendency of Civil Revision Petition case cannot be said to be proceeding and Revision is not an original proceeding and transfer by way of gift in favour of substituted opposite party Nos. 1(a) during pendency of Civil Revision case cannot be a transfer during a proceeding.

ii. On the verdict of appellate Court in favour of Pre-emptor Subitri Sundari Mali, the latter got the right to transfer and the right of pre-emption cannot be defeated by transfer during pendency of Civil Revision proceeding.

iii. Right of Pre-emption is heritable right and that heritable right cannot be defeated.

Inu Mia and others vs Mokhlesur Rahman and others, 45 DLR (AD) 171 and Khan Sahib Khan Muhammad Saadat Ali Khan vs Administrator, Corporation of City of Lahore, PLD 1949 Lahore 541 have been relied upon in support of contentions pressed.

10. Regard being had to the rival contentions pushed forward and fact and circumstances of the case the legal debate centres round on two core points which are:

I. Whether Pre-emptor incurred legal disability in having a verdict of pre-emption in view of loss or extinguishment of subsisting interest on the contiguous land of plot No. 334 for transfer of the said plot by way of a deed of gift in favour of substituted opposite party No. 1(a) who is son of Pre-emptor and

II. Whether decision allowing Pre-emption in favour of Pre-emptor in Civil Revision case can be reviewed.

11. In approaching and answering to the points posed it will be profitable to pay attention to the scope of Review first. Review Jurisdiction visualised by section 114 of The Code is to be traced to Order XLVII, rule 1 of The Code which contains prescribed condition and limitation in terms of requirement of that section. Order XLVII, rule 1 of The Code before Civil Procedure Code (Amendment) Ordinance of 1962 ran thus:

1. (1) Any person considering himself aggrieved

(a) by a decree or order from which an appeal is allowed, but from which no appeal has been preferred.

(b) by a decree or order from which no appeal is allowed,

or

(c) by a decision on a reference from a Court of Small Causes, and who, from the discovery of new and important matter or evidence which, after the exercise of due diligence, was not within his knowledge or could not be produced by him at the time when the decree was passed or order made or on account of some mistake or error apparent on the face of the record, or for any other sufficient reason, desires to obtain a review of the decree passed or order made against him, may apply for a review of Judgment to the Court which passed the decree or made the order.

12. The word "or could not be produced by him" or the words, "for any other sufficient

reason" stood omitted by Civil Procedure Code (Amendment) Ordinance of 1962 (Ordinance No. XLIV of 1962) which came into force on June 5, 1962.

13. Review now can be sought and made only on two specific grounds which are:

I. From the discovery of new and important matter or evidence which after exercise of due diligence, was not within his knowledge when the decree was passed or order made.

II. On account of some mistake or error apparent on the face of the record.

14. The status or legal character of pre-emptor after amendment of the petition under section 96 of The Act was ownership of contiguous plot No. 334 to the land transferred that is plot No. 335, the area of being 0.37½ acres. Under section 96 of The Act three categories of persons can exercise right of pre-emption. The first category is co-sharer by inheritance. The second category is co-sharer by purchase and the third category is holder of the land contiguous to the land transferred. The standing of holder of a contiguous land is inferior to the status of co-sharers by way of inheritance and co-sharer by purchase.

15. In Pre-emption Miscellaneous Case in paragraph 5 of the petition it is stated that Netai Mali had been owner of Eight annas thirteen gondas one kara and one kranti (।। ১৩√ক্রান্তি) and Netai Mali died leaving behind four (4) daughters, namely, Subitri Sundari Mali (Pre-emptor), Pulini Sundari Mali, Giribala Mali and Usha Rani Mali. In paragraph 6 it is stated that Pulini Sundari. Giribala and Usha Rani Mali by way of seven (7) separate deeds of conveyance transferred their all interest in favour of Subitri Sundari Mali (Pre-emptor).

16. In plot No. 334 area of the land is .74 acres. Predecessor-in-interest of Pre-emptor Subitri Netai Mali got less than .42 acres in eight anna, thirteen gondas, one kara and one kranti (।। ১৩√ক্রান্তি) share and Pre-emptor Subitri Sundari Mali by way of inheritance and sale deeds from her three sisters Pulini Sundari and others got less than .42 acres which her father Netai Mali got. From the deed of gift dated 27-10-1999 executed and registered by Pre-emptor Subitri Sundari Mali in favour of her son Sunil Chandra Biswas, substituted opposite party No. 1(a) it reveals that out of .74 acres she gifted .72 acres that is more .30 acres of land from plot No. 334. Thus, it becomes manifestly clear that after the date 27-10-1999 Pre-emptor Subitri Sundari Mali got no subsisting interest on the contiguous land of plot No. 334.

17. Admittedly, the deed of gift was made during pendency of Civil Revision case. Rule on Civil Revision Petition was issued on 24-10-1999. Deed of gift is dated 27-10-1999. Pre-emptor Subitri Sundari Mali died on 7-1-2001. Judgment in Civil Revision Case had been passed on 13-1-2002. Deed of Gift was executed and registered during pendency of Civil Revision proceeding before this Court.

18. In Mamijannessa vs Tazaruddin and another (Supra) the question that moved forward was whether Pre-emptor Tazaruddin could pre-empt the land purchased by Pre-emptee-petitioner when his own land by purchase of which he became a co-sharer had been pre-empted by another co-sharer. The question posed stood answered in the following way: The right of pre-emption has been given to a co-sharer in the holding, and if during the pendency of a proceeding for pre-emption started by him he ceases to be a co-sharer, his right of pre-emption comes to an end. This right is not an indefeasible right. It no doubt arises on the sale of a portion of a holding by a co-sharer but continues only so long as the Pre-emptor remains a co-sharer; and if during the pendency of the proceeding for pre-emption the Pre-emptor ceases to be a co-sharer, the right is lost and the pre-emption proceeding must fail, on the loss of his status as a co-sharer, his position and that of the stranger transferee are the same and he cannot claim a better right to hold the land than the other. In that view of the matter, since the opposite party ceased to be a co-sharer during the pendency of the appeal preferred by the present petitioner, the pre-emption proceeding must fail.

19. In Lakhi Kanta Patibar vs Sunil Kumar Patibar and others (Supra) two Pre-emptors in order to get pre-emption filed a Pre-emption case during pendency of Pre-emption proceeding, Pre-emptor No. 1 transferred all the interest in the holding. The question mooted was that the Pre-emptor No. 1 having all his interest in the holding got no locus standi to maintain a claim for Pre-emption. Principle enunciated is that in order to maintain a claim for pre-emption, the Pre-emptor must have interest in the holding not only at the time of filing of the petition for pre-emption but, also, throughout the whole proceeding. In the said case it had been, also, held that by this Pre-emptor No. 2, another co-sharer tenant, cannot be disentitled to get an order of pre-emption in her favour in respect of entire land under Pre-emption.

20. In Chandra Kumar Maladas vs Abdul Motaleb and others (Supra) purchase by respondent No. 1 Abdul Motaleb from Manmohan Parsana and Rajani had been pre-empted by other co-sharer holders and, as such, Pre-emptor had no subsisting interest in the holding to pre-empt the auction sale in favour of respondent No. 2. It has been laid down: A Pre-emptor must not only have a subsisting interest in the holding when he filed the application for pre-emption under section 26F of The Bengal Tenancy Act, but must continue to hold the self-same interest to the date when the case is finally disposed of. It has, also, been held: A co-sharer means a person whose interest subsists throughout the course of the application to pre-empt and not a person who held such an interest in the beginning, but lost it before its disposal. Equally, a fresh interest acquired at a latter stage cannot be tacked on to the interest held in the beginning but lost during the pendency of the application.

21. We are in respectful obedience to proposition of law propounded in the above authorities.

<u>22. The thrust of contention canvassed from the side of substituted opposite parties is that "Proceeding" means proceeding before the court of first instance as well as the appellate Court and the term "proceeding" cannot be stretched to the Revisional stage ie Revisional proceeding under section 115 of The Code.</u>

23. "Proceeding" is a term of wide amplitude. "Proceeding" is a prescribed course of action for enforcement of a legal right. The word "proceeding" has been stated in the Black's Law Dictionary, Sixth Edition page 1204 in the following way:

"An act which is done by the authority or direction of the court, agency, or tribunal, express or implied; an act necessary to be done in order to obtain a given end; a prescribed mode of action for carrying into effect a legal right. All the steps or measures adopted in the prosecution or defence of an action. Statter vs United States, CCA Alaska, 66 F 2d 819, 822. The word may be used synonymously with "action" or "suit" to describe the entire course of an action at law or suit in equity from the issuance of the writ or filing of the complaint until the entry of a final judgment, or may be used to describe any act done by authority of a court of law and every step required to be taken in any cause by either party. The proceedings of a suit embrace all matters that occur in its progress judicially.

In a more particular sense, any application to a court of justice, however made, for aid in the enforcement of rights, for relief, for redress of injuries, for damages, or for any remedial object."

24. The word “proceeding" what it connotes, came up before Full Bench of Madhya Pradesh High Court in Ratanchand Darbarilal Saina and others vs Rajendra Kumar Khoobchand and others, AIR 1970 MP 1(4) FB wherein it has been stated that a suit, appeal or second appeal can all be described as proceeding.

25. It is observed that provision of Second Appeal embodied in section 100 of The Code though stood omitted by Law Reforms Ordinance of 1978 which came into force on June 1, 1979 now stands replaced by section 115 of The Code. Before Law Reforms Ordinance Judgment and decree passed by Court of appeal were challenged in second appeal under section 100 and now those are being challenged under section 115 of The Code.

<u>26. "Pendency of proceeding" what it indicates came up for examination before a Division Bench of High Court Division in Jatindra Chandra Urang vs Md Shmnsuddin and others 34 DLR 265 when a narrow interpretation was endeavoured to put that proceeding before trial Court was only the proceeding. It has been ordained, that pendency of proceeding has a wider connotation, it means pending before the competent Court and awaiting final decision in the matter. In the case proceeding was very much before High Court Division.</u>

<u>27. The Pre-emption proceeding did not reach to its finality in the appellate Court. The propriety of decision rendered by appellate Court was called in question before High Court Division by Pre-emptee on presentation of a Civil Revision Petition for adjudication and proceeding before High Court Division was definitely a Proceeding. Any proceeding can be pushed forward even to the last ladder of hierarchy, that is before Apex Court the Appellate Division and proceeding before Apex Court for a final decision shall demonstratively be, also, a Proceeding.</u>

28. The argument put forward in bringing home contention that after the decision of the appellate Court and during pendency of Civil Revision case Preemptor Subitri Sundari Mali got right to alienate the property by way of gift has got no substance and the same stands ruled out.

<u>29. Evaluated in the above discourse, fact and circumstances of the case and taking into stock the authorities listed above we have no manner of hesitation to hold that since Pre-emptor Subitri Sundari Mali transferred by way of gift deed dated 27-10-1999 in favour of substituted party No. 1(a) the contiguous plot No. 334 and got no subsisting interest on the contiguous plot No. 334 to the plot transferred which is plot No. 335 she got no right to be graced with a verdict of preemption. Both Pre-emptor and the Pre-emptee acquired equal status, that is strangers to case holding.</u>

30. The rightness of the contention that the right of pre-emption is a heritable right and that heritable right cannot be defeated and the applicability of Inn Mia and others vs Moklesur Rahman and others 171 (Supra) in the fact and circumstances of the case in hand now shall be addressed.

31. It has already been set out that the gift deed was made on 27-10-1999 and Pre-emptor Subitri Sundari Mali breathed her last on 7-1-2001 and Judgment of Revision Case was passed on 13-1-2002. Loss of status or standing of Pre-emptor Subitri Sundari Mali to pre-empt the land under pre-emption proceeding as owner/holder of contiguous land that is plot No. 334 occurred long before her death and succession/inheritance opened in favour of substituted opposite party No. 1(a) long after extinguishment of interest on the plot No. 334 which conferred right upon Pre-emptor Subitri Sundari Mali to pre-empt case land. The right of pre-emption on Pre-emption proceeding land could be inherited only when during subsistence on interest Pre-emptor Subitri Sundari Mali would have been dead. The substituted opposite party No. 1(a) inherited nothing after Pre-emptor's disinvestment of the interest on the contiguous plot.

32. Inu Mia and others vs Mokhlesur Rahman and others (Supra) Respondents 1-9 filed a Pre-emption case under section 96 of The Act for an order of Pre-emption in respect of the land sold by respondent No. 10 in favour of Chand Mia, predecessor-in-interest of appellant Nos. 1 to 8 and respondent No. 52. Respondent Nos. 1-6 claimed to be co-sharers by inheritance and respondent Nos. 7-9 claimed to be co-sharers by purchase. Saadat Ali Kari, predecessor-in-interest of respondent Nos. 1-6 during his lifetime did not choose to file a petition for pre-emption. On the death of Saadat Ali right of pre-emption had been exercised by his sons, respondent Nos. 1-6. The question arose whether the legal heirs of Saadat Ali i.e. respondent Nos. 1-6 could exercise right of pre-emption. The observation of their Lordship is couched in the following terms:

Section 96 provides right of pre-emption to the co-sharers and, to the persons having land contiguous to the land transferred. In both the cases the person claiming Pre-emption must show his existing interest in the land, that is, in the case of a co-sharer it must be proved that the Pre-emptor has got subsisting interest in the holding and in the case of contiguous owner it must be proved that the Pre-emptor has got subsisting interest in the land contiguous to the land sold. In either of the cases the interest in the holding or in the contiguous land must subsist till the order of pre-emption is made. After filing pre-emption either claiming to be a co-sharer in the holding or claiming to be an owner of contiguous land, if the Pre-emptor ceases to have interest in the land in question the pre-emption case fails. On the death of the pre-emptor this right is not lost, because, the pre-emptor's heirs or their heirs inherit the right along with the land. In a pending proceeding the heirs are entitled to be substituted in the place of the deceased pre-emptor and proceed with the case. So also the right of pre-emption once accrued, the right of pre-emption does not lapse in the event of death, but it devolves upon his legal heirs. The legal heirs inheriting the land are competent to exercise the right of pre-emption in accordance with the law.

33. In the cited case, also, the principle that interest of Pre-emptor in the holding or in the contiguous land must subsist till final order had been reiterated. The authority cited is of no assistance to substitute opposite parties and rather it helps Pre-emptee-petitioner.

34. This takes us to another vital aspect of the matter. By way of amendment standing of the Pre-emptor to pre-empt was ownership of contiguous land to the land sold. In the Pre-emption case only the purchasers and sellers were made parties as opposite party Nos. 1 and 2 and 3 to 7 respectively.

35. Under sub-section 1 of section 96 of The Act (i) co-sharer-tenant of a holding and (ii) tenants holding lands contiguous to the land transferred can exercise right of Pre-emption.

36. Sub-section 2 of section 96 of The Act postulates that (a) when a petition for Pre-emption is made by a co-sharer-tenant all other co-sharer tenants and the transferee and (b) when a petition is made by a contiguous land owner (i) all co-sharer tenants and (ii) all other tenants holding land contiguous to the land transferred and the transferees are to be impleaded as parties in the petition for Pre-emption.

37. In view of standing of Pre-emptor Subitri Sundari Mali as contiguous land owner of the land transferred after the amendment, the contiguous land holders/owners were required to be impleaded as opposite parties but contiguous land owners were not made parties in Pre-emption Miscellaneous case and the Pre-emption case manifestly suffers from defect of parties and non-impleading of contiguous land holders in the case is an error apparent on the face of the record. In Revision Petition non-impleading of holders of contiguous land had been specifically taken as ground No. 1.

38. Khan Sahib Khan Muhammad Sandal Ali Khan vs. Administrator Corporation of City of Lahore, PLD 1949 Lahore 541 (Supra) got no manner of application in the fact and circumstances of the case and we are not at all inclined to make an idle parade of discussing the said case. It is not understood for what purpose the case has been relied upon.

<u>39. The transfer of subsisting interest in contiguous plot No. 334 by way of gift by Pre-emptor Subitri Sundari Mali to substituted opposite party No. 1(a) was not within knowledge of the Pre-emptee when the Civil Revision was heard and disposed of. This is a discovery of new, and important matter and this discovery is a good ground for Review of the decision passed in Civil Revision case. This can be, also, characterised as an error apparent on the face of the record.</u>

<u>40. Non-impleading of holders of contiguous land to the land transferred strikes at the root of Pre-emption case and non-impleading of contiguous land owners in Pre-emption Miscellaneous case and non-consideration of the ground can be, also, characterised as an error apparent on the face of the record.</u>

<u>41. In the touchstone of the laws and principles of Review, grant or refusal of Pre-emption on the loss of standing and extinguishment of subsisting interest on the land contiguous to the land transferred by way of gift and taking into account catena of authorities on the subject and, also, gauged in the fact and circumstances of the case we are of this view that Pre-emptee has made out a case of Review and the judgment passed in Civil Revision demands review.</u>

42. Two points formulated, thus, stand answered in the affirmative.

43. Corollary thereof is that Civil Rule arising out of Review Petition got merit and the same succeeds. Rule is made absolute. The Judgment dated 13-1-2002 passed by this Court in Civil Revision No. 3535 of 1999 is reviewed and Civil Revision case succeeds. Rule arising out of Civil Revision Petition under section 115 of The Cody is made absolute. The Pre-emption Miscellaneous Case No. 18 of 1994 of the Court of Subordinate Judge (now Joint District Judge), Munshiganj stands dismissed.

No costs.

End.

lawyer:
Fakhrul Islam, Advocate—For the Petitioner. 
Karunanmoy Chakma, Deputy Attorney-General—For the Respondents.
parties:
Zahirul Hoque Chokder ----- Petitioner
vs. 
Bangladesh and others ----- Respondents
full_judgment:
Nazmun Ara Sultana J: This Rule Nisi was issued calling upon the respondents to show cause as to why the inclusion of House No. 23, Road No. 2, Block-D, Section 1 Mirpur, Dhaka in the 'ka' list of abandoned property (Annexure-K) should not be declared to have been made without lawful authority and is of no legal effect and/or such other or further order or orders passed as to this Court may seem fit and proper.

2. The case of the writ petitioner Zahirul Hoque Chokder, in short, is that an area of 131 square yards of land of plot No. 23, Road No. 2, Block-B, Section 1, Mirpur, Dhaka was leased out by the 'Government in favour of Jamshed khan by a registered deed of lease dated 10-8-61 for a period of 99 years. That Jamshed Khan got possession of the said land and possessed the same peacefully, Jamshed Khan erected a pucca building on the said land and had been residing there with his family members on payment of all rents and taxes, etc., That the said Jamshed Khan was an employee of Rupali Bank, Dilkusha Branch, Dhaka and in respect of his service the Manager of the said Rupali Bank issued a certificate on 27-5-1980. That Jamshed Khan himself also swore an affidavit of allegiance before the Magistrate, 1st Class, Dhaka on 22-3-1973, That while he was in possession Jamshed Khan, being in need of money, sold the said property to the petitioner by a registered Kabala dated 31-5-1980, That the petitioner also was an employee of Rupali Bank, Dilkusha Branch, Since after purchasing the property in question from Jamshed Khan the petitioner has been living there with his family members. The petitioner erected a two-storied building on the said land by taking loan from the Rupali Bank keeping the said property under mortgage.

3. It has also been stated in the writ petition that Jamshed Khan migrated from India in 1950 and since then he was all along a Bangladesh citizen and his whereabouts were not unknown at any point of time, Jamshed Khan died on 6-10-86 and was buried in the graveyard of Section 10/A, Mirpur, Dhaka and the secretary of the said graveyard committee issued a certificate to that effect. That the Assistant Commissioner Settlement of the Ministry of Housing and Public Works by his Memo No. MH 301/61/9747 Kasha dated 21-8-1995 requested the Administrative Officer, Mirpur Housing Estate to enquire into the present position of the property in question and accordingly, an enquiry was held by the administrative officer and an inspector of Mirpur Housing Estate who submitted their enquiry report to the Assistant Commissioner, Housing and Public Works Ministry stating that the property in question was leased out to Jamshed Khan who paid the entire consideration money and Jamshed Khan while was in possession of the said property sold the same to this petitioner by a registered kabala dated 31-5-80. Further case of the petitioner is, that while was in possession of the property in question he went to Kuwait on 5-9-83 getting a job there and on 25-11-90 he came back from Kuwait. Since after his coming back from Kuwait the petitioner had been trying to get his name mutated in respect of the property in question. That the respondents, specially the Assistant Commissioner Ministry of Housing and Public Works and the Administrative Officer, Mirpur Housing Estate assured the petitioner that there was nothing to be worried, that he would get his name mutated in due time. But in the meantime the petitioner fell ill and had to remain under treatment for a long period and being cured, when he contacted the Assistant Commissioner, Housing and Public Works Ministry on 3-6-2003 he was informed for the first time that the property in question had been enlisted as abandoned property and thereafter the petitioner contacted his lawyer and on his advice he filed this writ petition. That the property in question was never abandoned property as the original allotted of this property was all along in possession of this property till the date of transfer of the same to the petitioner. That the enlistment of the property in question as abandoned property has been illegal.

4. The respondents though did not file any affidavit-in-opposition to oppose the Rule but the learned Deputy Attorney-General Mr Karunamoy Chakma, on behalf of the respondents, had made some submissions before us opposing the Rule.

5. We have heard the learned Advocate Mr Fakhrul Islam appearing for the petitioner and gone through the writ petition, the supplementary affidavit and also papers annexed thereto.

6. It is an admitted fact that the Jamshed Khan, son of late Monowar Khan, was given allotment of the property in question by the then Government of East Pakistan, in the year 1961 by a registered lease deed dated 10-8-61 the Annexure-A1. It is also not denied that the lease holder Jamshed Khan got possession of this property and also possessed the same. The learned Deputy Attorney-General  appearing for the respondents has supported the inclusion of the property in question in the 'ka' list of the abandoned property by saying that this Jamshed Khan ultimately abandoned this property during the relevant period of the liberation war of 1971 and his whereabouts could not be known and, as such, the property in question became abandoned property by the operation of law. The learned Deputy Attorney-General, however , could not say that the Government took over took possession of this property in question as abandoned property or anybody also went into possession of this property and possessed the same as abandoned property. On the contrary, it has been averred from the side of the petitioner that Jamshed Khan was an employee of Rupali Bank, Dilkusha Branch till long after liberation of Bangladesh and the Manager of the said Rupali Bank issued a certificate to that effect on 27-5-80, the annexure-C, and that Jamshed Khan himself swore an affidavit of allegiance before the Magistrate, 1st Class, Dhaka on 22-3-73, the annexure-B. The writ petitioner filed the photo copies of the annexures-C and B with the writ petition and at the time of the hearing of the Rule the learned Advocate for the petitioner showed us the original copy of the annexure-C. The annexure-G filed by the petitioner shows further that Jamshed Khan died within Bangladesh on 6-10-86 and he was buried in the graveyard of Section 10/A, Mirpur, Dhaka. The original copy of this annexure-G also has been produced before us at the time of hearing of the Rule by the learned Advocate for the petitioner. Besides the above-stated papers, the original lease deed of Jamshed Khan the Annexure A-1 also has been produced before us from the custody of the petitioner at the time of hearing of the Rule. The learned Deputy Attorney-General has examined all these papers filed from the side of the writ petitioner and though did not admit the genuineness of these papers except the lease deed of Jamshed Khan the Annexure-A1 but could not produce any material before us to tell against the genuineness of the annexure CB and G. Rather, the fact that the original copy of the lease deed of Jamshed Khan, the Annexure-A1, has come before this Court from the custody of the petitioner strongly supports the petitioner's case that Jamshed Khan being present in Bangladesh, sold out the property in question to the petitioner by a kabala dated 31-5-80. This fact supports the genuineness of the annexure CB and G.

<u>7. All these papers filed by the petitioner coupled with the facts that the original lease deed of Jamshed Khas has come before this Court from the custody of the petitioner and that there is nothing before us from the side of the respondent to show that Government or anybody else ever took possession of the property in question as abandoned property, sufficiently support the petitioner's case that Jamshed Khan was all along present in Bangladesh and he never abandoned the property in question. So, it appears to us that the property in question did not answer to the definition of "abandoned property" as defined in Article 2(1) of the President's Order No. 16 of 1972.</u>

8. The petitioner has asserted that since after purchase of the property in question he has been residing there with his family on payment of all rents and taxes, etc. This assertion of the petitioner has not been denied from the side of the respondents. The petitioner has filed the original copy of his purchase deed before us, the Annexure-B Besides this title deed, the petitioner has filed another important, paper which also tells strongly in favour of his case that he purchased the property in question from the original allotted Jamshed Khan by a registered deed in the year 1980 and since then he has been residing in the said property with his family. This is Annexure-1, an enquiry report submitted by the Administrative Officer, Mirpur Housing Estate. Dhaka to the Assistant Commissioner Settlement, Ministry of Housing and Public Works. From this Annexure-1 it appears that being directed by the Assistant Commissioner, Settlement, Ministry of Housing and Public Works the Administrative Officer of Mirpur Housing Estate along with an Inspector made an enquiry as to the property in question and submitted report to the effect that Jamshed Khan got lease of the property in question by a registered lease deed dated 10-8-61 and Jamshed Khan paid the entire lease money and also other taxes, etc., and subsequently, Jamshed Khan sold the said property to this petitioner Zahirul Haque Chokder by a registered Kabala deed dated 31-5-80 and this purchaser Zahirul Haque has been residing in this property with his family. The learned Deputy Attorney-General has examined this Annexure-I also but did not dispute its genuineness or correctness.

9. The learned Deputy Attorney-General has raised a question about the maintainability of this writ petition and has argued that there is a special forum for having any property excluded from the abandoned property list but the petitioner did not avail this forum and, as such, this writ petition cannot be maintained. From the side of the petitioner it has been averred by swearing an affidavit that the petitioner while was in possession of the property in question went to Kuwait on 5-9-83 getting a job there and on 25-11-90 he came back from Kuwait and after that he approached the appropriate authority for mutating his name in respect of the property in question and the authority also assured him that the property in question would be mutated in his name in due time. That thereafter, the petitioner became seriously ill and had to remain in complete rest for several years under the supervision of the physician and had to undergo intensive treatment during that period. Thereafter, being cured, he contacted the Assistant Commissioner, Housing and Public. Works Ministry in June, 2003 and at that time, for the first time he could know that the property in question was enlisted in the 'ka' list of abandoned property. In support of this averment, the photocopy of the passport of the petitioner, the Annexure-X, has been filed by a supplementary affidavit. The petitioner has stated by swearing affidavit that the original passport is in the custody of Bureau of Manpower Employment and Training. Dhaka for giving compensation to the petitioner who lost his job in Kuwait during the war of 1990. This writ petitioner has filed a receipt also the Annexure Y showing that he has already received Taka 75,513 as installment of compensation from the United Nations Compensation Commission award. From all the above papers, we are convinced that the petitioner after purchasing the property in question went away to Kuwait in the year 1983 and from there he came back to Bangladesh in the year 1990.

<u>10. The petitioner has specifically asserted that after his return from Kuwait he tried to mutate the case property in his name in the office concerned and the concerned authority also assured him that the property in question would be mutated in his name in due time. The assertion of the petitioner has not been denied from the side of the respondents. Considering all these facts and circumstances, we are convinced that the petitioner had no occasion to go to the Settlement Court within time provided by law and, as such, we find that this writ petition is maintainable.</u>

We have already found that the property in question is not abandoned property. So, this Rule deserves to be made absolute. Hence, it is ordered that the Rule be made absolute on contest without any order as to cost. The inclusion of House No. 23, Road No. 2, Block-D, Section 1, PS Mirpur Dhaka in the 'ka' list of the abandoned property (Annexure-K) is declared to be without lawful authority and is of no legal effect.

End.

lawyer:
MI Farooqui with M Saleem Ullah, Advocates — For the Petitioner.
Abdul Hameed Chowdhury with Md Aminul Islam, Advocates — For the Respondent No.4
parties:
Asma Begum ------ Petitioner
Vs. 
Bangladesh, represented by the Secretary Ministry of Works Government of the People's Republic of Bangladesh & others ------ Respondents
full_judgment:
AK Badrul Huq J: By this application under Article 102 of the Constitution, the enlistment of a property as an abandoned property and the judgment and order of the Court of Settlement has been called in question whereupon a Rule Nisi was issued calling upon the respondents to show cause why the enlistment of plot No.1-D, 5/12, Mirpur, Dhaka in the ''ka'' list of the abandoned properties published on September 23, 1986 in Bangladesh Gazette, Extraordinary at page No. 9762(34) against Serial No. 435, under the caption: name of areas "Mirpur" sections 1-2 and the judgment and order dated 25-1-89 of the Court of Settlement in Case No. 700 of 1987 (KA-435-Mirpur-Dhaka) should not be declared to have been made without any lawful authority and to be of no legal effect and why they should not be directed to hand over the physical vacant possession of holding in question to the petitioner.

2. Facts leading to the issuance of the Rule may be summarized as follows: One Abdul Kader Mullick became owner of the house with a piece of land measuring 131Sq. Yards at plot No.12 Road No.5 Block-D, Section-1, Mirpur Housing Estate, PS Mirpur, Dhaka hereinafter called the said property by way of registered deed of lease on January 8, 1962. The petitioner by way of registered deed of conveyance for valuable consideration on 3-6-68 purchased the said property. The petitioner after the liberation of Bangladesh in the last week of April, 1972 had been dispossessed by anti-social elements who occupied the said property. The petitioner made several representations to the concerned authorities for restoration of the said property. The petitioner filed an application to the Sub-Divisional Officer, Sadar (South), Dhaka on 12-7-73. The petitioner once again on 15-10-75 made another representation to the Officer-on-Special Duty of the President''s Secretariat. The petitioner, thereafter, made another representation on 26-10-84 to the Minister, Ministry of Works. The said property was enlisted as an abandoned property under the Abandoned Building (Supplementary Provisions) Ordinance No. LIV of 1985), briefly, the said Ordinance. The petitioner under the provisions of section 7(1) of the said Ordinance filed an application putting forward the claim that the property in question does not answer to the description of abandoned property. The said application was registered as Case No.700 of 1987 (KA-435-Mirpur-Dhaka).

3. The respondent Government although, did not file any written statement, contested the case taking the stand that the whereabouts of the petitioner were not known and she was absent in Bangladesh and left the disputed house un-cared for and the property vested in Bangladesh Government under the provisions of President Order No. 16 of 1972.

4. The Court of Settlement recorded the following findings:

(i) That from the copy of her own application dated 15-10-1975 addressed to the Secretary, Ministry of Works clearly indicates that she is a bonafide refugee from India in the year 1950 and the same is contrary to her submission that she was born at Goalpara, Dhaka.

(ii) That the petitioner has not come forward with any reliable evidence either oral or documentary to the effect that she was physically present in Bangladesh after the promulgation of President''s Order 16 of 1972.

(iii) That the certificate issued by the Chairman, Ward No.34 to the effect that she is a permanent resident of Malitola and she is a citizen of Bangladesh has not been proved in accordance with law.

(iv) That it does not also appear that she mutated her name with the Housing and Settlement Department or with any other Government authorities as owner.

(v) That the case is attracted within the mischief of Article 2 of President''s Order 16 of 1972 read with Ordinance No.54 of 1985.

5. The Court of Settlement with the above findings and views dismissed the case and maintained the inclusion of the Building No.1-D/5-12, Mirpur, Dhaka in the ''Ka'' list of abandoned buildings published on 23rd September, 1986 in Bangladesh Gazette (Extraordinary) as abandoned property.

6. Feeling aggrieved by the decision, the petitioner approached this Court in an application under Article 102 of the Constitution and obtained the present Rule.

7. One Abdur Rahman claiming himself to be a lessee in possession and also an allotted purchaser of the case property, by way of an application has been added as respondent No-4 in the Rule.

8. The respondent No. 4 filed an affidavit-in-opposition controverting all the material allegations made in the petition. In the Affidavit-in-opposition it is stated that the lessee Abdul Kader Mullick in violation of clause 3 of the lease agreement which provided that on the expiry of 15 years from the date of lease, the lessee would become the full owner of the house, made a paper transaction on 3-6-68 purported to be sale deed in favour of the petitioner before the expiry of the period of fifteen (15) years. It is further stated that the petitioner was a non-local and she did never take possession over the said case property on the basis of the said deed of conveyance nor did she ever mutate her name with the Housing and Settlement nor did she pay any rent. It is the further statement that the lessee Abdul Kader Mullick left the property uncared for as the War of Liberation started in the year 1971 and the said property had been abandoned under President Order No. 16 of 1972 by operation of law. It is further averred that the respondent entered into the possession of the disputed house just immediate after the independence of Bangladesh and she has been in possession of the said property. It is further pleaded that the Government finding respondent No. 4 in possession, treated him as an allottee and realised rent from him with effect from 1-5-72 and in pursuance of an offer for sale from the side of government, a Sale agreement for sale of the case property had been entered into between the Ministry of Works and the respondent No.4 on payment of consideration money of Taka 94,957.00. Lastly, it is averred that the Government was about to execute and register a sale deed in favour of the respondent but in view of the order of stay and pendency of the writ petition before the High Court Division, the sale deed could not be registered and there was delay in finalization of the deed.

9. The petitioner did not file any Affidavit-in-reply controverting the statements made in the Affidavit-in-opposition.

10. The respondent-Government, though, contested the case before the Court of Settlement did not enter appearance to oppose the Rule.

11. MI Farooqui, learned Advocate appearing in support of the Rule, contended, first, that the petitioner is a Bangladeshi by birth and a resident of Malitola, Dhaka and her husband being a Bangladeshi citizen and permanent resident of Dhaka, the property in question does not answer to the description of abandoned property under President's Order 16 of 1972 and the inclusion of the petitioner''s property as abandoned property is absolutely illegal and the impugned judgment passed by the Court of Settlement maintaining the inclusion of the property as an abandoned property is without lawful authority. Mere temporary absence or absence under certain circumstances, does not warrant the inference of abandonment of property and the desertion of the property must have coincided with the positive intention of giving up the right vested in the property and in the instant case, there had been no intention on the part of the petitioner of never returning back to the disputed property and the temporary physical absence of the petitioner could not bring the property under the description of abandoned property, Mr MI Farooqui, submitted, further.

12. Mr. MI Farooqui next submitted that the representation made to the Sub-Divisional Officer, Dhaka, President''s Secrfarint Secretary, Ministry of Works, Government of Bangladesh manifest the petitioner''s intention that she did not abandon her right on the property as she had been perusing the matter since before its final enlistment as an abandonment property and the Court of Settlement did not take into consideration the vital documents in determining the question of abandonment and went wrong in law and also went outside the jurisdiction calling for interference by this Court. In support of the contention raised, reliance has been placed on decisions in the case of Rex vs. Northumberland Compensation Appeal Tribunal, 1952 I KB 338, Baldwin and Francis Ltd. vs. Appeal Tribunal, 1959 AC 663, Pearlman vs. Governors of Harrow School, 1978 3 WLR 736, Bangladesh vs. Md. Jalil and others, 48 DLR (AD), 10.

13. Mr. Abdul Hameed Chowdhury, learned Advocate representing the respondent No.4 repelling the said contentions, on the other hand, submitted that the petitioner being non-local, during the liberation movement of Bangladesh left the disputed house uncared for and ceased to occupy, supervise and manage the property in person and her whereabouts were also not known and the disputed property had been very rightly enlisted as an abandoned property.

14. Mr. Chowdhury next submitted that the Court of Settlement did not act without jurisdiction nor in excess of jurisdiction in coming to the decision and there is no error of law apparent on the face of the record and the decision of the Court of Settlement, thus, does not warrant any interference in a Certiorari proceeding under Article 102 of the Constitution.

15. Mr. Abdul Hameed Chowdhury, then, strenuously canvassed that the deed of conveyance dated 3-6-1988 had been obtained in clear violation of the condition contained in clause 3 of the Standard Agreement for Allotment of House which enjoins that the lessee Abdul Kader Mallick, on the expiry of fifteen (15) years from the date of the lease, would become full owner and the deed of conveyance having been made before the expiry of the period of fifteen (15) years, the said deed became an invalid document in the eye of law.

16. The last submission advanced on behalf of the respondent No.4 is that the respondent, in pursuance of an offer of sale by the Government paid Taka 94,957.00 and sale agreement was made between the Ministry of Works, Government of Bangladesh and respondent No. 4 thus, acquired valid right over the disputed property.

17. In order to appreciate the contentions raised from both the sides, it is profitable to quote Article 2(1) of President Order No.16 of 1972.

18. President Order No. 16 of 1972 came into force on 28-2-1972 Article 2(1) reads as follows:

"2(1) "abandoned property" means any property owned by any person who is not present in Bangladesh or whose whereabouts are not known or who has ceased to occupy, supervise or manage in person his property".

<u>19. From the above provisions, it is manifestly clear that any property owned by any person who is not present in Bangladesh or whose whereabouts are not known or who ceased to occupy, supervise or manage in person his/her property comes under the definition of "abandoned property". The word "or" used in the aforesaid Article 2(1) in our, view is disjunctive and not conjunctive. So, the property of any person who is not present in Bangladesh can be declared as abandoned property: the property of the person whose whereabouts are not known can be too, declared as abandoned property, and, lastly, the property of the person who has ceased to occupy, supervise or manage in person his/her property can, also, be declared as abandoned property. The provisions, thus, make it clear that any of the aforesaid factors and conditions, if exist, the property can be brought under the definition of abandoned property under President Order No.16 of 1972.</u>

20. Annexure7C to the writ petition is a letter dated 12-7-73 by the petitioner addressed to the Sub-Divisional Officer Dhaka. In the said letter it was stated that just after Liberation of Bangladesh i.e. in the later part of the month of December, 1971, she was absent from the suit holding that is the disputed house. Annexure-C-1 is a letter dated 15-10-75 addressed to the President''s Secretariat by the petitioner wherein it was stated that following the Liberation movement of Bangladesh in the year 1971, that is after the Army crackdown on 25 March, 1971, she left the said house and lived in another rented house. In the said application it was further stated that at the time of liberation period some unknown persons forcibly entered and occupied the house. Annexure-C-3 is another letter dated 25-10-84 by the petitioner addressed to the Minister, Ministry of Works. In the said letter it was stated that after the War of Liberation she was forcibly evicted from the disputed house. It was further stated that she heard that the house had been allotted to another person.

<u>21. From all the annexures, it appears that the petitioner left the house either during the Liberation War of Bangladesh, and, accordingly, she ceased to occupy, supervise and manage in person they said property and her whereabouts were also not known till 12-7-73. Moreover, except the above stated three letters Annexure C, C1 and C2 there are no evidences to show that the petitioner took any effective steps including legal steps in any court of law challenging the declaration of the house in question as an abandoned property before the year 1987. This conduct of the petitioner, must also, be noticed. In accordance with Article 2(1) of President Order No. 16 of 1972, if the petitioner ceased to occupy, control or manage the property or her whereabouts were not known that would be sufficient to bring the property under the definition of abandoned property. The admitted position is that the petitioner was out of possession since the time of War of Liberation of Bangladesh. .The contention of the learned Advocate that mere temporary absence under some circumstances is not sufficient to treat the property as abandoned property does not appear to have any merit.</u>

22. The disputed property was enlisted in the "Ka" list of the abandoned property in pursuance of Ordinance No. LIV of 1985. It appears that by invoking section 5 of the said Ordinance, the Government enlisted the house in the "KA" list of abandoned building vide Notification in the Official Gazette.

<u>23. Sub-section 2 of section 5 of the Ordinance runs as follows:</u>

<u>"5(2) The list published under sub-section (1) shall be conclusive evidence of the fact that the buildings included therein are abandoned property and have vested in Government as such."</u>

<u>So, by operation of sub-section 5 of the Ordinance, the publication of the disputed house in the Official Gazette as abandoned-property is conclusive evidence of the fact that the said houses is an abandoned property and have vested in the Government. Support for this proposition is sought to be drawn from the opinion expressed by their Lordships of the Appellate Division in the case of Bangladesh vs. Md Jalil and others, 48 DLR AD 10 which has also been referred to by the learned Advocate for the petitioner in support of his contention. His Lordship ATM Afzal CJ in delivering the judgment expressed opinion in the following language:</u>

<u>"Section 5(2) of the Ordinance clearly provides that the list published under sub-section (i) shall be conclusive evidence of the fact that the buildings included therein are abandoned property and have vested in the Government as such. Section 7 says that a person claiming any right or interest in any such building may make an application to the Court of Settlement for exclusion of the building from such list, etc. on the ground that the building is not an abandoned building and has not vested in the Government under President''s Order No.16 of 1972 or that his right or interest in the building has not been affected by the provisions of that Order. The onus,therefore, is squarely on the claimant of the building to prove that the building is not an abandoned property. The Government has no obligation either to deny the facts alleged by the claimant or to disclose the basis of treating the property as abandoned property merely because the same is disputed by the claimant".</u>

24. Let us now come to answer to the other contentions addressed before us on behalf of both the sides.

25. It appears from materials on record that the petitioner did neither examine herself nor her husband nor other witnesses had been examined to lay proof that the petitioner had been present in Bangladesh and her whereabouts were known to the Government and the disputed property is not an abandoned property.

26. Record of the settlement case had not been called for at the time of issuance of Rule. Rule was issued on 20-2-90. But no attempt was made from the side of the petitioner to call for the record during this long period of seven (7) years. Learned Advocate for the petitioner at the time of hearing of the Rule placed certified copy of the order-sheet of the settlement case. On perusal of the order-sheet, it appears that the petitioner did not make any attempt to have herself and other witnesses examined to substantiate her claim that she had been in Bangladesh and her whereabouts were also known to the Government. It is the grievance of the petitioner that she, although, filed documents and papers under Firisthi in the Court, those papers and documents were not at all considered by the Court of Settlement and there had been an error on the face of the record. It is canvassed vehemently, on the other hand, from the side of the respondent that no document under Firisthi had been filed in the court. It is pointed out here that mere filing of the documents in the court is not enough for the proof of the case and the said documents are required to be proved in accordance with law.

<u>27. Provisions of sub-section (5) of section 10 of the said Ordinance is extracted hereunder:</u>

<u>"10(5). Court of Settlement shall, after such enquiry as it may deem necessary and after giving reasonable opportunity to the parties concerned of being heard and also adducing evidence, both oral and documentary, if any, make such decision on the prayer of the application as it deems fit."</u>

<u>28. From the above provisions, it is manifestly clear that the Court of Settlement shall make decision after giving the parties reasonable opportunity of being heard and also opportunity of producing evidences, both oral and documentary, on the prayer of the parties. It is pointed out here that the onus is heavy on the part of the applicant, here the petitioner, to prove that the building is not an abandoned property and the Government got no obligation to disclose the basis of treating the property as abandoned property. The petitioner, in this case, appears to have signally failed to prove by evidence, both oral and documentary, that the property does not answer to the definition of abandoned property.</u>

29. From the papers and documents annexed in the writ petition it is to be noticed here that the petitioner, for the first time on 12-7-73, long after the date 28-2-72, when President''s Order No.16 of 1972 came into force, filed an application to the Sub-Divisional Officer, Dhaka for handing over possession of the house in her favour. Thereafter, the petitioner on 15710-75, after a period of two (2) years and ''two (2) months filed two applications, one to the President''s Secretariat and another to the Secretary, Ministry of Works praying for restoration of possession of the house in question in her favour Lastly on 25-10-1984 after a period of 9 years, filed another application to the Minister Ministry of Works for returning back the house in her favour. It cannot, therefore, be said that the petitioner consistently persuaded the authority concerned to have the property released from the list of abandoned buildings as contended by the learned Advocate for the petitioner.

30. The petitioner in her application dated 15-10-75, Annexure-C-1, stated that she came from India in the year 1950. In the application under section 7 of the Ordinance, her date of birth had been shown on 1-1-1956 at Goal Nagar under PS Kotwali. In the writ petition, it is stated that she was born in the year 1954 at Goal Nagar. The Court of Settlement duly considered these aspects of the matter. It appears, further from the judgment of the Court of Settlement that the petitioner filed in the Court a certificate from a Ward Commissioner showing her nationality in Bangladesh. The said certificate has not been annexed in the writ petition. The Court of Settlement held that the Certificate dated 13-7-86 said to have been issued by the Chairman, Ward No. 34, Dhaka Municipal Corporation to the effect that she is a permanent resident of Malitola and that she is a citizen of Bangladesh has not been proved in accordance with law. The argument addressed before us on behalf of the petitioner that the Court of Settlement did not at all consider any document produced before it appears to have no substance.

31. The petitioner, although, claimed to have purchased the disputed property in the year 1968, did not file the original document of title that is the Standard Agreement for Allotment of House. The petitioner failed to show that she got her name mutated with the Housing Estate and paid rent. The petitioner did not file Non-option certificate and also the Nationality certificate from the competent authority. In the absence of those papers, it is difficult on our part to accept the contention that the petitioner, since the Liberation of Bangladesh, all along had been in Bangladesh and her whereabouts were known.

<u>32. It is well settled that this Court in the exercise of jurisdiction under Article 102 of the Constitution does not sit as a court of appeal. In Certiorari proceeding, this Court can only interfere with the judgment of a Court or Tribunal subordinate to this Court only when the same appears to have acted without jurisdiction or in excess of jurisdiction or made any finding without considering any material evidence or acted malafide or committed an error apparent on the ''face of the record. The Court or tribunal does not go beyond its jurisdiction merely by making a decision erroneous in law or fact.</u>

<u>33. In the case of Rex vs. Northumberland Compensation Appeal Tribunal, 1952 1 KB, 338, the Divisional Court of the King''s Bench Division held that Certiorari would issue to quash the decision of a statutory administrative tribunal for error of law on the face of the "record" although the tribunal was not a court of record and although the error did not go to the jurisdiction of the Tribunal. Morris LJ observed as follows:</u>

<u>"It is plain that certiorari will not issue as the cloak of an appeal in disguise. It does not lie in order to bring up an order or decision for rehearing of the issue raised in the proceedings. It exists to correct error of law where revealed on the face of an order or decision, or irregularity, or absence of, or excess of jurisdiction where shown. The control is exercised by removing an order or decision, and then by quashing it."</u>

<u>34. This decision led to a modest extension of the scope of judicial review both in England and in other common law jurisdictions which adapted the same Rule. But it could not fairly be characterized as a piece of judicial legislation: it is, in truth, a new application of a long established principle.</u>

<u>35. In the case of Baldwin and Frances Ltd. vs. Appeal Tribunal, 1959 AC 663 Lord Denning expressed the views in the following terms:</u>

<u>"An order of certiorari is sought upon the ground that there is an error of law on the face of the record, and on other grounds when certiorari is sought upon such a ground, evidence is not as a rule admissible. The error must appear on face of the proceedings without the aid of extrinsic evidence".</u>

<u>36. In the case of Pearlman vs. Governors of Harrow School 3 DLR 736, the observations of Lord Denning MR are couched in the following language:</u>

<u>"Those words "final and conclusive" have been considered by the courts a hundred times. It has been uniformly held that they preclude any appeal to a higher court in the sense of an appeal proper where the higher court reviews the decision of the lower tribunal and substitutes its own decision for that of the lower tribunal. But those words do not preclude the High Court from correcting the errors of the lower tribunal by means of certiorari—now called judicial review. Notwithstanding that a decision is by a statute made "final and conclusive", certiorari can still issue for excess of jurisdiction, or for error of law on the face of the record or declaration can be made by the High Court to determine the rights of the parties. It can declare the law by which they are bound, irrespective of what the lower tribunal has done. It can even consider the point of law by means of a case stated."</u>

<u>37. The scope for interference of the judgment or order of the Court/tribunal in Certiorari proceeding was also considered by the superior courts of this sub-continent in a good number of cases out of which two recent decisions of our Appellate Division are referred to.</u>

<u>38. In the case of Hosne Ara Begum vs. Chairman, Court of Settlement and another, 46 DLR (AD) 9, Mustafa Kamal J, emphasized:</u>

<u>"So long as the Court of Settlement acts within jurisdiction and does not commit any excess of jurisdiction the High Court Division will be right in not interfering on the ground of mere unsatisfactory disposal of the case"</u>

<u>39. In the case of Bangladesh vs. Md. Jalil and others, 48 DLR AD 10 ATM Afzal CJ observed in the following terms:</u>

<u>"The High Court Division was not a Court of appeal required to make determination of facts on its own. It could interfere with the findings of a tribunal of fact under its extraordinary jurisdiction under Article 102, only if it could be shown that the tribunal had acted without jurisdiction or made any finding upon no evidence or without considering any material evidence /facts causing prejudice to the complaining party or that it had acted malafide or in violation of any principle of natural justice."</u>

<u>40. The principles enunciated by the above referred authorities are well settled. But the question comes whether the Court of Settlement in its decision acted without jurisdiction or in excess of jurisdiction or committed an error apparent on the face of the record or acted malafide. From a reading of the decision of the Court of Settlement, the same does not appear to have acted without jurisdiction or in excess of jurisdiction or made any finding without considering any material evidence or acted malafide and also committed an error apparent on the face of the record.</u>

<u>41. It remains now to consider the submissions advanced before us on behalf of the respondent that in view of the violation of clause 3 of the original Agreement For Allotment of House, the deed of conveyance of the petitioner became invalid. We do not find any substance in the said submission. Annexure-B(1) is a document showing full payment of Taka 2700.00 to the erstwhile Government of East Pakistan. It appears that the lessee Abdul Kader Mullick before execution and registration of the deed of conveyance paid the entire consideration money of Taka 2700.00 by way of chalan to the Administrative Officer, Housing Estate and the lessee Abdul Kader Mullick being the full owner of the house property transferred the same to the petitioner.</u>

<u>42. From materials on record it appears that the respondent No.4 remained in possession of the disputed house since the year 1972 and the Government realized rents from him. It appears, further, that in pursuance of a sale offer by the Government, the respondent No. 4 paid Taka 94,957.00 and an Agreement for sale of the house property had been also made between the Government and the respondent No. 4 which is annexed as Annexure-4 to the affidavit-in-opposition. But in view of the order of stay in the Rule passed by this Court, the deed could not be executed and registered by the Government in favour of the respondent No. 4. It appears, thus, that the respondent No. 4 is an allotted purchaser of the house property on payment of entire consideration money of Taka 94,957.00.</u>

<u>43. It has already been found that the Court of Settlement did neither commit any illegality nor acted neither without jurisdiction nor in excess of jurisdiction nor did commit an error apparent on the face of the record, and, as such, there is no reason to disturb the said decision.</u>

44. In view of .the discussions made hereinbefore, we are of this considered view that the Rule is devoid of any substance and the same must be discharged.

45. In the result, the Rule is discharged, however, without any order as to cost.

Stay granted by this Court stands vacated.

End.

lawyer:
Syed Ishtiaq Ahmed with Dr. Kamal Hossain, M Amirul Islam, Idrisur Rahman and Ms Tanya Amir, Advocates — For the Petitioners. 
Kaiseruddin Ahmed, Deputy Attorney-General (Not argued) — For the Respondents.

full_judgment:
Md. Mozammel Hoque J : This Rule was issued calling upon the respondents to show cause as to why the Bangladesh Civil Services (Re-organisation) Order, 1980, purporting to incorporate the ''Judicial Service'' within the Bangladesh Civil Services as one of the Cadre Services vide paragraph 2 (X) thereof should not be declared as ultra vires the Constitution, unconstitutional in particular, violative of Articles 27 and 29 of the Constitution and why the impugned orders dated 28-2-94 and 2-11-95 suspending and then cancelling respectively the order dated 8-1-94 should not be declared arbitrary, malafide, discriminatory and violative of fundamental rights as guaranteed by the Constitution and to show cause as to why attempt to treat the Judges of the Subordinate Courts as part of the Civil Service Cadre meant for the executive branch of the Government and to subject them to any laws meant for the employees of the executive Government should not be declared as illegal and ultra vires the Constitution and why a separate set of Rules for the Judges of the Subordinate Courts should not be framed as contemplated under Article 115 of the Constitution. This Rule was issued on 19-11-95.

2. On the application of the petitioners another Rule was issued calling upon the respondents to show cause as to why the benefits allowed as per paragraph 3 of the impugned order dated 2-11-95 vide Annexure-F(1) to the officers of the other Cadre should not be given also to the Senior Assistant Judges and the Assistant Judges of the Judicial Service of the Republic.

3. In this Writ application there are 441 petitioners who are Judges of different Civil Courts of Bangladesh from Assistant Judges up to District and Sessions Judges. The petitioners have challenged the vires of the inclusion of this service in the name of BCS (Judicial) vide paragraph 2(X) of Annexure-A to the petition which is called Bangladesh Civil Services (Re-organisation) Order, 1980. The petitioners had several grievances of different kinds for which they made representations to the relevant authorities one after another for a long time. After considering their representations an Order, namely, Services (Pays and Allowances) Order, 1991, was issued on 8-1-94 by the Ministry of Finance. This Order, in fact, re-fixed the pay-scale of the year 1991. Earlier fixation was made by Gazette Notification dated 14 September, 1991 vide Annexure-D(3) by the self-same Ministry. The Annexure-E is, in fact, the amended Order of the re-fixation of salaries and allowances of the employees of different cadres. In this Annexure-E, that is, re-fixation of pay scale paragraph 3 is relevant for the purpose of the present Writ Petition which runs as follows:

৩। বি,সি,এস (বিচার) ক্যাডারের কর্মকর্তাগণের কাজের প্রকৃতি ও স্বতস্ত্রের প্রেক্ষিতে সরকার ১০. বি,সি, এস বিচার ক্যাডারের নিম্নে বর্ণিত পদসমূহের বর্তমান জাতীয় বেতন স্কেল, ১৯৯১ নিম্ন বর্নিত ভাবে পুনঃ নির্ধারণ করিয়াছেনঃ
