4. The effects of the re-fixation of pays and allowances of the Subordinate Judges, Additional District and Sessions Judges and District and Sessions Judges were given to which the petitioners, in fact, had no objection. This Order vide Annexure-E was issued on 8-1-94 and, in fact, it was given immediate effect. But by another Order dated 28-2-94 vide Annexure-F of this Writ Petition the operation of the previous Order dated 8-1-94 was stayed for indefinite period. Again on 2-11-95 the aforesaid Ministry issued another Order vide Annexure-F(1) to this Writ Petition and again re-fixed the scales of the pays and allowances of the officers of different cadres including those of the Subordinate Judges, Additional District and Sessions Judges and District and Sessions Judges vide serial Nos. 10, 11 and 12 of this re-fixation Order dated 2-11-95. Paragraphs 10, 11 and 12 of the aforesaid amended order dated 2-11-95 run as follows:

১০. বি,সি, এস (বিচার) সাব জজ ৪৮০০-৭২৫০/= ৫ বৎসর সিনিয়র স্কেলে সন্তোষজনক চাকুরীসহ ১ম শ্রেনীর ক্যাডার পদে ১০ বৎসর চাকুরীর পর জেষ্ঠতার ভিত্তিতে ৫০% হারে সিলেকশন গ্রেড ৬৩০০-৮০৫০/- প্রাপ্ত।
১১. বি,সি, এস (বিচার)জেলা ও দায়রা জজ। ৬৩০০-৮০৫০/= ৬৩০০-৮০৫০/= ২ বৎসর ৫ম গ্রেডে সন্তোষজনক চাকুরীসহ ১ম শ্রেণীর ক্যাডার পদে ১২ বৎসর চাকুরীর পর জেষ্ঠতার ভিত্তিতে ৫০% হারে সিলেকশন গ্রেড ৭১০০-৮৭০০/= প্রাপ্ত।
১২. বি,সি, এস (বিচার) জেলা ও দায়রা জজ ৭১০০-৮৭০০/= ৭৮০০-৯০০০/= জেলা ও দায়রা জজ পদে সিলেকশন গ্রেড ২০% বর্তমান জাতীয় বেতন স্কেলে ৮৬০০-৯৫০০/= তে অপরিবর্তিত থাকিবে।

5. Being aggrieved by the aforesaid two Orders dated 28-2-94 (Annexure-F) and the Order dated 2-11-95 (Annexure-F(1) as stated above the present Writ Petition was moved and Rule was issued.

6. In this Writ Petition the petitioners have raised several points including the vires of impugned Orders as contained in Annexure-F and F(1), so far the same relate to the petitioners, on the ground of being violative of fundamental rights of the petitioners as guaranteed by the Constitution. Further point was raised to the effect that inclusion of the Judicial Service with the executive vide Annexure-A to this Writ Petition in paragraph 2(X) as BCS (judicial) is also ultra vires the Constitution. It is their further case that the Subordinate Judiciary under Chapter-II is the part of Judiciary of Part-VI of the Constitution and thereby the Subordinate Judiciary has already been separated by the Constitution. Only the Rules under Article 115 of the Constitution and/or enactment, if necessary, are required to be made for giving full effect to this separation of judiciary. It is further stated that these Judges of the Subordinate Judiciary being Presiding Judges of the Courts cannot be subordinate to any Tribunal and, as such, the petitioners and other Judicial Officers are not subject to the jurisdiction of the Administrative Tribunal in asmuch as the Court cannot be subordinate to the Tribunal. Further, it is stated to the effect that the Assistant Judges and Senior Assistant Judges cannot be deprived of the pays and allowances as they are being given now and in any way they shall not be given lesser benefit in comparison with other officers as prescribed in paragraph 3 of Annexure-F(1) of the Writ Petition till fixation of their pays and allowances and other matters made along with the District and Sessions Judges, Additional District and Sessions Judges and Subordinate Judges under Article 115 of the Constitution.

7. In this case only an affidavit-in opposition has been filed on behalf of respondent No.3 who is the Secretary, Ministry of Finance, Government of Bangladesh, Bangladesh Secretariat, Dhaka, and no other affidavit-in-opposition has been filed.

8. This matter came up for hearing on 13-6-96 and on that day this court passed an order requesting the learned Attorney- General to appear in this case as this case involves important questions of law having far-reaching effect. The learned Attorney-General was notified and on 27-6-96 this matter came up in the list and was adjourned on the prayer of the learned Assistant Attorney-General. Again this matter came up for hearing on 29-1-97. On that day, the learned Attorney-General KS Nabi appeared and stated before the Court that he had already written to the Government with respect to the reliefs sought for by the petitioners in the instant Writ Petition and he prayed for some time in order to examine the matter by the government. Since the learned Attorney-General being the highest Law Officer of the Government was praying for time for consideration of the matter by the Government, this Court adjourned the matter up to 24th March, 1997. When this matter was taken up for hearing on 1-4-97, the learned Deputy Attorney-General Kaiseruddin Ahmed informed the Court that the learned Attorney-General has written to the Government expressing his favourable opinion about this case and the Government has not filed any affidavit-in-opposition. Since the learned Attorney-General had given his opinion favourable to the grievances and demands of the petitioners made in this Writ petition, the respondents have not appeared and contested this Rule. In such a situation it appeared to the Court that neither the Government had acted in the meantime in accordance with the opinion of the learned Attorney-General nor the Government is interested to contest this Rule. So, we heard the learned Advocates for the petitioners only in this matter.

9. When the Services (Pays and Allowances) Order, 1991, refixing pay scales of some services, was issued on 8-1-94, the petitioners did not raise any objection with regard to the re-fixation of their scales. But the petitioners are aggrieved by the subsequent order dated 28-2-94 by which the earlier order dated 8-1-94 was suspended and again another order dated 2-11-95 by which their scales of pays and allowances had been completely changed to their detriment putting certain conditions which are, in fact, against the fundamental rights guaranteed by the Constitution in favour of the citizens. It appears from Annexure-F (1), the impugned order dated 2-11-95 that with regard to the Subordinate Judges, Additional District and Sessions Judges and District and Session Judges scales of pays and allowances had been quite differently fixed from the earlier order vide Annexure-E to the petition. Not only that, several conditions have been attached against their pay scales which were not put in respect of the officers of other BCS Cadres.

10. Mr Syed Ishtiaq Ahmed, Dr Kamal Hossain and Mr Amirul Islam, the learned Advocates, have appeared for the petitioners and made their valuable submissions before this Court, but none argued for the respondents. Of them, Mr Amir-ul Islam had taken all the trouble of making the lengthy arguments. It is submitted by the learned Advocates for the petitioners that the benefits given by the authority in paragraph 3 of Annexur-E dated 8-1-94 in refixation of the pay scales of the Subordinate Judges, Additional District and Sessions Judges and District and Sessions Judges had been acted upon and the petitioners minus the Assistant Judges were given benefits out of them. Since the aforesaid order was acted upon and since they were getting the benefits out of it, abruptly the same cannot be suspended and subsequently amended to the detriment of their interest. As soon as this pay scales vide Annexure-E were given to the Subordinate Judges, Additional District and Sessions Judges and District and Sessions Judges, a vested right had been created in their favour which cannot be taken away abruptly. It is further submitted that the Annexure-F(1), that is, impugned Order dated 2-11-95 is a complete departure from the earlier Order in respect of their pay scales and not only that, some unfavourable conditions were added against them which were not, in fact, put against other BCS Cadre holders. The learned Advocates submit that this action of the respondents vide Annexures-F and F(1) in respect of the judicial officers is violative of the provisions of fundamental right Nos. 27 and 29 of the Constitution. Article 27 provides that" all citizens are equal before law and are entitled to equal protection of law." Article 29 provides that "there shall be equality of opportunity for all citizens in respect of employment or office in the service of the Republic."

11. It is their case that since fundamental rights of those judicial officers have been violated by issuing these two impugned orders dated 28-2-94 and 2-11-95, they should be declared ultra vires the Constitution being violative of Articles 27 and 29 guaranteed by the Constitution. We have carefully gone though the impugned orders along with the order dated 8-1-94 vide Annexure-E and it appears to us that some unreasonable conditions were attached with the pay scales of the Subordinate Judges, Additional District and Sessions Judges and District and Sessions Judges which were not attached in respect of pay scales and allowances of other BCS Cadre holders. In this view of the matter we find that these two impugned orders vide Annexure-F and F(1), so far the same relate to the petitioners and others, are ultra vires the Constitution being violative of the fundamental right Nos. 27 and 29 of the Constitution. Further, no reason has been assigned as to why the benefits with regard to the pays and allowances of those judicial officers were surreptitiously changed to the detriment of their interest although the same were given to them vide paragraph No. 3 of Annexure-E to the Writ Petition. Since the benefits with regard to the scales of pays and allowances of the Subordinate Judges, Additional District and Sessions Judges and District and Sessions Judges as given in paragraph No. 3 of the order dated 8-1-94 had been abruptly and aribitrarily taken away by the impugned orders vide Annexures-F and F(1) without showing any reason and since that order dated 8-1-94 was, in fact, acted upon and the same created a vested right in favour of the Judicial Officers mentioned above, the impugned portions of the orders vide Annexures-F and F(1) are liable to be declared to have been made without lawful authority and of no legal effect. At the same time it must also be declared that the re-fixation of pays and allowances with regard to the Subordinate Judges, Additional District and Sessions Judges and District and Sessions Judges made under Annexur—E dated 8-1-94 stand valid and such benefits given to them cannot be taken away by the authority. It is further held that by ad-interim orders passed by this Court the aforesaid Judicial Officers are continuing to have the aforesaid benefits vide Annexure-E, the same will continue till the new pay scales are fixed in future, by framing necessary enactment and/or rules pursuant to this judgment.

12. The petitioners have also challenged the inclusion of the Judicial Officers by paragraph 2 (x) BCS (Judicial) in Bangladesh Civil Services (Re-organisation) Order, 1980, vide Annexure—A dated 1st of September, 1980. It is their case that since the Judicial Service is a separate and distinct service as specified separately in the Constitution under Part-VI, the Judiciary, the same cannot be equated or amalgamated or tagged with the Bangladesh Civil Services in any manner whatsoever. In this connection we may refer to the Constitution of Bangladesh. In the Constitution, Part-IV containing Articles 48 to 64, deals with the Executive. Part-V of the Constitution deals with the Legislature having Article 65 to Article 93. Part-VI of the Constitution comprising Articles 94 to 117 deals with the Judiciary. It has three Chapters of which Chapter-II deals with the Subordinate Courts which, in fact, is the subject matter in the present Writ Petition. It is further contended that Article 136 is a part of Part-IX of the Constitution, that is Services of Bangladesh, and it is in no way connected with the Judicial Service. We find this contention reasonable and valid. Since the Subordinate Courts are part and parcel of Part-VI of the Constitution, the Judicial Officers cannot be equated or tagged with other services.

Article 136 of the Constitution runs as follows:

"Provision may be made by law for the reorganisation of the service of the Republic by the creation, amalgamation or unification of services and such law may vary or revoke any condition of service of a person employed in the service of the Republic."

13. This Article finds place in Part-IX, ''Services of Bangladesh'', Chapter-I, Services, whereas the Judicial Service has been specified under Part-VI, Chapter-II of the Constitution. Articles 114 to 116A of the Constitution which are under Chapter-II of Part-VI therefore, deal with the Subordinate Courts. Article 114 of the Constitution runs as follows:

"There shall be in addition to the Supreme Court'' such courts subordinate thereto as may be established by law."
Article 115 of the Constitution runs as follows:

"Appointments of persons to offices in the judicial service or as magistrates exercising judicial functions shall be made by the President in accordance with rules Made by him in that behalf."

Article 116 of the Constitution runs as follows:

"The control (including the power of posting, promotion and grant of leave) and discipline of persons employed in the judicial service and magistrates exercising judicial functions shall vest in the President and shall be exercised by him in consultation with the Supreme Court."

Article 116A of the Constitution runs as follows:

"Subject to the provisions of the Constitution, all persons employed in the judicial service and all magistrates shall be independent in the exercise of their judicial functions."

14. In this connection we may quote the definition of the ''Judicial Service'' as provided under Article 152(1) of the Constitution. In this Article 152(1), the definition of ''Judicial Service'' is given in the following manner:

"Judicial Service" means a service comprising persons holding judicial posts not being posts superior to that of the District Judge."

15. In this connection we may also quote Article 109 of the Constitution which runs as follows:

"The High Court Division shall have superintendence and control over all courts and tribunals subordinate to it."

16. ''Relying upon the aforesaid provisions of the Constitution the learned Advocates for the petitioners submit that since the Constitution itself has specified separate and distinct Judicial Service in several Articles of the Constitution and this Judicial Service is a part and parcel of the Part Judiciary as per Articles 114, 115, 116 and 116A of the Constitution, it cannot be considered as a part of Bangladesh Civil Service. The term BCS (Judicial) is a fundamental misconception as Judicial Service is recognised and treated separately in the Constitution itself. We find full force in the above submissions of the learned Advocates for the petitioners. In the Order, namely, Bangladesh Civil Service (Reorganisation) Order, 1980, the Judicial Service has been made a part of the Bangladesh Civil Services vide paragraph 2(X) of that order dated 1-9-80. It appears that Bangladesh Civil Services have been dealt with by the Constitution under Part—IX with the heading "Services of Bangladesh", and since the Judicial Service has been specifically mentioned in Articles 115, 116 and 116A of the Constitution and defined separately in Article 152(1) thereof, we hold that such inclusion of the ''judicial service'' under the Bangladesh Civil Service vide paragraph 2(x) of the aforesaid Bangladesh Civil Service (Reorganisation) Order, 1980 dated 1-9-80 as BCS (Judicial) is ultra vires the Constitution. Further, some amendments were made in 1986 with regard to the Bangladesh Civil Services (Reorganisation) Order, 1980, showing BCS (Judicial) Cadre at Serial No.16 which we also find ultra vires the Constitution in view of the provisions of Part-VI and the definition of the ''Judicial Service'' as given in Article 152(1) of the Constitution.

17. In this connection it may be mentioned that the Services (Reorganisation and Condition) Act, 1975, was enacted in pursuance of Article 136 of the Constitution. The aforesaid Act will, therefore, relate to other services "excepting the Judicial Service of Bangladesh. Since the Bangladesh Civil Services (Reorganisation) Order, 1980 includes the Judicial Service in the Bangladesh Civil Service: the same is found to be ultra vires the Constitution so far as it relates to such inclusion.

18. The learned Advocates for the petitioners further submit that in Articles 61 and 62 vide Chapter—IV of Part—IV of the Constitution, the Defence Services have been specified separately. Similarly, the Judicial Service has been specified in the Constitution under Chapter—II of Part—VI thereof. But the Civil Service, as such, has not been defined in any chapter or part of the Constitution. Rather the Services of Bangladesh have been dealt with in Part-IX of the Constitution. So, the framers of the Constitution had the intention to specify the two services, namely, the Defence Service and Judicial Service in the Constitution separately and in general the framers of the Constitution dealt with the Services of Bangladesh in Part-IX of the Constitution. In such a situation, the Defence Services have been correctly governed by separate Acts and Rules and in the similar way the Judicial Service shall have to be governed by separate provisions of Part-VI of the Constitution and the rules and enactments made thereunder. Since the Constitution itself has dealt with the Judicial Service separately as in the case of Defence Services, it must be given a specific treatment totally different and distinct from the Civil Services. The argument has substance in it and cannot be ignored.

19. The learned Advocates have drawn our attention to Articles 8(1), 8(2) and 22 of the Constitution. Article 8(1) runs as follows : "The principles of absolute trust and faith in the Almighty Allah, nationalism, democracy and socialism meaning economic and social justice, together with the principles derived from them as set out in this Part, shall constitute the fudamental principles of state policy." Article 8(2) runs as follows:

"The principles set out in this part shall be fundamental to the governance of Bangladesh, shall be applied by the State in their making of laws, shall be a guide to the interpretation of the Constitution and of the other laws of Bangladesh, and shall form the basis of the work of the State and of its citizens, but shall not be judicially enforceable."

Article 22 of the Constitution runs as follows:
"The state shall ensure the separation of the judiciary from the executive organs of the State."

20. Explaining these provisions of the Constitution the learned Advocates submit that though these principles are not justiciable under Article 8(2) of the Constitution, they are to be applied for the interpretation of the Constitution. In the instant case the petitioners have not come to enforce any fundamental principle judicially, but they have come for a declaration that judiciary had already been separated by the Constitution itself under Part-VI of the Constitution, namely, the Supreme Court, Subordinate Courts and Tribunals, and that the Respondents should be directed to implement and carry out the mandate of the Constitution in pursuance of Articles 109, 115, 116 and 116A of the Constitution. The petitioners have come before this Court under Article 102 of the Constitution which has empowered High Court Division to direct the persons performing any function in connection with the affairs of the Republic or of a local authority to refrain from doing that which he is not permitted by law to do or to do that which he is required by law to do. In the instant case the High Court Division is competent to direct the Legislature as well as the Executive to perform their functions which these authorities are required to do under the Constitution or any other law. So, it is submitted by the learned Advocates that the bar given under Article 8(2) of the Constitution will not be applicable in the facts and circumstances of the present case inasmuch as the petitioners are not praying for enforcement of fundamental principles. Rather they are praying for necessary direction and declaration as provided under Article 102(2) (a)(l)(II) of the Constitution with regard to Articles 115, 116 and 116A read with Article 109 of the Constitution, and urging upon this Court to apply the fundamental principles of State policies, particularly Article 22 of the Constitution, in the matter of interpretation of those provisions.

21. It is already stated above that Part-VI, Chapter-II, of the Constitution deals with Subordinate Courts. Presiding Officers of those courts are from Assistant Judges to the District and Sessions Judges. Article 109 has already provided that the High Court Division shall have superintendence and control over all Courts and Tribunals Subordinate to it. Article 115 provides that appointments of persons to offices in the judicial service and the Magistrate exercising iudicial functions shall be made by the President in accordance with rules made by him in that behalf. Article 116 provides that the control, including the power of posting, promotion and grant of leave, and discipline of persons employed in the judicial service and Magistrates exercising judicial functions hall vest in the President and shall be exercised by him in consultation with the Supreme Court. Article 116A provides that subject to the provisions of the Constitution, all persons employed in the judicial service and all Magistrates shall be independent in the exercise of their judicial functions. Relying on the aforesaid provisions of Articles 109, 115, 116 and 116A read with the definition of ''Judicial Service'', the learned Advocates submit that Judiciary has already been separated from the Executive in the Constitution itself vide Chapter-2 of Part—VI of the Constitution and, as such, question of enforcement of the fundamental principle does not arise at this stage. We find full force in the above submissions of the learned Advocates. As shown above, the judicial service has already been specified as a separate and independent entity in Chapter—II of Part—VI of the Constitution and the definition of the term "Judicial Service" in Article 152(1) of the Constitution has clearly identified it as a distinct service independent from any other services and, as such, the same cannot be a part of the civil, administrative or executive service or any other service of the country. In this connection we may refer to definition of ''Service of the Republic'' as given in Article 152 of the Constitution, which runs as follows:

"The ''Service of the Republic'' means any service, post or office whether in a civil or military capacity, in respect of the Government of Bangladesh, and any other service declared by law to be a service of the Republic."

22. This definition of the ''Service of the Republic'' is a broad definition embracing generally all services in Bangladesh including the defence service and the judicial service. But that does not mean that the judicial service or the defence service is a part of the civil or administrative services. Rather this is an independent service under the Constitution. The judicial service, as pointed out earlier, is totally distinct and separate from the civil services of Bangladesh. So, the definition clause of service of the Republic cannot in any way bring the ''Judicial Service'' within the ambit of executive or administrative service which is called civil service of Bangladesh. Now, if we consider the provisions of Articles 115, 116 and 116A together with the Article 109 of the Constitution, it will appear that in the Constitution itself the Judiciary has been separated and distinguished from the civil services of Bangladesh. Though the executive government is now controlling the judicial service in different manners along with the civil services of Bangladesh, in fact, under the Constitution it should be controlled, guided and administered by the High Court Division of the Supreme Court of Bangladesh. Articles 109, 115, 116, and 116A of the Constitution clearly indicate and provide for this.

23. So, it appears to us that the control of the judicial service by the Executive treating the same as BCS (Judicial) is ultra vires the Constitution, namely, Articles 109, 115, 116, and 116A of the Constitution. These provisions, in fact, relates to all the Judges of the Subordinate Courts from Assistant fudges to the District Sessions Judges and also the magistrates exercising judicial functions. We, therefore, find that in order to save, protect and show honour to the Constitution it is incumbent upon the State to immediately provide for bringing the entire judicial service, including the magistrates performing judicial functions, under the full and direct control and supervision of the High Court Division of the Supreme Court in all respects structurally and functionally by making or enacting necessary rules and/or laws. It also appears to us that the necessary law in pursuance of Articles 109, 115, 116 and 116A of the Constitution for giving total effect to the separation of the judiciary should be made in consultation with the Supreme Court of Bangladesh. In our view, for effective implementation of the provisions of Articles 115 and 116 necessary rules are to be made by the President which will be enough for the purpose. Under Article 115, the President is required to make rules for the purpose of appointment of persons to offices in the judicial service and magistrate exercising judicial function. As pointed out above, judicial service means a service comprising persons holding posts not being posts superior to that of a District Judge. That means, it comprises the posts of Assistant Judge, Subordinate Judge, Additional District and Sessions Judge and District and Sessions Judge. Therefore, under Article 115 the President shall have to make rules for the appointment of those Judges and magistrates exercising judicial function.

24. Though Article 115 has not mentioned about terms and conditions of service of these Judges, it is apparent, such matters shall also have to be determined by such rules, because appointment without such terms is meaningless. Article 116 lends clear support for this. Under this Article control and discipline of persons employed in the judicial service and magistrates exercising judicial functions vest in the President and this power is required to be exercised by him in consultation with the Supreme Court. The said control includes the power of posting, promotion and grant of leave also as will be seen from the words included in the bracketed portion of Article 116. But all these matters, namely, control, posting, promotion, leave and discipline relate to terms and conditions of service of those Judges and magistrates and the powers in respect thereof cannot be properly exercised without legal support. In other words, for these matters elaborate rules or legislation are necessary. Since these powers are vested in the President and since he can exercise these powers only in consultation with the Supreme Court, he may make rules governing these matters and he may do this after consultation with the Supreme Court. President may also legislate on some of these matters. By making appropriate rules or laws the provisions of Article 116 may be given effect to fully and this will ensure independence of the judiciary and its function in accordance with the Constitution without any linkage with the executive organs of the State as contemplated by Article 22 of the Constitution and Chapter—II of Part—VI thereof. For all these no amendment of the Constitution is necessary, though amendment providing for strengthening the independence of the subordinate judiciary by ensuring certain suitable specific provisions relating to appointment and conditions of service of the aforesaid Judges and magistrates will be welcome.

25. "In spite of the aforementioned clear provisions of the Constitution, the appointment of Judges of the Subordinate Courts and the terms and conditions of their service including disciplinary matter are regulated by rules made by the Government and these matters are all governed by common rules and laws meant for all Government servants. Nevertheless, to say this is clear violation of the provisions of Chapter II of Part—VI of the Constitution. All laws and rules relating to recruitment and terms and conditions of service of persons in the service of the Republic are made or in operation under Article 133 of the Constitution which has no application to Judges of the subordinate judiciary and magistrates performing judicial functions. When there are specific provisions of the Constitution governing such matters relating to the said Judges and magistrates, the provisions of Article 133 cannot be invoked for making laws or rules for regulating their appointment or conditions of their service. Part IX of the Constitution applies to service for which no specific provisions have been made elsewhere in the Constitution. For members of the defence service and Judges of the Subordinate Courts specific Constitutional provisions are there and those must be applied to them and laws for them must be made under those provisions, and not under Article 133. No person ever thought of making laws for defence service personnel under Article 133. Obviously, this is because their matters came within the ambit of Chapter IV of Part IV of the Constitution. Then there is no reason why the appointment and service matter of those Judges and magistrates should be governed by laws, rules or regulations made under Article 133, when such matters come within the ambit of Chapter-II of Part-VI of the Constitution.

26. It may be noted in this connection that there appears to be some misconception in the mind of some person that since the definition of the expression "Service of the Republic" as given in Article 152(1) of the Constitution refers to all services, posts or offices whether civil or military, and Article 133 thereof also relates to persons in the service of the Republic, persons in the judicial service or the magistrates automatically come within the mischief of Article 133. That conclusion is fallacious and it will become apparent from clear reading of the provisions of Chapter-IV of Part-1V, Chapter-11 of Part-VI and definitions of "judicial service" and "service of the Republic." Article 133 begins with the clause "subject to the provisions of the Constitution." It says that Parliament may by law, or the President, in the absence of such law, by rules, provide for appointment and condition of service of persons in the service of the Republic. As Chapter-IV of Part-IV of the Constitution deals with defence service, this article does not apply and has never been applied to such services. Similarly, as Chapter-11 of Part-VI of the Constitution deals with subordinate judiciary and matters relating to appointment and conditions of service of persons belonging to judicial service and ''magistrates, Article 133 has no manner of application to them. Further, one should note that the definition given in Article 152(I) of the Constitution is subject to the condition that they shall have the meanings given to them in that article except where the subject or context does not otherwise require. So, since Article 133 applies subject to other provisions of the Constitution and since the definition of "service of the Republic" will apply when the subject or context does not otherwise require, the clear provision of Chapter-II of Part-VI of the Constitution will apply to Judges and magistrates of the subordinate judiciary and these provisions will over-ride Article 133 in that regard. They are not persons in the service of the Republic for the purposes of Article and hence their appointment or conditions of their service can not be governed under that Article 133 of the Constitution.

27. In this connection the learned Advocates for the petitioners have referred to the case of All India Judges'' Association vs. Union of India (1991) I SCC 119. In the aforesaid case the separation of the judiciary, namely, the Subordinate Courts as well as the terms, conditions, benefits of the Judges and all other things relating thereof were subject matters before the Supreme Court of India.

28. In that Writ Petition reliefs were sought for by the Judges of the Subordinate Courts for bringing uniformity in the conditions of service for members of the subordinate judiciary throughout the country. Articles 32, 234 and 245 of the Constitution of India were the subject matter for consideration by the Supreme Court. In Article 235 of Indian Constitution provisions were made for controlling over the Subordinate Courts, and control and supervision were vested in the High Court. In that case the Supreme Court ultimately gave directions to the government in the judgment in the following terms:

(i) An All India Judicial Service should be set up and the Union of India should take appropriate steps in this regard. (ii) Steps should be taken to bring about uniformity in designation of officers both in civil and military.
(iii) Recruitment age of judicial officers be raised to 60 years and appropriate steps are to be taken by December 31,1992
(iv) As and when the Pay Commissions Committees are set up in the States and Union territories, the question of appropriate pay scales of judicial officers be specifically referred and considered.
(v) A working library at the residence of every judicial officer has to be provided by June 30,1992. Provision for sumptuary allowance as stated had to be made.
(vi) Residential accommodation to every judicial officer has to be provided and until State accommodation is available, Government should provide requisitioned accommodation for them in the manner indicated by December 31, 1992. In providing residential accommodation, availability of an office room should be kept in view.
(vii) Every District Judge and Chief Judicial Magistrate should have a State vehicle, judicial officers in sets of five should have a pool vehicle and others would be entitled to suitable loans to acquire two wheeler automobiles within different time limits as specified.
(viii) In-service Institute should be set up within one year at the Central and State or Union territory level.

29. The Union of India filed a review petition in respect of the aforesaid judgment of the Supreme Court which has been reported in (1993) 4 SCC 288. In the judgment of the Review Application some directions were partially modified by the Supreme Court. In this judgment on review the Supreme Court of India held that the judicial service is not service in the sense of ''employment''. The Judges are not employees. As members of the judiciary they exercise the sovereign judicial power of the State. They are holders of public offices in the same way as the members of the council of ministers and the members of the legislature. When it is said that in a democracy such as ours, the executive, the legislature and the judiciary constitute the three pillars of the State, what is intended to be conveyed is three essential functions of the State are entrusted to the three organs of the State and each one of them in turn represents the authority of the State. However, those who exercise the State power are the ministers, the legislators and the judges, and not the members of their staff Who implement or assist in implementing their decisions. The council of ministers or the political executive is different from the secretariat staff or the administrative executive which carries out the decisions of the political executives. Similarly, the legislators are different from the legislative staff, so also the judges from the judicial staff. The parity is between the political executive, the legislators and the judges and not between the judges and the administrative executive. The judges, at whatever level they may be, represent the State and its authority unlike the administrative executive or the members of the other services. The members of the other services, therefore, cannot be placed on a par with the members of the judiciary, either constitutionally or functionally. Therefore, while determining the service conditions of the members of judiciary, a distinction can be made between them and the members of the other services. There is no substance in the contention of the review petitioners that the directions given by the Supreme Court would lead to the demand from the members of the other services for similar service conditions.

30. In this connection we may also refer to the celebrated judgment of our Appellate Division, namely, Anowar Hossain Chowdhury vs. Bangladesh, reported in 1989 BLD (special issue), I, which is popularly known as ''8th Amendment Case." In this case exhaustive arguments were advanced by the learned members from the Bar and the learned judges also separately dealt with those submissions in that judgement. Justice Shahabuddin Ahmed (as he then was) observed that if by exercising the amending power people''s sovereignty is sought to be curtailed it is the constitutional duty of the court to restrain it and in that case it will be improper to accuse the court of acting as super legislators. Supremacy of the Constitution as the solemn expression of the will of the people, Democracy, Republican Government, Unitary State, Separation of Powers, Independence of the Judiciary, Fundamental Rights are basic structures of the Constitution. There is no dispute about their identity. In this judgment the learned Judge further observed that separation of powers and independence of judiciary are the two basic structures of the Constitution. It appears to us that independence of judiciary will not be completed if the judiciary is not separated from the executive. Since in the aforesaid judgment this separation of judiciary and independence of judiciary have been described as being basic structure of the Constitution, the same cannot be taken away in any manner whatsoever. In the instant case, the separation of judiciary, namely, separation of the Subordinate Courts from the executive organs has already been provided for in Articles 115, 116 and 116A, read with Article 109, of the Constitution and this separation of judiciary and the independence of judiciary being the fundamental structure of the Constitution, the same cannot be touched in any manner whatsoever.

31. In this connection we may also refer to a case, namely, Criminal Miscellaneous Case No.4927 of 1996 (Contempt of Court) The State vs. Shafique Rehman. This is an unreported case. In this case judgement was delivered on 10-12-96 by a Division Bench of this court. In that case some newspapers including one weekly Bengali newspaper the Jai Jai Din made some criticism of the lower courts with regard to granting bail to former president Hossain Mohammad Ershad. In that connection this court issued a suo motu Rule for contempt of court on the Editor of the Bengali weekly journal the Jai Jai Din. In that case also Mr. Syed Ishtiaq Ahmed as well as Dr Kamal Hossain, the learned Advocates, appeared and made their valuable submissions before the court. In that case also this question of separation of judiciary and independence of judiciary were argued by the learned Advocates. Referring to Article 7(2) and also Article 22 of the Constitution it was observed by the Division Bench that in considering the fact that the principles of State policy though not judicially enforceable like the fundamental rights, Article 22 is very much a part of the Constitution which is nothing but the solemn expression of the will of the people. Had it been enforceable like fundamental rights by the court, the court would not hesitate to pass a decree or make a declaration or direction for its implementation and fulfilment, as a long period of 25 years has already passed from the date of independence of Bangladesh. This Article No.22 was not meant for beautifying the Constitution as an ornament, but the will of the people was intended to be implemented within a reasonable time and this period of 25 years from independence is definitely a reasonable period to implement the cherished will and desire of the people. Absolute trust and faith in the Almighty Allah shall be the basis of all actions which is one of the fundamental principles of State policy as per Article 8 of the Constitution. This faith demands that we all should be true to our promise and Article 22 of the Constitution should be implemented in letter and spirit in no time. Since silver jubilee of our independence is being observed throughout the country and abroad, it is high time to show honour and respect to the solemn expression of the will of the people by ensuing separation of judiciary from the executive organs of the State as per Article 22 of the constitution. It is now the solemn duty of all of us particularly the people who are running the affairs of the State to do it.

32. In that case also the speech delivered by Hon''ble Prime Minister of Bangladesh on 3-12-96 in Bangladesh Civil Service BCS (Judicial) Association, the 16th conference, had been quoted from the Bengali newspaper the Daily Ittefaq in the following manner.

স্বাধীন, নিরপেক্ষ ও প্রভাবমুক্ত বিচার বিভাগ একটি গণতান্ত্রিক রাষ্ট্রের মূল ভিত্তি। বিচার ব্যবস্তার ধরণ ও প্রকৃত হইতে প্রতিটি দেশের সভ্যতা ও উন্নতি নির্নয় করা যায়।

আইনের শাসন প্রতিষ্ঠার জন্য জাতির জনক বঙ্গবন্ধু শেখ মুজিবর রহমানের নেতৃত্বে প্রণীত স্বাধীন বাংলাদেশের সংবিধানে নির্বাহী বিভাগ হইতে বিচার বিভাগের পৃথকীকরণের বিধান রাখা হইয়াছিল এবং স্বাধীন বিচার ব্যবস্থা নিশ্চিত করা হইয়াছিল।

প্রধানমন্ত্রী তাহার সরকারের কার্যনীতি প্রসংগে বলেন, সরকার নির্বাহী বিভাগ হইতে বিচার বিভাগের পৃথকীকরণ নিশ্চিত করিতে দৃঢ় প্রতিজ্ঞ। এ কাজ আগাইয়া চলিতেছে। বিচারকদের পেশাগত মান ও দক্ষতা বৃদ্ধির লক্ষ্যে বিচার প্রশাসন প্রশিক্ষণ ইনস্টিটিউট প্রতিষ্ঠা করা হইয়াছে।

33. In the case of Andhra Pradesh vs. Diksitulu, AIR 1979 (SC) 193 the Supreme Court of India considered Article 285 of the Indian Constitution with regard to control of the High Court over subordinate judiciary. Their Lordships held that the control over the subordinate judiciary vested in the High Court under Article 235 is exhaustive in nature, comprehensive in extent and effective in operation. It comprehends wide variety of nature. In the case of State of Assam vs. SN Sen, AIR 1972 (SC) 1028, Indian Supreme Court discussed the scope of Article 235 of the Indian Constitution with regard to control of the High Court over the subordinate judiciary. In AIR 1993 (SC) case, their Lordships clearly held that judiciary is above administrative executive. There cannot be link between service conditions of Judges and those of the members of other services.

34. As we have stated above, Part-VI of the Constitution deals with the judiciary. It has got three parts. Chapter I—The Supreme Court, Chapter II—Subordinate Courts and Chapter III—Administrative Tribunals, Under Chapter I, the Supreme Court is a separate and independent institution from the executive organs of the State. Establishment of this institution, appointment and removal of the Judges, their terms and conditions of service remunerations, salaries, allowances and all other privileges and benefits are guided, regulated and controlled by the Constitution itself, and by other Acts, Ordinance, Rules and Regulations made in pursuance thereof. Even the officers and staff of this Institution are governed by separate Rules. The Constitution itself has made its separation complete and its independence in all respects ensured.

35. Provisions for "Subordinate Court" i.e. Courts of Assistant Judges, Subordinate Judges, Additional District and Sessions Judges and the District and Sessions Judges have been made in Chapter-II of Part-VI of the Constitution. These Subordinate Courts are separate and distinct institutions being integral part of the Judiciary under Part-VI of the Constitution. The Constitution itself has given a separate, independent and distinct character to them. So, this institution i.e. Subordinate Courts can neither be made part nor brought under the control of the Executive organ of the State which is separately created and dealt with under different Parts and Chapters of the Constitution. The Subordinate Courts under Chapter-II of Part-VI must be regulated, controlled and managed within the framework of the Constitution and other enactments and rules made thereunder for carrying out the aforesaid purposes. It will be absolutely unconstitutional if the Subordinate Courts are tagged with or brought under the control of the Executive under Part-IV or any other Part excepting Part-VI of the Constitution.

36. Let us now analyse the relevant provisions of the Constitution one after another. Article 7(2) provides:

"This Constitution is, as the solemn expression of the will of the people, the Supreme Law of the Republic, and if any other law is inconsistent with this Constitution that other law shall, to the extent of the inconsistency, be void.

The above provision shows that the Constitution is the solemn expression of the will of the people of this country and it is the Supreme Law over all other laws.

37. Article 8(2) in Part-II provides that the fundamental principles enumerated in that part shall be fundamental to the governance of Bangladesh, shall be applied by the State in the making of laws, shall be a guide to the interpretation of the Constitution and of other laws of Bangladesh and shall form the basis of the work of the State and of its citizens, but shall not be judicially enforceable. The provisions enumerated. herein have been made compulsive, and binding by using the word "Shall" in almost all principles, including Article 8(2), and though not justifiable i.e. not enforceable through Courts of law, as such, they are nevertheless operative and meant to be followed and acted upon by all concerned. Being the solemn expression of the will of the people to whom all powers in the Republic belong, these principles shall be applied in the matter of governance of Bangladesh and shall form the basis of all State and individual actions. They are integral parts of the supreme law of the land i.e. the Constitution and cannot be avoided or ignored simply because they are not judicially enforceable. The provision for their non-enforceability judicially has been made for the obvious reason that implementation of the principles might take some time and so some breathing time for preparatory work was deemed necessary and by declaring the principles of non-enforceability, the framers of the Constitution simply wished that the State shall take appropriate steps in reasonable time to implement them. But this by no means indicates that the State could go on ignoring them indefinitely or till eternity and it could implement or not, implement them at its sweet will. ''Not justifiable'' does not mean non-binding and wholly optional. The principles are definitely binding and the State may brush them aside or avoid them only at the risk of violating the Constitution.

38. Article 22 provides that the State shall ensure the separation of the judiciary from the executive organs of the State. The word ''ensure'' is important for the purposes of this case. The ordinary Bengali meaning of the word ''ensure'' is নিশ্চিত করা বা নিরাপদ করা and Constitution''s Bengali meaning is নিশ্চিত করকরা. It means that the State shall see to it that the judiciary is kept separate from the executive organs. It urges upon the State to provide for all matters and to take all measures and steps that may be found necessary to ensure such separation. In other words, the State is required to give all logistic support for ensuring such separation, if necessary, appropriate laws are to be made. But this does not call for constitutional amendment. Constitution has already provided for separation of judiciary from the executive. What is now expected of the State is giving effect to and implementation of the Constitutional provisions in their true perspective.

39. Article 109 provides that the High Court Division shall have superintendence and control over all Courts and Tribunals subordinate to it. Bengali translation of the words superintendent and control is তত্ত্বাবধান ও নিয়ন্ত্রণ respectively. Ordinary Bengali dictionary meaning of the word superintend dence is তত্ত্বাবধান, নিয়ন্ত্রণ, পরিচালনা।English meaning according to Oxford English Dictionary is having or exercising the charge or direction, looking after, overseeing supervising the working or management of an institution, keeping watch upon. Ordinary Bengali dictionary meaning of the word ''Control'' is কর্তৃত্ব, দমন, শাসন, নিয়ন্ত্রণ পরিচালনা, Oxford English Dictionary meaning of the word ''Control'' is checking, directing action, function and power of directing and regulating, dominion, command, sway, restraint, check, exercising power or authority, to dominate, to curb, to restrain from action, to hinder, to prevent. So, according to this provision of the Constitution, it appears to us that the Courts and Tribunals subordinate to the High Court Division are under direct control and supervision of the High Court Division in all respects and, as such, no further Constitutional provision is necessary to bring the Subordinate Courts under the supervision and control of the High Court Division. By Constitutional mandate the Subordinate Courts have already been separated and made independent and brought under the High Court Division fully, finally and conclusively.

40. Article 115 provides that rules will be made by the President for appointment of persons to the offices in the judicial service and for appointment of magistrates exercising judicial function and he himself shall make such appointments. This means that the President is the appointing authority of Judges and magistrates of Subordinate Courts and he is also the authority to frame necessary rules for the purpose. Nothing like this is to be found anywhere in the Constitution in respect of appointment of officers or employees in the Executive branch of the Government. This shows that the Constitution has given special importance to the judiciary and like all constitutional posts appointment to the posts of Judges of subordinate judiciary are to be made by the Head of the State. Articles 115 and 116 also require that not only recruitment rules'' but also rules governing the conditions of service of these Judges and magistrates are to be made by the President. It is for the appointing authority to determine under what conditions or terms his appointees i.e. those Judge and magistrates, shall serve. So, the rules, as contemplated under Article 115 of the Constitution read with Article 116, will definitely include all relevant provisions ensuring the conditions of service, control, leave, transfer, promotion, discipline, etc. of the judicial officers and magistrates as aforesaid. If the rules as contemplated under Article 115 of the Constitution are not sufficient and complete to implement and carry out the purpose of effective separation, some other enactments may be made for complete and effective implementation of the same.

41. Article 115 provides that the appointment of the aforesaid judges and magistrates will be made by the President in accordance with the rules made by him. Such appointment includes all other matters relating to their service conditions. In this connection we may refer to the case reported in AIR 1979 (SC) 193. In paragraph 27 of the judgement their Lordships elaborately discussed the meaning and scope of ''appointment'' which runs as follows:

"Now, let us see what is the ambit and scope of the power of "appointment" in Article 229(1). In the context of Article 229, read as a whole this power is of wide amplitude. The word "appointment" in Article 229(1) is to be construed according to the axiom that the greater includes the less. This cardinal canon of interpretation underlies section 16 of the General Clauses Act which has been made applicable by Article 317(1) of the Constitution. Construed in the light of this juristic principle, the power of "appointment" conferred by Article 229(1) includes the power to suspend, dismiss, remove or compulsorily retire from service. In short, in regard to the servants and officers of the High Court, Article 229 makes the power of appointment, dismissal, removal, suspension, reduction in rank, compulsory retirement, etc. including the power to prescribe their conditions of service, the sole preserve of the Chief Justice, and no extraneous executive authority can interfere with the exercise of that power by the Chief Justice or his nominee, except to a very limited extent indicated in the provisions. In conferring such exclusive and supreme powers on the Chief Justice, the object which the Founding Fathers had in view, was to ensure independence of the High Court."

42. At any rate Constitutional amendment is not necessary at all. President has so long been exercising those powers through the executive organ of the State that is the Ministry of Law, Justice and Parliamentary Affairs. To implement and show respect to the constitutional provisions as explained above, instead of the said principles, the President shall have to perform all his powers and functions in this respect through the Supreme Court, High Court Division and necessary provisions by rules may be made in this behalf. Apart from the said administrative control, provisions have to be made for functional separation of the magistracy from the executive organ of the State. Under the Code of Criminal Procedure, 1898, Sessions Courts are functionally and institutionally separate from the executive organ. But the magistrates are members of the administrative service and work under the control of the District Magistrate who is also the Deputy Commissioner and controller of the district i.e. the top executive or administrative head of a district. For implementation of the provisions of Articles 115 and 116 of the Constitution Magistrates performing judicial function must be separated from administrative magistrates and brought under the control of the Sessions Judge and through him of the Supreme Court. This requires immediate amendment of the Code of Criminal Procedure.

43. It may be mentioned that absolute and unlimited power has been given to the President to make Rules under Article 115 of the Constitution. Even by making Rules the President can authorise the High Court Division to appoint the aforesaid Judges and magistrates and fix their terms and conditions of services including removal from service and all other connected matters with regard to their services. Rule making power has been given by the Constitutional provision and, as such, the President may make Rules as deemed fit and necessary for giving effective completion of the separation of the judiciary. Since the rule making power of the President is wide, unlimited and absolute, the President can make any provision under the rules which are necessary for carrying out all purposes of separation of judiciary from the executive.

44. In this connection it may be mentioned that in 1957 the Code of Criminal Procedure (East Pakistan Amendment) Act, 1957, was enacted, providing for judicial magistrates and separating them from executive magistrates, but it was never given effect to as no notification for its enforcement was ever made. The law is in the statute book even today. In this Act two categories of Magistrates were created, viz, Judicial Magistrates and Executive Magistrates. But because of the abolition of the post of sub-divisional magistrate and the other change in the administrative set-up the said law cannot be activated now in to. For bringing the judicial Magistrates under the control of the judiciary and separating them from the executive magistrates, necessary amendment in the Code of Criminal Procedure is required now. It may be mentioned that India and Pakistan have already done it and separated judicial magistracy from the executive magistracy and brought the judicial magistrates under the full and effective control of the judiciary. Since almost all the political parties in our country are openly in favour of separation of judiciary from the executive, we do not see any problem in getting the amendment of the Code of Criminal Procedure done soon.

45. Article 116 provides that the control, power of posting, promotion, grant of leave and discipline of the persons employed in judicial, service and the magistrates exercising judicial functions shall vest in the President who will exercise all those powers in consultation with the Supreme Court. Now it appears that all the above functions of the President are not being exercised by the President according to the true sense and spirit of the above Article 116. In our view, the President shall exercise all those functions not through the executive organ of the State, but through the Supreme Court by making suitable rules. It means, appropriate supporting legislation may be made.

46. Article 116A provides that all persons in judicial service and the judicial functions shall be independent in the exercise of their judicial functions. If Articles 115, 116 and 116A are read with Article 109 of the Constitution, it will give a clear and unambiguous picture that by inserting these provisions in the Constitution, the framers of the Constitution have already separated the judiciary i.e. the Subordinate Courts including the magistrates exercising judicial functions from the executive, and only necessary enactments and rules are required to be made to implement, give effect to and carry out the purposes of the said Constitutional provisions.

47. Article 136 provides for making law for recorganisation of services by creation, amalgamation or unification of services. It cannot include judicial service inasmuch as judicial service is a part of Part-VI of the Constitution. This judicial service cannot be legally brought within the ambit of Act No.32 of 1975, because if it is so done, it will offend the very fundamental and basic structure of the Constitution relating to separate and independent judicial service as ensured and made a part of Part-VI of the Constitution. Further, under the Constitution judicial service is one and indivisible. There is nothing to re-organise it either by amalgamation or unification of services or otherwise, as the same has been specified and separated in the Constitution itself.

48. Another aspect of the case should be considered with due seriousness. Everybody in the country is speaking about independence of judiciary which is reflecting from Article 116A of the Constitution also. It is a must and it should be a must to make the judiciary fully separate from the executive in all respects in order to attain the cherished goal of all—that is—the "Independence of Judiciary''. Without full and effective separation of judiciary, it is an impossibility to secure and achieve independence of judiciary and guaranteeing individual liberty. The present Government is also preaching highly about independence of judiciary in our country. What is expected of it now is serious early steps for effective completion of separation of judiciary from the executive should be taken in pursuance of this judgement.

49. Considering the provisions as laid down in Articles 109, 115, 116 and 116A of the Constitution we are of the view that the provisions for separation of judiciary are very much there in the Constitution itself and, as such, for separation of judiciary from the executive no new amendment of the Constitution is necessary. In exercising power under Article 102(2) (a)(i) of the Constitution this Court is competent to direct the respondents to make necessary rules and/or enactments in order to enable the judiciary to function as an independent institution free from any control or interference from the executive organs of the State and to carry out the intentions and promises of the framers of the Constitution as expressed in the aforesaid Articles of Constitution. Thereby the State will fulfil the wish and firm will of the people as reflected in the Preamble of the Constitution and in Article 22 thereof. In exercise of the said power under Article 102 of the Constitution, this Court is also competent to direct the President and legislature to make rules and/or enactments, if necessary, to make separation of judiciary from the executive complete and effective by bringing the Subordinate Courts along with the magistrates performing judicial functions entirely under the control, supervision and management of the High Court Division of the Supreme Court as the Constitution requires. Rules made under Article 115 should provide for an independent service commission for appointment of the Judicial Officers and Judicial Magistrates. Rules should also be framed or laws be made for the control and discipline of all the Judicial Officers and the Judicial Magistrates and to determine and regulate the terms and conditions of their service, salaries and remunerations and discharge of their judicial functions and all other connected and incidental matters. And those rules and enactments must also ensure that the Head of State shall exercise his functions only through, and in consultation with, the Supreme Court.

50. In this connection a question may be raised to the effect that since some judicial officers are challenging the revised pay-scales and they are persons in the service of the Republic, though in a limited sense, the remedy lies with the Administrative Tribunal and not in Writ Jurisdiction. This argument, though appears logical, is not sound or acceptable. Trued the petitioners are Judicial Officers and in a sense, as shown earlier, persons in the service of the Republic. But they are the presiding Judges of different Courts of Bangladesh. Their appointments and conditions of service are governed by Chapter-II of Part-VI of the Constitution and rules and laws made or to be made thereunder. Like the defence service they are independently and separately governed. Though the defence service personnel are also persons in the service of the Republic as defined in Article 152(1) of the Constitution, they do not come within the ambit of Article 117 of the Constitution. Similarly, Judicial Officers also do not come within the jurisdiction of the Administrative Tribunal as their service conditions are governed and determined by or under Chapter-II or Part-VI of the Constitution. President makes appointment to the persons of the judicial service, and control, discipline, etc. of persons in judicial service are vested in him, but he may exercise this power only in consultation with the Supreme Court, which is the highest Court in the country. Since the subordinate Courts are subordinate to the Supreme Court only and the judges function under the superintendence and control of the High Court Division of the Supreme Court, they do not come within the jurisdiction of the Administrative Tribunal. Administrative Tribunal is a Tribunal constituted under Article 117 of the Constitution. The very term ''Administrative Tribunal'' indicates that it is meant to give relief in service matters to those persons who are connected with the executive organs of the State. Though Article 117 refers to persons in the service of the Republic, yet for obvious reasons and as explained above such persons do not, for the purpose of this Article, include persons in the defence service or the judicial service, or the Magistrates exercising judicial functions. Courts or Judges are not subordinate of the said Tribunal and hence the Judges of Courts are not to seek relief from this Tribunal. As noted above, Administrative Tribunal is constituted primarily to settle disputes relating to service matters of executive officers or those persons who are not governed by specific provisions of the Constitution, or law or rules made thereunder. Since the Judicial Officers that is Judges are not in the service of the Republic within the meaning of the ''Services of Bangladesh'' under Part-IX of the Constitution, we are of the view that the Judicial Officers, that is, Judges of the Subordinate Courts and magistrates performing judicial function, are not required to submit to the jurisdiction of the Administrative Tribunal for any relief or redress in respect of the terms and conditions of their service as well as in connection with any other matter relating to their service.

51. So the present petitioners and other judicial officers are not required to go to the Administrative Tribunal for redress of their grievances. As we have stated above that the judicial officers should not be equated with the civil, executive or administrative officers or other officers performing functions in connection with the administration of the country and since the petitioners being Judges of different Courts are totally unconnected with the civil, administrative or executive service, we hold that they are not subject to jurisdiction of the Administrative Tribunal for any matter with respect to their service and other ancillary matters, as they are performing sovereign functions of the State specified under the Constitution.

52. Either in Annexure-E, that is, the Services (Pays and Allowances) Order, 1991 or in Annexure-F(1), that is the amended impugned order dated 2-11-95, the authority is quite silent about the Assistant Judges and Senior Assistant Judges. The impugned orders only relate to subordinate Judges, Additional District and Sessions Judges and District and Sessions Judges. But it appears that they are getting their salaries and other allowances as decided by the government. Let them continue to have the salaries and allowances and other benefits as they are getting now and they should not be given anything below the pays and allowances as specified in paragraph 3 of the impugned order Annexure-F(1) dated 2-11-95 till the framing of the Rules and/or any other enactment as required under the Constitution as per our above findings. Till completion of separation of judiciary the Assistant Judges and Senior Assistant Judges will be having their existing pays, salaries and allowances and/or other ancillary benefits as they are getting now. When the appropriate rules and/or enactment will be framed, their cases will be considered along with the Subordinate Judges, Additional District and Sessions Judges and District and Sessions Judges together.

53. Considering the facts and circumstances as stated above and the provisions of the Constitution which we have discussed in detail, we hold that the provisions of separation of judiciary are already there in the Constitution itself and it is to be implemented or carried out or given effect to only by making rules under Article 115, and enactment if it is so necessary. We further hold that the Supreme Court alone shall have overall control, supervision and management over the Subordinate Courts along with the Judicial Magistrates and the Executive will have no control, supervision and management over the same in any manner whatsoever.

54. We have already stated above that the Government is not contesting this Writ Petition. Further, we are informed by the learned Deputy Attorney-General that, in fact, the learned Attorney-General has given his opinion to the Government in favour of the grievances and demands of the petitioners in accordance with the Rules issued in this case. So, no State lawyer made any argument against the prayers made in this Writ petition. Since Government is not contesting, it is presumed, the Government has no objection if the Rule is made absolute and the prayers made by the petitioners in this Writ Petition are granted.

55. This Writ Petition filed by 441 Judges of different Courts of Bangladesh is allowed and the Rule is made absolute without cost in the following terms:

a). The impugned order dated 28-2-94 vide Annexure—F and the order dated 2-11-95 vide Annexure—F(1),(Serial Nos.10, 11 and 12) are hereby declared to have been made and issued without lawful authority and are of no legal effect, being ultra vires the Constitution so far the same relate to the Writ Petitioners and other Judges of Judicial Service.

b) It is declared that the service cadre made under paragraph 2(X) BCS (Judicial) as contained in the Bangladesh Civil Service (Re-organisation) Order, 1980 vide Annexure-A with amendment of 1986, is ultra vires the Constitution.

c) It is further declared that all the judicial officers of Bangladesh i.e. all the Judges of the different Courts from the Assistant Judges to the District and Sessions Judges are not required to go and submit before the Administrative Tribunal for any grievance or relief with regard to their service conditions and all other matters including punishment of any kind inasmuch as the Courts are not Subordinate to the Tribunal, and the said Judges and magistrates performing judicial functions shall be guided under Articles 115, 116 and 116A of the Constitution and according to our findings made above.

d) It is declared that in order to give effect, carry out and implement fully the separation of judiciary from the executive organ of the State no Constitutional amendment will be necessary as the provisions for such separation are there in the Constitution itself. It is directed that the services of the judicial officers and the Magistrates performing judicial functions shall be known as ''Judicial Service of Bangladesh'' under the direct control and supervision of the Supreme Court.

e) It is also declared that re-fixation of National Pay Scales, 1991, as enumerated in paragraph No.3 of Services (Pays and Allowances) Order, 1991, dated 8-1-94 vide Annexure-E to the Writ Petition, so far it relates to the petitioners and other judicial officers, shall stand valid and the same will continue until the necessary rules and/or enactment is made for the Judges of the Subordinate Courts with regard to salaries and allowances and all other matters in respect of their services.

f) It is also declared that the Assistant Judges and Senior Assistant Judges will continue to get their salaries and allowances as they are now getting, which will be not less than those as are admissible under paragraph No.3 of Annexure-F(1).

g) It is directed that the Respondent Nos.1, 2 and 4 shall take immediate steps to make necessary Rules under Article 115 of the Constitution and/or to make appropriate enactment in order to give effect, implement and carry out fully the purposes of the Constitution particularly of Article 109, 115, 116 and 116A read with Articles 8 and 22 of the Constitution for making separation of judiciary from the executive organ complete and effective.

h) If the present Pay Scales of the petitioners and other judicial officers are amended or enhanced or new pay scales are given before making rules by the President under Article 115 of the Constitution, the same of the said judicial officers and the Magistrates shall be made and/or done keeping conformity with the pay scales as are declared for them in this judgement.

I) Let a copy of this judgment be sent to the Hovile Prime Minister of Bangladesh and the Minister-in-Charge of the Ministry of Law, Justice and Parliamentary Affairs for information and necessary action in the light of this judgment and also in pursuance of Articles 109, 115, 116 and 116A of the Constitution of Bangladesh.

M Hassan Ameen J: I am completely in agreement with the decision of my learned brother. However, I like to add a few lines in order to get myself clear to my conscience. Our Constitution is based, among others, on three pillars—Executive, Legislature and Judiciary. The principles of state policy set out in Part II of the Constitution shall be fundamental to the Government of Bangladesh, shall be applied by the State in the making of laws, shall be guide to the interpretation of the Constitution and of the other laws of the country and shall form the work of the State and of its citizens. The Parliament is incharge of making the laws and Parliament Secretariat is to assist the former by giving logistic support. The duty assigned to judiciary is for interpretation of law and dispensation of justice by the Supreme Court and the Subordinate judiciary. And, finally, the duty assigned to the executive is to run the administrative and execute policy of the Government.

57. Articles 152(1) of the Constitution gives definition of ''Judicial Service'' which means a service comprising persons holding judicial posts not being posts superior to that of a district judge. The ''Service of the Republic'' means any service, post or office whether in civil or military capacity in respect of Government of Bangladesh and any other service declared by law to be a service of the Republic. It is curious to note that there is no reference about the name of any other cadre service of Bangladesh except the judicial service and defence service in the four corners of our Constitution. The judicial service is not service in the sense of employment. The judges arc not employees. As members of judicial service, they exercise the sovereign judicial power of the State under the Constitution. The Judges are not the judicial staff. The other services, in fact, exist which carry out the outcome of three pillars of the Constitution. Other services i.e. cadre services of the Republic carry out the decisions of these three organs of the State as representatives of the executive (Council of Ministers) one of the pillars of the Constitution being staff of the executive. So, natural corollary is that the judicial service cannot be equated with other services of the Republic and accordingly, the inclusion of judicial service as one of the cadre services of the Republic vide SRO No. 286-L/80/ED(IC)S11-92/80-98 dated 1-9-1980 (Annexure-A) is ultra vires the Constitution. As such, the "Judicial Service" shall be excluded from the above list which requires to be designated as "Judicial Service of Bangladesh" having no connection with other services of Bangladesh under direct control and supervision of the Supreme Court in view of separate control, clear and distinct nature of work of the members of Judicial Service of Bangladesh.

58. In this connection it may be recalled here that in spite of provisions as set out in Article 115 of the Constitution, the President of the Republic has failed to make Rules regulating the appointment and conditions of service of persons in the service of the Republic and we are sure this kind of anomaly (treating the judicial service as one of the cadre services of the Republic) would not have taken place had the Rules on this behalf been framed by the President. By this time long quarter century has passed and much water has flown through rivers of the country like Padma, Meghna and Jamuna and, as such, it is high time for the authority to give recognition to the separate identity of the ''Judicial Service of Bangladesh'' by making rules in view of their distinct nature of duties that a judge is called upon to discharge. Society''s expectation of the conduct of the Judges, the life style of the Judges, the occupational hazard, to which he/she is exposed to the need to keep Judges above their essential wants.


59. This distinction between the Judges and members of other services has to be consistently kept in mind yet for another important reason. Independence of judiciary cannot be secured by making mere solemn proclamation about it. It has to be ensured both in substance and in practice. The society has a stake in ensuring independence of the judiciary and no price is too heavy to secure it. Considering the facts and circumstances we are of the view that not only the scales of pay as announced in the impugned Memo being SRO No. অম/অধি(ব্যস্ত-১) বিবিধ-২৫/৯৩/২৪ তাং-২৯-২-৯৪ in respect of the judicial service (Annexure-E) should be retained but also the pay of judicial officers be substantially enhanced by constituting a separate Pay Commission in order to enable them (Judicial Officers) to maintain a proper standard of life and avoid obligations which may be embarrassing for him in the discharge of his duties by making the judicial service separate from other services of the Republic by making rules on this behalf.

End.
