13. From a bare reading of the Annexure-'E-2' dated 2-8-2008, it transpires that' the case property had already been released in favour of Hemendra Kumar Chakrabarty and the same was erroneously listed as a vested property. Taking the Annexure-'E' series and considering them in conjunction with the judgment and order dated 17-12-1969 tendered in Writ Petition No. 366 of 1967 (Annexure- ‘D’) we are left with no option but to hold that the case property Is not an enemy/vested property and erroneously the same was listed as a vested property as is apparent from Annexure- 'E-2' to the writ petition. This being the position, the Government cannot now make a volte-face and say that the case property is an enemy/vested property. It seems that Mr AB Roy Chowdhury has rightly contended that the Government is bound by promissory estoppel and that being so, it cannot deny the right and interest of the petitioners in the case property (49 DLR 557). On this point, we are at one with Mr. AB Roy Chowdhury.

14. Although it has been argued on the side of the respondent No. 4 that the case property is an enemy/vested property and the Government leased out some portions thereof to different persons including one Abdus Salam; yet strangely enough, no paper or document has been annexed to the Affidavit-in-Opposition in support thereof. What we are driving at boils down to this: the respondent No. 4 has signally failed to substantiate his case by annexing the necessary papers or documents. In such a posture of things, we have no hesitation in holding that the case of the respondent No. 4 has no legs to stand upon and, as such, it stands discarded. As a natural corollary thereto, we cannot accept the submission of the learned Deputy Attorney-General Mr. Md. Motaher Hossain (Sazu) that the case property is a vested property.

15. It is an indubitable fact that the petitioners did not approach the concerned অর্পিত সম্পত্তি প্রত্যর্পন ট্রাইব্যুনাল in Dhaka for necessary legal redress for inclusion of the case property in 'Ka' Schedule of the Gazette Notification dated 6-5-2012. According to the learned Advocate Mr. AB Roy Chowdhury, as the treatment of the case property as a vested property is clearly malafide, he invoked the writ jurisdiction of the High Court Division under Article 102 of the Constitution by filing the instant writ petition.

16. It is often said that malafides or bad faith vitiates everything and a mala fide act is a nullity. Now a pertinent question arises: what is malafides or bad faith? Relying on some observations of the Indian Supreme Court in some decisions, Durgadas Basu J held, "It is common place to state that malafides does not necessarily involve a malicious intention. It is enough if the aggrieved party establishes: (i) that the authority making the impugned order did not apply its mind at all to the matter in question; or (ii) that the impugned order was made for a purpose or upon a ground other than what is mentioned in the order." (Ram Chandra vs Secretary to the Government of WB AIR 1964 Cal 265).

17. To render an action malafide, "There must be existing definite evidence of bias and action which cannot be attributed to be otherwise bonafide; actions not otherwise bonafide, however, by themselves would not amount to be malafide unless the same is in accompaniment with some other factors which would depict a bad motive or intent on the part of the doer of the act" (Punjab vs Khanna, AIR 2001 SC 343).

18. Reverting to the case in hand, there is no gainsaying the fact that the case property was released from the list of enemy/vested properties by Annexures-'13' and 'E-1' and subsequently by Annexure-'E-2', the Government necessarily admitted that the listing of the case property as a vested property was through inadvertence. The release of the case property from the list of enemy/vested properties as evidenced by Annexures- 'E' and 'E-l' was in consequence of the judgment and order dated 17-12-1969 rendered in the earlier Writ Petition No. 366 of 1967 (Annexure-'D'). The Annexure-'E-2' clinched the whole matter.

<u>19. Taking the entire gamut of the situation enumerated above and in the facts and circumstances of the case, a man of ordinary prudence will necessarily come to the conclusion that the authority concerned was prompted by malafides or bad faith in including the case property in 'Ka' Schedule as a vested property in the Gazette Notification dated 6-5-2012. In this context, we feel tempted to say that it is a settled proposition of law that an aggrieved party may invoke the writ jurisdiction of the High Court Division under Article 102 of the Constitution straightaway provided the action impugned is malafide, even though there may be an alternative remedy available for him. Since we have found that the inclusion of the case property in 'Ka' Schedule of the Gazette Notification dated 6-5-2012 as a vested property is rnalafide, the instant writ petition, as we see it, is maintainable. Besides, it has been clearly, categorically and unequivocally held in the decision in the case of the Government of Bangladesh represented by the Ministry of Works no Syed Chand Sultana reported in 51 DLR (AD) 24 that the writ-petitioners can come directly to the High Court Division for protection of their fundamental right, even though an alternative remedy is available. So our definite finding is that the petitioners can come directly to the High Court Division for protection of their right to property as contemplated by Article 42 of the Constitution of Bangladesh, even though an alternative forum, that is to say, অর্প্রিত সম্পত্তি প্রত্যর্পণ ট্রাইব্যুনাল is available for necessary legal redress.</u>

20. Section 6(ka) of অর্পিত সম্পত্তি প্রত্যার্পন আইন, ২০০১ Contemplates that প্রত্যর্পনযোগ্য সম্পত্তির তালিকায় নিম্নবর্ণিত সম্পত্তি অন্তর্ভূক্ত করা যাইবে না। যথাঃ- (ক) কোন সম্পত্তির অর্পিত সম্পত্তি নহে মর্মে এই আইন প্রবর্তনের পূর্বে যথাযথ আদালত চূড়ান্ত সিদ্ধান্ত প্রদান করিয়া থাকিলে সেই সম্পত্তি.  As the then Dhaka High Court made the Rule absolute in Writ Petition No. 366 of 1967 and held the treatment of the case property as an enemy property without lawful authority, the provisions of section অর্পিত সম্পত্তি প্রত্যার্পন আইন, ২০০১ you will, for certain, come into play in this case. On this count also, the inclusion of the case property in 'Ka' Schedule of the Gazette Notification dated 6-5-2012 as a vested property cannot be sustained in law.

21. From the foregoing discussions and regard being had to the facts and circumstances of the case, we find merit in the Rule. The Rule, therefore, succeeds.

Accordingly, the Rule is made absolute without any order as to costs. The inclusion of the case property at serial Nos. 468 and 618 in 'Ka' Schedule of the Gazette Notification dated 6-5-2012 pursuant to EP Case No. 152 of 1966 and EPMC Case No. 1057 of 1961 (Annexure-T to the writ petition) is declared to be without lawful authority and of no legal effect.

End.

caseno: Civil Petition for Leave to Appeal No. 1559 of 2005
lawyer:
KZ Alam, Senior Advocate, instructed by Md Nawab Ali, Advocate-on-Record—For the Petitioner. 
None Represented—For the Respondents.
parties:
Marziana Khatun ------ Petitioner.
Vs.
Government of Bangladesh ------ Respondents.
case_source: (From the judgment and order dated 24-8-2005 passed by the High Court Division in Writ Petition No. 2279 of 2001).
full_judgment:
Md Fazlul Karim J: This petition for leave to appeal at the instance of the petitioner is directed against the judgment and order dated 24-8-2005 passed by the High Court Division in Writ Petition No. 2279 of 2001 discharging the Rule and refusing to declare that inclusion of the property in question in the 'Ka' list of abandoned properties appeared at Serial No. 190 in the gazette notification dated 23-9-1986 was illegal and the direction of respondent No. 3 dated 8-9-1998 to the petitioner to deposit Taka 58,261.00 as house rent for the said property was also illegal, without any lawful authority and is of no legal effect.

2. The case of the petitioner, in short, is that she is the owner in possession of the case property being House No. J-59, Sherioil, Police Station Boalia, District Rajshahi by virtue of 5 (five) registered title deeds of the year 1974. Since 1974 she has been possessing and enjoying the same peacefully and uninterruptedly by getting her name mutated in various departments with reference thereto. After mutation of the name of the petitioner vide Mutation Case No. 382/91/91-92, she paid rent to the revenue office and municipal taxes in respect of the case property. However, on 16-10-1974 the Executive Engineer, C&B, Rajshahi and Secretary, Abandoned Property Management Board, Rajshahi served a notice upon the husband of the petitioner for eviction from the case property on the score that the said property is an abandoned property. Thereafter the petitioner instituted OC Suit No. 408 of 1976 in the Court of Assistant Judge, Rajshahi Sadar, Rajshahi praying for permanent injunction against the Government in relation to the case property. The said Title Suit was subsequently transferred to the Additional Court of Assistant Judge, Rajshahi and renumbered as OC Suit No. 119 of 1983 Ultimately, the said OC Suit No. 119 of 1983 was decreed on contest on 24-4-1983. While the petitioner had been enjoying and possessing the case property in accordance with the aforesaid judgment and decree of the Civil Court, she came to know in the month of October, 1996 that the said property was enlisted in the "Ka" list of abandoned buildings. Thereafter, she made a representation to the respondent No. 1 paying for release of the property from the 'Ka' list of abandoned buildings, but in vain. However, the respondent No. 3 sent a notice to the petitioner directing her to deposit a sum of Taka 58,261 within 15 (fifteen) days from the date of receipt of the notice on account of the rent of the property in question vide Memo No. Je: Pra:Ra/Ra:Mu:1256 dated 8-9-1998. On receipt of the aforesaid notice dated 8-9-1998, the petitioner being a sexagenarian made all out efforts to get the case property released, but without any result. Be that as it may, the petitioner being a purdanshin ordinary woman was not aware of the inclusion of the case property in the he 'Ka' list of abandoned buildings till October, 1996 and, as such, she could not make any application for release of the same before the Court of Settlement concerned within the given time frame. The Government did not take over possession of the case property prior to its inclusion in the 'Ka' list of abandoned buildings in accordance with the provisions of section 5(1)(a) of the Abandoned Buildings (Supplementary Provisions) Ordinance, 1985 (Ordinance No. 54 of 1985). The case property is not an abandoned property within the meaning of the Bangladesh Abandoned Property (Control, Management and Disposal) Order, 1972 (PO No. 16 of 1972). Hence the inclusion of the property in the 'Ka' list if abandoned buildings is without lawful authority and of no legal effect.

3. Mr KZ Alam, learned Counsel appearing for the petitioner submits that the petitioner and her vendor being present in Bangladesh having possession and occupation of her property in question, the property could never be declared as an abandoned property and the learned Judges of the High Court Division erred in law in not declaring that the inclusion of the petitioner's property in the "Ka" list or for that matter having declared the same as an abandoned property contrary to the provision of law, and, as such, the same is liable to be set aside by this Court; that the petitioner having proved her purchase of the property in question from the owners who were and are present in Bangladesh living in the territory since 25th March, 1971, the learned Judges of the High Court Division were in error in discharging the Rule under Article 102 of the Constitution; that the petitioner being a citizen of Bangladesh and so are the petitioner's vendors on the date when the PO 16 of 1972 came into operation, the property could not be treated as abandoned property and the learned High Court Division were wrong in holding the same as and abandoned property; that the petitioner under duress and coercion acted in a most silly way without realising that her application to the respondent No. 4 would be treated as her application for allotment and in any view of the matter a property which could not be treated as an abandoned property in law, the High Court Division were in error in declaring her property to be an abandoned property and needs to be rectified by this Court; that the High Court Division was in error in not considering the judgment and decree dated 24-4-1983 in OC Suit No. 408 of 1976 (renumbered as 119 of 1983) passed by a competent Civil Court decreeing the suit for permanent injunction and hence the same could not be declared as such and needs to be rectified by this Court; that the property if it was to be included in the list of abandoned property, it was incumbent upon the respondents to show that it was within the mischief of law clearly for it betrays the fundamental right of the petitioner to hold her own property; that no notice as contemplated under the President's Order No. 16 of 1972 or Order LIV of 1985 issued to petitioner, inclusion of her property in the 'Ka' list of the abandoned buildings being without lawful authority and this Court will be pleased to set aside the judgment and order dated 24-8-2005 passed by the High Court Division on an erroneous view and direct the respondents to take off the petitioner's property from the list of abandoned property; that the petitioner purchased the case property in 1974 from one Halima Khatun and her two sons namely Mahbubul Alam and Rafiqul Islam respectively by 5 registered deeds and since her purchase she has been owning and possessing the same and though the abandoned property office issued notice for vacating the house and though underduress she took allotment of the same from the property authority but at no point of time the property in question was enlisted as abandoned property because Rabeya Khatun, the previous owner, was all along in Bangladesh during the war of liberation and to that effect she affirmed an affidavit in 1974 and in spite of Court's order in Other Class Suit No. 119/1983 Government failed to produce any paper to show that the case property was an abandoned property and in the judgment Munsif clearly found title and possession in favour of the petitioner but the High Court Division, on an erroneous view of the matter and without considering the judgment of Other Class Suit No. 119/1983, found that the case property was an abandoned property and its subsequent inclusion in the 'Ka' list was not illegal and accordingly, discharged the Rule causing serious miscarriage of justice and prejudice to the petitioner; that the Other Class Suit No. 119/1983 the petitioner by examining 6 PWs proved that Rabeya Khatun was in Bangladesh on or before the promulgation of PO 16 of 1972 and Rabeya Khatun by affirming an affidavit before a Magistrate, 1st Class, Dhaka on 13-12-1974 stated the fact that she was all along in Bangladesh at the relevant time and, as such, her whereabout was very much known and the property in question could not be declared as such nor could be included in the list of the abandoned property and the respondents having failed to produce and prove as to the property being an abandoned property as per the provisions of law had claimed illegally and arbitrarily but the High Court Division by misinterpreting Article 2(1) of PO 16 of 1972 arrived at a wrong finding that the property is an abandoned property and the same was vested in the Govt. by operation of law and accordingly discharged the Rule which has caused a grave failure of justice; that as per advice of the lawyer, the petitioner instituted Other Class Suit No. 119/1983 for permanent injunction, title and possession of the plaintiff as a condition precedent for getting permanent injunction and considering the same, a decree was passed by the Munsif in favour of the plaintiff-petitioner and the respondents having contested the suit but did not prefer any appeal against the said judgment and order dated 24-4-1983 and, as such, keeping the judgment of a competent Civil Court un-challenged before any higher forum, subsequent inclusion of the property in question in the 'Ka' list of the abandoned properties is illegal, arbitrary and without jurisdiction but the High Court Division on an erroneous view of Article 14(1) of the PO 16 of 1972 held, that granting injunction by the Munsif was illegal because Article 14(1) of PO 16 of 1972 was a bar and the subsequent inclusion in 'Ka' list was lawful and accordingly, discharged the Rule and, as such, the same should be set aside by this Court; that the original owner of the property in question, namely Rabeya Khatun, was in Bangladesh during the war of liberation and thereafter her property could not be taken over as an abandoned property and since it was not in the abandoned property list, Article 6 of PO 16 of 1972 being not applicable and the High Court Division, without at all considering facts and circumstances of the case arrived at a wrong conclusion thereby erred in law in discharging the Rule contrary to the clear finding of the Munshif in the judgment of OC Suit No. 119/1983; that the petitioner being an elderly pardanashin lady having no support from members of her family or from any relation or friend, she under duress took allotment which was stated in the plaint of OC Suit No. 119/1983 but never paid any rent as an allottee and she instituted Other Class Suit No. 408/1976 (renumbered as OC Suit No. 119/1983) and obtained an order of permanent injunction restraining the respondents from taking over possession of the house in question from the petitioner and also not to collect rent from her in respect of the same though this fact was inadvertently omitted from the Writ petition and not an intentional suppression of fact, and the High Court Division failed to consider the moot point in law and discharged the Rule causing serious miscarriage of justice which is to be set aside by this Court; that as per provision of section 5(1) of PO 16 of 1972, notice taking over possession of an abandoned property is a condition precedent for its inclusion in 'Ka list of abandoned properties and in the instant case at no point of time the respondents took over possession and though the petitioner took allotment of the same in 1975 she was dispossessed by the respondents and though she took allotment from Government but never paid any rent and thereby the allotment was not acted upon and, as such„ its inclusion in the 'Ka' list on 23-9-1986 in the Bangladesh Gazette was violative of the provisions of law and on a total misreading of the evidence on record of the High Court Division discharged the Rule which has caused grave failure of justice and need be rectified by this Court; that in the light of the decision by this Court in respect of any property allegedly taken over or included in the list of abandoned property or trying to be taken over as an abandoned property, the High Court Division erred in law and on facts in not declaring that the appellant-petitioners property included in the 'Ka' list of the abandoned properties is without any lawful authority and is of no legal effect, and need be so declared by this Court; that in any view of the matter the High Court Division erred in holding that inclusion of the property of the appellant-petitioner as an abandoned property lawful, the same is liable to be set aside by this Court.

4. It appears from the record that the definite claim of the writ-petitioner is that during the promulgation of the PO No. 16 of 1972 Rabeya Khatun possessed the case property. But the High Court Division found that no scrap of paper has been filed on the side of the writ-petitioner evidencing that Rabeya Khatun possessed the case property during the relevant period. It also appears from the record that the case property is a abandoned property. In this context Article 14(1) of the PO No. 16 of 1972 may be called in aid. Article 14(1) of the order provides that an property vested in the Government under this order shall be exempted from all legal process, including seizure, distress, ejectment, attachment or sale by any office or a Court or any other authority and no injunction or other order of whatever kind in respect of such property shall be granted or made by any Court or any other authority and the Government shall not be divested or dispossessed of such property by operation of any law for the time being in force. So, it is crystal clear that no injunction shall be granted by any Court or any other authority in respect of an abandoned property. The High Court Division had no hesitation in holding that the judgment and decree passed in the suit for perpetual injunction simpliciter (OC Suit No. 119 of 1983) is hit by Article 14(1) of PO No. 16 of 1972.

<u>5. The High Court Division observed that admittedly the writ-petitioner took lease of the case property as a DN holder of the Government in 1975. To put it differently, the Government has been possessing the case property through its allottee. As the Government has been in possession of the case property through the writ-petitioner, the Government did not take over possession thereof from its own allottee before enlistment thereof in the 'Ka' list of abandoned building published in the Bangladesh Gazette on 23-9-1986. In such a situation the submission is that the Government must have taken over the possession of the case property before its inclusion in the 'Ka' list of abandoned building falls to the ground.</u>

6. In the facts and circumstances of the case and in view of the findings of the Court below, we find no substance in the submissions of the learned Advocate for the petitioner.

Accordingly, the petition is dismissed.

End.

lawyer:
ZI Khan Panna, Advocate with Md Sagir Hossain—For the Petitioners. 
Shahidul Islam, DAG with Sukumar Biswas, AAG—For Respondent No. 2.
parties:
Nazrul Islam Mollah (Md) & others ------- Petitioners
Vs.
Chairman, 1st Court of Settlement & another -------- Respondents
full_judgment:
Mahmudul Hoque J: In this application under Article 102 of the Constitution of Bangladesh a Rule Nisi has been issued at the instance of the petitioner calling upon the respondents to show cause as to why the inclusion of premises being House No. 19/7 Pallabi, Mirpur, Dhaka in the "Kha" list of abandoned building as appearing in the Bangladesh Gazette Extra-ordinary on 23-9-1986 at page 9764 (25) in serial No. 35 should not be declared to be without lawful authority and of no legal effect, and/ or pass such other or further order or orders as to this Court may seem fit and proper.

2. Facts relevant for disposal of this Rule, in short, are that the petitioners are the citizen and permanent residents of Bangladesh. The properties in question was originally belonged to one Idu Mollah who got the same by a deed of Heba-bil-Ewaz dated 18-12-1946. While he was in possession and enjoyment of the same, he sold the properties to 1) Sultan Ahmed Mollah, 2) Nur Islam Mollah, 3) Nur Mohammad Mollah and (4) Del Mohammad Mollah by a registered deed of sale being No. 10801 dated 20-8-1960. Since then the petitioners have been possessing the property in question peacefully without any disturbances and on payment of all taxes to the Government. They mutated their names in the relevant khatian, got WASA and gas connection in their names.

3. The petitioners are the heirs of Nur Islam Mollah. Said Nur Islam Mollah while in possession of the property in question died in Bangladesh on 4-4-1986 and was buried in Mirpur Graveyard. Local Ward Commissioner issued a certificate to that effect on 3-1-2001.

4. Further case of the petitioners is that the owner of the property Nur Islam Mollah is a national of Bangladesh by birth and he never left the country at the time of Liberation period and he was a permanent resident and inhabitant in Mirpur area, Dhaka. He was a voter in Mirpur area and his name appears in the voter list prepared on 7-12-1976 at serial No. 254 (Annexure-J). It is to be noted that the name of the petitioner No. 5 is also to be found listed at serial No. 191 (Annexure-K).

5. It so transpired that one Shamima Rahman, through her constituted attorney M/s Eastern Housing Ltd, as plaintiff instituted Title Suit No. 3 of 2003 in the Court of Joint District Judge, 6th Court, Dhaka for declaration of title, recovery of possession and permanent injunction in respect of the suit land against the petitioners along with others. After contested hearing the learned court dismissed the suit vide judgment and decree dated 3-11-2011 (decree signed on 22-11-2011) (Annexure L and L-I to the Supplementary Affidavit).

6. After the death of said Nur Islam Mollah the present petitioners as heirs got their names mutated in the Khatian (annexure-G to the supplementary affidavit) and the latest City Record of Right Stands recorded in the names of the petitioners (Annexure-H). They paid taxes to the Government and City Corporation as well and constructed building thereon upon obtaining sanction and approval of the plan from RAJUK (Annexure-B series) and took loan from House Building Finance Corporation for construction of the building.

7. The petitioners predecessor died in Bangladesh and was buried at Mirpur Graveyard at a time when the petitioner Nos. 1- 4 were minors and the petitioner No.5 was merely a housewife and was not aware of the worldly affairs and it was not possible to know about the affairs of the property in question on their part and it was also not known to them that the property has been enlisted as abandoned property in the Gazette published on 23-9-1986. For the first time on 15-9-2003 they came to know that their property has been enlisted as abandoned property in the abandoned buildings list. The petitioners on coming to know the fact of enlistment of the property as abandoned collected relevant papers and documents and filed an application before the Court of Settlement praying for release of the property from the abandoned list.

8. The said case was heard by the Court of Settlement and after hearing was dismissed by its judgment and order dated 15-10-2003 on the ground of limitation without entering into the merit of the case.

9. The petitioners assert that they as well as their predecessor-in-interest are nationals of Bangladesh by birth and have been in possession of the property in question, supervising and managing the property in person and the property in question was never abandoned. Accordingly, question of petitioners or their predecessor's whereabouts being unknown does not arise and, therefore, the very inclusion of the property in the 'Kha' list shows that the petitioners are in possession and, as such, the inclusion of the property in question in the 'Kha' list is ex facie illegal and violative of Article 42 of the Constitution. It is also claimed that no notice for surrendering or taking over possession of the property in question as abandoned property was ever issued or served under Section 7 of the Abandoned Buildings (Supplementary Provisions) Ordinance, 1985 (Ordinance No. LIV of 1985 ("Ordinance")upon the petitioners. It is contended further that the property in question is not an abandoned property as the same does not come within the definition of abandoned property given in the Bangladesh Abandoned Property (Control, Management and Disposal) Order, 1972 being President's Order No. 16 of 1972 (P.O. No. 16 of 1972) and thus indusion of the same in the list of the abandoned buildings is illegal and without lawful authority. The Court of Settlement having rejected the application for being barred by limitation the petitioners moved this Court by filing this Application under Article 102 of the Constitution challenging the enlistment of the case property in the 'Kha" list and the judgment and order of the Court of Settlement and obtained the present Rule and Order of status quo.

10. The respondents contested the Rule by filing Affidavit-in-opposition alleging that since the whereabouts of the original owner was not known to the Government after the commencement of PO No. 16 of 1972, the Government has rightly declared the said property as abandoned property. Furthermore, it is asserted that from 'House to House' survey report of survey team dated 5-11-1984 it is found in the remark column that "the present occupant failed to produce any paper". Thereafter, the authority concerned issued a notice to the occupant Nur Islam Mollah on 1-6-1985 asking him to appear before the office of the respondent No.2 within 7 days along with original lease deed and other documents placing the addressee further on notice that any failure to so comply would entail the risk of the said house being treated as an abandoned property as per provision of Article 2(1) of the PO No. 16 of 1972. Admittedly, Nur Islam Mollah did not appear before the authority. Again on 19-7-1986 another notice was issued to Nur Islam Mollah fixing 26-7-1986 to appear before the authority but he failed to appear notwithstanding ostensible due service upon him. It is submitted, therefore, that the petitioners' plea of non-service of notice and lack of knowledge is not sustainable in the eye of law and that also the Court of Settlement has rightly rejected the application on the ground of limitation. The core argument put forward in this regard for and on behalf of the respondents is that the listing of the property as abandoned property without service of notice as per provision of Ordinance is not material because the Ordinance has encumbered the claimants to establish that the property in question is not an abandoned property i.e., whether the claimant had ceased to occupy, supervise or managed the case property in per-son at the very point of date at first.

11. It is also stated that the question of service of notice is a question of fact and this can only be determined upon taking evidence. Since no rebuttable evidence has been adduced to show that the original owner was present in Bangladesh and he occupied, managed or supervised the disputed house when PO No. 16 of 1972 came into operation i.e., 28-2-1972 and, as such, listing of the property as abandoned property in the "Kha" list is lawful and conclusive proof of facts.

12. Mr. ZI Khan Panna with Mr Md Sagir Hossain the learned Advocates appearing for the petitioners submit that the property in question was under the possession of Nur Islam Mollah bona fide citizen and permanent resident of Bangladesh by birth on the basis of a purchase deed dated 20-8-1960 till 4-4-86, the date of his death and thereafter the present petitioners as Bangladeshi nationals by birth till to date and that not for a single day it was abandoned or held by any other person or persons for which there was no scope to find it without effective control and supervision of the original owner and subsequently the present petitioners. It is submitted that, therefore, it was quite illegal to include the said property in the abandoned property list being in violation of therules and regulations in this regard.

13. Mr. Khan referring to the Preamble of the Bangladesh Abandoned Property (Control, Management and Disposal) Order, 1972 further submits that since the case property was constantly under effective occupation, control and supervision of the original owner and, thereafter, the petitioners themselves having never ever deserted the property with the positive intent to give up their rights vested in the property, the inclusion of the property in the list of abandoned buildings was done by abuse of authority and arbitrarily and, as such, it is unjust, improper, illegal and bad in law.

14. It is also argued that pursuant to section 5(I)(b) of the Ordinance No. 54 of 185, no notice was served upon the petitioners and in that view of the matter the enlistment of the case property in the 'Kha" list of the abandoned buildings is ex facie illegal and without any lawful authority. Mr Khan further submits that the case has become time-barred for no fault of the petitioners as they were minors when the property got included in the 'Kha' list and immediately on coming to know that the case property has been enlisted in the 'Kha' list the petitioners had filed a case but at that time the remedy available before the Settlement Court had become time-barred and there was no competent court to go to and no alternative effective remedy for the petitioners to avail of. In this situation the petitioners can indeed invoke writ jurisdiction under Article 102 of the Constitution to enforce their fundamental rights inclusive of the right to property even though they availed the alternative remedy, but failed on a technical ground of limitation. He also submits that the title of the petitioners in respect of the disputed house has been decided in favour of the petitioners by a competent court in Title Suit No.3 of 2003 filed by one Shamima Rahman. In this view of the matter also the case property cannot be an abandoned property. In support of his submission he referred to the cases of Jebon Nahar and others vs Bangladesh reported in 49 DLR 108, Bangladesh vs Chand Sultana reported in 1 MLR (HC) 310 = 48 DLR 547 & 51 DLR (AD) 24 and Sarwari Begum vs. Bangladesh reported in 45 DLR 571.

15. Mr. Shahidul Islam, the learned Deputy Attorney-General with Mr Sukumar Biswas, the learned Assistant Attorney-General appearing for the respondents submits that under section 7 of the Ordinance any person disputing the enlistment of a property as abandoned property may make an application to the Settlement Court within 180 days. The petitioners having filed the case long after the period as prescribed by the Ordinance, the Settlement Court rightly rejected the said settlement case for being time barred.

16. It is also argued by the respondents that the case property was duly listed in the 'Kha' list after issuance of a notice under section 5(1) (b) of the Ordinance to the predecessor of the petitioners which the petitioners deny to have received. By the said notices Nurul Islam Mollah was asked to appear before the office of the respondent No. 2 along with necessary papers pertaining thereto and it was duly served upon him. The learned Deputy Attorney-General further submits that the burden of proof squarely lies on the petitioners to prove that Nur Islam Mollah occupied, managed or supervised the case property on the relevant date, i.e., 28-2-1972 to establish that the said property is not an abandoned property. But the petitioners having failed to prove the same, the inclusion of a building in the 'Kha' list is proof of its being an abandoned property and the Government has nothing to prove or deny. In the present case the petitioners could not show that Nur Islam Mollah was present in Bangladesh on material dates or that he occupied, managed or supervised the case property when PO No. 16 of 1972 came into operation, assuch the listing of the property in the 'Kha' list as abandoned property is lawful and conclusive proof of facts. In support of his submission he referred to the cases of Bangladesh & others vs Md laid and others reported in 48 DLR (AD) 10, Secretary Ministry of Works vs Rowshan Ara Begum reported in 57 DLR (AD) 167 and an unreported judgment dated 29-10-2009 passed in the case of Md Feroz Mia vs Bangladesh in Writ Petition No. 4971 of 2001.

17. Heard the learned Advocates for the parties, perused the petition, supplementary affidavits, Affidavits-in-opposition and the annexure annexed thereto.

18. Before entering into the merit of the case the provisions of law in this respect may be looked into. The purpose of PO No. 16 of 1972 is to make provisions for the control, management and disposal of certain property abandoned by certain persons who are not present in Bangladesh or whose whereabouts are not known or who have ceased to occupy or supervise or manage in person their property, or who are enemy aliens.

19. From the language as used in the Preamble it appears that the purpose of PO 16 of 1972 is not to declare as abandoned the property of citizens who are very much present in Bangladesh and who have been occupying, supervising and managing their property at all times. The petitioners have made clear averment in the writ petition about themselves and their predecessor's Bangladeshi nationality, their continuous residence in Bangladesh and their possession over the case property all along. In support of their claim they have annexed to the writ petition and supplementary affidavits the title deed dated 20-8-1960 (Annexure-A), rent receipts, municipal tax receipts, duplicate carbon receipt, sanction letter issued by RAJUK granting permission to construct building on the case property, present city record of right, voter list of the year 1976 evidencing that the predecessor of the petitioners was a voter, death certificate of Nur Islam Mollah issued by the ward Commissioner, Mirpur and judgment and decree of the court of Subordinate Judge, Dhaka passed in Title Suit No. 03 of 2003. All these papers and documents show that the predecessor of the petitioner and the present petitioners are all Bangladeshis and they have always been in possession of the case property, supervising and managing the same. There is nothing on record to suggest that at any point of time they have ceased to occupy, supervise and manage the case property in person and the property was ever resultantly abandoned. These documents further attest to the fact that their whereabouts cannot possibly have remained unknown to the Government. Moreover, the respondent No. 2 also do not claim that the predecessor of the petitioners and the present petitioners are not Bangladeshi or that they are nationals of any other country which at any time after 25-3-1971 was at war with Bangladesh or that they are not in possession of the said property. Rather given these facts and circumstances, the very fact of inclusion of the property in the "Kha" list itself proves that the petitioners have been in possession all along. This Court finds, accordingly, that the case property in no way answers to description of the abandoned property as defined in Article 2 of 16 of 1972 and, as such, the inclusion of the case property in the 'Kha' list violates the petitioners, fundamental right under Article 42 of the Constitution of Bangladesh to own and hold property. Such right this court finds cannot be taken away without the backing of law.

20. Furthermore, the voter list dating back to as early as 1976, manifests to this Court and by reference to Article 122 of the Constitution, in the very minimum the status of the voter as a citizen and resident of Bangladesh and of one having at least attained the age of 18 on the material date of preparation of such voter list.The inclusion of the names of Nur Islam Mollah and his wife, the petitioner No. 5 must, therefore, in the absence of any conclusive evidence to the contrary, be assumed to manifest the same.

21. Furthermore, it is always to be borne in mind that in any case as this it must be accepted as a truism that the act of abandonment implies two fundamental factors:

(i) Desertion of the property and

(ii) Giving up one's right to the property.

<u>22. The word "abandonment" connotes in this sense the idea of the owner not merely temporarily vacating but deserting the property with the intention of never returning to it. Such absolute desertion must be concomitant with the positive intention to give up the right vested in the property. It follows, therefore, that (mere temporary or occasional absence of physical possession shall not of itself suffice to treat the property as abandoned. These two determinants of the notion of "abandonment" appear not to have been established in this case.</u>

23. This Court, accordingly, finds that the case property does not in any way answer to the description of abandoned property as mentioned above and defined particularly under Article 2 of the PO 16 of 1972 as there was no desertion of the property accompanied by giving up of the right to the property by the owner.

24. It is also argued by the respondents that notice contemplated under the Ordinance was duly served upon the predecessor of the petitioners. Provisions in section 5(1)(b) of the Ordinance may be looked into in this regard:

"Section 5(i) The Government shall, after the commencement of the Ordinance and before the 31st day of December, 1988, publish, from time to time, in the official Gazette... (b) Lists of buildings in respect of which notices for surrendering or taking possession as abandoned property under the said Order have been issued. "

25. A perusal of the Government file pertaining to the case property indicates that a notice being Memo No. AP-8M-898 dated 1-6-1985 was claimed to be served upon the petitioner's predecessor Nur Islam Mollah. It is prudent to produce the notice, the contents of which are reproduced below:—

গণপ্রজাতন্ত্রী বাংলাদেশ সরকার

পূর্তমন্ত্রনালয়

শাখা-৮

তারিখ-১-৬-১৯৮৫ইং

স্মারক নং এপি-৮ম-৮৯৮

প্রেরক-টি,সি,চাকমা,

উদ্ধতন শাখা প্রধান।

প্রতিঃ জনার নুরূল ইসলাম মোল্লা,

১৯/৭, পল্লবী, মিরপুর , ঢাকা।

বিষয়ঃ ১৯/৭, পল্লবী, মিরপুর , ঢাকা প্রসংগে।

মিরপুরস্থ ১৯/৭ পল্লবী, মিরপুর , ঢাকা-নং বাড়ীটিতে বসবাসের স্বপক্ষে মূল দলিল/কাগজপদ্র এক প্রস্থ ফটোকপি সহ অত্র পত্র প্রাপ্তির ৭(সাত) দিনের মধ্যে অত্র মন্ত্রনালয়ে হাজির হওয়ার জন্য নির্দেশক্রমে আপনাকে অনুরোধ করিতেছি। অন্যথায় পি,ও,১৬ এর ১৯৭২ আইন মোতাবেক উল্লিথিত বাড়ীটি পরিত্যক্ত সম্পত্তি হিসাবে ঘোষনা করার প্রয়োজনীয় ব্যবস্খা গ্রহণ করা হইবে।

(টি,সি, চকমা)

উদ্ধর্তন শাখা প্রধান।

26. There is nothing found on record to show when and how it was issued and how it was served upon the petitioner’s predecessor by the respondent No.2. Another notice dated 19-7-1986 alleged to have been issued and served upon the petitioners' predecessor Nur Islam but facts remain said Nurul Islam Mollah died on 4-4-1986 i.e. before the issuance of said notice as evident from death certificate dated 3-1-2001.

27. Article 7 of the PO 16 of 1972 also provides for giving notice in certain cases which runs as thus:—

7. (1) Where any abandoned property is not in possession of any person, the Deputy Commissioner or the Sub-divisional Magistrate [or the authorized officer] shall take possession of the property in such manner as may be prescribed.

(2) Where any abandoned property is in possession of any person, such person shall, within seven days of the commencement of this Order, surrender such property to the Deputy Commissioner or the Sub-divisional Magistrate [or the authorized officer.]

(3) Where the person in possession of any abandoned property fails to surrender such property as he is required to do under clause (2), the Deputy Commissioner or the Sub-divisional Magistrate for the authorized officer shall serve a notice on him in the prescribed manner requiring him to surrender possession of the property, within seven days of the service of the notice, to the person mentioned in the notice or to show cause against such surrender within the said period and if he fails to do so, the Deputy Commissioner or the Sub-divisional Magistrate [or the authorized officer] shall take possession of the property in such manner as may be prescribed. 4)

28. Therefore, after the issuance of the notice leaving the matter hanging without pursuing it further or taking possession of the property as required under Article 7 of PO 16 of 1972 proves mala fide.

29. The petitioners claimed that no notice under section 5(1)(b) of the Ordinance, was issued and served upon the predecessor of the petitioners or the petitioners, as a result they were not aware of inclusion of the case property in the `Kha' list. By the time they came to know about the inclusion of the case property in the `Kha' list after long lapse of time and they failed to file application before the Court of Settlement for exclusion of the case property within the period as provided in section 7 of the Ordinance. Consequently, their application was rejected and they are now without any relief unless this court invokes its writ jurisdiction and interferes with the inclusion of the case property in the `Kha' list. In this situation in our view this court in its writ jurisdiction has every reason to react to the manifest injustice and try to remedy it.

<u>30. It appears from the annexure '2' to the affidavit-in-opposition that a survey was held by the respondent No.2 to find the position of the case property which proves that the owner Nur Islam Mollah was in possession on material dates. Later enlistment of the case property by the respondent No.2 in the 'Kha" list shows bad faith, dishonesty and improper motive on their part. The petitioners, therefore, do have an entitlement under Article 42 read with Article 27 and 31 that should now be protected under due process of law. The right to enforce a fundamental right under Article 44 is another fundamental right which gives the petitioners right to move this court even though their application was rejected by the Settlement Court on the ground of limitation.</u>

31. It is also noted that there is nothing on record to show that the petitioners or their predecessor was ever asked to show cause about inclusion of the property or to surrender the same which has definitely denied the right of natural justice to the petitioners.

32. In the case of Syeda Chand Sultana vs Bangladesh reported in 1 MLR (HC) 310 which was affirmed by the Appellate Division and reported in 51 DLR (AD) 24, it has been held that,Where the owners as Bangladeshi nationals having lawful title have been in possession of the property all through and never having ceased to manage or supervise the same and not having left the country and when there was no proper service of notice upon the petitioners as required under Article 7 of the PO No. 16 of 1972, the inclusion of the said building in the "Kha list" of abandoned properties being violated of the fundamental rights as contained in Article 42 of the Constitution is illegal, without jurisdiction and of no legal effect and, as such, the petitioners are entitled to invoke the writ jurisdiction for enforcement of fundamental rights.

33. In the facts and circumstances, this Court finds itself fully subscribing to the ratio above and finding on its applicability to the case at hand is now inclined to make the rule absolute.

34. In the result, the Rule is made absolute, without any order as to costs.

35. It is hereby declared that the inclusion of House No. 19/7, Pallabi, Mirpur, Dhaka in the "Kha" list of abandoned buildings, published in the Bangladesh Gazette Extra Ordinary on 23-9-1986 under serial No. 35 at page 9764 (25) is without lawful authority and is of no legal effect and the respondent No. 2 are, hereby, directed to exclude the petitioners building from the 'Kha' list of the Abandoned Buildings within 30 (thirty) days from the date of receipt of the certified copy of this Judgment and Order.

36. There is no Order as to costs.

Communicate a copy of this Judgment and Order to the Court of Settlement concerned at once.

End.

caseno: Civil Petition for Leave to Appeal No. 536 of 2005.
lawyer:
Sufia Khatun, Advocate-on-Record—For the Petitioner. 
None represented—For the Respondents.
parties:
Achyutananda Das ------ Petitioner. 
Vs.
Government of Bangladesh, represented by Secretary, Ministry of Land ------ Respondents.
case_source: (From the judgment and order dated the 8th December, 2004 passed by the High Court Division in Writ Petition No. 3981 of 2003).
full_judgment:
Md Fazlul Karim J: The petition for Leave to Appeal at the instance of the petitioner is directed against the judgment and order dated 8-12-2004 passed by the High Court Division in Writ Petition No. 3981 of 2003 discharging the Rule.

2. The facts of the case are that the petitioner is a citizen of Bangladesh by birth. The petitioner was born in 1927 and he was living in the homestead in plot Nos. 839 and 840 of Khatian Nos. 257 and 256 of Mouza Sylhet Municipality at Mahalla Roynagar in the Sylhet Town. The petitioner passed the matriculation examination in the year 1943 and passed intermediate in the year 1946. While he was working in Hardeo Glass Factory in Dhaka he left for the United Kingdom in 1957 to secure higher study. In the United Kingdom he got a job in the British Railway and thereafter in London Transport. In order to improve his efficiency he got admitted into the Institute of Transport, an institution incorporated by the Royal Charter in 1926 and after 4 years of his study he pissed the Associate Membership Examination in May, 1961 and he was given the Associate Membership of the Institute of Transport on 12 March, 1962. The petitioner continued to serve in the London Transport and retired from service in 1989. The petitioner was granted citizenship of United Kingdom in December, 1965 and he got British Passport in 1966 as a citizen of United Kingdom. At the same time he is also a citizen of Bangladesh holding dual citizenship. The petitioner came to Bangladesh on the 1st August, 2001 and went to Sylhet to see his ancestral house and to renovate land to reside there at the end of his life, and to his utter Surprise he came t6 learn that the property has been declared as enemy property, now vested and non-resident property and the Government has taken up the management of his ancestral property. Thereafter, he instructed one of his relations to collect the papers regarding the property and left for United Kingdom on the 8th August, 2001. The petitioner again came to Bangladesh on the 15th January, 2002 and he made a prayer to the Deputy Commissioner, Sylhet on the 21st January, 2002 for release of the property from the list of vested property stating that the petitioner was never an enemy subject nor he was a citizen of any country with which the erstwhile Pakistan was at war and, as such, treating his property as enemy property or vested property is illegal and without jurisdiction.

3. Upon the said application to the Deputy Commissioner (Rev) Sylhet Miscellaneous Case No. 40/2001-2002 was started and the Additional Deputy Commissioner called for a report from the Assistant Commissioner (Land), Sylhet, Sadar upon inquiry and the inquiry was held and the Assistant Officer, Land, Chak Sultanpur Union, Land Officer, Sylhet Sadar submitted a report to the effect that the land belonging to the petitioner comprising plot No. 840 has been declared an enemy property in VP Case No. 24/66-67 and the land of plot Nos. 838 and 839 has been declared an enemy property in VP Case No. 313/ 66-67 and those were leased out to the lessees and the Government is in possession of the said land. The Assistant Commissioner (Land), Sylhet having received the aforesaid inquiry report forwarded the same by his memo dated 5-4-2003 to the Upazila Nirbahi Officer, Sylhet Sadar and in his forwarding the Assistant Commissioner opined that the petitioner came to Bangladesh after retirement and he never left the country for good, but in view of the promulgation of অর্পিত সম্পত্তি প্রত্যর্পণ আইন, 2001 (sic) the property cannot be released. The Additional Deputy Commissioner (Rev.) on the basis of the inquiry report rejected the prayer of the petitioner for release of the land from the list of enemy property (now vested property) by his order dated 24-4-2003. The petitioner claims that the petitioner's father purchased the property and after his death the petitioner and his elder brother inherited the said property. During last settlement operation the land has been recorded in the name of Sachidananda Das, the elder brother of the petitioner and the petitioner Achyutananda Das in equal share in the property, the petitioner having 0.79 acres of land in plot No. 840 and 0.7½ decimals of land in plot No. 838 0.25½ decimals of land in plot No. 839. Thus, the petitioner owns in total 0.53 decimals of land comprising of the aforesaid plots. As the brother of the petitioner, a co-sharer, died in India, the petitioner does not make any claim in respect of his brother's share.

4. The Chairman of the Sylhet Pourashava issued a certificate to the effect that the petitioner is a citizen of Bangladesh. In the supplementary affidavit the petitioner has annexed the photocopy of the passport showing his dual citizenship and also a copy of the voters' list of 2002 showing that the petitioner's name was registered in the voters' list which was published on 25-11-2002.

5. Mrs Sufia Khatun, Advocate-on-Record appearing for the petitioner, submits that the High Court Division erred in passing the impugned judgment and order that there was no material before the High Court Division to show that the petitioner was ever an enemy subject or alien enemy within the meaning of Defence of Pakistan Rules, 1965 and, as such, the impugned judgment and decree are liable to be set aside; that the petitioner being a citizen of Bangladesh, he having not denounced his citizenship at any point of time, the inclusion of his property in the list of enemy property and keeping the same as vested property is illegal but the High Court Division failed to consider this aspect which has caused miscarriage of justice; that the petitioner was never an "enemy" as defined in Rule 161 or "enemy subject" as defined in Rule 169 of the Defence of Pakistan Rules, 1965 as he never went to India when the Defence of Pakistan Rules was in force and, as such, the enlisting of the property belonging to the petitioner as enemy property and treating the same as vested property at present is illegal but the High Court Division erred in law in not considering this vital aspect and, as such, the impugned judgment and order of the High Court Division is liable to be set aside; that the petitioner has inalienable right to enjoy his property as enshrined in Article 42 of the Constitution of Bangladesh and, as such, enlistment of his property as enemy property and continuing to treat the same as vested property is violative of Article 42 of the Constitution and the High Court Division failed to consider this important aspect and thus impugned judgment and order is liable to be set aside; that the High Court Division held that the petitioner filed writ petition at a belated stage, but failed to consider that the petitioner was absent from the country and used to reside in United Kingdom in course of his employment there and soon after his return in August, 2001 in Bangladesh for the first time he has taken appropriate steps to get back his ancestral properties and he is not guilty of any lathes or inaction and, as such, the impugned judgment and order is liable to be set aside.

6. The High Court Division made a wrong approach to the case and held that the petitioner was to establish his title without considering that the petitioner's title was denied by the respondent and that he has title in the suit land is an admitted fact and that the respondents also did not deny the fact that the petitioner was never an enemy subject and thus erred in the impugned judgment which is liable to be set aside; that the High Court Division committed a serious error in holding that the question of ownership of the property is to be decided by the Civil Court without properly appreciating the case of the petitioner that the SA record has been prepared in the name of the petitioner in respect of the land as enlisted and, as such ,the ownership was not in dispute and only the question was, that whether the petitioner ever became enemy subject and the respondents have not asserted so and in that view of the matter the impugned judgment and order is liable to be set aside.

<u>7. It appears from the record that admittedly the property in question belonged to two brothers. The elder brother went to India before 1965 and the petitioner was also absent in the area since 1965 and since the elder brother died as enemy in Indian territory the Government initiated two VP cases immediately after the Defence of Pakistan Rules was promulgated and treated the property as enemy property. The petitioner had not been in possession of the property and the Government having treated the property as enemy property or vested property allotted the property to the different allottees. The petitioner claims that he is a co-sharer of the property which was taken over by the relevant authority as vested property initiating VP cases. The property is admittedly in possession of the vested property authority. Unless the petitioner establishes his title over the land and recovers possession by a decree obtained in competent Civil Court no effectual remedy can be obtained by the petitioner. The question of ownership of the petitioner in the property and his citizenship could only be determined by a competent civil Court in a properly framed suit. The petitioner during the last more than 45 years never looked after the property, never made any claim before the authority before an application was made on 21-1-2002 to the Deputy Commissioner, Sylhet and consequently, there have been great ladles on the part of the petitioner which will disentitle the petitioner to come before this Court to invoke writ jurisdiction.</u>

8. In view of the above, we find no substance in the submissions of the learned Advocate for the petitioner.

Accordingly, the leave petition is dismissed.

End.

lawyer:
Md. Nurul Huq, Advocate-on-Record ------ for the appellant.
Syed Ishtiaq Ahmed Sr. Advocate, B.B. Roy Chowdhury, Sr. Advocate, instructed by Md. Aftab Hossain, Advocate-on-Record ------ for respondents Nos. 2. 3. and 7. 
No one ------ for respondents No. 4-6.
parties:
Mst. Aftabunessa
Vs.
Md. Shamsul Huq Talukder
full_judgment:
Badrul Haider Chowdhury, J. This appeal by special leave is directed against the judgment and order in F.A. No. 57 of 1975.

2. Plaintiff is the appellant. She instituted T.S. No. 21 of 1079 in the Court of 4th Subordinate Judge, Dhaka against the respondents praying for declaration that the plaintiff had acquired title by adverse possession of the suit property namely premises No. 6/1 Kailash Ghosh Lane, P.S. Kotwali, Dhaka and (b) the Memo No. 3623/6-EP dated 4.12.1969 issued by the defendant No. 3, Assistant Custodian of Enemy Property (L &B) is without any lawful authority and is of no legal effect.

3. Facts in short are as follows: property in suit originally belonged to one Jnan Ranjan who gifted the same to his son Mono Ranjan Banerjee with an authority to make further construction (ext. 8). Mono Ranjan recorded his name in the Municipality in 1923-24 Ext. 5 and the Municipality sanctioned his plan for further construction on 4.10.29. Mono Ranjan died leaving behind three sons namely Sattaya Ranjan Banerjee, Kumud Ranjan Banerjee and Shanti Ranjan Banerjee and his wife Brinda Banerjee. It appears that this house was taken on lease in 1926-27 by the Dhaka Nawab Estate. The plaintiffs husband was an officer of the estate. He occupied one portion of the building living there with his family. In 1947 the office of the Nawab Estate was shifted to a different place. The plaintiffs husband, however, continued occupation of the entire suit premises as monthly tenant under the proforma defendants 4 to 6 namely Sattya Ranjan, Kumud Ranjan and Shanti Ranjan Banerjee. The Banerjees left the then East Pakistan and asked the Evacuee Property Management Board to take over the property for management in their absence whereupon a Gazettee Notification was made by the Government under section 8(1) of Act XXIV of 1951 dated 31.12.53. Thereafter the plaintiffs husband paid rent upto 1954 to the Evacuee Property Management Committee and recognised him as tenant Ext. 1 series. In 1954 the plaintiff started paying rent in her name and continued payment of rent from January 1954 to 1969.

4. Now the second round. In 1961 it seems Suresh Chandra respondent, purported to sell his property to Shamsul Huq Talukder, respondent No. 1. Suresh Chandra filed an affidavit before 1st Class Magistrate on 15.1.63 claiming to be the sixteen annas owner of the suit property. Shamsul Huq Talukder filed a petition on 3.5.61 claiming premises by right of purchase from Suresh Chandra Banerjee before the Evacuee Property Management Committee. The matter was heard by the Committee on 12.10.61 and by resolution No. 4 the petition of Talukder for releasing the property was rejected (Ext. 9) and true copy of this resolution was forwarded to Shanti Ranjan and Kumud Ranjan. The Management Committee considered the objection of Santi Ranjan dated 6.8.61 denying the claim of Suresh Chandra Banerjee and the Committee resolved "the objections asked to establish their right and title, if any, in the properties in the proper court of law". Suresh chandra however, did not file proceeding in Civil Court and the plaintiff continued payment of rent as tenant to the Evacuee Property Management Committee and subsequently to the Assistant Custodian, Enemy Property informed the plaintiff " to hand over possession of the holding to the owner after expiry of the present terms of the lease on 31.12.69". The letter was written to Shamsul Huq Talukder informing him that the holdings had been released from the Schedule of the Enemy Property with effect from 29.11.69". The plaintiff reacted sharply and through his lawyer informed the Assistant Custodian that Shamsul Huq Talukder was never the owner of the property and as such the question of handing over possession of the same does not arise Ext 2(6). The respondents, however, attempted to take forcible possession of the suit premises on 24.3.70. She then filed the present suit.

5. Plaintiffs main contention is that the property had been released from the category of Enemy Property. Her original tenancy under the owners namely respondents 4 to 6 revived and she was never tenant of Suresh Chandra, defendant No. 2 nor she could attorn to defendant No. 1 Shamsul Huq as the owner of the premises.

6. Defendants contested the suit by filing written statement and their main case more or less was that the property having been released from the category of Enemy property in favour of Suresh Chandra, the plaintiff has no cause of action nor the suit is maintainable because she was the tenant of the Government and since Suresh Chandra is sixteen annas owner of the property the plaintiff is obliged to hand over the possession to Shamsul Huq Talukder who purchased from Suresh Chandra. The trial Court came to the conclusion that the plaintiff and her husband were in possession since 1957 and that the property originally belonged to Jnan Ranjan Banerjee and thereafter he gifted to Mono Ranjan and the property devolved after his death on his son defendants 4 to 6. The claim of Suresh Chandra Banerjee was repelled and finding of the trial was that not even a scrap of paper was produced to show that Niranjan was ever owner of the suit property. Be it noted that Suresh Chandra claimed through Niranjan. The trial Court, considered the oral evidence and has found that Monoranjan was a pleader and by the deed of gift Jnan Ranjan gifted this property to his son Monoranjan. It was found that the defendant No. 1 did not acquire any title in the suit property in pursuance of the Ext. A the sale deed dated 7.2.61 showing a transfer from Suresh Chandra Benerjee to Shamsul Huq Talukder. The trial Court found that the plaintiff acquired title by adverse possession against the claim of Suresh Chandra.

7. The High Court Division, however, in F.A. found that the suit was wholly misconceived and considered that the plaintiff was a tenant under Evacuee Property Management Committee and consequently the plaintiff had a very little cause. The learned Judges then considered section 4(3) of the E.P. Enemy Property (L & B) (Administration) Order which provided the tenant "shall not acquire any right of occupancy in such property and shall not be entitled to hold over after the expiry of the period of the lease." Relying on this provision of law the High Court Division reversed the judgment and order of the trial court and allowed the appeal.

8. Leave was granted to consider the correctness of the decision of the High Court Division and to consider whether the suit was maintainable by the plaintiff.

9. Suresh Chandra Banerjee deposed as D.W. 2. He did not contest the suit by filing written statement. He stated that he was deposing in support of the case of defendant No. 1. He gave the genealogy and that the property originally belonged to Ishan Chandra, who died leaving behind two daughters Bama Sundari and Shyama Sundari. Both the daughters were married to one Mahesh Chandra. Jnan Ranjan Banerjee was the son through Bama Sundari and Niranjan Banerjee was the son through Shyama Sundari. He is the son of Niranjan. According to him Jnan Ranjan had two sons Nayan Ranjan and Pran Ranjan. Pran Ranjan died unmarried during the lifetime of his father and Nayan Ranjan died issueless after his father. After their death the property devolved upon Niranjan entirely and he is the sole heir of Niranjan. Monoranjan according to him was not a son of Jnan Ranjan. He, however, corrected himself in cross-examination by saying that Monoranjan was the adopted son of Jnan Ranjan. Then in re-examination corrected himself again by saying that Monoranjan was not an adopted son but foster son of Jnan Ranjan. He admitted that he had no paper to show that property, at any time before, stood in the name of his father or in his name. He conceded that he had no paper to show possession of himself or of his father prior to 1950. He stated that he used to reside in the holding No. 6 with Monoranjan, Shanti and Kumud between 1920 and 1950. He admitted that he appeared for the first time in the scene in 1956 when he stated that he filed an objection to the Evacuee Property authority but he could not file any paper to show that he really filed any objection in 1956. He stated that he knew defendant No. 1 5/6 years before partition, who was an inhabitant of adjoining village. He stated that after the sale of the suit property he resided with the defendant No. 1 at Hrishikesh Das Road. His father died in 1928. He denied in cross-examination that he got his name mutated in the Municipal records in collusion with the defendant No. 1 and Settlement employees. He stated that the deed of give Ext. 8 dated 6.12.18 was created by the plaintiff. He was confronted with Ext 4 C.S. Khatian which stood in the name of Jnan Ranjan and later Monoranjan recorded his name in the Municipality Ext. 5 and obtained permission for further construction dated 4.10.29 (Ext, 10).

10. Suresh Chandra could not give any satisfactory explanation as to these documentary evidences and hen the Gazette Notification dated 31.12.53 under section 8(1) of Act XXIV of 1951 show that the property was taken over at the request of the owner, namely, Satya Ranjan, Kumud Ranjan and Santi Ranjan and Bindu Bashini, the heirs of Monoranjan Banerjee. Section 8 postulates that the Evacuee Property Management Committee can take charge of any evacuee property if the Evacuee applies to the Committee for such management and make a declaration in such application that he does not intend to return before a certain date, whereupon the Committee by sub-section (2) is required by public notice calling for objection to such proposal. Suresh Chandra according to his own statement did not file any objection when the notification was made. He made feeble attempt by saying that he filed an objection petition in 1956 although he could not substantiate his contention. On his own admission he never lived in the suit premises after 1956, but before 1950 he lived with Monoranjan and his sons in the suit-premises between 1928 and 1950. He could not show any document that the property ever stood in the name of his father Niranjan. The only paper he could show the rent receipt of much later date Ext. B series of 1961 to 1968. These rent receipts were all of a later period. He sold his property on 7.4.61 to Shamsul Huq and his rent receipts are all of the date since the date of purchase. His first attempt to get the property released in his name was by petition dated 7.9.61 and the Evacuee Property Management Committee by its letter dated 4.10.61 Ext. D asked him to appear before the Committee which he did. Before that he filed a petition before the Government on 3.1.61 and the Government replied by Ext. D(1) that the property "were taken over for management and protection by Evacuee Property Management Committee. Dhaka with effect from 25.11.53 on the application of the Evacuee owners, M/s Sattya Ranjan, Kumud Ranjan, Santi Ranjan Banerjee all sons of late Monoranjan Banerjee". He was directed to prove his claim before the President, Evacuee Property Management Committee, Dhaka for the release of the property. After hearing the Board resolved as under:

‘‘In view of the facts that the properties were taken up for management and protection under East Bengal Act XXIV of 1951 with effect from 25.11.53 on the application of the Evacuce, Mr. Santi Ranjan Banerjee and others, who actually owned and possessed the properties under objection since long before they left for India after 15.8.47 and that the present claimant, Babu Suresh Chandra Banerjee never possessed nor realised rent from the tenants in occupation nor even raised any objection or tried to have the properties released from the charge of management of the Committee as a Pakistani Citizen before the properties could be sold by him, the objection raised cannot be considered admissible on any reasonable and legal point of view. Resolved, there-fore that the objections made be rejected and the objectors asked to establish their right and title if any, in the properties, in the proper court of law.

11. Suresh Chandra did not file any suit to prove his title. Analysis of the evidence show that here is no attempt on behalf of Suresh Chandra for releasing the property from the Evacuee Management Committee between 1953 and 1956, nor any evidence was led to show that he did anything for releasing the same between 1956 and 1961. In 1961 he appears in the scene as Vendor and when the Evacuee Management Committee refused his prayer for releasing the same in his favour he did not take any step for establishing his claim either. Now Shamsul Huq Talukder appears in the scene and his prayer for release of the property by petition dated 3.5.61 was rejected by the Management Committee-

‘‘Unless Babu Suresh Chandra Banerjee, who is said to have sold the properties to you applies and proves his legal right and claim to the satisfaction of the Committee.

Nothing was done either by Suresh or by Talukder. The plaintiff continued payment of rent right upto 1960 when suddenly she was informed that the property had been released from the Schedule of the Enemy Property with effect from 29.11.69. The trial Court had rightly concluded that unless Suresh Babu had proved his title to the suit premises. Shamsul Huq Talukder could not step into his shoes. The plaintiff took the stand that Suresh was not the owner of the suit premises. He being an outsider, she took the stand that she was adversely possessing the property so far defendants 1 and 2 are concerned. She maintained that once the property had been released from the category of Enemy Property her tenancy with the original owners revived and therefore she is not obliged to hand over possession to Shamsul Huq or any body else. The High Court Division relied on the section 4 sub-sections (3) and (4) for coming to the conclusion that she had no locus standi to maintain the suit. Sub-sections (3) and (4) are as follows:

(3) Notwithstanding anything contained in any other law for the time being in force or in any agreement, a person to whom any enemy property is leased or let out under sub-paragraph (2) shall not acquire any right of occupancy in such property and shall not be entitled to hold over after the expiry of the period of lease.

(4) Notwithstanding anything contained in any other law for the time being in force or in any agreement, the lessee or tenant in respect of any enemy property leased or let out under sub-paragraph (2), shall be liable to be evicted without notice from such property at the expiry of the term of the lease."

12. Mr. Nurul Huq appearing for the plaintiff contended that once the property had been released from the category of Enemy in the same Act have no manner of binding effect on the plaintiff because the plaintiff was claiming adversely against the defendants 1 and 2 and claiming tenancy under defendants 4 to 6. Be it noted that when both Suresh and Shamsul Huq were trying to secure release of the property Santi Ranjan Banerjee filed objection to the Evacuee Management Committee and the Board recorded:

‘‘considered the objection along with the letter dated 6.8.61 received from one of the Evacuee owners, Mr. Santi Ranjan Banerjee vehemently protesting against the claim of Babu Suresh Ch. Banerjee.”

The clinches the issue because Suresh Chandra's title had never been established and since it is not enemy property restriction contained in the said enactment have no binding effect on the plaintiff. Mr. Nurul Huq put the proposition that the Enemy Property cannot be released and therefore when the property was released it was not enemy property and consequently the rules and regulations and restriction contained in the Enemy Property Act have no manner of application. This contention has force.

<u>13. Mr. Syed Ishtiaq Ahmed argued on the point that the plaintiff is just a tenant and she could not claim any better title nor acquire any right of occupancy in such property and the law says that "she shall not be entitled to hold over possession after expiry of the period of lease" and further sub-section (4) says: "she shall be liable to be evicted without notice from such property at the expiry of the terms of the lease." This contention is begging the particular point. The property is not an enemy properly. The restrictive provisions have no manner of application. The point now comes to focus who is the owner of the property. It is evidence that the plaintiff and her husband are in occupation since 1947 as a tenant of the sons of Monoranjan Banerjee. The title of Monoranjan Banerjee and his son apparently is so clear that even no attempt was made by the defendant to assail these documents in support of the title. As has been mentioned Ext. 4 is the C.S. Khatian which stands in the name of Jnan Ranjan. On 6.12.18 Jnan Ranjan gifted the property to his son Monoranjan with authority to make further construction (Ext. 8) Monorajan recorded his name in the Municipality (Ext. 5) and obtained sanction for further construction on 4.10.29 (Ext. 10) The evidence of Ramani Mohan Dutta (P.W. 2) shows that Monorannjan died in said premises. P.W. 3 Lakmi Kanta Pal, an Advocate stated that Monoranjan was his senior and the said holding belonged to him. On the face of the documents and oral evidence Mr. Istiaq Ahmed simply contended that Monoranjan might have been gifted a portion of the suit property but the other portion belonged to Niranjan and the share of Niranjan devolved upon his son Suresh. Here lies the crux of the problem. Suresh then must prove his title in a Civil Court. As a matter of fact Evacuee Management Committee advised him accordingly because Santi Ranjan son of Monoranjan challenged his title. Without doing so. Suresh resorted to transfer his share to Talukder. The plaintiff challenged the order of the Custodian for handing over possession to Suresh. Hence she claimed adversely against both Suresh and Talukder. It is contended that plaintiff is entitled to claim adverse possession against the defendant Suresh and his vendee Talukder and precisely that in what they contended in the trial court. The High Court Division, however, unfortunately missed the point as to the right of adverse possession. The plaintiff is not a trespasser. She and her husband were tenants of the owners since 1947 and after 1953 they paid rent to the Management Committee and thereafter to the Custodian, Enemy Property. Her possession is therefore legal possession which can be termed as juridical possession. She did not get possession either by fraud or by force. She is a tenant in possession and cannot be terminologically considered as a squatter nor a way-farer or trespasser. When the Custodian, Enemy Properly released the property on the ground that the same is not Enemy Property he could not direct the plaintiff to release the property to a particular individual whose title is denied by the owner. As has been noticed that Santi Ranjan objected to the petition of Suresh Chandra in 1961 and the Management Committee advised Suresh Chandra to establish his title in a Court of law. Instead of doing so, it seems, he waited since 1961 and started paying rent in his name from 1961 and mutated his name in the S.A. Khatian which was challenged by the plaintiff as collusive. The plaintiff is holding adversely to Suresh Chandra and his vendee Shamaul Huq Talukder who allegedly stepped into shoes of his vendor but unless Suresh has established his title Talukder is just no body. In Varada Pilliai Vs. Jeevarathaal AIR 1919 PC 44 it was held that where one of the heirs of the donor holds possession as donee under an imperfect gift and subsequently the donor dies and succession opens to the other heirs also, the character of the possession of the donee which was adverse does not cease to be so by reason of his becoming a part owner along with other heirs. In this case, the gift to Monoranjan was made in 1918 and the heirs of Monoranjan exercised their right, title and interest and the plaintiff was the tenant of the sons of Monoranjan since 1947 and the attempt of Suresh for securing 'the release of the property from Evacuee Management Committee was challenged by the sons of Monoranjan. These facts indicate that the plea of adverse possession against Suresh had been taken on formidable grounds even assuming, but not holding, that Suresh became part owner through Niranjan. The Trial Court therefore rightly decreed the suit and this point unfortunately were missed by the High Court Division.</u>

14. In the result, therefore, this appeal is allowed. The order of the High Court Division is set aside and the judgment and decree of the trial Court is hereby restored. No costs.

End.
